                  Chance one                                   Chance one


                   Possible starts:       same write
                   blank or zero                                End: zero
                      Half the                                 Chance one
                  chance on each
The first preparation loses no uncertainty. The second loses one bit. The transition rule is the
                           same; the input preparation is different.
    Keeping an exact answer among N independently possible alternatives needs at
least N representational states, or ⌈log2 N ⌉ bits in a fixed-length binary encoding.
That is a capacity bound. Identifying an arbitrary one of three possibilities can
require two binary questions in the worst case; testing just “is this cell blank?” is a
different, binary task. Neither count proves that a known blank was prepared by an
erasure or that a heat bill has already been paid.


1.3 A reversible machine keeps nothing

Bennett’s reversible machine never lets two of its states lead to the same next state;
that’s what reversible means. Put one on finitely many states and watch it. By the
pigeonhole it has to revisit a state within as many steps as there are states. The step
law says the first revisit is a merge or a return to the start, and a merge is impossible
for it, so it returns to its start, and once it’s back at its start it does everything again.
Any reading it raised has come back down. A reversible finite machine with a next
state for every state keeps nothing, and that’s a theorem, not a slogan. One that
stops slips past, as the stopping hole above says, and keeps what it halted on. It
is the recurrence Zermelo threw at Boltzmann (Section 3 tells that story), in its
finite form, proved from the step law and the pigeonhole and nothing else. What
Bennett’s machine keeps is the fresh states it’s handed: on an endless tape it can
34   1 A distinction that stays


                keep its whole history and never come back, taking a state it has never used at every
                step, and the tape was paid for before the first step by whoever built it. A reversible
                machine dodges the merge and its floor. For a specified thermal implementation, a
                finite-time change of distribution can also require entropy production. Fresh states
                and physical dissipation are different quantities; contact with surroundings alone
                supplies no numerical bound.


                Theorem 1.6 (Reversible keeps nothing). Let a one-to-one step act on finitely many
                states. From any start the run returns to the start within as many steps as there are
                states, and any reading that is no at the start and never goes from yes to no is no at
                every step.

                Proof. Among the first (number of states) plus one states of the run, two are equal,
                by the pigeonhole. Take two equal positions and cancel the one-to-one step back
                from both the same number of times, until the earlier one reaches the start; the later
                one then equals the start. So the run returns to the start after at most that many
                steps, and from then on repeats. If the reading were yes at some step, it would stay
                yes from there, in particular at a later multiple of the period, where the state is the
                start, which reads no.


                1.4 Noisy steps

                Real states are noisy. The bead hops on its own. So take the step to be a table
                of chances: from each state, the chance of landing on each state next, every row
                adding to one. A permanent reading is a set of states you never leave once you’re in
                it. And “no merge” has an exact noisy meaning: the step preserves the even spread.
                Start with everybody spread evenly over the states, take one step, and they’re still
                spread evenly; which is to say every column of the table adds to one as well as every
                row. Such a step squeezes nothing on average.
                    Then the cell’s count goes through with chances in place of people. A step that
                preserves the even spread cannot raise a permanent reading from any state outside
                it, and not merely with small chance but with none. Count the chance flowing
                into the yes-states from everywhere. Column by column that’s one per yes-state, so
                it equals the number of yes-states. The yes-states alone already send exactly that
                much, because they never leave. What’s left over for the outside states is zero, and
                it’s a sum of chances, so each is zero. The count never used that the spread was
                even, only that every state had some chance and the step gave the spread back. A
                lopsided memory that keeps its own lopsided spread can’t raise a reading that stays
                either: weight each state by its chance and the same sum comes out.
                                                                                     1.4 Noisy steps   35


   And it runs the other way too. A step that can raise a permanent reading does
not preserve the even spread, so after one step from the even spread the crowd is
more bunched up than it was. Here is a way to measure that bunching. Draw a
state twice, independently, using the same spread of chances. Ask whether the two
draws match. For two equally likely states, the matching pairs have chances one
quarter and one quarter, so a match occurs half the time. Put three quarters of the
chance on one state and one quarter on the other: the matching chances are now
nine sixteenths and one sixteenth, adding to ten sixteenths. Bunching has made a
match more likely.
   In general, a state with chance q contributes q2 to this matching chance: q for
the first draw, times q for the independent second draw. Add those squares over all
states. I call that total the collision weight. The step just described raises it above the
value for an even spread.
   There is another measure of the same change, Shannon entropy, which measures
uncertainty in the spread. It is largest when all states are equally likely, so leaving
that even spread lowers it. This is the quantity that enters the heat bound under
Landauer’s premise. Section 3.7 works through its meaning in bits; the proof here es-
tablishes the drop. Finally, when a step preserves the even spread, it cannot increase
the collision weight of any starting spread. That last claim needs a calculation too.



Theorem 1.7 (Noisy steps). Let a step on finitely many states be a table of chances
with rows adding to one, and let a set of states be closed: from inside, the chance
of leaving is zero. (1) If every column also adds to one, the chance of entering the
closed set from any state outside it is zero. (2) If some state outside can enter the
closed set with positive chance, then some column does not add to one, and one
step from the even spread strictly raises the collision weight, the sum of the squared
chances, which is least for the even spread, and it leaves a Shannon entropy strictly
below the logarithm of the number of states. (3) If every column adds to one, one
step never raises the collision weight of any spread.

   Part (1) needs only the closed set to be finite, the rest as large as you like, and
part (3) needs no finiteness at all; part (2) needs the even spread, so it needs finitely
many states.
Proof. (1) Count the total chance sent into the closed set. Each of its columns sums
to one, so the total equals the number of states in that set. The rows belonging to
states already inside send all their chance inside, and they already supply that entire
total. Nothing remains for an outside row to contribute. Because every contribution
is nonnegative, each outside contribution is zero.
36   1 A distinction that stays


                   (2) Suppose instead that an outside state contributes a positive chance of entry.
                Then the conclusion of (1) fails, so its column-sum condition cannot hold: at least
                one column sum differs from one. Call the number of states N and the sum of
                column j c j . Starting evenly puts chance 1/N at each source, so the chance at
                destination j after the step is c j /N. The column sums themselves add to N, because
                the N rows each add to one. Expand the following squares and use that total:

                                  ∑(c j − 1)2 = ∑ c2j − 2 ∑ c j + N = ∑ c2j − N.
                                   j              j           j              j

                At least one square is positive. Thus ∑ j c2j > N. Dividing by N 2 says that the new
                collision weight is greater than 1/N, the old even spread’s collision weight. Now
                compare the uncertainty before and after. Write q j = c j /N for the new chances.
                At least one differs from 1/N. Shannon’s entropy weights each possible state’s
                logarithmic uncertainty by its chance. Using the natural logarithm, written ln, its
                value is
                                               H (q) = −    ∑ q j ln q j .
                                                           j:q j >0

                The sum leaves out states with zero chance; they contribute nothing. An even spread
                has N equal terms, giving H = ln N. Subtract the new entropy from that value.
                Since the chances add to one, you can put ln N inside the sum:
                                          ln N − H (q) =     ∑ q j ln( Nq j ).
                                                            j:q j >0

                I need to show that this difference is positive, even though some individual terms
                may be negative.
                   Use the elementary logarithm inequality ln y ≤ y − 1, with equality only at y = 1.
                One way to see it is to look at y − 1 − ln y: its slope is 1 − 1/y, negative below one
                and positive above one, so its least value is zero at one. Apply the inequality with
                y = 1/( Nq j ) and multiply by q j . Rearranging gives

                                              q j ln( Nq j ) ≥ q j − 1/N,

                with equality only when q j = 1/N. A zero chance contributes zero to the entropy
                difference, which is strictly greater than its comparison term −1/N. Add the
                comparisons over all N states. Their right sides sum to 1 − N/N = 0. At least one
                comparison is strict because the new spread is not even, so the entropy difference is
                positive.
                   (3) Fix a destination column. Because its entries add to one, its new chance is an
                average of the old chances, with those entries as weights. An average of squares is
                never less than the square of the average. To see why, call the weights wi , the old
                                                                                     1.5 Unitary steps   37


chances pi , and their weighted average m. Expanding gives

        ∑ wi ( pi − m)2 = ∑ wi p2i − m2 ≥ 0,          ∑ wi = 1,     m = ∑ wi p i .
         i                   i                         i                   i

So the new chance squared is at most the weighted sum of the old chances squared.
Add this comparison over all destination columns. Each old chance squared gets
weights from its whole row, whose sum is one. The result is exactly the old collision
weight, bounding the new one from above.


1.5 Unitary steps

The quantum version needs a different picture. Draw a sheet through the centre of a
room. Call every direction along the sheet YES, and the direction straight through it
NO. Turn the whole arrangement without stretching it. Can the sheet stay within its
old plane while the direction through it turns into that plane? No. The turn keeps
right angles. If the sheet still fills that plane, the direction that was at right angles to
the whole sheet is still at right angles to it.
    Here is what carries from that picture into the quantum statement. A quantum
state is described by a vector. A reversible quantum step preserves lengths and
overlaps between vectors; such a step is called unitary. The YES part is a subspace: a
collection of directions that also contains their linear combinations. The directions
with zero overlap with every YES direction make up its orthogonal complement.
These are the NO states in this argument. Permanence means that a vector in the
YES subspace stays in it after the step.
    There is one detail to settle before the right-angle argument works. The old
YES directions must fill the whole YES subspace after the step, leaving no missing
direction. Choose a finite list of directions from which every YES vector can be
assembled, with none of the listed directions assembled from the others. Such a
list is called an independent spanning list, or a basis. A unitary step keeps the list
independent, since any relation between its images could be reversed to give the
same relation before the step. The images are still inside the YES subspace, and
there are just as many independent directions as before. They therefore still span it.
That is why the step fills the YES subspace, rather than merely landing somewhere
inside it.
    Now take a NO vector. Before the step it has zero overlap with every YES vector.
After the step those overlaps are still zero, and the stepped YES vectors still fill the
whole YES subspace. The stepped NO vector is therefore still NO. Repeat the step
and the same argument applies again.
    Finite dimension was used exactly once: a full finite list of independent YES
directions still fills the YES subspace after the step. Drop it and the bilateral shift,
38   1 A distinction that stays


                which is unitary on an endless ladder of states, raises “past the start” on the first
                step and keeps it forever, taking a state it has never used every time. A reading
                that stays, which no unitary step can raise in finite dimension, is paid for either
                by fresh states, a ladder of states that never comes back around, or by a step that
                squeezes the even spread, which, when the squeezed states were really possible,
                owes Landauer’s floor. Not every step that fails to be unitary squeezes: one that
                keeps the even spread, as pure dephasing and an unread projective measurement
                do, can’t raise a reading that stays either. The balance argument is the same one
                used for noisy steps. Choose a complete set of mutually perpendicular directions,
                some filling the YES subspace and the rest filling its orthogonal complement. Spread
                the chances equally over those directions. This is the fully mixed state: choosing a
                different complete perpendicular set gives the same mixture.
                    Suppose there are N directions altogether and m of them are YES. The mixture
                has chance m/N of YES. A step that preserves this mixture must leave that chance
                at m/N. But the YES part already supplies all of it: it started with weight m/N,
                and permanence keeps that whole weight inside YES. Every contribution from the
                other directions is nonnegative, so none can contribute any chance of entering YES.
                You can include any chosen NO vector among the perpendicular directions of the
                complement. The same balance then rules out entry from that vector. That is why
                the outside cannot get in. In finite dimension nothing is kept without one of the
                two. Which way a quantum measurement pays when its outcome is kept isn’t settled
                here. The collapse models people test keep the even spread too, so the heat the
                experiments look for is the heat of the noise those models add, not a Landauer price
                on a kept outcome; I come back to them below.


                Theorem 1.8 (Unitary steps). Let a unitary map a finite-dimensional subspace into
                itself. Then it maps the orthogonal complement into itself: a state orthogonal to the
                subspace remains orthogonal after every step.

                Proof. Call the step U and the YES subspace Y. Choose a basis of Y, meaning an
                independent list from which every vector in Y can be assembled. The step sends that
                list to an equally long independent list inside Y, so its images are another basis of Y.
                    Take any vector x orthogonal to Y. To test whether Ux is still orthogonal, choose
                any vector y in Y. Because the images fill Y, there is a vector z in Y with Uz = y.
                Unitarity preserves the overlap, written with angle brackets, so

                                          ⟨Ux, y⟩ = ⟨Ux, Uz⟩ = ⟨ x, z⟩ = 0.
                                                                     1.6 Going faster gives off more heat   39


The last equality holds because x is orthogonal to every vector in Y, including z. The
choice of y was arbitrary, so Ux is orthogonal to all of Y. This is the same condition
I started with, and it survives every further step.


1.6 Going faster gives off more heat
Everything so far was what keeping takes. What comes next is a dissipation result for
a particular stochastic model. Bennett’s Brownian computer is a walker on a line that
is pushed forward a little: at each tick it steps forward with some chance and back
with the rest. Its speed is the difference between the two. A forward translation is
one-to-one, and so is a backward translation. The random choice between them is a
stochastic rule, not one deterministic translation; the deterministic merge count does
not apply to it as though it were. The entropy it gives off per tick is Schnakenberg’s
formula for a biased walk, the speed times the logarithm of the forward-to-backward
ratio, and that number is strictly positive at any speed other than zero, because both
factors have the same sign. The only walker that gives off nothing is the one with
no drift, as likely to step back as forward. This is the point that going slower doesn’t
get you out of paying, now as a theorem: at any speed you actually run it, every tick
gives off heat on average.
    The exchange rate has a floor as well. Heat per net step forward, counted in
units of kT, is the logarithm of the forward-to-backward ratio, and that logarithm is
at least the speed. So walking a distance costs at least distance times speed in heat
and takes distance over speed in time, and heat times time is at least the distance
squared. At low speed, halve the speed and the heat roughly halves while the time
doubles; the product never drops below the square of how far you went. Going
slowly makes the mean heat for a specified amount of directed progress smaller and
its drift time longer. These are averages. With no bias, the walker still moves, and it
can reach a nearby target on the first tick.
                                                         One place back
                                                         Half the chance


                Start at zero


                                                    Target: one place ahead
                                                        Half the chance
The mean displacement is zero. Half the paths reach this target on the first tick. Zero drift
                 does not mean no movement or no completed paths.
   Below, distance divided by speed is the time scale for the mean displacement to
advance that distance. It is not the duration of every path that happens to finish.
40   1 A distinction that stays




                Theorem 1.9 (Heat against time). For a walker stepping forward with chance p and
                back with chance 1 − p, with 0 < p < 1, the entropy it hands to its surroundings
                                        p
                per tick, (2p − 1) ln 1− p , is zero at p = 21 and strictly positive otherwise. With speed
                v = 2p − 1 in (0, 1) and distance N ≥ 0, the mean heat in units of kT for drift
                progress N, N ln 11−+v , times the drift time N/v is at least N 2 .
                                     v

                Proof. For p > 12 both factors are positive and for p < 12 both are negative, by
                the monotonicity of the logarithm; at p = 12 the first factor is zero. For the floor,
                ln(1 + v) ≥ 0 and ln(1 − v) ≤ −v since ln y ≤ y − 1, so ln 11+ v
                                                                             −v ≥ v, and the product
                is N 2 times that logarithm divided by v.
                   That is the surroundings’ share of the entropy production. The whole of it adds
                the change in the walker’s own spread, which on a line keeps growing but ever more
                slowly, so per tick that share goes to zero and the long-run rate is the heat’s.
                   The sharp floor is twice that. The difference ln 11− +v − 2v is zero at v = 0 and its
                                                                         v
                              2
                derivative, 1−v2 − 2, is never negative on (0, 1), so the logarithm is at least 2v and
                the product is at least 2N 2 . I state N 2 because the one-line bound gives it, and what
                matters is the square, not the factor in front of it.
                   Keeping something costs, on top of that, either a merge, which under Landauer’s
                premise owes a floor of kT ln 2 per bit that no slowness removes, or a state the
                device has never used before. Taking a fresh state escapes the floor and does not
                settle the implementation’s finite-time dissipation. And a finite set of states, where
                every state has a next one, forces the merge.


                1.7 Every scale pays the same way

                One more question, and it’s the one that decides whether any of this is about the
                world or only about my pictures. A state is a description. The dial on a lab bench is
                a state, and so is each atom in it, and so is each atom together with the light it gave
                off. Describe the same thing coarser or finer and you get different states. Does what
                keeping takes change with the zoom?
                    It doesn’t, and the reason fits in one picture. Draw the fine states, and draw a
                fence around each group of them that counts as one coarse state. Say the coarse
                picture merges: two coarse states step to one coarse state. Then, when the fine
                states are finitely many, the fine step can’t keep them all apart either. Count them.
                If the fine step sent different fine states to different fine states and none of them
                stepped out of the fenced set, it would be a reshuffle of the fine states, with every
                fine state landed on exactly once afterwards. But some fenced group is now landed
                                                                   1.7 Every scale pays the same way   41


on by nothing, because the coarse step missed a coarse state (two coarse states went
to one, so on a finite set some coarse state is stepped to by nothing), and so nothing
lands on any fine state in that group. A reshuffle leaves no state out. So something
gave: the fine step merges too, or some fine state stepped out of the fenced set,
or the fenced set has no end. The three ways come back one level down, though
stepping out of the fenced set isn’t taking a fresh state; it’s where the coarse picture
stops tracking the fine one.


Theorem 1.10 (Every scale pays the same way). Let a fine machine have one rule
F on a set X of states, let A be a set of its states, and let a coarse description be a
map π from X to a set S of coarse states that takes A onto S, with a coarse rule f
on S such that π ( F ( x )) = f (π ( x )) for every x in A. If the coarse rule merges two
coarse states, then at least one of these holds: F merges two states of A; F takes
some state of A outside A; or some run of F from a state of A stays in A and never
comes back to a state it has visited.

Proof. Suppose the fine machine avoids all three ways out. It stays inside A, keeps
different states apart, and every run eventually visits a state it has visited before.
Follow one run to its first repeat. The two visits have the same state, so their
predecessors must agree too: different predecessors are never allowed to land
together. Walk backwards like that until the earlier visit reaches the start. The later
visit has reached the same start. The run is a loop from the start, with no loose
approach leading into it.
    Now watch that loop through the coarse window. Every fine step gives the coarse
step specified by f . When the fine state returns to its start, its picture returns too.
Every coarse state has a fine state above it, because π takes A onto S. So every
coarse state also lies on a loop.
   That rules out a coarse merge. Suppose two different coarse starts had the same
next state. Call the lengths of their loops L1 and L2 . Wait L1 L2 steps from the starts:
that is a whole number of circuits for both loops, so each must be back at its own
start. But after their first step they were together. The same rule cannot separate
them afterwards, so at the end of that wait they are still together. Their starts must
have been the same after all.
   The coarse rule does merge, by hypothesis. The fine machine therefore cannot
avoid all three alternatives. In the last alternative, every tick visits another state of
A, so no finite collection can hold the run.
   When I say a coarse description is exact about a set of fine states, I mean what
the theorem asks: it follows the fine step on the set, and every coarse state describes
some state in it. Put it next to the permanent flip. On a finite coarse picture, a
42   1 A distinction that stays


               reading that goes up and stays up is raised by a merge (the cell above, on three
               states; Theorem 3.1, two chapters on, in general). By this theorem, at every finer
               description that the coarse one is exact about, keeping that reading is again a merge,
               though not always where the reading rose, or a step off the described states, or a run
               that takes a fresh described state at every step. The dial and its light are the example.
               In the dial’s own picture, two blends of readings decay to one either-or, a merge
               (Section 18). In the picture of dial and light together, the step is one-to-one, and it’s
               the second case: the light starts blank and leaves carrying the copy, so the fine step
               leaves the set of states where the light is still blank. At the fine scale nothing merges;
               the step leaves the states the coarse picture describes. And the heat floor sits where
               the merge really is. Landauer’s premise charges the scale whose step merges states
               that were really possible; a description that merges only because it stopped looking
               at the light owes that floor nowhere merely because of that projection. Leaving
               the set where the light is blank is not the same as visiting a fresh full state at every
               later tick. To infer an endless fresh-state run, the theorem needs its third alternative.
               To infer heat, specify the physical preparation and what happens to the light or
               reservoir.


                1.8 What keeping takes, and where the toll comes in

                So that’s the whole of what keeping takes, set out before anybody writes a price on
                anything. The toll, which the next chapter states, is what keeping takes, written into
                a step. It’s the price of something being the case: a reading that goes from no to yes
                and stays is a distinction that stays, and a distinction that stays is a state the run has
                used and can’t give back. Anything whose state includes distinctions it can’t give
                back pays what the toll prices: the bead, the cell, the memory bit, a world with a
                past. Give one a price list that obeys the toll and it’s a Thiele machine, and when the
                cell could have held anything, Landauer’s premise puts a heat floor under that raise,
                because on a finite cell the raise is a merge. The toll keeps its shape there, charged
                in heat instead of units of cost. And what keeping takes, deterministic or noisy
                or quantum, comes to this: the Brownian walker has a positive dissipation rate at
                nonzero drift, and the cited diffusion and jump models give finite-time distributional
                bounds under their own hypotheses; keeping something costs on top of that either a
                merge, with Landauer’s floor when the merged states were really possible, or a state
                never used before; and a finite machine, where every state has a next one, forces
                the merge. The step law, the noisy steps and the unitary steps are proved, and the
                table above says how near the laboratory has come to each; the heat is physics.
                   That’s also why the rule sits on the raise and not on the merge. The toll charges
                for what is kept whichever column pays for it, merge or fresh state. A price on
                merges charges only the merge column, so it misses something kept by taking a
                                                 1.8 What keeping takes, and where the toll comes in   43


state never used before: the machine that keeps every history, the first way out two
chapters on, raises its reading at zero cost under it. And it charges merges that keep
nothing, like the reset that lowers a flag. The toll doesn’t ask that reset for a unit
of cost, and it still merges two states, so in a real device it owes Landauer’s floor
whenever the bit it lowers was really unknown; the ledger leaves that to physics,
the same as the dissipation of happening.
   Next comes the smallest model that keeps that cost on its own ledger: two boxes
on a sheet of paper, a tally, and one rule.
CHAPTER 2




A record and a toll

The last chapter found what keeping takes and kept no count of it. Now give it a
ledger. This is where the machine gets stated once, exactly: a state, a reading of
it into an order, moves, and a price in each move, with one rule tying the price to
the order. Then take the smallest record that can carry a charge for its change, two
positions, blank and written, and build it on paper, with a pencil. Write the charge
into its rules and see what follows. Keeping it this small is what lets you see which
part of the construction does which part of the work.
    The usual models charge a computation for two things: how long it runs and
how much space it uses. The bits it destroys have been counted too, as the opening
said, by Li and Vitányi and by Demaine and his coauthors. What this part charges is
something else: what the computation keeps and can’t take back. This part is about
that charge, which gets paid in a merge, carrying a heat floor when the merged
states were really possible, or by taking a state never used before, and which the
last chapter showed can’t be talked down to zero. The record built below is the
smallest thing that can carry the charge, and the tally next to it counts every time
the record goes up. Whether a machine has to charge it as a unit of cost, and on
which premises, is the next chapter.
    One thing needs saying about what a flag stands behind, because it stays out of
the picture a while. What I’m about to build prices vouching for anything at all: a
flag goes up, and the rule doesn’t ask what the flag is standing behind. A sorting of
a pile into groups, the kind of structure Part II starts from (Section 6), is the first
kind of claim I care about. It isn’t the only kind, and the book comes back to what
a flag stands behind in Section 9, and on a machine in Section 15, where a flag
stands on a checked claim. Until then nothing about the flag leans on groupings.
The floor in this section, the reason for it in the next, and the latch in Part II all work
whatever the reading is about, partition or no partition. When groupings come in,
in Section 9, it’s as a theorem: a reading that says a grouping has been checked
and committed sees the grouping only through its partition, and what it entitles is
exactly the groupings that refine it (Theorem 9.2). So the grouping gets a job, and
an exact one.


                                   44
                                                                2.1 A demon, and the step that pays   45


   But first one neighbour, because the charge I’m about to write down has a famous
cousin in physics, and I want it on the table before the toy is, so you can see which
step it prices and which it doesn’t.


2.1 A demon, and the step that pays
Here is that neighbour, and it’s the one that gets closest. In 1867 the physicist James
Clerk Maxwell, in a letter to his friend the Scottish physicist Peter Guthrie Tait,
imagined a “very observant and neat-fingered being” sitting at a tiny door between
two halves of a box of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and slow ones
the other, so that one side heats up and the other cools with no work done, which is
supposed to be impossible. The being got called Maxwell’s demon, and physicists
have been arguing about it for a hundred and fifty years, which should tell you
something.
    In 1929 Leo Szilard, a young Hungarian physicist working in Berlin, cut the
demon’s box down to a single molecule, and that made information part of the
accounting. The tempting move, and the one Szilard’s own accounting made, is
to put the whole heat floor on finding out which side the molecule is on. Bennett
separated finding out from restoring the memory for another round: measuring
onto a blank record can, in principle, be thermodynamically reversible, and resetting
an unknown record is a different operation. That does not mean a real measuring
device costs nothing to build or run. It says that learning and resetting do not carry
the same unavoidable entropy cost, and I’m about to pick a step to charge, so I need
that distinction before I do.
    Bennett’s version of the rule, in a 2003 paper you can read, is that what must cost
is “the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths.” That is erasing,
or taking two possible situations and making them one. And in the same paper he
lists copying unknown data onto a blank place to write among “the most important
logically reversible operations,” the kind he says can, at least in principle, be run
thermodynamically reversibly. So, in the one place in all of this where a record is
priced by physics, the unavoidable erasure charge belongs to forgetting the unknown
record. Making a record on a blank place carries no such charge of its own. It does
use up the blank place, which is a state the machine hasn’t used yet. Resetting it for
reuse has a Landauer bound when that reset removes entropy under the thermal
premises. Read that twice, because it’s not what I expected either.
    Making a record on a blank place is one operation. Landauer’s 1961 paper names
another: set a bit to one whatever it held. If that bit is the whole state, down goes to
up, up stays up, and two possible states become one. Landauer called this “restore
to one.” On an uncertain input it removes information, and a heat bound then needs
the thermodynamic premises.
46   2 A record and a toll


                   A larger machine has more state than its flag. Two starts can both finish with
               the flag up while remaining different elsewhere. The next chapter proves that, on
               a finite machine whose reading is permanent, any instruction that raises it must
               merge some full states. It does not say the state whose flag just rose is one of that
               pair. Put one state outside the set that reads yes and two states inside it. Send the
               outside state to the first inside state, and send both inside states to the second. The
               flag rises for the outside state, but the two inside states are the ones that merge.
               These arrows describe alternative starts, not three things happening in one run.
                   That is the distinction the one-bit picture hides. The instruction has a collision
               somewhere, and the actual distribution of starting states determines whether that
               collision removes uncertainty. A known starting state loses none under the entropy
               premise, even when its flag rises (Theorem 3.17, next chapter). A separate uncertain
               memory may have a reset cost, but neither its existence nor an earlier heat payment
               follows from specifying a known start. The ledger can still charge the instruction
               under merge pricing. A ledger charge, information loss and a device’s heat are three
               quantities to keep apart.
                   A few more neighbours, quickly, because they all point the same way. Regulators
               who make brokers keep records on media that can’t be rewritten (the SEC required
               exactly that, write once and read many, from 1997 until 2022, when it allowed an
               audit trail as the other way to comply) are pricing the hardware. The rule puts no
               charge on the act of writing. Haber and Stornetta in 1991, the timestamping that
               Bitcoin’s footnotes lead back to (Section 14 follows them), chained time-stamped
               records together with hashes so that changing an old entry breaks every entry
               after it (and Ralph Merkle’s hash tree, from his 1979 Stanford thesis on secrecy
               and authentication, lets one short value vouch for a great many records); try the
               dependency with five entries, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, adding each to the running total: 1, 3,
               6, 10, 15. Keep that sheet and make another with the second entry changed to
               3. Its totals are 1, 4, 7, 11, 16. The change travels down the chain. Now lower
               the third entry to 2, and the last total is 15 again. Simple addition can be fooled
               by compensating changes. A cryptographic chain needs a stronger function, and
               someone must retain a trusted value to compare against. This trial shows the
               dependency between entries; it supplies neither that function’s security nor a price
               on the record. Proof-of-work, which the computer scientists Cynthia Dwork and
               Moni Naor proposed in 1992 to make junk mail expensive and which Bitcoin later
               chained, is the one framing where a record genuinely costs, and what it charges for
               is a search: how many tries it took to find a lucky number. At the same difficulty,
               an empty and a full block face the same target for the header hash. The expected
               number of hash attempts agrees; the attempts on two actual blocks need not, and
               handling their transactions is additional work. So the work prices the search. Proof-
               of-work charges nothing extra for the moment anything becomes certified. Robert
                                                     2.2 The smallest thing that could carry the charge   47


Floyd and Tony Hoare, two computer scientists asking how you’d prove a program
does what it’s supposed to, attached claims to points in a program in 1967 and
1969 (“whenever you get here, this is true”), and the claim is backed by a proof
that’s paid for off the machine. And the certificates of complexity theory, which
go back to Stephen Cook’s 1971 work on NP, are strings designed to be cheap to
check: hand me the certificate and I can confirm the claim quickly. Whether they’re
also expensive to find is the famous open question of the field, P versus NP, and
nobody knows; the definition promises polynomial-time verification. Polynomial
time need not be small in practice, and it need not be less than the time to find
every particular witness. This is a bound on checking, not a separate charge for
setting an accepting flag. And from statistics, a ledger that runs the other way: Dean
Foster and Robert Stine’s alpha-investing (2008) runs a long string of tests against
a budget of allowed false alarms, where every test spends some of the budget and
each observed rejection earns budget back, even though some rejections can be false.
That’s the other way round from a price on vouching: the testing rule spends and
earns an error-control budget; a reward does not certify that the discovery is true.


2.2 The smallest thing that could carry the charge
Take a sheet of paper. Draw two boxes and label them NO and YES. The two boxes
are the reading, a single yes-or-no question asked of the state, and I’m going to
be careful about what the question is, because after five thousand years of seals
and witnesses the word “vouch” is carrying a lot and this toy carries almost none
of it. The question is only: “has the designated flag been set.” It is not “is some
claim about a grouping true,” and it is not “did anyone check.” There is no claim in
this toy, no evidence, no checker, nobody standing behind anything. There is a flag.
Whether a flag can ever be made to mean that something was checked and can be
relied on is a real question, and it’s not this section’s; I’ll build toward it later, and
until then please read YES as “the flag is up” and nothing more. The state is which
box you’re in, and that’s the whole state, one bit. Then draw a line under the boxes
for tally marks. The marks sit outside the state. They’re the running total you keep
beside it as you play, the way you’d keep score beside a board game.
    Now give yourself three moves. STAY: you don’t move, and you make no mark.
WORK: you don’t move either (it’s a stand-in for every ordinary step a machine
takes), and you make no mark. VOUCH: from NO you move to YES; from YES
you stay in YES; either way you make one tally mark, because in this toy the price
belongs to the move’s name, and where you were standing doesn’t enter into it. Now
play. Start in NO, make any sequence of moves you like, and stop in YES. Count the
marks. Then try to reach YES with zero marks. You can’t, and you can see exactly
why: the only move that crosses from NO to YES is VOUCH, and VOUCH makes
48   2 A record and a toll


               a mark. Now erase the mark from VOUCH’s rule and play again. You reach YES
               with no marks, every time. The entire content of what I’m about to call a rule is
               this, and I want you to see how little it is before I dress it up: I’ve decided that the
               move which crosses the line makes a mark. Nothing in the toy’s rules forces the
               mark. VOUCH does merge, NO and YES both landing on YES, which is what the
               last chapter says a kept raise on two states has to do; what nothing yet says is that
               a merge has to cost a mark. Here it’s a choice, what the last chapter says keeping
               takes, written down as a rule. The next chapter is about when a machine has no
               choice.
                   Why tally marks, by the way? Because they’re about the oldest receipt there is.
               The real ones, the English treasury’s notched sticks split down the middle, get their
               own story in Part II (Section 7), fire and all. The tally on your paper is nothing
               like those. Nobody holds the other half. You keep it, beside the board, and you
               could rub a mark out and nobody would ever know. Hold on to that, because by the
               end of this section it’s the reason the toy is a scorekeeper’s receipt and not a record
               anybody else could rely on.
                   Here is the machine, stated once, carefully, because this is the one place in the
               book where I state it exactly and everything later points back here. The point listed
               the five parts in a sentence; here they’re pinned down. A Thiele machine has five
               parts.
                   A set of states.
                   A set of move names.
                   A step: for each state and each move name, where you land.
                   A cost for each move name: a whole number of units, zero or more.
                   A record: a reading of each state into an order, a set of places on which, for any
               two, you can ask whether one is at or below the other. Higher is more settled.
                   Those five parts are the whole of it. Add the one rule, the toll, and it’s a Thiele
               machine: a move that carries the record somewhere not at or below where it stood
               costs at least one. A machine whose moves never climb is the flat case, and the rule
               has nothing to say to it; every ordinary computer is one.
                   The thing on your paper is the smallest case that isn’t flat. Its record has two
               places, the blank box and the written one, which I’ve labelled NO and YES, with NO
               below YES; its states are the two boxes and nothing else; its move names are STAY,
               WORK and VOUCH; its costs are zero, zero and one, in tally marks. Everything in
               this section is proved for the two-place record, because it’s the one you can point
               at. Section 4 proves the same for any order and gets the two places back as a case
               (Theorem 4.2).
                   I also want to be exact about what’s not in it. There’s no counter stored inside the
               state that’s forbidden from going down; the marks are the side tally from the board
               game, and the tally only ever grows because the costs are whole numbers, zero
                                                    2.2 The smallest thing that could carry the charge   49


or more. (A machine could keep the total inside its state too; that’s an extra part
beyond the five, and Section 7 builds it.) There’s no window, no observer who sees
only part of the state; that’s a later question and it gets its own section. And the cost
depends only on the move’s name; where you are when you make it doesn’t matter.
That’s on purpose: the charge is on the attempt, so you pay for making the move,
whatever it turns out to do. It’s also a real simplification, and where a result needs
a price that depends on where you are, Section 8 says so and uses one. Last, the
step gives every state and every move exactly one place to land. A choice becomes a
move name, and a machine that has stopped steps to itself. A step that can land in
several places by chance is a different picture, and the noisy steps in Section 1 take
it up. To apply the step law, fix the move being repeated, or include the program
and its control in the full state so that one autonomous rule chooses the next step.
Arbitrarily choosing different moves from outside is a different case, worked through
in the next chapter. Deterministic instructions alone do not supply that fixed rule.
Separately, giving every move a successor even when the flag is already up keeps a
price per move name from charging exactly the raises: a move that raises the flag
and has no next step once it’s up could cost one and never charge for anything else.
    On two places the toll reads like this. For every state and every move: if the
reading is NO before the move and YES after it, the move’s cost is at least one.
That’s the whole rule there. It says nothing about any other move. It says nothing
about how big a mark is in anything you could measure. One mark is one mark;
what a mark is worth, why the smallest charge is one (why not two, or a half?), and
whether I had any right to decide that, come next. The middle question has a short
answer I’ll give away now. What the next chapter forces, on its premises, is that
a raise that stays up, with only finitely many yes-states, merges two states, so any
price on merges lands on it. Costs here are whole numbers, which I chose so the
ledger counts acts, and the least whole number above nothing is one. The “at least
one” comes from there.
    And one theorem, which is the only thing the toy actually proves, and you’ve
already proved it by playing. Take any run of moves that starts in a NO state and
ends in a YES state. Then the marks it made add up to at least one. The argument
in words is short enough that you can hold the whole thing. Walk the run move by
move, reading the box at each step. It read NO at the start and YES at the end, and
every move either leaves the reading alone or flips it, so at some move it went from
NO to YES. The toll says that move cost at least one. Every other move cost zero
or more. Add them up and the total is at least one. Notice what the argument did
not need. It didn’t need the reading to stay YES afterward; if a later move flipped
it back to NO and another flipped it to YES again, the toll charges twice, and the
argument still goes through. It didn’t need the machine to be finite. It didn’t need to
know what any move does besides what the reading says before and after. It needed
50   2 A record and a toll


               the toll, and two things the five parts already hand it: no cost is below zero, and the
               reading has only two values, so a move that changes it from NO lands on YES. Give
               the reading a third value, a “maybe” between the two, and the one-bit toll as written
               here charges nothing for NO to MAYBE; the toll over any order in Section 4 charges
               every step that climbs, MAYBE included. That difference is the whole reason the
               record is a place in an order and not a bit.
                  That’s the whole theorem, and I’ll state it once more in the exact form, because
               from here on the book carries two layers side by side: what I mean, in words, and
               what’s stated and proved, in symbols you can hold me to. The symbols are few. N is
               the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on. S and I are just names for “the set of states”
               and “the set of move names.” Writing step : S × I → S means “hand it a state and a
               move name and it hands back a state.” A run is a list of move names, t = [i1 , . . . , in ],
               played from a start s0 , one after another. The double arrow =⇒ reads “then”: the
               thing on its left forces the thing on its right. For this first proof, keep your finger
               on the run and stop at the first YES. The move immediately before that is the one
               whose charge matters.

               Definition 2.1 (Thiele machine). A Thiele machine consists of a set S of states, a set
               I of move names, a step function step : S × I → S, a cost cost : I → N, and a record
               rec : S → R into a set R with an order ≤ that is reflexive and transitive, subject to
               one rule, the toll: for every state s and move i,
                                      rec(step(s, i )) ̸≤ rec(s) =⇒ cost(i ) ≥ 1.

               Nothing more is assumed of the order.


               Definition 2.2 (Thiele machine with a two-place record). Take R = {no, yes} with
               no below yes. The record is a reading cert : S → {no, yes}, it leaves the down-set
               exactly when it goes from no to yes, and the toll reads: for every state s and move i,
                              cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes =⇒ cost(i ) ≥ 1.

               The run of t = [i1 , . . . , in ] from s0 ends at run(t, s0 ), the result of applying the steps
               in order, and its total cost is cost(t) = cost(i1 ) + · · · + cost(in ), with the empty run
               costing 0.

                  The first definition is the machine. The toy on the paper is the second, and most
               of Parts I and II is told on it; Section 4 carries every result here over to any order. I
               write the two-place reading as cert, because on the machine of Part III it names a
               flag that says a claim was certified. What earns a flag its meaning will depend on
               the machine’s rules.
                                                      2.2 The smallest thing that could carry the charge   51


   The one theorem comes first in its general form, because it’s three lines and it
shows that nothing about two places is doing the work.
Observation 2.1 (The floor over any order). In any Thiele machine, a run whose
record ends somewhere not at or below where it started has total cost at least 1.
Proof. Read the records along the run. The last is not at or below the first. Walk
forward and take the first state whose record is not at or below the start’s. The state
before it reads at or below the start, so if this one read at or below the state before it,
it would read at or below the start too, since the order carries across, and it doesn’t.
So the move between them climbed, and the toll charges it at least one. No other
charge is below zero.
   On two places it reads as follows, and that is the version the toy proves.
   A word on the label before the first result. I call a result an observation when its
proof does little more than unfold the definitions, and in an axiomatic cost model
that’s what the definitions are meant to do: the work is in choosing them, so the
results that follow from them in a few lines are labelled that way and the theorems
with more in them stand out.
Observation 2.2 (The universal floor). In any Thiele machine, every run that starts
at a state reading no and ends at a state reading yes has total cost at least 1: if
cert(s0 ) = no and cert(run(t, s0 )) = yes, then cost(t) ≥ 1.
Proof. Read the states of the run from left to right. The first reads no and the last
reads yes, so there is a first state on this list that reads yes. It cannot be the starting
state. The state immediately before it reads no: otherwise the chosen YES would
not be the first. The move between them therefore costs at least one, by the toll.
   Now add the charges for the whole run. That one charge is already at least one,
and none of the other charges is negative. The total is at least one. The flag may
come down later and go up again; that cannot remove the charge I have found.

The tabletop and the stamp
Put two boxes on the table. Each has tiles on top, and the tiles spell the same answer.
On the side of one box the stamp is up. On the other it is down. Hang a camera
directly above them. The photographs are identical.
    Now hand me the photographs and ask which box was stamped. Take a better
photograph. Enlarge it. Count every tile. None of that gets the side of the box into
the picture. The difference is there, in the boxes. It has been left out of what you
handed me.
    That is the window I want to name. S is the set of full states of the boxes, and
B is the set of tabletop pictures. The map π : S → B takes a full state and returns
its picture. Every picture in B comes from a box; that is what onto says. Pick one
52   2 A record and a toll


               picture, b, and gather every full state that gives that picture. That whole collection
               is the fibre above b, written π −1 (b).
                   Keep the whole collection in mind. The tiles can agree while the boxes differ in
               which checks ran, which earlier pages were certified, and what was kept when those
               pages were wiped. The fibre holds all the differences this camera leaves out. There
               can be two states in it, a million, or infinitely many.
                   I started with one question: is the flag up? That gives me one yes-or-no reading
               of the full state. A hundred different states can all answer yes. Reading that one
               flag tells me where they stand on that one question; the other differences are
               still there. Chapter 14 opens the gauge wider. It asks which checks passed and
               which editions were certified, and counts how many states those answers require.
               Keep independently chosen histories across arbitrarily many editions, all recoverable
               above the same final picture, and the fibre has to be infinite; the count is a pigeonhole
               on the editions.
                   To see exactly what the tabletop can do by itself, give these boxes two kinds of
               move. The tile moves are horizontal. They cost zero, leave the stamp alone, and
               move the tiles according to what is on the tabletop. The stamp never reaches into
               their gears. The stamp moves are vertical. They leave the tiles alone and can raise
               the stamp or leave it where it is. Once raised, it stays raised. A raise pays the toll
               already defined above.
                   These are the rules of the sliced machine. They give me a view of the flat part
               that runs on its own and a record that survives beside it.

               Which question does the toll charge?
               Slide a tile one place to the right. Let that move cost nothing. Now ask a new
               question: is the tile in the place it just reached? Before the slide the answer was
               no. Afterward it is yes. If every question had to obey the same toll, that slide would
               have to cost at least one.
                  Try the same trick on any free move that changes the full state. Ask whether
               the machine is in its destination state. Again the answer changes from no to yes.
               Charging every question would stop every free change. The reading in the definition
               therefore matters: I have to say which question the toll belongs to before I can say
               which moves are free.


               Theorem 2.3 (Charging every question stops free changes). Suppose equality of
               full states is decidable. The same instruction prices satisfy the toll for every Boolean
               reading exactly when every zero-cost instruction leaves every full state unchanged.
                                                        2.2 The smallest thing that could carry the charge   53


Proof. For a changed state, the question “am I at that destination?” supplies a
crossing, so the move cannot be free. In the other direction, a move that leaves the
state unchanged cannot change any reading. Every remaining instruction already
costs at least one, since prices are nonnegative whole numbers. It therefore pays for
any crossing it makes.
   Now keep one question and require its yes to stay yes. A free move cannot raise
that reading, because a raise pays the toll. It cannot lower it, because the reading is
permanent. It has to leave it alone.


Theorem 2.4 (Free moves leave a permanent reading alone). The toll and perma-
nence force every zero-cost instruction to preserve the reading on every state.

Proof. Starting at no, a free move cannot reach yes by the toll. Starting at yes, it
cannot reach no by permanence. Those are the two possible starting readings.
   This gives two ways to state the reading part of the sliced rules. Require horizontal
moves to leave it alone and vertical moves never to lower it; then every move keeps
a yes. Or require that every move keeps a yes, keep the toll and free horizontal
prices, and recover horizontal preservation by the two sentences above. The window
rules still do their own work. A paid move could change both the tiles and the
stamp; permanence does not make the tiles stand still.

Definition 2.3 (Sliced Thiele machine). A sliced Thiele machine is a Thiele machine
with an onto view π : S → B and its move names split into horizontal moves IH and
vertical moves IV . Write r (s) = cert(s), with no < yes, and Fi (s) = step(s, i ). For
each i ∈ IH there is a map hi : B → B such that

             π ( Fi (s)) = hi (π (s)),    r ( Fi (s)) = r (s),     cost(i ) = 0.
For each v ∈ IV ,
                        π ( Fv (s)) = π (s),      r (s) ≤ r ( Fv (s)).
The toll remains: r (s) < r ( Fv (s)) implies cost(v) ≥ 1.

   These laws hold on every state of the specified domain. In contrast, the counter
example’s later live-state slice is a restricted interface: a failed check leaves its
domain. It is not a claim that all six native instruction kinds satisfy these equations
globally.
   The states can be counter configurations, tape configurations, or any other states
meeting these rules. The same horizontal argument works with a whole set of claims
54   2 A record and a toll


               as the record: every horizontal move preserves the set and evolves the picture using
               only that picture. The number of possible records never enters that argument.
                   Now give the two boxes the same horizontal moves. After one move the pictures
               still agree. After two they still agree. Every next picture comes from the previous
               picture and the move you named, and those agree at every step. Meanwhile one
               stamp stays up and the other stays down. You can watch the tabletop for the whole
               run and never see the difference you started with.
                   Give somebody permission to read the stamp and choose a different tile move
               because of it, and they can signal through the tiles. Here both boxes receive the
               same moves. That is how I keep the question fixed while asking what the window
               can reveal.


               Theorem 2.5 (What the tabletop can tell). In a sliced Thiele machine, every hori-
               zontal word projects to the corresponding word of the maps hi on B, and preserves
               r. Two states with the same view and different records therefore keep the same view
               and different records after any common horizontal word. No function of the view
               alone can recover r on both states. A vertical move that changes r supplies such a
               pair: s and Fv (s).

               Proof. Start with two states showing the same picture. Give them the first horizontal
               move. Its rule chooses the next picture from the current picture alone, so the next
               pictures agree too. Neither record changes. You are back in the same situation,
               ready for the second move. Repeating this argument covers every move in the word,
               including a word with no moves. On each side the picture follows the corresponding
               hi , and the original record stays put.
                    A proposed reader of the picture now receives the same input from both states. It
               must give the same answer to that input, so it cannot return two different records
               correctly. Finally, a vertical move that changes the record gives you exactly such
               a pair: before and after, the picture agrees and the record differs. Those must be
               different full states.
                   The stamp remains in the full state through every one of those moves. The camera
               keeps missing it for exactly the same reason it missed it in the first photograph. In
               Part III a failed check can stop the gears. Hiding that stop while asking the picture to
               predict every later free move would also hide the difference between gears that turn
               and gears that cannot. Theorem 15.1 works through that obstruction; the live-state
               slice there keeps this boundary explicit.

The smallest price on the instruction
Put three price cards beside a button: zero, one and two. Somewhere in the machine
there is a state with the lamp down where pressing that button raises it. Cross
out zero. It fails there. One pays the toll; two pays it too. The toll has picked the
smallest card, even though it has not forbidden the larger one.
   Now take a button that never raises the lamp, from any state. Zero works. Go
through the buttons this way. Put one beside each button that can raise the lamp
and zero beside each button that cannot. The price stays on the button when you
use it somewhere else. A button that raises the lamp once still costs one when the
lamp is already up.


Theorem 2.6 (The least instruction price). Fix the transitions and reading, and
supply a finite list covering the states. The schedule just described is the unique
pointwise least nonnegative whole-number schedule satisfying the toll. It is also the
least schedule giving every trace from no to yes, from every start, total cost at least
one.

Proof. For each instruction, inspect the list for a state where it raises the reading. If
one is found, every valid schedule must charge at least one there, and the instruction
has the same price everywhere. If none is found, the toll puts no positive demand
on that instruction, so zero suffices. Our schedule meets every demand and is no
larger than any schedule meeting them. Two least schedules must each be no larger
than the other at every instruction, so their prices agree. The trace claim follows
by finding the first crossing; conversely, a crossing by one instruction is already a
trace.
    The list makes that search finish. With infinitely many states, searching forever
without finding a crossing does not tell me that none exists. For the lift, there is a
direct answer whenever each mark has an event witness: put the lamp down over
a base state where that mark’s event holds, and press it. It raises the lamp. Every
mark therefore needs one, and computing moves need zero because they leave the
lamp alone. That proves the least zero/one schedule even over an infinite base. A
mark whose event never holds can cost zero under the toll. Giving that mark a tally
of one on every use is an additional accounting rule. The unit in all of this is the
unit of the definition; to price a physical device in joules I still need its physics.
    The universal floor is about every Thiele machine, a system with the toll among
its conditions, and about no system without it. One edge matters: the theorem does
not assume that a YES state exists. If no state ever reads YES, no run meets the
theorem’s hypothesis, so it’s true of every run and tells you nothing about any of
them, which is a mathematician’s way of saying it’s true and useless. The toy on
56   2 A record and a toll


               your paper has a YES box, so it isn’t useless there. It would be natural to assume the
               system has to have at least one NO state and one YES state; the statement has no
               such clause, and that’s on purpose, because a theorem that applies to no run is still
               a theorem and the toy is where you supply the runs.
                   The theorem also runs backwards, and that direction is one line. Suppose every
               run from a state reading no to a state reading yes costs at least one, whichever state
               you start from. A single move is a run of length one, so a move that takes no to yes
               costs at least one, which is the toll. The floor from every start and the toll are the
               same rule, and nobody has to choose between them. From one fixed start that reads
               no, the floor asks for the toll only at the crossings you can reach without paying
               anything; a crossing you can only reach by paying has already cost at least one by
               the time you get there.
                   And the bound of one is the smallest case of a count.
               Observation 2.7 (One unit per crossing). In any Thiele machine, a run costs at least
               the number of its steps that take the reading from no to yes, with no permanence
               assumed. Conversely, a system in which every run costs at least its number of such steps
               obeys the toll. And the bound is reached for every count: on the one-bit machine with a
               set that costs one and a reset that costs nothing, setting and resetting n times from no
               crosses n times and costs exactly n.
               Proof. Each crossing step costs at least one by the toll, every other step costs at least
               zero, and each step is counted once, so the total is at least the number of crossings.
               Conversely, a single move that crosses is a run with one crossing, so it costs at least
               one, which is the toll. On the one-bit machine, each set from no is a crossing costing
               one and each reset costs nothing, so n rounds cost n and cross n times.
                  And one more edge, because it’s the first thing to bite when you ask a machine
               to stand behind more than one thing. The two-place record has one question in it:
               one flag, and one crossing the toll charges. Once the flag is up, a second claim has
               nowhere to go, because raising a flag that’s already up doesn’t move anything. So
               a second claim needs a reading of its own, and a third claim a third: one reading
               per claim, each with its own crossing. Part II builds that properly, as a family
               of flags, one per threshold, with a step that raises any of them charged at least
               one (Theorem 11.10). A step that raises three at once still owes at least one, and
               nothing in the toll makes the charges add up flag by flag. Charges that add need
               the composition assumptions for independent machines (Appendix D). The same
               theorem has a count in it that is what finiteness takes. Picture the record as a row of
               switches that only ever get turned on. Ten switches can change at most ten times in
               one run, one switch per change, and then the row is full. (Across different runs the
               row can end in any of its thousand and twenty-four settings; along any one run it
               climbs through at most eleven.) A finite machine can keep only so many things up
                                                               2.3 How the receipt earns its meaning   57


for good in its whole life. That’s “you can’t keep all of it,” which Section 14 says of a
full trace, turned into a count.


2.3 How the receipt earns its meaning
Give the worker a whiteboard and a pen. Ask for an answer and a line underneath
saying “CHECKED = YES.” The worker can write both. So can somebody who copied
the answer and did no check at all. The extra line has told you nothing about which
happened.
    Follow that problem into the machine. If an unchecked run can reach the same
accepting state as a checked run, there is nothing in that state that tells the two
apart. To make the receipt carry the difference, the machine has to close the
unchecked route. The worker can request the check; the worker cannot simply write
its successful result into the accepting record. That restriction is what gives the
record its force.
    Put a variable called checked beside the answer and you have another place to
write. The name does not give it authority. A program that can write yes there
without doing the check can manufacture the same display as the program that
earned it.
    For an earned receipt, I want the machine’s rules to close that route. Every per-
mitted program must go through the required check before it can reach acceptance.
The program can ask for the check. It cannot give itself the successful verdict. That
is the difference between carrying words about a check and enforcing what those
words stand for.
    So when somebody offers a simulation, showing me where its bits go is the
beginning. Show me which instructions the simulated program can actually use,
and prove that none of their allowed sequences can forge acceptance. Preserving
that boundary is part of implementing this machine. A copy of the flag alone has
not done it.
    Now put the camera back over the tabletop. The same answer can sit above
an accepting record or an unearned one. The record has to survive, and the rules
governing access to it have to survive too. Those are the things I am asking the
machine to keep.

Look before the concrete covers it
The inspector arrives after the concrete is poured. The question is about the rebar
underneath. On one job it was sound. On the other it wasn’t. Give both jobs exactly
the same finished appearance, and give the inspector only that appearance.
   There is no amount of staring that tells those jobs apart. Searching for a sound
arrangement that could have produced this surface doesn’t do it either. A sound
58   2 A record and a toll


               arrangement was possible on the bad job too. What matters is which arrangement
               was there.
                  Write x for what was there, f ( x ) for what remains to be inspected, and P( x ) for
               the yes-or-no question about it. A good x+ and a bad x− leave the same f ( x ). The
               inspector receives one identical input and is supposed to give two different answers.
               Here is the whole obstruction.


               Theorem 2.8 (An erased distinction cannot answer its old question). Let f : X → Y
               and P : X → {no, yes}. If f ( x+ ) = f ( x− ) but P( x+ ) = yes and P( x− ) = no, there
               is no d : Y → {no, yes} with d( f ( x )) = P( x ) for every x. If P is available before the
               loss, the enriched observation ( f ( x ), P( x )) does answer the question exactly and
               distinguishes these two cases above their common view.

               Proof. The proposed d would return both yes and no at f ( x+ ) = f ( x− ). The
               enriched observation returns its second coordinate. Its two values are ( f ( x+ ), yes)
               and ( f ( x− ), no): the first coordinates agree and the second coordinates differ, so
               the enriched states remain distinct.
                   While the rebar is exposed, you can inspect it and keep the answer. Or preserve
               enough evidence to inspect later. Either way, something that distinguishes the good
               case from the bad one has to survive. Wiping an unrelated detail causes no trouble.
               Wiping the last difference your question depends on leaves the next inspector with
               the same surface and two possible pasts.
                   For one known question repeated along a run, the receipt can be very small. Start
               a bit at yes and, at each check, replace it by the old answer AND the new answer.
               It says exactly whether all checks so far passed. A later failure turns it down. The
               permanent flag that says “some certification occurred” stays up. Put those gauges
               beside each other and you can see why they answer different questions.

               When the stamp merges two states
               Draw two boxes with the same tiles: Unstamped and Stamped. Pressing the stamp
               takes the first to Stamped. Pressing it on the second leaves that whole box exactly
               where it is. Draw both arrows. They land in the same place.
                  Call the press V. At a state s where it raises the record, s and V (s) are different. If
               another press leaves the full state fixed, then V (V (s)) = V (s). Those two different
               states have the same successor.
                  Give the stamped box a hidden wheel that turns on every press. Now the picture
               has more states in it. If every state reached after stamping still reads yes, and there
               are only finitely many such states, a merge is forced somewhere along the continued
               pressing. It can be later than the first press. Keep the entire move injective instead,
                                                               2.3 How the receipt earns its meaning   59


and the run has to keep finding distinct stamped states. Call that finite accepting
region H and the entering state u. The move sends all of H ∪ {u} into H. There
are | H | + 1 distinct sources and only | H | possible targets, so two sources share
a successor. The move preserves the working picture, so both sources and their
common successor lie in that same fibre.
    An internal ledger belongs in that full-state picture too. If each press increments
it, two presses have different ledger values even when the stamp looks unchanged.
Count those states with the others. The toll tells me what to charge for a raise; the
next chapter gives the premises that connect charges to mergers. I want the arrows
and the bill on the same page, with the rule connecting them where you can see it.
    Notice also that it asks nothing about how strong the system is, in either direction.
A system is Turing-complete when it can imitate a Turing machine, and no stronger
than one when a Turing machine can imitate it. The theorem asks neither question.
Whether the system is stronger than a Turing machine, weaker, or exactly as strong
makes no difference to the floor. Bring the five parts, charge the toll on the crossing,
and you’re in scope. The floor doesn’t check what you can compute, because it was
never about what you can compute; it’s about what a move is allowed to do without
costing anything.
    That brings up the objection a theorist makes in about four seconds, so I’ll make
it first. The toll is a floor, and a floor is easy to meet. Charge one unit for every
move, whatever it does, and the toll holds for any reading you like, since every
crossing is a move and every move costs one. So any computer with a step counter
beside it, and any yes-or-no question at all about its state, is a Thiele machine, and
a clock passes. Nothing about that is a loophole; it’s what the definition says, and it
means the definition, on its own, doesn’t tie the cost to anything kept or certified. It
only says a crossing can’t go unpriced. (It’s also why “a machine that can compute
anything plus a flag that obeys the toll” says little on its own: a clock meets it, and
so does the flat case, which never raises anything.) Two things later in the book
tie the cost down. The first is a ceiling: demand that a run’s total never exceed the
number of times the flag went up. With a price that can depend on where the step
starts, that and the floor leave exactly one way of charging, one unit per raise and
nothing else (Sections 7 and 8). With a price per move name, as in my definition,
no system whose flag ever rises meets both, because the raising move, played again
