from yes, which every move can be, raises nothing and still costs one. A clock fails
the ceiling the first time it charges a step that raised nothing. The second is order, on
any certified machine, and the example of Part III is one: there, from a clean start,
the flag can’t go up unless a passing check of a claim came first, then a commitment
to that same claim, and a clock can’t fake that, because it’s about which moves
happened, and a clock only charges (Theorem 15.11).
60   2 A record and a toll


                   There is also the matter of why the ledger doesn’t charge for heat. A physical
               ledger would need the actual dynamics, distribution and protocol. A ledger that
               simply charged every nontrivial move would charge by that rule, and that’s the clock
               again: it can’t tell a run that kept something from a run that only ran. So the ledger
               leaves the dissipation of happening to physics and counts one thing, the rise of a
               reading that stays. A zero abstract charge says nothing about physical dissipation; it
               just prices no crossing.
                   The other side of that is that nothing is in scope just for being a computation. A
               Turing machine’s run isn’t an instance of this theorem because it’s a run. It becomes
               one when somebody supplies all five parts for it, says which states read yes, and
               proves the toll for that cost. Until then the theorem says nothing about it, and I
               won’t pretend it does; that limit is the toll’s scope. What keeping takes has no scope
               to supply, because every run of anything with one next state per state takes a fresh
               state at every step, joins exactly one pair of its states into one, or goes round a loop
               through its start and keeps nothing (Theorem 1.1). The reading this isn’t the state
               I started in rises at the first step and stays up exactly on the runs that never come
               back to their start, the first two kinds, and those pay, in states never used before or
               in their one merge.
                   That’s also where the hunch this book started from ended up, once I checked it:
               the night a video about Flatland convinced me there was another axis, a direction
               ordinary computing is blind to (the Afterword, Section 24, tells it). It isn’t a direction
               an ordinary computer can’t reach. Hand a Turing machine a reading, charge the toll
               on its crossing, and it’s in scope like anything else. The possibility was always there.
               What the usual rules leave out is the price.
                   The same goes for a system with no reading at all. If nothing in it answers “is
               the flag up,” then nothing in it can say, from the inside, that anything is entitled to
               be relied on. Whatever entitlement it ends up with gets carried in from outside, by
               somebody who signs their name to it, and nothing in the system priced it. Smuggled
               entitlement isn’t entitlement for the system, no matter whose name is on it. Be
               careful which way that cuts, though. Whoever reads the signature can be perfectly
               entitled on their own account; that’s what an auditor has, and it’s honest as long
               as it’s called the auditor’s. It isn’t the system’s. On the example I build later, the
               reason to believe its checker says yes only when the claim is true is exactly that
               kind: a proof, done outside any record the machine keeps, and I’ll say so when I get
               there (Section 15). What outside entitlement never is, is something the system itself
               earned.
                   There’s also a question I’ll only start on here: bolt two Thiele machines together,
               and do you get one? Run them side by side, each move being a move of one or the
               other, and add up the costs. It depends on the reading you give the pair. Take a
               reading that can only go up when one of the parts’ readings goes up, like “either
                                                              2.3 How the receipt earns its meaning   61


flag is up” or “both are”: then any crossing of the pair is a crossing of a part, that
part’s toll charged it, and the pair obeys the toll. Take “the first flag is up and the
second is down,” and it doesn’t: that reading turns on when the second flag falls,
and nothing charges a fall. The first two readings are proved in Appendix D: read
through “either flag is up” the pair is a Thiele machine whose floor is one. Read
through “both are,” a run that starts with both flags down and ends with both up
costs at least two, and two is reached when each part can raise its own flag for one.
From a start with one flag already up, one raise is enough, so two is a floor for the
clean start only. The third needs nothing beyond the one unpriced fall above. A
related composite keeps the toll too, a host machine running a guest, read through
“the host’s own flag or its copy of the guest’s.” Whether every way of building one
machine out of others keeps the toll is a bigger question, and Appendix D takes it as
far as I could: some ways do, some provably don’t, and it says which.
    So why bother with the toy at all? It isn’t because anybody was looking for it.
People have been making marks that other people rely on for five thousand years,
and what they were after was durability, evidence, authenticity, catching slips; none
of them was trying to put a price on the moment a flag goes up, and I shouldn’t
pretend they were. The reason is narrower. Everywhere somebody did locate a cost,
but one, it sat on a step next to the flag. The flag itself went unpriced as a flag:
Szilard on the measurement, Bennett on the wiping, proof-of-work on the search,
Boyle on the instrument and the room, Foster and Stine on the test. One entry prices
the crossing’s own shape, and I put it beside the toll on purpose: Landauer’s restore
to one, the literal two-state version of the crossing, whose heat bound depends on
the input uncertainty and the thermal premises. The flag’s job never came into it.
The toy is the first thing I could build where the cost sits on the crossing itself, and
it proves that if you price that step, the floor follows everywhere, for any machine
with the five parts. That’s not an answer; it’s the question made exact enough to
be wrong. And of the jobs a record does, the toy supplies only a limited kind of
retention: its three permitted moves never lower the flag. The abstract definition
allows other machines with a reset. Adding that reset would change this toy, and
the cost that doesn’t go away is kept by you, the scorekeeper, beside the board. The
machine keeps none of it. What the toy has is a scorekeeper’s receipt for the crossing.
Whether the machine can be made to keep that receipt itself, where a step could
reach in and change it, is Section 7’s question. Authenticity, evidence, accounting,
cheap checking: none of them is in here, and I’ll say so again when it’s tempting to
forget.
    Let me say what I’ll owe you by the end. Whether the toll is a choice or a
necessity: the next section, and I’ll tell you now that the answer surprised me. What
a unit of cost is worth in anything physical: later, and only partly. What an observer
who sees only a window can and cannot recover, including whether they can even
62   2 A record and a toll


               tell which step paid: its own section. And whether the definition can be met by a
               machine that computes everything a Turing machine does, with its record earned
               and not declared, and what it costs to vouch for structure in one: Part III shows that
               with an example, and takes most of its length on it.
                   For now you have a sheet of paper with two boxes, three moves, one rule that
               writes what the last chapter says keeping takes into the step, and one theorem you
               proved yourself in about a minute. Don’t let go of it. It’s the smallest version of
               everything that follows, and if it’s wrong here, it’s wrong everywhere.
CHAPTER 3




Why the toll isn’t arbitrary

The first chapter of this part proved what keeping takes by counting states: a
run of one rule that raises a flag and keeps it up either lands two of its states on
one somewhere or never uses a state twice, so keeping is paid in a merge or by
taking states never used before; and a thermal implementation can incur additional
dissipation under the specified dynamics. The merge-or-fresh-state part needs no
premise beyond one next state for every state; the heat is physics, which I proved
for Bennett’s walker with Schnakenberg’s formula taken as the model, and cited for
devices whose states jump or drift at random in surroundings at a temperature. This
chapter counts the fresh states exactly, and asks what it takes to turn what keeping
pays into a unit on a ledger. The flag I built is one thing that stays; the result is
about anything that stays.
    The last chapter wrote what keeping takes into a toy as one rule, and in the toy
the move that raises the flag costs one because I said so. If that’s all it is, the ledger
is a long way of describing a preference, and you should treat it the way you’d treat
someone telling you their favourite colour is a law of nature. So this chapter is
me trying to find out whether a machine has to charge it. I’ll tell you the shape
of the answer up front, because I don’t want you reading forty paragraphs to find
out whether there’s a point. What keeping takes needs no “if” beyond a next state
for every state: on any machine, keeping something is paid in a merge or in states
never used before, and physical dissipation is a separate, model-dependent question;
that’s the paragraph above. Getting from what keeping takes to my rule, one unit
on the ledger for the step that raises the flag, takes three “ifs”: there are finitely
many states that read yes, so the fresh states run out; the flag, once raised, stays
up; and the ledger charges every move that forgets. Then the move that raises the
flag has to forget something, two of the states it acts on landing on one, and pays.
Forgetting is also the step Landauer’s principle, my premise, puts a heat price on,
when what’s forgotten wasn’t already known; a known preparation alone supplies
no positive entropy-loss floor. If the input is correlated with another memory, that
larger physical account has to be specified too. Each of the three “ifs” is a way out of
the theorem, and I’m going to walk through each one, because what’s on the other


                                                   63
64   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                side of each is where the content is. None of them is a way out of what keeping
                takes. Where the first fails, the machine pays by taking states it has never used.
                Where the second fails, the flag comes back down, so nothing is kept and there’s
                nothing to charge. Where the third fails, the step still forgets, and only the ledger
                looks away.
                    One more thing before the three ways out, and it comes first on purpose. Nothing
                in the argument uses the word certify. It uses a reading that can go from no to yes
                and never back. A fuse that has blown is one. So is a seal that has been broken, a
                bit in write-once memory, a block a chain has finalized, a measurement somebody
                wrote down and won’t take back. The argument below sends what keeping takes to
                whichever of them you point at, and the latch chapter (Section 11) proves it doesn’t
                matter which one you pick. Certification is the instance I build, for reasons I give
                in Section 18 and don’t claim to have proved. So read this section as being about
                anything that stays. The flag is only the one I keep on the table.


                3.1 A closed room with no spare chair

                Do this one with real objects, because the whole section rests on it and it’s about
                ninety seconds of work. Draw a box on the table and call it the yes room. Put three
                chairs inside the box and one chair outside, by the door. Four people, one per chair;
                the people are the states your machine could be in, and the three inside are the ones
                whose flag is already up. One move of the machine moves everybody at once: each
                person stands up and goes to the chair the rule sends them to. There are two rules.
                First, nobody inside the room may end up outside, because the flag, once up, stays
                up. Second, the person by the door must end up inside, because this move is the
                one that raises their flag.
                   Now try to finish the move with one person in each chair.
                   You can’t. Three people start inside and have to stay inside, so they take the three
                inside chairs between them, with nobody left out, because nobody may leave. The
                person from the door has to come in, there is no fourth chair inside, so somebody
                has to share a chair, and two of the machine’s possible states have landed on one
                state. Now use the chairs as a guessing game: secretly choose one starting chair,
                apply the rule, and report only the finishing chair. If two starts are sent there, the
                report cannot tell your partner which start you chose. Watching the people move
                would tell them, but that would be keeping information outside the finishing chair,
                and the chair alone has forgotten something.
                   The whole argument is in that shared chair, and I want to name the piece of
                mathematics that did the work, because it’s old and it’s not mine. If you put things
                into fewer boxes than there are things, some box gets two. People call it the
                pigeonhole principle; it’s the one from “The point,” where Jean Leurechon used
                                                                 3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   65


it in 1622 to argue that two people somewhere have the same number of hairs,
and the first name for it I could find came from Dirichlet, who used it in 1842
and later called it the drawer principle. It’s the kind of fact a child accepts and a
mathematician spends a career finding new uses for. Here the use is that a step
which forgets nothing is a one-to-one shuffle, a one-to-one shuffle of a finite set of
chairs lands on every chair, so the inside chairs are all taken by insiders and none
is left for the newcomer. Finiteness, permanence and the flip are the three things
that force a collision in the instruction’s map. The two starts that collide need not
include the outsider: send the outsider to one inside chair and send two insiders
to another. A run from a known outside chair can still have a uniquely identifiable
start. The collision is a fact about the instruction over possible states.
    The precise statement of the argument is a theorem a few lines down, and it
needs one word first. “Injective” is the mathematician’s word for “forgets nothing”:
a step is injective when two different starts always give two different ends. The
theorem says exactly what the people and the chairs said and takes exactly the three
premises: a duplicate-free list that names every state (finite), a reading that no step
ever turns off (permanent), and one state that reads NO before the step and YES
after it (the flip). There is no price in it anywhere; it is pure counting. I’ll come back
to what counts as physics, but notice that nothing so far has been physics.
    The exact words follow. For this whole section the setting is the five parts from
Section 2 without the toll: states S, move names I, a step, a reading, and (later) a
cost.

Definition 3.1 (Finite, permanent, injective). The machine is finite when there is
a list of states with no repeats that contains every state. The reading is permanent
when no move ever turns it from yes back to no: for all s and i, cert(s) = yes implies
cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A move i is injective (forgets nothing) when different starts
give different ends: step( a, i ) = step(b, i ) implies a = b. A move that is not injective
merges.



Theorem 3.1 (A permanent flip merges). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading, if cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then the move i merges.

Proof. Suppose i were injective. Let C be the list of states that read yes: go down
the list of every state and keep the ones that read yes. It has no repeats. (That is the
only use of finiteness: all the proof needs is a duplicate-free list of the yes-states.)
By permanence, used only for the move i, step(·, i ) sends every member of C into C.
Being injective, it sends the members of C to members of C with no two landing on
the same one, so its images are as many as C itself, and a list of that many distinct
66   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                members of C is all of C. So the yes-state step(s, i ) equals step(c, i ) for some c in C,
                and injectivity gives s = c, so s reads yes. It reads no, and that is the contradiction,
                the same one the four people and the three inside chairs ran into.
                   A list with no repeats, as long as the set it draws from, contains the whole set.
               Leave one member of the set out and you have packed the list into one place fewer
               than it has members. That can’t be done: take away one occupied place and the
               member sitting in it, and the list is still one too long for the places left, and it stays
               one too long until there are no places left at all. This is the pigeonhole in the form
               Leurechon would recognise.
                   None of that is new. It has been sitting in two places for a long time, one in
               physics and one in the theory of automata, and a physicist will recognise it on sight,
               so I’ll start there. In 1876 Josef Loschmidt pointed out, against Ludwig Boltzmann’s
               account of how a gas settles down, that the laws of mechanics run just as well
               backwards: reverse every molecule’s velocity and the gas retraces its steps, so
               mechanics alone can’t make entropy only ever climb. Twenty years on, in 1896, a
               young assistant of Max Planck’s in Berlin pushed harder. He took Henri Poincaré’s
               recurrence theorem of 1890, which says that in a system preserving a finite measure
               of its accessible states, almost every starting state returns arbitrarily close to itself,
               again and again, and used it to argue that nothing in such a system can climb
               forever: give it time and it comes back down. The assistant was Ernst Zermelo,
               the same Zermelo who’d put set theory on axioms twelve years later, axioms that
               keep out the paradox that had sunk Frege’s foundations of arithmetic (Section 6
               tells that one). Boltzmann answered the same year, not very politely, that the times
               you’d have to wait for a return are so enormous that nobody would ever see one.
               (Jos Uffink, who wrote the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on Boltzmann’s statistical
               physics, calls that reply drenched in sarcasm and bitterness, and calls Zermelo’s own
               paper a careful logical argument.)
                   Now look back at the table. A step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, is a
               reshuffle: it moves everybody around in loops, and every loop comes back to where
               it started. A flag that goes up and stays up is exactly a quantity that climbs and
               never comes back down. So a reshuffle can’t carry one, which is Zermelo’s objection
               with the infinities taken out. On a finite set the loops are enough, and Poincaré’s
               theorem isn’t needed. And the wait is at most as many steps as there are states,
               nothing enormous. Zermelo was aiming it at the second law, and flags never came
               into it. A quantum recurrence result came in 1957, when P. Bocchieri and A. Loinger
               proved returns arbitrarily close to the initial state under their conditions on a closed
               quantum system. That is a neighbouring recurrence argument, not this finite-state
               proof: even a finite-dimensional quantum system has continuously many states.
                                                              3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   67


Applying it to a physical record requires saying how that record is read and how
robustly it distinguishes nearby states.
    The second place stings more, because it’s in computer science, and somebody
got here first, again. Picture a finite machine that reads letters, one move per
letter. If every letter just reshuffles the states one for one, automata theorists call
it a permutation automaton, and the sets of inputs such machines can pick out
are called group languages. Jean-Éric Pin’s 1992 paper on reversible automata,
machines whose letters act as one-to-one maps, sorts out exactly which languages
those machines recognise, and in that world this counting argument is folklore.
The short version runs like this. Start at a state that reads no, and collect every
input that ends at a yes. Because yes is permanent, adding letters to the end of a
collected input keeps it collected. A group language with that property is either
empty or everything, and everything would include the empty input, which ends
where it started, at no. So it’s empty, no run of reshuffles raises the reading, and
that’s Theorem 3.1 with the moves as letters. Pin’s paper is where I’d send you to
check the automata side. It isn’t about flags or prices, and I’m not claiming it says
anything about them.
    There is a broader way to look at the same obstruction. Suppose every allowed
move can be undone by another allowed sequence of moves. Start outside YES and
try to enter it. Once inside, permanence says every allowed sequence keeps you
there. But the undoing sequence must take you back outside. Those two demands
cannot both hold.
    On a finite set, a move that keeps all states apart is a reshuffle. Repeat that
reshuffle enough times and every state comes home; all but the last repetition
therefore undo one application. So the undoing sequence needed in that argument
is available. Morgan Rogers studies systems of composable moves in his 2019 and
2021 papers on toposes of monoid actions. That more general language gives this
fact another home. Here the chairs and the undoing sequence already show why it
holds.
    Going quantum doesn’t get around the automata version either. Alex Brodsky and
Nicholas Pippenger (2002) showed that a quantum finite automaton that measures
only once, at the very end, accepts with bounded error exactly the group languages,
the reshuffle kind. One that’s allowed to measure after every letter, and to stop on
what it sees, does better: it accepts every piecewise testable language, and “has
seen a b somewhere” is one of those. A measurement that can stop the machine is a
record that stays, and it’s the extra thing that lets the bigger class in.
    The third place is the closest, and it isn’t old at all. In 2023 Thomas Ouldridge
and David Wolpert derived the thermodynamics of a finite automaton built the way
real computers are: the same physical step run again and again, each time touching
only the part of the machine that changes. They sorted languages into two kinds by
68   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                the smallest automaton that recognises each one. If that automaton has a letter that
                sends two states to one, every automaton for the language has such a letter too, and
                on their derivation recognising the language on a device like that produces entropy,
                waste no cleverer design gets back, unless the inputs are so finely arranged that
                only one of the merged states ever actually turns up. If the smallest automaton only
                reshuffles, they find the language can be recognised with no unavoidable entropy
                production at all. One of their worked examples is the strings with no b in them,
                which is my flag turned inside out: the runs that raise it are exactly the strings that
                have seen a b. So the counting argument, a real price on it, and the case when you
                already know which state you’re in are all in their paper, three years before this
                book. Their price is derived from the physics of the device, and mine is assumed.
                    There’s a fourth neighbour, and I’d call it a cousin, because it speaks another
                language. Constructor theory is David Deutsch and Chiara Marletto’s programme for
                stating physics as which transformations a device that runs in a cycle can and can’t
                bring about, and in it a task is irreversible when it’s possible and its inverse isn’t.
                Marletto’s version of thermodynamics (posted in 2016) leans on exactly that: tasks
                that are possible while their transposes aren’t. Marletto, the physicist Vlatko Vedral
                and coauthors (2022) made an irreversible task out of the quantum homogeniser, a
                machine of reservoir qubits that interact by partial swaps, and ran it with photons.
                Maria Violaris and Marletto (2022) then argued that the same machine, run in a
                cycle, can turn a pure qubit into a mixed one and can never turn a mixed qubit
                back into a pure one, even though every interaction in it is reversible, and that
                this suggests erasure may cost something beyond Landauer’s bound. The counting
                argument is a classical, finite, exact cousin of that sentence: a set of states a step can’t
                leave, a task that’s possible, and no way back. Theirs is quantum and approximate
                and aimed at physics’ price; mine is counted, and assumes its price. Deutsch and
                Marletto’s paper on information (2015) has a neighbour of the counting argument in
                its section 8.6: measuring one observable disturbs another irreducibly, and nothing
                can undo the disturbance afterwards while the outcome stays in an information
                variable. It’s a second, theory-independent way of saying that a record that stays
                makes the step irreversible.
                    So what I can claim here is narrower again, and I’d rather say exactly how. Even
                the pricing form is, in physics and on their derivation, Ouldridge and Wolpert’s:
                a merge the language can’t avoid costs entropy. A price assumed rather than
                derived isn’t mine either: Li and Vitányi (1996) took a unit charge for every bit
                irreversibly erased, with steps that can be undone priced at zero, as axioms of a
                model of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016) put a price on named
                instructions that destroy bits, a unit for an AND or an overwrite. What I didn’t
                find anywhere I looked is what a price on merging moves forces on a reading that
                stays, charged on a ledger whether or not anybody’s physics is right (put a price on
                                                               3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   69


merging and the flip has to pay it, which is the next subsection), and what I get out
of that: the toll, as a theorem about the ledger, the merge-or-revoke split for a single
move, the exact match between “forced to be priced” and “merges”, the squeeze
bound counted in whole units and its entropy form, a built machine walking out
through each of the three ways out, and every proof on the page. Those are the
forms I didn’t find stated anywhere I looked, and I’d sort them the same way: the
counting core classical and somebody else’s, the pricing form only partly mine. The
core move is older than the computer, it had two homes before it got to mine, and
its physical price had a third.

Count the alternatives before putting a price on them
Write N different starting configurations on cards and spread them across the bench.
Run each through the same rule once. When several cards give the same full
configuration, put them in one pile. Run the rule again and gather the new piles.
Once cards agree on the full state, the same rule gives them the same next state too.
   Count the different configurations after each tick. Call their set Qt and their
number qt , with q0 = N and Qt+1 = F ( Qt ). The difference qt − qt+1 tells you how
many alternatives disappeared on that tick. Four distinct configurations landing at
one state lose three alternatives in one landing pile. Keep those two counts beside
each other: three alternatives lost, one landing place.


Theorem 3.2 (The alternatives balance exactly). For a total deterministic rule F
and N distinct starts,
                              T −1
                              ∑ (qt − qt+1 ) + qT = N.
                              t =0

If all endpoints fit in K < N full states, a transition at some t < T identifies two
different members of Qt . If all endpoints are one full state, the total loss is N − 1.

Proof. An image has no more elements than its source, so every difference is non-
negative. Add the differences: each intermediate qt cancels, leaving q0 − q T . If
q T < N, at least one difference is positive; at that step a map from more states to
fewer cannot be one-to-one. In particular, one final full state leaves a loss of N − 1
alternatives.
    Turn the cards over before counting them together. Two runs might show the
same answer on the front and still carry different inputs on the back. Those are
different full configurations. The count follows everything the machine kept.
    Now put a price rule beside the piles. Let pt be the price at tick t, and require
every landing pile to have at most 2 pt distinct sources. The number arriving is
70   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                then at most 2 pt times the number of places they land: qt ≤ 2 pt qt+1 . Multiply that
                inequality through the run and you get
                                                   N ≤ 2∑ t < T p t q T .

                The rule connects the bill to how tightly the machine can pack the alternatives.


                3.2 Now charge for forgetting, and the toll falls out
                This is the step I’d been circling since the counting on states. In the last chapter I
                told you Bennett’s rule as he states it: what has to cost is erasing a bit or merging
                two paths a computation could have taken. I didn’t ask you to believe it. I’m not
                going to ask you now either. I’m going to write it down as a rule you can accept or
                refuse, in the smallest form that does any work: any move that forgets something
                costs at least one. Any move that is not injective has cost at least one. Notice what it
                does not say: nothing about certifying, nothing about flags. It’s a price on forgetting
                and only on forgetting.
                   Put the two together. The first theorem says: on a finite machine with a perma-
                nent flag, the move that raises the flag forgets something. The price says: a move
                that forgets something costs at least one. So the move that raises the flag costs at
                least one. That is the toll, the rule the toy was handed because I said so, and now a
                machine has to charge it. The proof is two lines: the first theorem says the flipping
                move merges, the premise says merges are priced, done. I’ll keep saying “premise,”
                because that’s what it is, and because a section further on (Section 5) is about what
                happened to some very smart people who put a price where a premise goes and then
                treated it as a law of nature, and about half of this one is me trying not to do that.

                Premise 3.2 (Merge pricing). Every move that merges costs at least one: for all i, if
                i is not injective then cost(i ) ≥ 1.
               Observation 3.3 (The toll from finiteness, permanence, and merge pricing). On
               a finite machine with a permanent reading whose cost satisfies merge pricing, every
               move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. That is, the machine
               with that cost is a Thiele machine in the sense of Definition 2.2, and the universal floor
               (Observation 2.2) applies to it.
                Proof. A move that flips the reading merges, by Theorem 3.1; merge pricing charges
                it at least one.
                   The theorem asks for more than it uses. Only the yes-states need to be finitely
                many: with a permanent reading and finitely many states reading yes, the rest of
                the machine as large as you like, merge pricing still gives the toll. With infinitely
                many it can fail: the first way out below builds a machine that raises a permanent
                                                  3.2 Now charge for forgetting, and the toll falls out   71


flag at zero cost while charging every merge. That machine hasn’t got out of paying.
It pays by taking a state it has never used, and a price list that charges only merges
never looks at the fresh states it takes. And merge pricing asks for more than the
toll needs. Under those same two conditions the toll holds exactly when every move
that flips the reading somewhere and merges is priced. Merge pricing gives that,
and the eight-state machine described later in this section, with its jump repriced at
zero, meets the toll without merge pricing.
    That “more” has an exact size. On a finite machine a move merges exactly when
it turns on some reading that it never turns off. If it merges, take the reading “this
move can land here.” The move never turns it off, because everywhere it lands
reads yes; and some state reads no, because a move that sends two states to one
lands on fewer states than the machine has, and from that state the move turns
the reading on. If it doesn’t merge, it turns on no reading it never turns off: that’s
Theorem 3.1, whose proof asks permanence only of the one move. So on a finite
machine a price list meets merge pricing exactly when it meets the toll for every
reading at once, each move answering only for the readings it never turns off. The
charge on forgetting isn’t a second kind of price beside the toll. What the premise
chooses is which readings the toll answers to: the flag alone, or every reading a
move keeps.
    There is one more way to see the same thing, and I give it because it answers a
rival I’d otherwise owe you. The rival says: leave certification alone. Price erasure,
and keep an honest flag that reports when something was erased. Fine; but a system
can set its certificate at cost zero with its erasure flag reporting nothing, exactly
because the certifying move merged two states and the flag didn’t say so. Make
the erasure flag honest, so that it reports every move that forgets, and on a finite
machine with a flag that stays up the erasure law charges the same cost the toll
does. The toll isn’t a rival to honest erasure accounting; it’s what honest erasure
accounting says about the certifying move.
    So, is the toll arbitrary? The honest answer is that the toll is a consequence of
three things: finitely many states that read yes (a finite memory is plenty), a flag
that stays up, and a charge on forgetting. If you accept all three, you don’t get to
refuse the toll; it’s forced. If you refuse any one of them, the toll on my ledger goes
back to being my preference. The cost stays where it was; what’s gone is the proof
that my ledger has to charge it. So the question “did I have to pick it” has turned
into three smaller questions, which is what progress usually looks like: a better set
of things to argue about. Let me take the three ways out in order, and for each
one build the machine that leaves through it, because a premise you can’t see the
counterexample to is a premise you’re taking on faith.
72   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                3.3 The first way out: keep everything, and pay by taking fresh states
               Take a strip of paper that never runs out of boxes. The machine’s whole state is the
               strip. Each move writes a 1 in the next empty box, and the flag is up as soon as any
               box has a 1 in it. Check the three premises. It is permanent: once there’s a 1, there’s
               always a 1. It flips: the empty strip reads NO, and after one move it reads YES. It
               forgets nothing: every move can be undone by erasing the last 1, so two different
               strips never become the same strip. So this is a machine that raises a flag, keeps
               it up, and never merges anything. The theorem that a permanent flip on a finite
               machine merges has no grip on it, and a price list that charges only merges doesn’t
               charge it. But look at what each move does: it writes in a box nobody has written in
               before. The raise takes a fresh box, and so does every step after it, forever. It hasn’t
               got out of paying. It’s paying in the other column, by taking a state it has never used,
               and a price list that only charges merges isn’t looking at that column. (Each physical
               write may incur a model-dependent finite-time cost; what the strip dodges is the
               floor a merge would add on top.) In the exact form its state is a row of 1s of any
               length, which is how you say the strip has no end.
                   If the endless strip feels like a cheat, it’s a famous one. David Hilbert, in a lecture
               course in the winter of 1924–25, told a story about a hotel with infinitely many
               rooms, every one of them taken, where a new guest still gets a room: everybody
               moves from room n to room n + 1, and room 1 is left empty. The hotel is that
               other column, the fresh states, told as a joke about a front desk: nobody shares,
               and every guest in the building packs up and moves one room along, into a room
               that’s occupied as he moves, by a guest who’s moving on at the same moment, so
               that one room at the front is left empty. The guests go one-to-one into a part of the
               hotel, with a gap left over. The part worth checking is that Hilbert never published
               it. The hotel became famous because George Gamow put it in a popular book in
               1947, and for a long time it wasn’t clear Hilbert had told it at all. The historian
               of science Helge Kragh first guessed that Gamow had made it up. Then Tilman
               Sauer, a historian of science who had co-edited a volume of Hilbert’s lectures on the
               foundations of physics, pointed him to Hilbert’s lecture notes, which had just been
               printed in 2013, and in 2014 Kragh took his guess back in a paper called “The True
               (?) Story of Hilbert’s Infinite Hotel.” Keep the question mark. Even Kragh’s own
               paper puts the lecture in January 1924 in one place and January 1925 in another.
               Still, this time a story everybody repeated turned out to have a real lecture behind it.
               I’ve learned not to count on that happening. Bring it back to the table. In the closed
               room, the person from the door had nowhere to sit because the chairs ran out. In
               Hilbert’s hotel they never do, so everybody shifts one over and nobody has to share.
               The strip machine is that hotel. The argument stays the same. What the hotel shows
               you is that the whole argument was about running out of states all along.
                                    3.3 The first way out: keep everything, and pay by taking fresh states   73


    What walked out is the finiteness premise. Now cut the strip to eight boxes. Keep
the same rule: fill the next blank box from the left, leaving every earlier mark alone.
There are nine possible strips, including the blank one. After eight moves the strip is
full. What should the ninth move do? If a full strip stays full, the seven-mark strip
and the full strip both go to the full strip. That is the collision. If the machine stops
instead, its next-step rule is partial. If it clears the strip, its YES reading comes down.
Each escape changes a premise.
              Marks so far    Strip       Next strip under the stay-full rule
                  0           00000000    10000000
                  1           10000000    11000000
                   ..         ..          ..
                    .          .           .
                  7           11111110    11111111
                  8           11111111    11111111
Eight unrestricted bits have 256 configurations. These nine are the ones this
particular prefix-filling rule permits. A fresh configuration need not use a fresh
physical box; changing a pattern can reach one too. Keeping the whole history is
exactly the move Bennett made in 1973, when he showed that any computation can
be done without forgetting if you let it keep a copy of everything it did; Landauer,
back in 1961, had already written that for a machine able to run a program that
doesn’t stop, the space to hold every intermediate result “cannot be there.” Keeping
the history is a real way to pay. It costs a memory that never fills, and every machine
you can buy has a memory that fills.
    Bennett wasn’t the first there, or the last. Yves Lecerf, in a short note to the
French Academy of Sciences in 1963, had already shown that reversible Turing
machines can simulate arbitrary ones, and the note went largely unnoticed. The
computer scientist Tommaso Toffoli (1980), and Edward Fredkin and Toffoli together
(1982), both then at MIT, built reversible logic: gates and circuits that compute
any function and lose nothing, by carrying constant inputs in and extra outputs
out. Their basic gate wasn’t new even then. Landauer’s own 1961 paper writes
down a three-bit device that replaces r by p · q when r is 0 and by the negation of
p · q when r is 1, calls it logically reversible and capable of an AND, and says each
AND then needs its own supplied ZERO and leaves its extra outputs behind. He
doubted such a machine could be useful. What Toffoli added was the proof that
it computes everything. And the computer scientist Kenichi Morita (1996) proved
that reversible two-counter machines are universal, so even a machine as small as
the one Section 15 builds, handed its input encoded, can compute everything with
every move one-to-one. Every one of them keeps what it doesn’t forget somewhere:
a history, garbage outputs, a counter that codes the past. The strip is one of those: it
keeps the whole history, box by box.
74   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                    There are three separate claims here, and I need to keep them apart. The strip
                machine is permanent and forgets nothing. It also has infinitely many states: no
                finite list holds every finite strip. Neither of those involves a cost. The third does: the
                strip can raise its reading at zero cost. Count the strip’s length as a whole number
                and let each move add one at a price of zero. Nothing merges, merge pricing holds,
                and the toll fails. This is what a price list that charges merges and nothing else looks
                like on a machine with endlessly many states to take: the raised reading shows up at
                no charge on the ledger because the column it’s paid in is one the price list doesn’t
                charge.
                    The same thing holds for one move instead of a run, and in that form it says
                exactly how many states the move needs.


                Proposition 3.4 (A raise with no merge takes endlessly many states). Let a move
                never turn a reading from yes to no, let it raise the reading at some state s (no at
                s, yes where the move sends s), and let it send no two different states to the same
                state. Then it sends the states that read yes one-to-one into a part of themselves that
                leaves at least one of them out: the state the move sends s to. So there are infinitely
                many states that read yes. With finitely many, the raising move merges two states.

                Proof. The move sends every yes-state to a yes-state, because it never turns yes
                to no, and it sends different states to different states. It sends s to a yes-state. If
                some yes-state c were also sent there, the move would send s and c to one state,
                so s = c; but s reads no and c reads yes. So the yes-states are sent one-to-one into
                the yes-states with that one left out. If there were only n yes-states, that would put
                n things one-to-one into n − 1 places, which the pigeonhole forbids. So there are
                infinitely many.
                    The proposition is Hilbert’s front desk as a theorem, and it’s also exactly how
                Richard Dedekind defined an infinite collection in 1888: one that can be matched
                one-to-one with a part of itself that leaves something out. So with no merge, every
                raise has to send the kept things one-to-one into a part of themselves with a gap
                left over, and only endlessly many of them have a gap to spare. Taking a fresh state
                isn’t the absence of what keeping takes but the other way of paying it, and only a
                machine with endlessly many states can keep paying that way.
                    Which state is being counted. Whether a move merges depends on what the state
                keeps. The strip keeps its history, so nothing merges; cut it to eight boxes and the
                stay-full rule merges. Section 19 proves the general form (Theorem 19.2): keep the
                list of every earlier state alongside the current one and every fixed-instruction step
                is one-to-one. (Keeping only the one state before isn’t enough: two states that differ
                only in what came before them still land together.) So a merge price is a fact about
                                    3.3 The first way out: keep everything, and pay by taking fresh states   75


a move on a stated state space. Each price derived in this book is derived on the
whole state its definition gives, and three things go with it: which state that is, what
lies outside it (nothing outside it is charged), and whether the move is one primitive
instruction or a composite run of several. Relabelling the states one-to-one changes
no price, since it sends merges to merges and one-to-one moves to one-to-one moves.
Adding history to the state, or projecting part of the state away, changes the machine
being modelled, and the price can change with it.
    The first way out deserves a number, because “a memory that never fills” is doing
all the work and I’d rather see what keeping takes than take it on trust.



Proposition 3.5 (Merge, or a fresh state every step). (1) Let a machine run by
one rule, so that every state has exactly one next state, and let its reading never go
from yes back to no. Take any run in which the reading goes from no to yes. Then
either some step of the run merges two of its states (two different states of the run
have the same next state), or the run never visits the same state twice. So on a
machine with M states, a run that keeps a record and never merges has fewer than
M steps. (2) Let an operation send every value to one fixed value and leave that
value alone. Take a machine with M states run by one rule, a reading of its states,
and N different starting states, exactly one of which already reads the fixed value,
such that from every start each of the next T states reads the fixed value. If no two
different states among those the runs sit in at steps 0 to T − 1 have the same next
state (the operation is carried out through T repetitions without merging), then
M ≥ 1 + ( T + 1)( N − 1). When N ≥ 2, a bounded memory delays the merge and
does not avoid it; with only the resting start there need be no merge.

Proof. (1) Suppose no two different states of the run share a next state, and suppose
the run still visits some state twice, once early and once later. Walk the two visits
back together, one step at a time: two equal states whose predecessors are both in
the run had equal predecessors, because nothing merged. The early visit gets back to
the start first, and the later visit is then at the start too. So the run comes back to its
start after some number p of steps, and since one rule gives the next state, it comes
back again after 2p, 3p, and so on forever. The start reads no: a yes there would
stay yes all along, and the reading does go from no to yes. Some of those returns
come after the raise, where the reading is yes and stays yes, and each of them is the
start, which reads no. So the repeat was impossible. A run that never merges takes
a state it hasn’t used at every step, and with M states that’s at most M − 1 steps. (2)
Count the states along paths. Walking two equal states back together, as in (1), is
allowed at any step from 1 to T, because the states one step earlier are at steps 0 to
T − 1. Each of the N − 1 starts not already in the fixed reading, followed through
76   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                T repetitions, occupies T + 1 states, and none twice: a repeat would walk back to
                the start equalling a later state of its own path, and every later state reads the fixed
                value while the start does not. Two of those paths cannot share a state either: walk
                back to the earlier time, and either two different starts are one state, or a start is a
                state that reads the fixed value. That is ( T + 1)( N − 1) states. The start that already
                reads the fixed value, followed through T repetitions, ends in one more: if that state
                were on one of the paths, walking back would again put a start at a state that reads
                the fixed value. One more is all that start is owed, not T + 1: every state on its own
                path reads the fixed value, so walking back along it finds no contradiction, and the
                path may fold onto one state, as it does in the machine built below.
                    The number is exact, not only a floor, and you can build the machine that reaches
                it. One state for the start that already reads the fixed way; the operation leaves it
                there. For every other start, lay out a row of states, one state longer than the number
                of repetitions you want to survive. The first state in the row reads the way that
                start reads, the rest read the fixed way, and the operation walks the row, sending its
                last state to the common fixed state. This also works for zero requested repetitions,
                when a row contains only its start. Count the states: one, plus a row for each of
                the other starts. For as many repetitions as you asked for, no two distinct visited
                source states land on one. If there is at least one other start, the next repetition
                merges its row’s last state with the fixed state: both go to the fixed state. With no
                other start, the one fixed state idles forever and no finite retention horizon follows.
                A single fixed reading isn’t needed either. If the operation sends every state to one
                of a few resting states and leaves each resting state alone, and every resting state is
                one of the starts, the same walking back counts the same rows inside each resting
                state’s own catchment, the starts that end at it. The total comes to one state per
                start, plus, for every repetition, one more state for each start that isn’t a resting state.
                With one resting state that is the bound in the proposition, and the same rows in
                each catchment show it exact. In the exact form: N starts, L of them resting states,
                T repetitions, at least N + T ( N − L) states, and that many are enough. In bits: a
                memory of B bits has at most 2B states, so surviving T repetitions with one resting
                                                             
                state takes B ≥ log2 1 + ( T + 1)( N − 1) . The memory grows with the logarithm
                of how long the history is kept; a fresh state at every step isn’t a fresh cell at every
                step.
                    So the strip uses fresh configurations for as long as its record stays up without a
                collision. Cut its permitted state space to a finite size and the counting bound applies.
                A configuration is a pattern, not a newly allocated cell. Bennett’s 1989 construction
                saves storage by undoing and redoing intermediate work while retaining enough to
                recover it. Those extra transitions buy a time–space tradeoff. They do not let a fixed
                autonomous run under this fresh-state premise reuse a configuration.
                                     3.3 The first way out: keep everything, and pay by taking fresh states   77


    Bennett’s Brownian model supplies a separate tradeoff: reducing its bias reduces
its mean forward speed and its heat per net forward step. At zero bias its mean
drift is zero, although individual random walks still move. Theorem 1.9 concerns
that model, not every physical step. There are two accounts: configurations in the
structural argument, and entropy production under specified thermal dynamics.
The total autonomous run just counted, after a new permanent raise, must have
a collision somewhere in its continued orbit or take endlessly fresh states. The
collision need not be on the entry arrow. Counting gives that alternative; a physical
implementation determines its resource costs.

Two levers, and whether their hidden moves commute
Put two reset levers on the box. Pull left then right, and look at the tabletop. Now
start over and pull right then left. The picture agrees. Open the box as well: are all
its hidden parts in the same places? That is the extra demand in this example. The
order of the levers must leave the whole machine the same.
    Use three tabletop values, 0, 1, 2. The first lever wipes only 1 to 0. The second
wipes only 2 to 0. They commute on the tabletop. Choose one starting full state
above each value and allow every word of at most T lever pulls. Call everything
reached by depth t Rt . Through the promised horizon, each lever must give different
successors to different states in R T −1 , even if those states were reached at different
times. You know which lever was pulled, so the two levers may reuse a landing
state.


Proposition 3.6 (The exact room for exclusive resets). For T ≥ 1, the minimum
finite installed carrier has T + 3 states without a commutation requirement, and
2T + 2 with commuting hidden levers. These are also the respective minimum sizes
of R T when larger carriers are allowed. With commuting levers that are one-to-one
on their whole domain, the minimum | R T | is 2T + 3, attained for every T by one
infinite machine. At T = 0 the reachable minimum is three in each class.

    Count the zero states first. Write F, G for the hidden levers and z, a, b for the
starts reading 0, 1, 2. At depth t, let Zt contain the states reading zero. The first
lever takes every state in Zt , and also a, into Zt+1 . Their successors must be distinct.
So | Zt | ≥ t + 1. Add a and b and there are at least T + 3 states.
    A single line of zero states reaches that number. Use z0 , . . . , z T , advance the line
with either lever, and fix its last state. Put F ( a) = z0 , G (b) = z0 , G ( a) = a and
F (b) = b. The final zero state stays outside R T −1 . Try the levers in opposite orders
at a, though, and the hidden states disagree. To make them commute, count again.
78   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                Counting when the hidden levers commute. Start above 1 and pull only the lever
                that leaves 1 alone on the tabletop. The hidden box can still move. Watch its first
                T + 1 states, a, G ( a), . . . , G T ( a). Do the matching experiment above 2, watching
                b, F (b), . . . , F T (b). The first list reads 1 throughout; the second reads 2. If either list
                never repeats, its T + 1 states, the at least T + 1 zero states already counted, and
                the other starting state give 2T + 3. There is enough room already.
                    So suppose both lists repeat. A deterministic run first follows an approach and
                then enters a loop. Let the first approach take r pulls and its loop take p pulls; let the
                second take s and q. The loop lengths p, q are at least one. Call their first loop states
                α = Gr ( a) and β = F s (b). There are r + p different states on the first approach and
                loop, and s + q on the second. All have been reached within the promised horizon.
                    At those loop states, switch levers. From α, the first F pull changes the reading
                from 1 to zero. From β, the first G pull changes 2 to zero. There are L = T − r pulls
                left in the first experiment and M = T − s in the second. Write the resulting two
                rows of zero states as
                                 A = { F (α), . . . , F L (α)},       C = { G ( β), . . . , G M ( β)}.

                Neither row repeats. If two entries agreed, walk their predecessors backwards
                together. All those predecessors occur by depth T − 1, where the lever keeps sources
                apart. Eventually the earlier entry would reach the nonzero seed while the later one
                still read zero. That is impossible. The rows therefore contain L and M states.
                    Can the rows cross? Suppose their ith and jth entries are the same state. Pull F
                another q times. Seen from the second row, commutation lets you do those pulls
                at β before its j pulls of G. They take β once around its loop and bring it back.
                So the shared state returns to itself after those q pulls of F. The same argument,
                exchanging the levers, returns it after p pulls of G:

                                         F i + q ( α ) = F i ( α ),   G j + p ( β ) = G j ( β ).
                I have just proved there are no repeats within either displayed row. The returns
                must therefore lie beyond their ends: i + q > L and j + p > M. Only the last q
                entries of the first row and the last p of the second can be shared. There are at most
                min( p, q) shared states.
                   Now add the two nonzero lists and both zero rows, subtracting the shared entries
                once:
                          | R T | ≥ (r + p) + (s + q) + L + M − min( p, q) = 2T + max( p, q).
                The approach lengths disappear because every pull spent on an approach leaves one
                fewer pull for its zero row. If either loop has length at least two, the count is at least
                2T + 2.
                                      3.3 The first way out: keep everything, and pay by taking fresh states   79


    Only two one-state loops remain: p = q = 1. If the zero rows do not meet, adding
them without a subtraction gives 2T + 2. If they meet, the crossing restriction puts
their only shared state at both ends. Call it c. It is fixed by both levers. The initial
zero state z must now supply another place. To see why, suppose it lay on one of
the rows. Starting there would reach c in at most T − 1 pulls. The state just before
c on the first row is also reachable by then, and is different from c. The first lever
sends both to c, violating its promise on R T −1 . Thus z lies outside both rows. Count
it, and the total is 2T + 2 again.
    Finally strengthen the promise: each lever keeps different sources apart every-
where, even beyond the horizon. A crossing would give the return Fi+q (α) = Fi (α)
above. Now you may walk backwards all i steps, without a horizon restriction,
giving F q (α) = α. The left side reads zero and the right side reads 1. So in this case
the rows cannot cross at all. Their count with the nonzero lists is 2T + p + q, which
is at least 2T + 3 unless both loop lengths are one.
    In that last case you need one more state. If z is outside the rows, it is the extra
state. If it lies at Fi (α) on the first row, pull F from z another T times. This is allowed
from an initial state and reaches F T +i (α). The whole zero row can never repeat
under the global promise, by the same backward argument used earlier. This new
state lies past its displayed end. It cannot be on the other row either, because the
crossing argument still applies, however far you go. Its zero reading also keeps it off
the two nonzero lists. If z lies on the second row, pull G instead and make the same
count. Every case gives at least 2T + 3.
     Build the finite box with two arms and a shared endpoint. The F-arm has
a0 , . . . , a T −1 ; the G-arm has b0 , . . . , bT . Each lever advances its own arm and fixes
the opposite arm. Both fix the common end. Read a0 as 1, b0 as 2, and everything
else as zero. Start at those two heads and at z = b1 .
     At horizon one, there are just four places. Write every arrow down:
                        State    Tabletop    Pull F   Pull G    Start?
                          a0        1         end       a0       yes
                          b0        2          b0       b1       yes
                          b1        0          b1      end       yes
                         end        0         end      end        no
On the three starts each column has three different destinations. On the whole
four-state carrier each column has a repeated destination. The horizon promise and
the everywhere promise are different. Try both orders at b0 : either order ends at
b1 . The other three rows also agree in both orders. The endpoint first appears at
depth T. By then every one of the 2T + 2 states has been reached, and until then
each lever keeps its sources apart.
    For one-to-one levers on the whole machine, keep the two arms disjoint and let
them run forever. Give them a separate fixed zero state, and start at that state and
80   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                the two heads. After T pulls the reachable population is exactly 2T + 3. The same
                box works at every horizon.
                   Change the tabletop and the chairs can fit differently. Give it two bits, with one
                lever clearing the first and the other clearing the second. Lay out an infinite grid
                with nonnegative integer coordinates (i, j) and a separate blank state. One lever
                adds one to i, the other to j, and both fix blank. Read a grid point as ([i = 0], [ j = 0])
                and blank as (0, 0). Start at blank and the three grid points (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1).
                                           grid (0, 0)    first lever    grid (1, 0)
                                          reads (1, 1)                  reads (0, 1)


                                        second                                second


                                           grid (0, 1)                   grid (1, 1)
                                          reads (1, 0)    first lever   reads (0, 0)

               Both orders reach the very same grid point, not just the same reading. The separate
               blank state also reads (0, 0) but is fixed by both levers; it is not the grid’s origin.
                   A pull adds one to i + j. The three grid starts have sums zero or one, so no word
               of length at most t can go beyond i + j = t + 1. Conversely, the origin is a start.
               For any other point in that triangle, start at (1, 0) if i > 0, and at (0, 1) otherwise.
               Exactly i + j − 1 ≤ t pulls reach it. That gives the whole triangle. Its rows have
               1, 2, . . . , t + 2 points. Pair the first row with the last and count, then add blank:
                                                           (t + 2)(t + 3)
                                                 | Rt | = 1 +             .
                                                                 2
                Adding to one coordinate is one-to-one on the grid, and neither grid shift reaches
                blank. Adding to different coordinates in either order gives (i + 1, j + 1), so the
                levers commute on the whole carrier. The reading follows the two clears because
                incrementing a coordinate makes its zero-test false and leaves the other zero-test
                alone.
                    This count also meets the lower bound. Each one-cleared fibre starts with one
                state. The appropriate clear sends that fibre and at least one (1, 1) state into it
                injectively, so its population increases by at least one per depth: at depth t it needs
                t + 1. The (0, 0) fibre also starts with one. At depth j + 1, one clear sends both
                its j-depth population and a one-cleared fibre of at least j + 1 states into (0, 0)
                injectively. Its population therefore increases by at least j + 1. Summing from j = 0
                to t − 1 gives 1 + t(t + 1)/2. Add the one (1, 1) state and the two one-cleared
                populations: 1 + 2(t + 1) + 1 + t(t + 1)/2 = 1 + (t + 2)(t + 3)/2. The three-value
                box needed extra room for commutation. This two-bit box fits its best count while
                keeping commutation intact.
                                                  3.4 The second way out: let the flag come back down   81


3.4 The second way out: let the flag come back down
Take one coin. The rule is: turn it over. Heads is YES, tails is NO. Every move is
undoable (turn it over again), so nothing is forgotten. Tails goes to heads, which is a
flip, NO to YES, and heads goes to tails, so the same move takes the flag back down
somewhere else. There are two states, as finite as it gets, and the move that raises
the flag forgets nothing, so a schedule that charges only for forgetting is allowed to
charge it nothing. The move is injective and can switch the reading both on and off.
Pricing the turn at zero meets merge pricing, since no move merges, and fails the
toll. The premise dropped on this way out is permanence.
    There’s a fact here sharper than the premise it replaces, and it was the thing in
this section that surprised me. Drop permanence entirely and keep only finiteness,
and take any move that raises the flag anywhere. Then one of two things is true: the
move forgets something, or the same move lowers the flag somewhere else. There’s
no third option, and the proof below is a search: go through the finitely many YES
states looking for one this move turns to NO. Find one, and that’s the revocation;
find none, and the move is permanent at least for itself, which is all the argument
from fresh states needs. So a flag that goes up without a merge is a flag the same
move can take back. A flag that nothing takes back is paid for. You can’t have a raise
at zero cost that stays raised, not on any finite machine, not with any price schedule
that charges for forgetting. The sentence is narrower than “every certificate costs.”
It’s true, and I’ll take it. The broad one would only be mine.


Theorem 3.7 (Merge or revoke). On a machine with finitely many states reading
yes (no permanence assumed), if cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then either
i merges, or there is a state t with cert(t) = yes and cert(step(t, i )) = no.

Proof. Check every yes-state on the finite list for one that i sends to no. If there is
one, that is the second alternative. If there is none, then i keeps every yes-state at
yes, which is permanence for the single move i; the argument of Theorem 3.1 uses
permanence only for the move it is about, so it applies, and i merges.
    I’ll give you the three-card version too, because it shows that a move can be
forced to be priced without writing anything permanent, and I don’t want you to
think the picture is tidier than it is. There are three cards, T0, T1, T2, with a star on
T1. The rule is that T0 goes to T1, T1 goes to T2, and T2 goes to T1. T0 gains the
star (a flip). T1 loses it (a revocation). T0 and T2 both land on T1 (a merge). So this
move is priced, by the forgetting rule, and yet it writes nothing permanent; it takes a
star away in the same breath. “The priced moves are exactly the permanent records”
is false, as the three cards just showed. What’s true is one direction: on a finite
82   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                machine, every permanent raise is a priced move. The other direction has the three
                cards standing in it. And “priced” here has an exact meaning worth one sentence: a
                move is forced to be priced when every schedule that charges for forgetting charges it,
                and that holds exactly when the move forgets something, with no finiteness needed
                at all.

                Definition 3.3 (Forced to be priced). A move i is forced to be priced when every cost
                function satisfying merge pricing (Premise 3.2) charges i at least one.



                Theorem 3.8 (Forced price is merging). A move is forced to be priced exactly when
                it merges. No finiteness is needed.

                Proof. If i merges, merge pricing charges it at least one, whatever the cost function.
                If i does not merge, define the cost that is 0 on i and 1 on every other move. It
                satisfies merge pricing, since every merging move is some move other than i and
                costs one, and it charges i nothing, so i is not forced.
                   A cost here is any rule from move names to whole numbers, so that one is there
                whether or not anything can tell i from the other names. A test that tells them apart
                comes in only when a cost has to be computed by a program, and then the program
                needs it to tell i from the rest.


                Corollary 3.9 (Permanent records are forced). On a finite machine, a move that
                never turns the reading off and turns it on somewhere is forced to be priced. (By
                Theorem 3.7 it merges, and merge pricing charges every move that merges, whatever
                the cost function.) The converse fails: the three cards are forced, because they
                merge, and they revoke.


                3.5 The third way out: don’t charge for forgetting

                The third way out is the easiest to describe and the hardest to argue about, so I’ll
                describe it and then spend the rest of the section on the argument. Take a sheet of
                paper and let its reading be just BLANK or STAMPED. There is one move: stamp
                it if blank, and leave it alone if already stamped. It is finite, with two readings. It
                is permanent, since STAMPED stays STAMPED. It has a flip, since BLANK goes to
                STAMPED. Both possible readings now end at STAMPED. The paper’s fibres, the ink
                and your memory are outside this two-state description; the merge is a loss from
                the reading, not the disappearance of every physical trace. Everything the argument
                                                    3.5 The third way out: don’t charge for forgetting   83


from fresh states needs is here, and the move merges. Now set the price of that
move to zero. The toll fails, and you can watch it fail: the flag went up at zero cost.
The premise dropped on this way out is the charge on forgetting. (A price of one
on that move satisfies all three premises, so the premises can hold together; the
third way out is about whether they must.) Nothing in counting stops you from
setting that price to zero. Only a claim about the world does. The nearest such
claim is Landauer’s, and I have to be exact about the gap between the two: the
premise as written charges every forgetting move, whether or not you knew which
state you were in, and Landauer’s own heat, as the coin under the cup below will
show, is owed only for what you didn’t know. Merge pricing keeps only a yes-or-no
distinction: whether any pair can merge. The one-bit reset is where it comes from,
and it measures neither the full worst-case entropy loss nor the heat of any particular
preparation. The counting needs only that rule.
    Here is what Landauer said, in 1961, as exactly as I can put it. I went past the
summaries and read the paper itself. A logical operation with no single-valued
inverse (a step that forgets, in this book’s words) must produce heat, “typically
of the order of kT” per operation, where k is Boltzmann’s constant and T is the
temperature; and for the specific case of resetting one bit whose value you don’t
know, the minimum is kT times the natural log of 2, about 0.69 kT. I want you to
hear two things in that. First, “of the order of”: he was not handing out a number
to three decimals. Second, and this surprised me, he did not measure anything.
The paper is argument, with models. He writes that he can “show, or at least very
strongly suggest” the conclusion, and that his reasoning gives “no guarantee that
this minimum is in fact achievable.” That’s the founding paper of the whole subject,
and it’s a careful man saying “I think this is right and here’s why.” I like him more
for it.
    Was it measured, eventually? Yes, and only recently. In 2012 a group at the École
Normale Supérieure in Lyon, Antoine Bérut and Sergio Ciliberto’s lab working with
Eric Lutz, trapped a single glass bead, two millionths of a metre across, in a double
well made of laser light, and used the two wells as the two values of a bit. Then they
erased the bit, by lowering the barrier, tilting the trap, and raising it again, many
times over, slower and slower, and measured the heat each time. The average heat
came down toward Landauer’s kT ln 2 as the erasure got slower, closer the slower it
went, and never under it, on average. Single runs went under it; the bound is about
the average, and any one erasure can beat it. And if you only succeed in erasing half
the time the floor drops to zero, which the paper’s formula shows and which I think
is the most honest line in it. Others have done it since with different devices. So it
was predicted in 1961 by argument and seen in a laboratory fifty-one years later.
    And is it settled? No, and I’d be lying by omission if I left that out, because the
people who doubt it are not cranks. John Norton, a philosopher of physics, has
84   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                argued since 2005 that the usual proofs of the principle quietly assume what they’re
                trying to prove, and that the kinds of process they assume, combined, could be made
                to break the very law the principle is supposed to guard. An earlier objection, made
                in 1998–99 by Norton and his Pittsburgh colleague John Earman, also a philosopher
                of physics, was that the principle can’t be independent of the second law. Charles
                Bennett, who did more than anyone to build the subject, rated that one “in my
                opinion the one of greatest merit,” and then disagreed with it. Others replied to
                Norton; Norton replied back. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry on the topic, written
                by a philosopher of physics who works on exactly this, ends without a verdict. I’ve
                read what I could of both sides and I’m not qualified to referee them, and I’m not
                going to pretend the laboratory settles a question about what the principle means in
                general, because measuring one bead doesn’t do that.
                    What I did with it is this, and I think it’s the only honest thing to do. The charge
                on forgetting is written into this book as a named premise. It’s a definition the
                theorems take as an assumption, and nowhere is it proved as a general fact, because
                it isn’t provable from counting; for a particular machine with a particular price
                list you can see it hold (the stamp at cost one, above), which is a different thing.
                If Norton turns out to be right, every theorem in this section still holds; they just
                have one premise fewer that the world agrees to. If Landauer’s side turns out to be
                right, it supports a thermal price under its conditions; the whole-number charge
                on every merging move is still the ledger rule stated here. Either way, nothing in
                this section says a device does anything until someone measures the device. The
                counting is mine to prove. The physics is a premise I’ve named, and what settles it
                is a measurement, which a proof can’t do.
                    Naming a premise, though, isn’t the same as leaving it unplaced, and a hedge
                isn’t a position, so I’ll give mine. Earman and Norton’s objection is a dilemma. Either
                an information-theoretic exorcism of the demon assumes the second law, which
                they call the sound horn, and then it adds nothing the second law didn’t already
                give; or it rests on a new principle tying information to entropy, the profound horn,
                and nobody has given that principle independent grounds. A named premise is the
                sound horn, on purpose. That’s where Bennett ended up in 2003, and Norton’s “Too
                Good to Be True” (written in 2025, published in 2026) says the careful literature
