                almost always accepts that horn, and argues that whatever succeeds there is ordinary
                thermodynamics relabelled. I’ll take that. Ordinary thermodynamics, relabelled
                onto a ledger, is all this section asks of the physics. And on the counting I’m on
                Norton’s side outright. His 2018 paper “Maxwell’s Demon Does Not Compute”
                exorcises the demon with Liouville’s theorem and nothing else, no information and
                no computation: dynamics that keeps every patch of states the same size can’t crowd
                a big set of states into a small one. The counting core of this section, that a step
                losing nothing can’t carry a no-state into a set that stays up, is that point in finite,
                                                    3.5 The third way out: don’t charge for forgetting   85


discrete form. And if you want the best case for the premise itself, the one I found is
James Ladyman, Stuart Presnell, Anthony Short and Berry Groisman (2007): from
one of the standard statements of the second law, the one named for Kelvin, they
derive that a logically irreversible operation can’t be carried out thermodynamically
reversibly by any of their L-machines. That’s a physical argument under their stated
model of a machine. It deserves to be argued with on those terms; it does not by
itself establish the book’s whole-number ledger charge.
    One question a physicist asks before any of that, and it’s a good one: the laws
underneath never merge anything. Classical mechanics carries each exact state
forward to exactly one next state and could carry it back again, and Liouville’s
theorem adds that a patch of states keeps its size as it moves; quantum mechanics
is unitary, which is one-to-one too. So when this section says a step merged two
states, where did the difference go? It went out of the machine. The merge is in the
machine’s own description, the states its reading is about. The machine together
with everything around it still runs one-to-one, and the distinction the machine
forgot survives. It gets pushed out into the surroundings. The surroundings are the
endless strip of the first way out, the machine that keeps every history: the column
of states never used before, which the universe as a whole may have to spend and
the machine doesn’t, because the machine isn’t the universe and its memory fills.
Pushing a distinction out isn’t yet heat: another memory could keep it as a readable
record. It’s heat when the reset removes real uncertainty into a thermal reservoir,
and then Landauer’s premise bounds the mean heat handed over. None of that
heat has to be heat wasted. Takahiro Sagawa’s 2014 analysis says that erasure can,
in principle, approach a process that produces no entropy overall: the reservoir’s
entropy goes up by what the machine’s goes down. A positive mean heat transfer
can then be unavoidable without being wasteful. A known input has no uncertainty
to remove, and this entropy-loss premise alone sets no positive heat floor for it.
The reset can dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions, and a reset
device that wasn’t built for that one input keeps a floor that survives going slowly
(Section 3.7).
    Ladyman and his coauthors and Sagawa aren’t disagreeing. They use “reversible”
for two different things. Ladyman’s L-machines are devices, and a device counts as
reversible only if it produces no entropy on every input it’s fed, each one known
(their section 4: “the L-machine is thermodynamically reversible if and only if”
every one of its processes, one per input, produces no entropy). Sagawa’s reversible
erasure is a process on one given spread of inputs, with the device tuned to that
spread. The standard eraser is reversible in Sagawa’s sense and not in Ladyman’s: on
an even mix of 0 and 1 it produces no entropy, and on each known input it produces
k B ln 2. One identity holds the two together. For a fixed device that sends every
input to one output, and any spread q of its inputs, the average over inputs of the
86   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                entropy produced on each known input equals the entropy produced on the spread
                q, plus k B times the Shannon entropy of q. The identity holds because the heat is the
                same average either way, the device being fixed, and the output is the same either
                way. The only difference is at the start: the spread’s own entropy includes k B H (q)
                for not knowing which input it is, and each known input’s doesn’t. Sagawa makes
                the first term on the right zero; Ladyman reads the left side, which is then k B H (q),
                and more than zero.


                3.6 How much: the price grows with the squeeze

               The toll charges at least one unit, and that’s a floor for raising one flag. The counting
               of states says more if you let it. Say there are m states that already read yes and k
               more are turned to yes in one move. (That’s a different k from the one in Landauer’s
               kT; when the two meet, below, Boltzmann’s constant gets a little B hung under it,
               k B , so you can tell it from a count of states.) All m plus k of them end up on the
               m yes-states. That’s a squeeze by a factor of (m + k) over m, and if you accept a
               slightly stronger version of the forgetting price, that each unit of cost pays for at
               most one halving of the number of distinguishable states, then the move costs at
               least the number of halvings in that squeeze, which is the base-two logarithm of (m
               + k)/m.
                    Back to the stamp from the third way out, but give the reading four possible
               values this time: A, B, C and YES. Write them on four cards. Choose one secretly,
               then cover its face with an identical opaque YES label. Read only the new face: all
               four possibilities now give YES. Before the move, identifying the original face took
               two yes-or-no questions (one of the first two? then which one?); afterward there
               is only one possible face to report, so that reading has lost two bits, which is two
               halvings. Peeling the label off would recover the old face, so this tabletop version
               models the loss from the reading; it does not demonstrate physical erasure. So that
               move costs at least two units, and two is enough, since a cost of exactly two satisfies
               the halving rule. The general statement is m + k at most 2 to the cost times m,
               and there is also a logarithm form that rounds both logarithms up and is weaker
               for it (three states and one newcomer round to the same two bits on both sides,
               and the rounded form says nothing). The halving premise, like the one before it,
               is a definition used as an assumption. The units are halvings. To turn a halving
               into joules of heat you multiply by k B T ln 2, and that multiplication is physics; the
               counting stops before it.
                    That little k B deserves a short trip of its own, because it sits exactly where count-
               ing turns into physics, and its name is a small history lesson. Ludwig Boltzmann’s
               grave in Vienna has S = k log W carved on it (that k is the same k B , before anyone
               hung a B under it): entropy is a constant times the logarithm of the number of ways
                                                       3.6 How much: the price grows with the squeeze   87


the parts could be arranged. The idea is his. The constant, and the equation written
that way, came from Max Planck, in his work on radiation around 1900. In his
Nobel lecture in 1920 Planck said the constant “is frequently termed Boltzmann’s
constant, although to the best of my knowledge Boltzmann himself never introduced
it,” and guessed that Boltzmann never believed anyone could measure it accurately.
I’d assumed Planck named it after Boltzmann. His own words point the other way:
it was other people calling it that, and who first did, I couldn’t pin down. So the
most famous constant in this corner of physics wears the name of a man who didn’t
write it down. Does that change the heat floor? It doesn’t, but look at the job the
constant does in that equation. Take it away and what’s left is the logarithm of a
count, which is a number of halvings, which is what the squeeze bound hands you.
The constant is the exchange rate, and whether the world honours that rate for a
merge is the premise. No theorem here settles it.
    The premise, stated exactly, needs one new piece of notation: for a list D of
states, write | D | for how many it has, and imgi ( D ) for the number of different states
the move i sends them to.

Premise 3.4 (Halving price). Each unit of cost pays for at most one halving: for
every move i and every list D of states with no repeats, | D | ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ( D ). (It
implies merge pricing, since a merge sends two different states to one and so needs
cost(i ) ≥ 1.)
    There’s a plainer way to read that premise, and it’s worth having because it says
what the premise is about. Look at one landing spot of a move and count how many
states land there; call the biggest such count the move’s worst pile-up. The premise
holds exactly when the cost covers the worst pile-up in halvings: a cost of one allows
piles of two, a cost of two allows piles of four, and a pile of three already needs a
cost of two. In one direction, hand the premise one whole pile. It lands on a single
spot, so the premise says the pile has at most that many members. In the other, any
list of states splits by where its members land, each part sits inside one pile, so the
list is at most the number of landing spots times the worst pile-up, which is what
the premise says. So the halving price asks a move to pay for the worst it could
ever do, whichever state it’s actually handed. The worst case is on purpose, and it
has a home in physics. In the branch of thermodynamics that prices a single run
that has to succeed every time, with no averaging over many runs, Philippe Faist,
Frédéric Dupuis, Jonathan Oppenheim and Renato Renner derived in 2015, in that
framework, what they give as the least work any logical process needs, and when
every input might occur and no error is allowed, their bound comes to k B T ln 2 times
exactly that logarithm. Take an AND gate as the example: three inputs land on 0,
so it needs at least log2 3, about 1.6, halvings’ worth of work (two units, in whole
88   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                numbers). The premise asks for that bound of a device that has to work whatever
                it’s handed, and it counts it in units of cost. Joules don’t come into it.


                Theorem 3.10 (The squeeze bound). On a finite machine with a permanent reading
                and a cost satisfying the halving price, let m be the number of states that read yes,
                and let a move i turn k different no-states to yes. Three numbers are in play: m
                counts every yes-state of the machine, reachable or not; k counts a list of distinct
                no-states that the move turns to yes, and the move may turn others too; and cost(i )
                is the price the cost assigns to the move. Then
                                                                                            m+k
                      m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · m,      and, when m ≥ 1,         cost(i ) ≥ log2       .
                                                                                             m
                When m ≥ 1 the two displayed bounds say the same thing. (When m = 0 there is
                nowhere for a newcomer to land, so k = 0 too.)

                Proof. Put the m yes-states and the k newcomers in one list; it has m + k different
                members. By permanence every yes-state lands on a yes-state, and by hypothesis
                every newcomer does too, so all m + k land among the m yes-states: imgi ≤ m. The
                halving price gives m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ≤ 2cost(i) · m.
                    The four card readings are the case of one yes-state and three newcomers, where
                the bound is reached. With one newcomer the bound says the move costs at least
                one, which is the toll again. The counting argument also shows that at least as many
                states collapse as there are newcomers, without any price premise.
                    The bound is reached, whatever the numbers. Pick how many states already
                read yes and pick a cost. As long as the old yes-states and the newcomers together
                fit under that cost’s pile-up allowance (a cost of one allows twice the yes-states, a
                cost of two allows four times), there is a finite machine with a permanent reading
                and the halving price that has exactly that many yes-states and a move of exactly
                that cost turning those newcomers to yes. The move turns every other no-state of
                that machine to yes as well, filling the allowance to the brim. No cost meeting the
                halving price on that machine charges the move less. So the least whole-number
                cost that meets the bound is exactly the rounded-up logarithm, ⌈log2 mm+k ⌉.
                    Four more facts about the halving price, and the last one is a limit. First, the
                plainer reading above is a theorem on a finite machine: the halving price holds
                exactly when no move has a landing spot with more than 2cost(i) states landing on it.
                Second, for the eight-state machine described later in this section that’s a theorem
                about its own price list: no move has a larger pile-up than 2cost , so the halving
                price holds, and the toll follows from it; and the price list is the least that meets the
                halving price, since any price list that does charges every move at least what this
                                                3.7 The same bound, written in bits, and when it’s zero   89


one charges. Third, the squeeze bound is met with equality there: its stamp turns
on the four states whose flag is down, beside the four whose flag is already up, and
4 + 4 = 21 · 4. Fourth, and this is the limit, the small machine of Part III (Section 15)
as a whole does not meet the halving price, whatever procedure you use to decide
whether two of its states are equal, because one of its zero-price moves, the one that
takes one off a number the machine holds, lands two different states of the whole
machine on the same state (the pair is in Theorem 15.22), and a pile of two at price
zero is all it takes to break the halving price. What does hold there is merge pricing
asked of the record’s part of the state alone, and it gives the toll on that machine
too (Theorem 3.19, below).


3.7 The same bound, written in bits, and when it’s zero

There’s one more way to say all this, and I include it because it’s the way physicists
say it and because it says exactly when the heat floor is zero: when no two states
you might be in land on one. Its two ends are a move that forgets nothing and a
move on a state already known, and the second I find more instructive than any
case where it isn’t.
    Claude Shannon, in 1948, gave a number to “how much you don’t know”: if
something could be in any of n states and you have no idea which, your uncertainty
is log base two of n bits, and that’s the most it can be for n states. If you push
your uncertainty through a step that forgets nothing, it stays the same; through a
step that merges two states you might have been in, it drops. Now push it through
the permanent flip. Before the move, you might be in any of the m + k states in
play. After it, you’re in one of m. So your uncertainty afterward is at most log2
of m, whatever you believed before. If you started with no idea at all, every one
of the m + k states equally likely, your uncertainty was exactly log2 of (m + k),
and the move removed at least log2 of (m + k)/m bits: the same number as the
halving count, now in Shannon’s units. Landauer’s principle, in the form physicists
write it, then says a step that removes that many bits from the state gives off at
least k B T ln 2 of heat per bit. Put the two together and the flip gives off heat, and
the exact statements below say how much and under which side conditions, one
of which (the temperature has to be taken as zero or above) is easy to skip and
shouldn’t be.
    Why does Shannon’s number share a name with the physicists’ entropy at all?
There’s a story about it. Shannon wanted to call it uncertainty, and the mathemati-
cian John von Neumann told him to call it entropy instead, for two reasons: the
same formula already lived in statistical mechanics under that name, and nobody
really knows what entropy is, so in an argument he’d always have the upper hand.
It’s a great story. It comes from Myron Tribus, who spent years tying information
90   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                theory to thermodynamics, who said Shannon told it to him in 1961, and who
                printed it, with Edward McIrvine, in Scientific American in 1971. Then in 1982 an
                interviewer, Robert Price, asked Shannon about it, and Shannon said he didn’t think
                von Neumann had told him any such thing. So it’s a legend with one witness, and
                the person the witness quoted doesn’t remember saying it. What doesn’t hang on the
                story: the two formulas really do have the same shape, and it still takes Landauer’s
                premise, a named assumption, to turn a count of bits into heat.
                   Now the exact version, with the notation built first. A spread (probabilists say
                distribution) is a way of giving each state a chance p( x ) ≥ 0, with the chances
                adding to 1. Its Shannon entropy, in bits, is

                                            H ( p) = −      ∑          p( x ) log2 p( x ),
                                                         x: p( x )>0

                where the big sigma means “add up, over every state x with a chance above zero,”
                and each term is a state’s chance times the bits it would take to single that state
                out. That comes to log2 n when n states share the chance evenly and less when the
                chance is lopsided. Pushing a spread through a move i gives the spread of where
                you land: q(y) = ∑ x: step( x,i)=y p( x ). The bits the move removes are H ( p) − H (q).
                   Try four equally likely cards, A, B, C and D. Send A and B to a box marked X, C
                to Y and D to Z. Beforehand each card has chance 1/4, so the four terms in the sum
                are each 1/2: two bits. Afterward the box chances are 1/2, 1/4, 1/4, and the three
                terms are each 1/2: one and a half bits. Half a bit was lost on average. You can
                see where: half the time the box is X and leaves one binary question unanswered:
                A or B? The other half of the time Y or Z tells you the starting card exactly. An
                actual draw never loses half a card; the half belongs to the average uncertainty over
                repeated draws.
                                                                               X: one half
                                A: one quarter
                                                                         Origin could be A or B

                                B: one quarter


                                                                              Y: one quarter
                                C: one quarter
                                                                               Origin was C

                                D: one quarter


                                                                              Z: one quarter
                                                                              Origin was D

                 Half the time one binary question remains unanswered; half the time the origin is known.
                                               The average loss is half a bit.
                   Start with the half of the claim that removes no bits, Bennett’s half. A move that
                forgets nothing sends each state somewhere different, so the chances are carried
                                                  3.7 The same bound, written in bits, and when it’s zero   91


along to new places, one for one, and nothing piles up and nothing spreads out. The
uncertainty is the same number before and after.


Theorem 3.11 (A move that forgets nothing removes no bits). Let the states be
finite, listed once each, and let f send states to states with f ( a) = f (b) only
when a = b. Then for every assignment of chances p, the pushed spread q has
H ( q ) = H ( p ).

Proof. An injective map on a finite list of distinct states is a reshuffle of that list:
every state is hit exactly once. So q( f ( x )) = p( x ) for every x, and the sum defining
H (q) is the sum defining H ( p) with its terms in a different order.
   That’s why a price on removed bits can leave every reversible move costing
nothing, which is the shape the toll needs: the ledger’s cost lands only where
something was forgotten.


Theorem 3.12 (Entropy after a permanent flip). On a finite machine with a per-
manent reading, let m be the number of states that read yes, and let a move i turn
k ≥ 1 different no-states yes. For any spread p whose chance lies on those m + k
states, the spread after the move has H (q) ≤ log2 m. For the even spread on the
m + k states, the move removes at least log2 mm+k bits and at least m2k
                                                                     +k bits; the first
is reached when m divides k, the second when k ≤ m.

Proof. All the starting chance lands among the m yes-states: the old ones stay yes
and the newcomers turn yes. There must be at least one landing state, so m ≥ 1.
The first question is how much uncertainty those m places can hold.
   Here is the small fact about logarithms that does the work. For y > 0, ln y ≤ y − 1.
Picture the gap y − 1 − ln y. Its slope is 1 − 1/y: negative below 1, zero at 1, positive
above 1. The gap falls to zero and then rises, so it never goes below zero.
   Call the positive landing probabilities q1 , . . . , qr . There are at most m of them
and they add to one. Compare each with the even share 1/m. Apply the logarithm
fact to the ratio 1/(mq j ) and multiply by the chance q j :
                                            1    1
                                  q j ln        ≤ − qj.
                                           mq j  m
Now add over the occupied places. On the right the even shares total r/m ≤ 1,
while the actual shares total exactly 1. The sum is therefore at most zero. On the
left, splitting the logarithm gives − ln m − ∑ j q j ln q j . Move ln m across and divide
92   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               by ln 2 to count in bits. This says precisely H (q) ≤ log2 m: no arrangement of the
               chance among those places holds more uncertainty than the even arrangement.
                   Before the move, the m + k starting states were equally likely. Their uncertainty
               was log2 (m + k). Subtract the greatest possible uncertainty left at the end: the loss
               is at least log2 ((m + k)/m). If k is a multiple of m, keep each old yes-state where it
               is and send an equal number of newcomers to each. The landing chances are then
               even too, so this bound is reached.
                   For the other bound, count one landing pile at a time. A pile of s equally likely
               starts receives chance s/(m + k). Once you know that pile was reached, there are
               still s equally likely origins to distinguish: log2 s bits have disappeared there. Its
               share of the total loss is therefore s log2 s/(m + k).
                   A pile of one contributes zero. A pile of two contributes 2/(m + k). For every
               larger whole number s, s log2 s ≥ 2(s − 1). To check that inequality, subtract 2(s −
               1): the difference is zero at s = 2, and its slope for s ≥ 2 is log2 s + 1/ ln 2 − 2 > 0.
               It grows from there. Thus each pile costs at least 2/(m + k) for every origin after
               its first. There are m + k origins and at most m piles, leaving at least k such extra
               origins. The loss is at least 2k/(m + k ). When k ≤ m, send each newcomer to a
               different old yes-state and leave the old states fixed. All piles then have size one or
               two, exactly the sizes where the inequality is an equality. That construction reaches
               the second bound.

                Premise 3.5 (Landauer’s principle, as a premise). For the chosen physical memory
                and its input distribution, assume that a step lowering its logical-state entropy by
                ∆H bits transfers mean heat Q ≥ k B T ln 2 · ∆H to a bath at temperature T, where
                k B is Boltzmann’s constant. Here Q is an average over that preparation, not a bound
                on each individual trial. Applying this premise requires a physical model in which
                the logical entropy loss has this thermodynamic meaning; a bare state-transition
                table does not supply one. In particular the memory is symmetric, its logical states
                alike in their own entropy, as Landauer assumed; for a memory whose states differ,
                the floor changes (Maroney 2009), and erasure work in an asymmetric double well
                has been measured below k B T ln 2 (Gavrilov and Bechhoefer 2016).



                Corollary 3.13 (Heat floor of a permanent flip). Under Premise 3.5, with k B T ≥ 0,
                the flip of Theorem 3.12 from the even spread gives off at least k B T ln mm+k , and at
                least m2k
                        +k k B T ln 2; with k B T > 0 that is strictly positive.

                Proof. Theorem 3.12 gives an entropy loss of at least log2 ((m + k )/m) bits, and
                of at least 2k/(m + k) bits. Multiply by the nonnegative factor k B T ln 2 and use
                Premise 3.5. The identity ln 2 log2 x = ln x gives the displayed floor. Here m > 0
                                                3.7 The same bound, written in bits, and when it’s zero   93


and k > 0, so (m + k)/m > 1 and its logarithm is positive; if k B T > 0, the heat
floor is strictly positive too.
    How big is that? Take the case where the squeeze is two, one state flipping in
beside one that was already yes, and the floor is k B T ln 2. At room temperature,
about 300 kelvin, that’s roughly three zeptojoules: three thousandths of a billionth
of a billionth of a joule. And that’s the biggest floor a one-state flip gets from this
corollary. With one newcomer the floor shrinks as more states already read yes,
because the squeeze gets thinner: with a thousand of them it’s 2 ln 2/1001 of k B T,
about a seven-hundred-and-twentieth, some five hundred times less than the case
of two. So, for an even spread over the states in play, one unit of cost is not one
halving. It’s one halving exactly when the squeeze is two; for any thinner squeeze
and an even spread, the physics asks for less than a halving, and the toll still charges
a whole unit, because the cost comes in whole numbers. The entropy road to the
toll, a little further down, doesn’t need that rounding: entropy pricing asks about
every spread, and the worst one takes a full bit. Read in the worst case over what
the machine might be holding, the way the halving price reads a move, it’s at least
a full bit every time. A permanent flip merges two states (Theorem 3.1); put half
the chance on each, and the move removes a full bit, however many states already
read yes. So the gap between the unit of cost and the bits is a fact about the even
spread, and in the worst case the flip removes at least the full bit the unit pays
for. Whatever the size, it’s heat only if you grant the premise; nothing on this page
measured anything. The bead experiments above probe this energy scale. Ordinary
CMOS switching is a different comparison: the implementation figures cited next
are much larger than this floor. One 2023 tally of the numbers puts switching a
single CMOS gate at a hundred attojoules at the low end, over thirty thousand times
this. The point of the number isn’t that a permanent flip is expensive but that, on
the premise, it isn’t zero.
    A related logarithm appears in a different physical question. Yûto Murashita,
Ken Funo and Masahito Ueda (2014) study processes whose reverse histories can
include ones with no forward counterpart. They call this absolute irreversibility. If
the reverse histories with no forward partner carry some share of the probability,
their bound on mean entropy production picks up the logarithm of one over what’s
left. In their free-expansion example, gas that starts confined to a tenth of a box
gives the logarithm of ten.
    Make the confined fraction the old yes-states’ share of the pile, the yes-states over
the yes-states plus the newcomers, and out comes the same logarithm as the squeeze
bound. That numerical match does not identify two physical processes. The arrows
specify neither a thermodynamic reverse experiment nor its path probabilities, so
they don’t determine that share of reverse histories. The state count alone says noth-
94   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                ing about absolute irreversibility, its absence, or a heat equality. Gonzalo Manzano,
                Gülce Kardeş, Édgar Roldán and David Wolpert (2024) study such trajectory-level
                questions for computations with one-way transitions and random stopping times.
                Their physical premises are additional to the counting done here.
                   The even spread is the easy case, and it’s fair to worry that the heat depends on
                picking it. It doesn’t. Any spread that gives a real chance to every yes-state and to
                the state that flips will do.


                Corollary 3.14 (Positive heat for any full spread). On a finite machine with a
                permanent reading, let move i turn a no-state s yes. Take any spread p that gives
                positive chance to s and to every yes-state. Under Premise 3.5 with k B T > 0, the
                heat the move gives off is strictly positive.

               Proof. After the move, s and the yes-states all land among the yes-states, and there
               is one more of them than there are yes-states, so two distinct states with positive
               chance land on the same state. That merge removes a positive number of bits
               (Theorem 3.18 below), and a positive temperature times a positive number of bits is
               positive heat.
                   There’s a third road to the toll here too, and it’s the same shape as the merge
                road, with the bits removed, in place of whole units, as the price of forgetting.

                Definition 3.6 (Entropy-priced). On a finite machine, a cost is entropy-priced when,
                for every move i and every spread p, the cost of i is at least the bits the move
                removes: cost(i ) ≥ H ( p) − H (q), where q is p pushed through i.



               Theorem 3.15 (The toll from entropy pricing). On a finite machine with a perma-
               nent reading and an entropy-priced cost, every move that turns the reading from
               no to yes costs at least one. So the machine with that cost is a Thiele machine
               (Definition 2.2), and every run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least one.

                Proof. Let move i turn s yes. By Theorem 3.1 it lands two different states on one.
                Put half the chance on each: the move removes one bit, so the cost of i is at least one.
                The run-level floor is the universal floor (Observation 2.2) applied to that system.
                    There are three roads to the toll, with two different strengths. Entropy pricing
                and the halving price are equivalent: the most bits a deterministic move can remove
                is the base-two logarithm of its largest pile of starts sharing a destination. Merge
                                               3.7 The same bound, written in bits, and when it’s zero   95


pricing asks only for a cost of at least one whenever any pair collides. It is the
two-state restriction of the stronger conditions.
   Try eight equally likely cards all sent to one box. The loss is three bits. A charge
of one meets merge pricing but fails entropy pricing and the halving price, which
require at least three. All three conditions give the permanent-record toll; only the
stronger two give the full squeeze bound.


Theorem 3.16 (Entropy pricing, halving, and pairwise merge pricing). Take a finite
machine and a move i. (1) If no state has more than K ≥ 1 states landing on it
under i, every spread loses at most log2 K bits through i; and if some state has
exactly K states landing on it, the even spread on those K loses exactly log2 K bits.
(2) A cost is entropy-priced (Definition 3.6) exactly when it satisfies the halving
price (Premise 3.4). (3) A cost satisfies merge pricing (Premise 3.2) exactly when it
satisfies the halving price for every list of at most two different states, and exactly
when it satisfies entropy pricing for every spread whose chance sits on at most two
states. The first of those two equivalences uses no finiteness.

Proof. (1) Sort the possible starts into piles according to where the move sends
them. Suppose the landing place is y and its total chance is q(y) > 0. Knowing
that you landed there leaves only the starts in that pile in question. Their chances,
now measured within the pile, are p( x )/q(y). They add to one, and there are at
most K of them. The logarithm argument in the preceding entropy bound says their
uncertainty is at most log2 K bits.
    Average that remaining question over the landing places, giving each its chance
q(y). This is exactly the information the move discarded. Indeed, a start x con-
tributes
                                     q(y)
                         p( x ) log2        , y = step( x, i ),
                                     p( x )
and summing these terms gives H ( p) − H (q) by grouping the output terms by their
landing places. An average of numbers no greater than log2 K cannot exceed log2 K.
For equality, put equal chance on every member of one pile of size K. There are
log2 K bits at the start and none at the single landing place.
    (2) An entropy price must cover that even preparation on every pile. A pile of
size n therefore requires cost c ≥ log2 n, or equivalently n ≤ 2c . That is the halving
rule: no landing place accepts more than 2c starts. Conversely, if the halving rule
holds, part (1), with K = 2c , says no preparation loses more than c bits. The same
price covers them all.
    (3) Now allow at most two starts. If they land separately, the move loses nothing.
If they land together, the halving rule reads 2 ≤ 2c , which asks for at least one
96   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                whole unit. This is exactly merge pricing. Nothing in that two-start argument needs
                the rest of the machine to be finite.
                   The chance calculation makes the same demand. Two possible starts hold at most
                one bit, so a charge of one covers every spread over a merging pair. Equal chances
                on that pair lose exactly one bit and force that charge. A single possible start, or two
                that stay separate, lose zero. So restricting entropy pricing to at most two possible
                starts gives merge pricing too.
                   So merge pricing is weaker than full entropy pricing, though both force the
                one-unit toll under the permanence and finiteness premises. The prices are rules on
                moves. Reading one as physics takes Landauer’s premise for the actual spread and a
                stated exchange rate from bits or units of cost to heat.
                   Now for the case where the floor is zero. Take the coin under a cup: toss a fair
                coin under it without looking at how it lands, and let the rule be to set it heads up.
                You might have had tails; now you have heads; one bit of what you didn’t know is
                gone, and that’s the bit the principle charges for. Now lift the cup, see heads, put the
                cup back, and apply the rule again. Nothing you didn’t know changed, and no bit
                was lost. And the principle, applied to a state you already knew, demands nothing:
                the premise holds exactly when the heat is zero or more, which is to say it sets
                no positive floor. Setting a coin known to be tails to heads may have a finite-time
                cost under the chosen thermal dynamics; setting one you know is heads changes
                nothing. What the premise gives up either way is a floor that survives going slowly.
                Whether the hand that sets the coin keeps one is a question about the hand, and
                I come to it below. If you lift the cup after an uncertain toss, you have also made
                a record correlated with the coin. Resetting that record has to be analysed with
                those correlations and with the controls available. If instead the coin was supplied
                heads with certainty, there was no uncertain toss to record. These are different
                preparations. Knowing the result does not by itself locate a heat payment in the
                observer.
                   The entropy-loss bound depends on the preparation and on what the move does
                to it. Here “known” means a preparation concentrated on one logical state, or a
                conditional ensemble whose side information is explicitly included in the account.
                Merely telling a spectator which way the coin landed does not change an unchanged
                device’s heat. This is the generalized form of Landauer’s principle, worked out by
                Owen Maroney in 2009, in a paper he wrote at the Perimeter Institute in Canada (he
                has been a philosopher of physics at Oxford since 2011), and by Sagawa in 2014,
                and Landauer himself had the seed of it in 1961: for a row of bits all already ONE,
                he wrote, there’s no need to carry out any operation, so no entropy changes and no
                heat is given off, and resetting a row all ZERO to ONE involves no entropy change
                either, because neither row carries any information.
                                               3.7 The same bound, written in bits, and when it’s zero   97




Theorem 3.17 (A known state gets no heat floor from the premise). On a finite
machine, if the spread puts all its chance on one state s, then any move removes
zero bits, and Premise 3.5 for that move holds exactly when Q ≥ 0.

Proof. A spread on one state has entropy 0, and so does its image, which is again on
one state. So ∆H = 0 and the premise reads Q ≥ 0.
    Be careful with that one, because it’s easy to overread. “The premise sets no
heat floor for a known state” does not mean a stamping machine run on a known-
blank sheet dissipates nothing. A model of the stamping apparatus may impose a
finite-time cost, but the logical change alone does not establish it. The restricted
thermal results are proved here for Bennett’s walker (Theorem 1.9), found for a
dragged bead by Schmiedl and Seifert and for the specified classical jump-process
models by Shiraishi, Funo and Saito, and how much depends on the device’s physical
implementation, its control protocol and how fast it goes. What the theorem says is
only that the premise sets no floor there. The floor comes from what you didn’t know.
That’s a sentence about the premise’s floor, and the device is a separate matter. And
notice that the toll still charges the known-state stamp one unit, because the toll is a
rule about the move, and the move doesn’t know what the observer knows. That’s
the worst-case gap from the third way out showing up again, and it’s the price of
having a rule a machine can follow without asking who’s watching.
    The physics of all this has a standard review, the physicists Juan Parrondo, Jordan
Horowitz and Takahiro Sagawa’s “Thermodynamics of information” (2015), which
sets Landauer’s bound, its generalized form and the costs of measurement and
feedback side by side. And the gap between a device and the spread it runs on has a
physicist’s number on it. Artemy Kolchinsky and David Wolpert (2017) showed that
a fixed process built to dissipate as little as possible for one spread over its states
pays extra when it runs on another, and the extra is how much closer the process
brings the two spreads, measured in relative entropy; the extra was later named
mismatch cost. That’s the worst-case gap again, priced for an actual spread, where
the toll prices the move.
    Fix a thermal protocol with the entropy-balance identity just described, using the
same controls and environment for each input. A floor then comes from comparing
its inputs. Take K inputs the device sends to the same output, and spread your
chances evenly over them. The identity of Section 3 that ties Ladyman’s reading
to Sagawa’s says the average, over the K, of the entropy the device produces on
each one known equals the entropy it produces on the even spread, plus k B ln K.
The second law makes the entropy produced on the spread zero or more. So the
average is at least k B ln K, and the worst of the K is at least the average: on some
98   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                one of them the device produces at least k B ln K of entropy, and, when dissipated
                work is temperature times entropy production, at least k B T ln K of dissipated work.
                Slowing this same protocol does not remove that worst-input bound. Kolchinsky
                and Wolpert’s formula says, under their conditions, which input pays: the one the
                device’s own best spread gave the least chance. A device can make one input cheap
                only by making another dear. Choosing different controls for different known inputs
                changes the protocol being compared. The bound above concerns one fixed protocol
                across them. So the floor sits on the merging move, on its worst input, whatever
                anyone knows, and that’s the shape of the toll. The bound on a device left to relax
                from a known start, in the next subsection, is one more floor of this kind.
                   There’s a second piece of fine print on Theorem 3.17, and it’s about who works
                the controls. The entropy-loss bound supplies no positive floor for a known input.
                Whether a device can approach that floor also depends on its controls: lower this
                barrier, tilt that well, raise the barrier again. Those operations have a timing and a
                physical implementation. The entropy calculation alone does not price either.
                   Paul Riechers, Alexander Boyd, Gregory Wimsatt and James Crutchfield (2020)
                analyse metastable memories under time-symmetric control: the prescribed control is
                the same played forwards or backwards, with the relevant time-reversal conventions.
                A symmetric clock pulse can meet that restriction; an arbitrary clocked pulse need
                not. For memory states unchanged by time reversal, their low-error result singles
                out the memory states that the desired logical map, applied twice, fails to bring back
                to where they started. They call those transitions nonreciprocal. With equal local-
                equilibrium free energies, the leading minimum-work term as the error allowance ε
                tends to zero is proportional to
                                                                            
                                             k B T ln(1/ε) Pr C (C (m)) ̸= m .

                The probability is over the initial memory states. This is a low-error scaling with
                physical premises, not an exact finite-error heat charge on every execution.
                   A permanent flip from no to yes is nonreciprocal at that no-state: a second
                application cannot return it to no. A known input at that state can then face the
                extra work cost in their restricted control setting, even though its initial logical
                entropy is zero. Their class also includes a three-state cycle, which merges nothing.
                The distinction is about the permitted controls as well as the logical map. It neither
                changes Theorem 3.17’s entropy calculation nor identifies the book’s abstract merge
                price with a universal physical heat floor.
                   A deterministic run from a known start has a known state at every step, so
                the premise sets no floor under any of its steps; each that changes something can
                dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions, and a fixed device keeps the
                floor above on each step that merges. One more limit, about which states collide.
                The counting guarantees a collision among the already-yes states together with the
                                                 3.7 The same bound, written in bits, and when it’s zero   99


entering no-state. It does not guarantee that the entering state takes part in the
collision. Take four states with only the first reading no, and a move that sends the
first state to the second, the second to the third, and leaves the third and fourth
where they are: the second and third both land on the third, and the first never
shares with anyone. For an input distribution supported only on no-states, this
counting argument alone forces no positive entropy loss. Whether other states in
that support merge depends on the move. The operation-level ledger toll still follows
under merge pricing.
    What this section earns comes to this. A finite machine’s permanent flag-raising
instruction has two allowed starting states that land on one state. Prepare those
two with equal chances: that instruction removes one bit, and under the adopted
physical premise its mean heat is at least k B T ln 2. That is a worst-case preparation,
not a positive charge on every execution. A known start gives no positive entropy-
loss floor. Any finite-time dissipation depends on the device’s dynamics, controls
and speed; under the fixed-protocol entropy-balance assumptions above, merging
K inputs forces at least k B ln K of entropy production on one of them. The ledger
charges the merging move whatever the preparation, because merge pricing says
so. The counting proves a collision, the preparation determines the uncertainty
removed, and the physical premises connect that removal to heat.
    The general case is the one that shows you where the bits go. Split the bits
removed state by state. Each state x you might be in carries its chance p( x ) along
to where it lands, step( x, i ), and finds whatever other chance landed there too. If
nobody else landed there, its term is zero. If others did, its term is the difference
between how crowded its landing spot is and how much of the crowd it brought.


Theorem 3.18 (The bits removed, one term per state). On a finite machine, for any
move i and any chances p( x ) ≥ 0, with q the pushed spread,

                              ∑ p(x) log2 q(step(x, i)) − log2 p(x) .
                                                                    
         H ( p) − H (q) =
                               x: p( x )>0

Every term is zero or more, so a move never adds bits. If two different states x ̸= x ′ ,
both with positive chance, land on the same state, the sum is strictly positive.

Proof. Group the sum for H (q) by where things land: the chance q(y)
at a landing spot is the sum of the p( x ) that land there, so H (q) =
− ∑ x: p(x)>0 p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )). Subtract from H ( p) term by term. Each
term is non-negative because the landing spot holds at least what x brought,
q(step( x, i )) ≥ p( x ), and the logarithm keeps order. If x and x ′ share a landing spot,
that spot holds at least p( x ) + p( x ′ ) > p( x ), so the term for x is strictly positive.

                3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not
               Let me total it: what have you earned the right to conclude, and where is there still
               a way out?
                   You’ve earned this first, and it needs no premise but one next state for every
               state: on any machine run by one rule, finite or endless, a run that raises a reading
               and keeps it up either merges two of its own states or never repeats one, and
               on any machine at all a single move that raises a kept reading without merging
               anything has to send the kept states one-to-one into a part of themselves with a
               gap left over, which takes endlessly many of them. Either way it is a merge, or an
               endless supply of states never used before. You’ve earned this: on any machine with
               finitely many states, a move that raises a flag either forgets something or takes a
               flag down somewhere else. That is pure counting, with no physics and no premise
               beyond finiteness, and the half of it where nothing comes down is the pigeonhole
               on four states. You’ve earned this: on a finite machine, if a flag, once up, stays up,
               then raising it has a collision somewhere. If it raises several no-states at once, the
               yes-states together with those newcomers land on at least that many fewer spots
               than there are of them. This does not say that each newcomer shares its destination;
               this one is counting again. And you’ve earned this: if forgetting is charged for, the
               toll follows, and if forgetting is charged per halving, the size of the toll follows
               too; each of those derivations hands back a system with the five parts and the toll,
               so Section 2’s floor applies to it as it stands. This is the rule from Section 2, now
               derived, with every premise named, for any finite machine with a flag that stays up.
               In that section I only declared it.
                   Now for what you haven’t earned, which I list so you don’t assume it. You haven’t
               earned that forgetting costs anything in the world; that’s Landauer, it’s measured for
               beads and argued over for the general case, and in this book it’s an assumption with
               a name. And even granting it, Landauer’s entropy-loss bound demands no positive
               heat from a run whose state is known (the lifted cup of the coin example), so what
               the physics forces is a floor on a device that has to work whatever it’s holding. An
               individual run can fall below an ensemble average bound. Knowing a state does
               not by itself prove that another person or memory paid the difference. You haven’t
               earned that any machine you’d actually want to build is of this kind, either, and
               there are two easy ways to miss. A machine that keeps its running total inside its
               own state, as a number with no ceiling, has infinitely many states, so the finite
               premise fails for it as a whole. And you can’t patch that by giving the total a ceiling.
               A total that only climbs, held in finite memory, eventually either stops at its top, and
               then two different histories leave the same top value, which is a merge, or rolls back
               over to zero, and then it doesn’t only climb. So any running total a finite machine
               keeps for itself has a horizon: it’s honest up to its width and no further. And a
                                                   3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   101


machine whose price list charges the step that raises the flag, but lets some other
step merge two states at no cost, raises the flag honestly and still doesn’t charge
for forgetting in general, so the merge-pricing premise fails for it. Either one puts
a machine outside these theorems as stated, though a finite piece of it can still sit
inside. The example I build later (Section 15) misses in both ways. It keeps counters
with no ceiling, so it’s infinite outright, and some of its ordinary steps, counting a
counter down among them, can land two different states on one at no charge on
the ledger. So the counting, as stated, doesn’t reach it: it forces the toll only on
machines with finitely many yes-states that price every merge, and that example is
neither. It doesn’t need the counting, though: the moves that raise its flag merge
states themselves, so the same cost lands on them directly (Theorem 3.19).
    A finite piece can still sit inside, and the smallest one I could build where every
premise can be seen to hold is this. None of them is left as a hypothesis. It has four
slots times a flag, eight states, and three kinds of move: stamp (set the flag, go to
the next slot, cost one), jump to a chosen slot (cost two), next slot (cost zero). It’s
finite and permanent; the next-slot move forgets nothing; the stamp and the jump
merge; merges are priced, and priced per halving. So this section’s two conclusions
hold on it outright. The counting lemma underneath, that a duplicate-free list in
which no landing spot is hit by more than a set number of members has at most that
many times as many members as landing spots, is the plainer reading of the halving
price above. Merge pricing alone would take any price of at least one for the jump.
The jump’s price of two is what the halving price asks, since the jump squeezes four
states into one. One more fact about it: each move’s price is exactly the number of
halvings in its largest squeeze. A move that costs one has no spot hit by more than
two states, a move that costs two has none hit by more than four, and some spot is
hit by exactly that many (stamp squeezes at most two states into one, jump to a slot
squeezes four, and next-slot squeezes nothing).
    The example Part III builds runs this eight-state machine. Seen through a window
that shows only a line number, read modulo four as the slot, and a flag, a short
program of that machine, once a two-instruction setup has run, does what the
eight-state machine does, one move at a time, and pays exactly what the eight-
state machine charges. The example as a whole prices its record and not every
merge: some of its zero-price steps merge states, and whatever those merges cost
the hardware is off the ledger, so the finite piece is a piece. The toll on the whole
example comes from the record’s part of the state (Theorem 3.19).
    Finiteness did one job in the counting. It forced the step that raises a permanent
flag to merge two states. On the machine of Part III no count over the whole machine
has to force that, because the merge is in plain view. Its record moves are the check,
the commitment and the raised flag that the opening’s lock puts in order, and it
names them CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY: COMMIT names a checked claim in
102   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               a slot called the channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. CERTIFY takes a state with
               the flag down and the same state with the flag up to one place, since a flag that’s
               already up just stays up. Its COMMIT overwrites the channel, so two states that
               differ only in what the channel names land on one state. Part (1) of the theorem
               below shows both. So any price list that charges every merge of that machine’s own
               step charges the flag-raising step, with no premise that the machine is finite. It isn’t:
               its versions and its ledger grow without bound.
                   Finiteness is still there, in the smallest place it can be. Hold every part of the
               state but the flag fixed, and the flag has two readings, down and up. CERTIFY sends
               both to up, and it does the same to everything else from either, so the two states
               land together. That is the counting of Theorem 3.1 on a set of two. So the choice I
               made in the opening’s list isn’t the merge, and it isn’t the shape of CERTIFY. It’s that
               the step never reads the flag: the rest of the state moves by its own rule and the
               ledger adds the instruction’s price, whichever way the flag reads, so no instruction
               keeps a copy of the old reading, and any that raises the flag lands its two readings
               together. Make CERTIFY trap instead when the flag is already up, and the merge
               moves rather than goes away: the state it traps lands with the state that was trapped
               already, since a trapped machine only pays. That’s the halted state stepping to itself
               again, and it holds of every record move: any of the three that fails lands with the
               same state already trapped. The one way out of the flag’s merge is to write the old
               reading into a part of the state that grows, a list of every reading so far, say, and
               that is a state never used before, the other column. A ledger that adds more for a
               re-raise than for a raise doesn’t do it: the state with the flag up and the ledger a
               little lower lands where the raise lands, and the merge has only moved again.
                   That leaves the other miss, the unpriced merges. The example’s price list, in
               Part III, puts its flat moves at zero, and a flat move merges (DEC, counting a counter
               down, lands two states on one), so full merge pricing and that price list can’t both
               hold on that machine. They don’t have to. Split a state into its base part, which is
               what a two-counter machine would show (the line number and the two counters),
               and its record part, which is everything else: the versions (each counter’s count of
               how many times it has been written), the table of facts, the channel, the trap latch
               (which goes up when a record move fails, after which only the ledger moves), the
               ledger and the flag. Then price only the merges the record layer makes.

               Premise 3.7 (Record-layer merge pricing). A move that sends two different states
               with the same base part to one state costs at least one.

                   Part of where that line falls is forced. The line number has to be in the base
                part, or DEC, which can land two lines with the same counters on one, makes a
                record-layer merge at no cost; each counter has to be there, or its version, or DEC’s
                                                     3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   103


own merge gets charged; and the flag or the trap has to be outside it, or nothing
charges CERTIFY. Where the versions, the table, the channel and the ledger sit
moves nothing below.
   The merges among base parts are the flat part’s business, the ones any two-
counter machine makes, and whatever heat they cost is the flat part’s heat. The
premise prices only merges between states with the same flat part. A step like DEC,
which changes that part, can lose a version number at no cost, and the premise
doesn’t object. Merge pricing implies this premise, so it asks less, and on the record
distinctions it is still an assumed operation-level price; identifying it with heat needs
a physical model. And it is a price on this machine, not a source of the toll on any
machine. A certifying move whose effect on the base read the flag, say one that
moved a counter up when it raised the flag and left the counter alone when the
flag was up already, would raise the flag and send no two states with the same
base to one state, and the premise would have nothing to charge at the raise. It
would still merge: the state with the flag down and the state with the flag up and
that counter one higher land together, across two base parts, where the premise
doesn’t look. And on this machine its trap would still be charged when it fails. The
small machine’s record moves treat the base the same whichever way the flag reads,
which is why the premise does its job there, and the theorem below is stated for that
example and no other.


Theorem 3.19 (The toll on the example machine). For the small machine of
Section 15, with no finiteness premise: (1) CERTIFY merges, and so do COMMIT
and CHECK of every claim, and each joins two different states with the same line
and counters. (2) Every cost that satisfies merge pricing for that machine’s step
charges CERTIFY, every COMMIT and every CHECK at least one, and obeys the toll,
so the machine with that cost is a Thiele machine. (3) No INC, DEC or HALT sends
two different states with the same line and counters to one state. So the machine’s
own prices, base moves at zero and each record move at one, satisfy Premise 3.7,
they’re the least prices that do, and merge pricing fails for them. (4) Every cost
that satisfies Premise 3.7 obeys the toll, so the machine with that cost is a Thiele
machine.

Proof. (1) For CERTIFY, prepare two states identical except for the flag. Give both a
channel holding a commitment. One flag is down and one is up. CERTIFY raises
the first and leaves the second up. Both advance one line and add the same charge;
every other field agrees. They have become the same full state.
   For COMMIT, put the requested fact, at the counter’s current edition, in both
tables. Leave one channel empty and put that very commitment in the other.
104   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               COMMIT writes the same commitment into both channels and treats every other
               field alike. Again the full successors agree.
                   For any CHECK, fill the fact table to its sixteen-entry limit. CHECK then fails,
               whatever claim it was asked to test. Compare that untrapped state with an otherwise
               identical state whose trap is already up. The first sets its trap; the second is already
               frozen. Neither changes the other core fields, and both pay the same charge. Their
               successors agree. In each construction the starting line and counters agree as well,
               so these are record-layer merges.
                   (2) A price on every merge charges each of those instructions at least one. Only
               CERTIFY can raise the certificate. Its merge therefore supplies the toll.
                   (3) Check the free instructions by asking whether two states with the same line
               and counters could become one. The table, channel, trap, ledger and certificate
               are left alone, so any difference in those fields survives. On a live state the shared
               line and counters choose the same instruction branch. A counter write adds one
               to its edition; different edition numbers stay different after the same addition.
               All unchanged editions stay different too. Hence no remaining field can hide a
               difference between those sources.
                   A trapped state stays exactly where it is under a free instruction. Two different
               trapped states therefore stay different. A live state remains live under these instruc-
               tions, so it cannot meet a trapped one. That exhausts the cases. The free instructions
               make no record-layer merge, and all three kinds of record instruction do. Charging
               the former zero and the latter one satisfies the premise and is the smallest such price
               list. Full merge pricing still fails: the zero-price DEC pair in Theorem 15.22 starts
               with different counters and lands together.
                   (4) Any record-layer merge price charges the CERTIFY pair from (1). Since no
               other instruction raises the flag, this gives the toll for every raise.
                    So this section reaches the example machine. On it the toll follows from record-
                layer merge pricing, and the example’s own price list, flat moves at zero included,
                satisfies that premise. This is a result about its ledger, not a heat bound. There’s
                a second way to settle the clash, which I note and didn’t take. Morita’s reversible
                two-counter machine runs every step backwards and is still universal: with its input
                encoded, it computes anything a Turing machine can. Put the record over a base
                like that, with the base’s step taken as the program’s own step from line to line and
                the halt left with no next step, and every base step is one-to-one, and full merge
                pricing permits those base steps to cost zero. That price list would put the flat
                moves at zero; the lower-bound premise alone does not require zero charges. It
                isn’t the example’s flat part, though. The example has a move for each two-counter
                instruction, acting from every live state, not a step for each line of one program,
                and DEC c j sends states on any two lines with the same counters, c above 0, to the
                                                    3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   105


same window, so whether it merges turns on the rest of the state and not on the
program being reversible. That base wouldn’t be getting anything for nothing: what
it doesn’t forget it keeps in its counters, which is the column of states never used
before, again. I haven’t built that machine.
    And you haven’t earned anything about what the flag means. The pigeonhole on
four states doesn’t know what it’s certifying. The cost is for raising a flag that stays
up. Whether raising that flag ever amounts to standing behind a structural fact, the
“vouching” I keep promising and keep not delivering, is a question for the certified
example in Part III, and here it has moved exactly this far: on a finite machine that
charges for every merge, if that flag stays up, it was paid for.
    One last thing, because it should nag at you. The toll is forced by the premises,
but the premises were chosen, and “permanent” in particular was chosen by me.
Why should a flag stay up? Why not let it come down, pay nothing, and be honest
about it? That’s a fair question, and merge or revoke is the start of an answer (the
three-card machine only showed that the converse of Corollary 3.9 fails): on a finite
machine that charges for every merge, a flag that goes up at zero cost is a flag the
same move takes back somewhere, and a record that can be silently taken back is
the thing a hash chain and a write-once disk were built against. “Permanent” here
is exactly that: the flag can’t be lowered. The toy in Section 2 has it only because
none of its three moves happens to lower the flag, and durability is the one job of a
record it has; I chose it. Whether that was the right job to pick is something you can
argue with me about, and I’d want you to.
    And “permanent” is an idealization, which I should say before a physicist does. No
physical record lasts forever. A bit held behind an energy barrier leaks over it at some
rate, however slow, and a closed finite system comes back around, which is Zermelo’s
point from the counting (Theorem 1.6 is the finite form). The toll theorems in this
section, the ones that start from a flag that stays up, need permanence on every
state the machine can reach, including states a given run never visits, forever; on
states nothing reaches it never comes into it, and merge or revoke does without it.
Weaken that to “the flag stays up on the states that actually turn up, for as long as
anyone cares,” and merge-or-revoke tells you what goes wrong: the move could
take the flag down somewhere the machine could go and never does, and then it
isn’t forced to merge at all. A version of the toll stated in chances is the noisy steps
of Section 1: a step that squeezes nothing on average can’t raise a reading that stays,
and one that can strictly bunches the even spread. A version stated in time spans is
a different theorem, and what I have of it is below.
    One piece of it I can hand you, and the step law of Section 1 is its general form.
Take one move and repeat it from one start, forever. On a finite machine the states
that run passes through are finitely many, so it falls into a loop. If the move forgot
nothing on those states, it would be a reshuffle of them, and a reshuffle brings every
106   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               one of them back around, the start included, where the flag was down. So if the
               flag goes up along that run and stays up from some point on, the move merges two
               states the run itself visits. The state they share is one the machine actually passes
               through. And it doesn’t touch the known-state point above: a merge among states
               the run visits still receives no positive lower bound from the entropy-loss premise
               when its state is known. The argument holds for any map on finitely many states
               iterated from a start whose flag is down, with the flag up at every step from some
               point on; no permanence premise is used.
                   Runs that mix different moves split two ways, and the answer is short enough to
               give here. If the moves are picked from outside, in any order at all, the answer is
               no. Take two states, one reading no and one reading yes. One move swaps them;
               the other does nothing. Run the swap once and then the do-nothing move forever:
               the flag goes up at the first step and stays up for good, and neither move merges
               anything anywhere. The swap would take the flag down from the yes-state if it ever
               ran there; on this run it never does, and that’s exactly the weakened permanence
               this paragraph is about. But if the machine is closed, picking its next move from its
               own state, the run is the orbit of one map, the step with whatever move the state
               picks, and the single-move argument applies to that map as it stands. Now say the
               moves come in a pattern that eventually repeats, one phrase of moves played over
               and over. Suppose the flag is down at some step after the repeating starts, and goes
               up and stays up after that. Count the repetitions from a step where the flag was
               down (start the phrase at that move if you have to) and run the same argument on
               the whole phrase treated as one move, at the states where each playing of it begins.
               It merges two of those states, both visited; follow the two through the phrase, and
               the first move where their paths meet merges two states the run visits at that move’s
               place in the pattern. So the answer is no for moves picked from outside, and yes for
               a closed machine, or for a repeating program once the flag is down somewhere after
               the repeating starts.
                   Two chapters remain in this part. The next takes the record off its two places and
               lets it sit anywhere in an order, to see what the two places were doing. The one after
               is about a different way out entirely. Forgetting has had its chapter; the question
               after that is whether finding out costs, because the demon’s whole trick was that it
               knew which way the molecule was going, and I owe you a straight answer on what
               knowing costs.
CHAPTER 4




The whole direction

The record in Definition 2.1 is a place in any order, and the toll charges any move
that climbs. Up to here the proofs were done on two places, blank and written,
because that’s the record you can point at. Established never felt like a switch to me,
though. It feels like a direction with lines drawn across it, and the switch is just the
first line. This section does the proofs on the whole direction, and finds out that the
two-place case was a case: nothing the switch needed gets left behind, and the one
thing a single switch can’t do, hold three or more stages, falls out as a count.
    A row of cells that only ever go from blank to written is a direction: you can tell
how far along it a state is, and nothing walks it back. A single cell, a cup turned
once, has two positions. The question for this section is blunt: with the record
anywhere in an order, which of the results so far (the universal floor, the merges,
the squeeze) come along as they stand, and which ones need the order to be more
than a preorder?


4.1 A row of cups
Get four cups and a pencil. Write five stages of an experiment on a strip of paper,
left to right: proposed, set up, run, read, recorded. Agree to do them in that order.
Put an upside-down cup between each pair of neighbours. The first means “the
setup happened,” the second “the run happened,” the third “the result was read,”
the fourth “the result was recorded.” As you complete a stage, turn over its cup.
Cups only ever get turned right side up; none has a reset wire. These are records
of completed acts. A fourth cup up does not make a false conclusion true, and a
different experiment may need a different order.

                 Read down the drawing. Zero means cup down, one means cup up. Four cups give five
                        stages along this run because each new stage turns up one unused cup.
                  Two things to notice with the cups in front of you. Each cup by itself is the
               two-place record: it reads yes or no, and once yes it stays yes, which Part II will call
               a latch (Section 11). And four cups were enough for five stages. Try it with three,
               and you’ll find you can’t: three cups that only ever turn up, in order, give you at
               most four different arrangements along the way. I’ll prove both of those in a minute,
               and the proof is about as short as the experiment.
                  Now a harder strip. Some checks don’t line up. One person repeats the experi-
               ment; another independently works through the calculation. Neither act includes
               the other. Draw a diamond: neither at the bottom, experiment repeated on the left,
               calculation checked on the right, both at the top. There are two ways up, and the
               middle points don’t compare, which is what a partial order allows. Put a cup on
               each point except the bottom, one for the repeat, one for the calculation, one for
               both. Each cup is still a latch. The three cups tell you which acts have happened.
               They do not decide whether the experimental model or the calculation’s premises
               were appropriate.
