   Whatever the shape of the strip, a straight line of stages or a diamond or some-
thing with a hundred points, I’ll call the set of places the record can be the direction,
and each question “has the record reached at least this place?” a line across it. One
line is one cup.


4.2 The order, said exactly
The strip and the diamond each come with an order you can see by looking: whether
one place is at or below another. Said exactly, the order is a test. For any two places
x and y it answers “is x at or below y?” with yes or no, and I write a yes as x ≤ y.
The test has to obey two rules: every place is at or below itself, and if x ≤ y and
y ≤ z then x ≤ z. An order that obeys just those two is called a preorder. If it also
obeys a third rule, that x ≤ y and y ≤ x together force x = y, it’s a partial order,
and that third rule is called antisymmetry. The two-point order, no below yes, is the
cup. The whole numbers in their usual order are a straight strip that never ends.
    The cups say the same thing in their own terms. For a place a, the cup for a asks
“has the record reached at least a?”, so with the record at x it’s up exactly when
a ≤ x, and I write its answer as [ a ≤ x ]. In the row of cups I said the cups together
tell you which place the record is at. On the strip and the diamond you can check
that with your eyes, and Part II proves it again from the latch side whenever the
order is partial (Theorem 11.10), though the first time through I hadn’t asked what
in that proof was doing the work. My first guess was that it held for every order.
    Why bother with the bare preorder at all, when every strip on the table is a
partial order? I bothered because I wanted to see what the third rule was doing,
110   4 The whole direction


               and the way to see what a rule does is to take it away. Take a preorder with two
               places, call them left and right, where each is at or below the other. There are two
               cups, one asking “at least left?” and one asking “at least right?”, and both are up at
               left and both are up at right. Look at the table and you can’t say where the record
               is. Now build a record that swaps between left and right on every single step and
               charges nothing. Every rule I’m about to state is satisfied. The record never drops
               below anywhere it was, because each place is at or below the other. No cup ever
               moves, so the toll in the next subsection has nothing to charge. The record moved
               on every step and nothing on the table noticed.



               Theorem 4.1 (The cups fix the place, and only with antisymmetry). (1) In a partial
               order, if two places x and y leave the same cups up, [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y] for every
               a, then x = y. (2) In a preorder that isn’t a partial order this can fail: there’s a
               preorder with two different places that leave the same cups up, and a record over it,
               driven by the computation and growing in that preorder, that changes on every step
               while no cup moves.

               Proof. (1) Look at the cup for x. It’s up when the record is at x, since x is at or below
               itself, so it’s up at y too, and that says x ≤ y. The cup for y gives y ≤ x the same
               way. Antisymmetry gives x = y. (2) Left and right above, with the record swapping
               every step.
                   So in a partial order the cups are the place, and in the preorder I built they aren’t.
               That second half holds in every preorder that isn’t partial, by one line: if x ≤ y and
               y ≤ x with x ̸= y, then a cup that’s up at either one is up at the other, by transitivity.
               So the cups fix the place if and only if the order is partial. My first guess was right
               on every strip I could draw, and it was right because of a rule I hadn’t noticed I was
               leaning on. On a bare preorder, putting two places on the same rung tells the toll
               not to care about moves between them, and it doesn’t. I don’t think that’s a defect;
               it’s the order telling you what you agreed to count.


               4.3 The toll, over the whole direction
               One cup had one rule: the step that turns it right side up pays. Now there’s a row of
               cups, or a diamond of them, and a single step can turn over several at once. The
               rule I’d guess first turns out to be the right one: a step that turns over any cup pays
               at least one. A step that turns over three cups at once still only has to pay one. The
               rule asks whether a step turned something over. It doesn’t ask how many.
                   That rule buys the same thing one cup bought. Take any run, and suppose some
               cup is up at the end that was down at the start. Somewhere along the run a step
                                                              4.3 The toll, over the whole direction   111


turned that cup over, and that step paid. So the run paid at least one. Count the
same way and you get more: the run paid at least once for every step that turned
anything over.
   Now look at what that argument didn’t use. It didn’t care whether the cups sat in
a row or a diamond or something with a hundred points. It didn’t care how many
there were. It didn’t even use the fact that cups never get turned back down. If
something could knock a cup back over, the argument still works, because all it
needs is the one step where that cup went up.
   To say it exactly I want to translate it into places. The cup at a place a is up
exactly when the record is at or above a. Say a step takes the record from x to y.
The cup at y is up afterwards, since y is at or above itself, and it was down before
exactly when y isn’t at or below x. And if y is at or below x, any cup that’s up at y
was already up at x. So a step turns over some cup exactly when it lands somewhere
that isn’t at or below where it started. The same reasoning says a run ends with
some cup up that was down at the start exactly when it ends somewhere that isn’t
at or below where it started.


Theorem 4.2 (The toll over any direction). Take a machine whose record is a place
in any preorder, and say a step turns a cup over when it takes the record from x to a
place that isn’t at or below x. (1) Every step that turns a cup over costs at least one
exactly when every run, from whatever state it starts, that ends somewhere not at
or below its start costs at least one. (2) When that holds, a run costs at least the
number of its steps that turn a cup over. (3) It holds exactly when every cup, on its
own, obeys the two-place toll: for every place a, a step that turns the cup at a from
down to up costs at least one. (1) is the floor over any order (Observation 2.1) said
in cups, and the universal floor (Observation 2.2) is (1) with one cup.

Proof. (1) and (2) are the walk above. For the other half of (1), a run of one step
that turns a cup over ends somewhere not at or below its start. (3) is the translation
above.
   When the cups only ever go up, as on the strip and the diamond, a step that turns
a cup over is just a step up.
   That surprised me a little, because I’d filed the floor away as a fact about one bit,
and nothing in it was about one bit. It was about one cup going up, and anything
you build out of cups has that.
112   4 The whole direction


               4.4 One line isn’t enough
               Now comes the payoff I promised at the start of this section. Could a cleverer single
               cup do the job of all four, with one latch and some decoding that reads the record’s
               place off the latch and whatever the machine shows? Section 11 rules that out in the
               smallest case: over a machine with one visible state, a record that climbs through
               three places can’t be produced by one latch and a decoding, because one latch and
               one visible state make two outcomes and the record has three.
                  So try a second guess, closer to the cup’s own rule. The cup’s rule was “new
               value is old value or the event.” The obvious rule for a whole row is “new place is
               old place joined with the event’s place,” where joining two places means going to
               the lowest place at or above both. On the row, the event names a place, and you
               turn up every cup as far as that place. To see it break, take the strip 0 < 1 < 2, a
               cup at 1 and a cup at 2, over a machine with one visible state, so the event has to be
               one fixed place. Let the record jump from 0 straight to 2, turning up both cups in
               one step, and stay put at 1 and at 2. From 0 the event has to turn up both cups, so
               the fixed place is 2. From 1 the same event would turn up the second cup as well,
               and the record stays at 1.
                  What works is giving every cup its own event, and letting the event for a cup
               look at where the record already is. Theorem 11.10, in Part II, says exactly that, and
               this is why it has to. That leaves the question of how many cups. In the row of cups
               I asked you to try five stages with three and said you couldn’t. Here is the count,
               with the matching example added, and with an arrangement of k cups read as a
               k-bit word, a one for every cup that’s up.


               Theorem 4.3 (Lines a direction needs). (1) A list of different arrangements of k
               cups, each keeping up every cup the one before had up (a chain of different k-bit
               words in which each word’s set bits are among the next word’s), has at most k + 1
               members, and for every k there’s such a chain with exactly k + 1. So a straight strip
               of n + 1 stages needs exactly n cups. (2) Over a machine with one visible state, take
               the record on the strip 0 < 1 < 2 that jumps from 0 to 2 and stays put at 1 and at 2.
               It grows and is driven by the computation, and no rule of the form “join the record
               with a fixed place” reproduces its steps.

               Proof. (1) Going from one arrangement to the next, which is a different one, turns
               up at least one more cup, and there are k cups, so there are at most k steps and k + 1
               arrangements. For the matching chain, take no cups up, then the first, then the first
               two, and so on, packed to the left: that’s the row of cups. (2) Joining 0 with a fixed
               place g gives g, and from 0 the step has to give 2, so g is 2. Joining 1 with 2 gives 2,
               and from 1 the step has to stay at 1.
                                                                4.5 Why crossing a line has to cost   113


   So five stages need four cups, and neither one nor three will do it, as long as the
cups only turn up. An ordinary binary counter holds a thousand stages in ten bits,
because its bits go down as well as up, and the theorem says nothing against that.
The switch isn’t wrong: it’s the first line, and a straight strip with more than two
places needs more of them, exactly one fewer than it has stages. A direction that
branches needs at least as many cups as the steps in its longest strict climb, and at
least as many as it takes to tell its places apart, the rounded-up logarithm of how
many there are. Put three places above a bottom, none of them above another: the
longest climb is one step, and one cup can’t tell four places apart, so it takes two,
and two do it, though not two lines: one cup that goes up at the first and the third,
and one that goes up at the second and the third. It can need more than both. Take
two places each below two others: one step of climb, four places, and two cups still
won’t do, because both upper places would have to keep up every cup either lower
one has up, and two cups allow at most one arrangement like that besides the lower
places’ own.


4.5 Why crossing a line has to cost
The last chapter showed that the cup’s toll isn’t an arbitrary rule. It’s forced by
three premises, and the argument that ties them together was the pigeonhole: on a
machine with finitely many states, the move that raises a record that goes up and
stays up has to land two possible states on one state (Theorem 3.1), and a step
that lands two states on one is a step that forgets which one it came from. Does
that survive the whole row of cups? Mostly, and the parts that don’t survive are the
interesting ones.
    The counting needs a flag, because what it counts is the collection of states with
that flag up, and now there are many cups, each one a yes-or-no reading that could
serve as the flag, so the first job is to pick one. My first guess was the cup for the
place where the record starts. That goes nowhere: the starting state already has
that cup up, so it’s already in the collection, and there’s no state coming in from
outside. The cup that works is the one the step turns over, the cup for the place
where the record lands. It’s up after the step, since a place is at or above itself, and
it was down before, which is what turning a cup over means. So the collection is
every state with that landing cup up, and the state the step starts from is the one
coming in from outside. If the move keeps every state in the collection inside it and
never lands two states on one, the states already inside use up every state in the
collection between them, and there’s none left for the newcomer. So one of two
things happened. Either two states landed on one, or some state that was in the
collection got moved out, which means its landing cup went back down. I’ll call that
second thing a revocation.
114   4 The whole direction




               Theorem 4.4 (Turning a cup over merges). On a machine with a record in any
               preorder, where each place has finitely many states with its cup up: (1) if a move
               turns a cup over at some state and lands the record at a place a, then either the
               move merges two states, or there’s a state with the cup at a up that the same move
               takes to a state with the cup at a down, which is a revocation; (2) if the record only
               grows, so that no cup ever goes back down, the move merges; (3) if the record only
               grows, the toll holds exactly when every move that turns a cup over at some state,
               and merges, costs at least one, so merge pricing gives the toll.

               Proof. (1) Gather every state with the cup at a up. There are finitely many. If the
               move keeps each of them there and is injective, it maps that collection into itself
               without two landing on one, so it hits all of them, including the state it sends the
               starting state to; injectivity then says the starting state was in the collection already,
               and it wasn’t, because its cup at a was down. So either some state in the collection
               has its cup at a knocked down, or the move isn’t injective. (2) Growth rules out the
               knocking down. (3) If the toll holds, every move that turns a cup over somewhere
               pays, merging or not. The other way, a move that turns a cup over merges by (2), so
               the hypothesis charges it.
                   It’s the old counting argument again, run once for every cup.
                   Each premise there can be knocked out, and I wanted to see each one go, because
               a premise you’ve never seen fail is one you don’t understand yet.
                   Knock out finiteness. Take the whole numbers as the states, which gives a row
               of cups that never ends, and let the record be the state itself, one more on every
               step, at no charge. Every step turns up one more cup. The step never merges
               anything: different numbers go to different numbers. Merge pricing holds, because
               there are no merges to price, and the toll fails on every single step. The counting
               broke at the one place it needed the collection to be finite. Every state moved one
               along, and there was always another state to move to. That’s Charles Bennett’s
               1973 construction in miniature: a machine that keeps its whole history never has
               to forget, so it never has to merge. It hasn’t got out of paying. Every step lands it
               on a state it has never used, and that’s the fresh-state column. The toll fails here
               because merge pricing only charges merges and this machine pays by taking a state
               it has never used, which that price list doesn’t charge. Take the infinity away and
               the supply of fresh states goes with it.
                   Knock out growth. Take a two-state machine whose record flips back and forth
               between two places, so a cup goes up on one step and gets knocked back down on
               the next. The two states just swap with each other, so nothing merges, and the price
               list is honest about merges. The step that turns the cup up pays nothing. It takes the
                                                               4.5 Why crossing a line has to cost   115


other branch of (1) and revokes: the state that had the cup up gets moved to where
it’s down.
    Knock out the price on merges. A two-state machine that stamps every state
with yes turns the cup up wherever it was down, merges at the stamp, and charges
nothing. Of course the toll fails; nobody asked the merge to pay.


Theorem 4.5 (Each premise does work). (1) There’s a machine with infinitely many
states, a growing record and an honest merge price on which every step turns a cup
over and the toll fails. (2) There’s a two-state machine with an honest merge price
whose record doesn’t grow, which turns a cup over and fails the toll. (3) There’s a
two-state machine with a growing record whose merges aren’t priced, which fails
the toll.

Proof. The three machines above, in order.
   So the toll over a whole direction rests on exactly the three things the cup’s toll
rested on: finitely many states with each cup up, a record that doesn’t come down,
and merges that pay. Nothing extra got smuggled in when one cup became a row,
and nothing the one cup needed got left behind.
   I’d half expected the diamond to need something new, some extra rule for the
two middle cups that don’t compare. It didn’t. Every cup gets its own collection of
states, and the argument on each is the old one.
CHAPTER 5




Learning borrows, committing
pays

I ended the chapter on the toll’s reason owing you an answer about knowing. What
keeping takes so far sits on forgetting: under merge pricing, a finite machine’s
permanent flag-raising instruction was paid for because it merges two states some-
where. But there’s a thing that looks like the opposite of forgetting and feels like it
ought to cost at least as much, probably more, and that is finding out. Every time a
machine rules out a possibility, it knows more than it did. If forgetting a bit costs,
does learning one cost too? I had a strong feeling about this, and you probably have
it too, so I’ll say it first: learning is the expensive part. Most physicists had that
feeling as well, for a long time. It’s why the demon took a hundred and fifteen years
to exorcise, or didn’t. “Exorcise” is the word the people who think it worked like
to use. John Earman and John Norton, the doubters from the last chapter, called
their two-part paper on it “Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell’s Demon,” and I read
that Roman numeral as a joke about how many times the demon has been declared
gone. So hold the word loosely. This section is me finding out where the feeling
goes wrong, and where it’s right. I’ll give the answer up front. Looking can have a
physical cost; its value needs a model of the measurement. But it doesn’t have to
merge anything, so it owes no floor, and a ledger that charges merges can charge
it nothing. What it does use up is a blank page to write on. Learning borrows that
page. Wiping the page to use it again is a merge, and that’s where the floor gets paid.
Committing, making a record nobody can hand back, is paying for good. I’m going
to tell you the version where the exorcism worked, Charles Bennett’s, because it’s
the version that says where the heat goes, and the third way out in the last chapter,
the one Landauer’s premise is there to close, stays open behind it.


5.1 Bennett moves where the heat is paid
In 1982 Charles Bennett, who’d already shown in 1973 that computation can be
done without forgetting if it keeps its whole history and pays by taking states it


                                 116
                                                          5.2 Two different things called “narrowing”   117


has never used instead, took the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks
at a molecule and writes down which side it’s on. Is writing that down a merge?
Picture the being’s notepad, which starts blank. After looking, the notepad says
“left” or “right.” There are two possible worlds before the look (molecule left, pad
blank; molecule right, pad blank) and two possible worlds after it (left, “left”; right,
“right”), so nothing merged: two went in, two came out, and you can read the
before off the after. Copying what you see onto a blank page forgets nothing, and a
step that forgets nothing owes no floor under Landauer’s premise. Any finite-time
physical cost additionally depends on the chosen dynamics and protocol. But it did
use something up: the blank page. Before the look, the pad was blank and ready;
after it, the pad is full. Brillouin had priced one particular way of looking (bouncing
light) and took it as the price of getting information at all. Bennett gave a way of
looking that, on his account, doesn’t pay that price. It borrows a page instead.
    So where is the heat floor? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules.
After the first molecule the page is full, and to do the next one it has to wipe the page.
Wiping takes two possible worlds (pad says “left”; pad says “right”) to one (pad
blank), and that’s the merge, the step with no way back. For a complete reusable
engine under the stated thermal assumptions, the memory reset and the feedback
process must be accounted for together. The cycle cannot turn information about
the molecule into net work from a single bath while restoring every other resource
for free. It’s the rule from his 2003 notes that I quoted in Section 2: erasing and
merging carry the unavoidable charge, and copying onto a blank place to write
doesn’t. The look borrows the page. Resetting an uncertain page without using its
correlation with the molecule has the corresponding entropy-loss floor under the
thermal assumptions. While the molecule is still available, the joint operation can
instead undo the copy; the four-state example below does that. A blank supplied at
the start is an initial condition. To charge its preparation, specify what uncertain
state was reset and how.
    Section 2 separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see exactly
which step pays, and why the other one was tempting, because looking feels like the
active part, the thing the being does, while wiping feels like housekeeping. In that
reset protocol, the housekeeping is where the entropy-loss floor applies. If there’s
one sentence in this section I’d want you to carry out of it, it’s that one, and the idea
in it is Bennett’s.


5.2 Two different things called “narrowing”

Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense,
and I’ll give it to you as a picture because that’s how I eventually got it.
118   5 Learning borrows, committing pays


                   Draw the machine’s possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row
               above it: the dots that you, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are two
               different rows: the first is a fact about the machine, and the second is a fact about
               you, about what you’ve seen and what you’ve ruled out. Both rows can shrink, but
               they shrink for different reasons, and only one of them costs.
                   The machine’s row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state, which
               is a merge, and a merge is what the price charges. Under the halving rule from
               Section 3, a run can’t shrink the machine’s own row by more halvings than it paid
               for. That’s the theorem just below, and it’s that section’s halving price run forward
               along a whole program, where that section took it one step at a time. There is no
               new idea in it, only the same counting of states.
                   To state it exactly, write ⌈log2 n⌉ for the index-bit count of n: the smallest
               whole number k with 2k ≥ n, the fewest yes-or-no questions that can guarantee
               identification among n things when arbitrary binary splits are allowed. It is 0 at
               n = 1, and 0 at n = 0 too, since 20 ≥ 0; the definition covers empty lists, where the
               logarithm of zero isn’t a number. Wherever I write an ordinary logarithm without
               the rounding, its argument is positive. For a run t and a list D of starting states,
               let imgt ( D ) be the set of states the run can end in, starting from somewhere in D,
               and write |imgt ( D )| for how many there are (in Section 3 the symbol for one move
               already meant the count; here I need the set and its size both). Let cost(t) be the
               run’s total cost.


               Theorem 5.1 (The machine’s own narrowing is priced). If the cost satisfies the
               halving price (Premise 3.4), then for every run t and every list D of starting states
               with no repeats,
                | D | ≤ 2cost(t) · |imgt ( D )|,   so     ⌈log2 | D |⌉ ≤ cost(t) + ⌈log2 |imgt ( D )|⌉.

               Proof. After each move, gather the states still possible and count each different state
               once. If the first move costs c1 , the halving rule says the original count is at most
               2c1 times this new count. If the next move costs c2 , the new count is at most 2c2
               times the count after that. Put the inequalities together: the original count is at
               most 2c1 2c2 times the count after two moves.
                  Carry on to the end. The factors multiply, their exponents add, and the added
               prices are exactly cost(t). The last collection is imgt ( D ), giving the first inequality.
               An empty run contributes no factor and leaves the collection unchanged, so it fits
               too.
                  For the rounded count, let k bits suffice to number all the endpoints. There are
               then at most 2k endpoints, and the first inequality gives at most 2cost(t)+k starts.
               That many bits therefore suffice for the starts. This also covers an empty starting
                                                               5.3 The demon on a sheet of paper   119


collection, whose stipulated index-bit count is zero, without taking a logarithm of
zero.
   Rounding throws some information away. Four starts and three endpoints both
need two index bits, so the rounded comparison alone permits zero cost. The
unrounded comparison still sees that four is more than three and forces a positive
charge.
   The run itself is the witness; nothing else is handed in. That will matter in
Section 9, and I’ll say why at the end of this section.
   Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn’t
have shown you, and you cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the
machine. It didn’t merge anything; it didn’t know you were watching; it would have
done the same thing with nobody there. The physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name
for mixing these up, and I think it’s one of the most useful names in all of science:
the mind projection fallacy, treating what you know about a thing as if it were a
property of the thing. Your list of candidates is in your head, and the machine’s
row is in the machine. The halving price is about the machine’s row, and crossing a
candidate off yours doesn’t move it.
   And here I have to be fair to Jaynes, because he’d argue with where I just took
his phrase. In a 1965 paper on Gibbs’s and Boltzmann’s entropies he wrote that
entropy is “an anthropomorphic concept” (a phrase he credited to the physicist
Eugene Wigner), and by that he meant a property of the particular experiments you
or I choose to do on a physical system. On his account the system alone doesn’t
carry it. So for Jaynes the second law is about what’s known too, and the line I’d
have liked to draw, that the second law has opinions about the machine and none
about you, is exactly the line he’d refuse. Who’s right is one of the oldest fights in
statistical physics, Jaynes’s reading against Boltzmann’s, and I can’t settle it and
don’t have to. The spreads in Section 3’s entropy theorems are spreads over the
states the device might be in when the step runs, and every theorem there holds
whether you read those chances as ignorance or as physics; “the floor comes from
what you didn’t know” is the same sentence in either reading, with “you” being
whoever built the spread. What I need from the fallacy is only this: the two rows
are different rows, and only one of them is the machine’s.


5.3 The demon on a sheet of paper
Build it, because the whole claim is four dots and two arrows and you should see it
merge or not merge with your own eyes.
   The machine has a hidden bit (think of it as the molecule’s side) and a display
(the notepad). It has four states, written as pairs, hidden bit then display: 00, 01,
10, 11. It has two moves.
120   5 Learning borrows, committing pays


                  MEASURE copies the hidden bit onto the display, by adding it in the way that a
              light switch adds: if the hidden bit is 1, flip the display; if it’s 0, leave it. Draw the
              arrows: 00 goes to 00, 01 goes to 01, 10 goes to 11, and 11 goes to 10. Look at the
              arrowheads: every state has exactly one arrow landing on it, so nothing merged and
              MEASURE forgets nothing. Look at the two states where the display starts blank: 00
              goes to 00 and 10 goes to 11, which is the copy onto a blank page, (hidden, blank)
              to (hidden, hidden), and it’s the use that matters here. And the light switch isn’t
              one way of copying among several. A MEASURE that merges nothing, copies onto a
              blank display and leaves the hidden bit where it was has nowhere else to send 01
              and 11: each has one landing left on its own side.
                  WIPE sets the display to 0 whatever it held. 00 goes to 00; 01 goes to 00 as well.
              10 goes to 10; 11 goes to 10 as well. Two arrows land on 00 and two on 10, which
              is a merge, twice over.
                               Hidden bit, display before   After MEASURE   After WIPE
                                           00                      00           00
                                           01                      01           00
                                           10                      11           10
                                           11                      10           10
              Now follow only the prepared cases: 00, 10 become 00, 11 after the copy. WIPE
              sends those two to 00, 10, still two different full states. The hidden bit retains the
              distinction. The instruction price nevertheless charges WIPE because its rule merges
              other possible pairs, as the full column shows. That worst-case charge is not a
              one-bit entropy loss on this particular correlated preparation. Under any price that
              charges per halving, WIPE costs at least one, while MEASURE is allowed to cost
              zero. Zero on the price list isn’t zero spent: a physical MEASURE can dissipate under
              its specified dynamics, and it uses up the blank display. What it doesn’t do is merge,
              so it owes no floor.
                   Now be the observer. You can see the display and not the hidden bit. What you’re
              shown, the display here, is what I’ll call a window: the part of the state an outside
              observer gets to see. Section 8 is about windows in general; here the window is
              just the display. The display starts blank, so your list of candidates is {00, 10}: two
              possibilities, one bit you don’t know. The machine runs MEASURE and you look at
              the display. If it shows 1, the only candidate that could have produced it is 10, and
              if it shows 0, only 00, so your list went from two to one and you learned the hidden
              bit. The machine’s price for that move, on a list that charges merges, is zero, and
              what it spent was the blank display. Its own row of possible states went from {00,
              10} to {00, 11}, still two; nothing it could have been got merged with anything else.
              You narrowed and it didn’t. That’s the measuring half of Bennett’s argument on four
              dots, and WIPE’s charge is the wiping half. So the demon just broke something: one
              bit gained, nothing charged. The thing it broke, written out so you can see exactly
                                                                 5.3 The demon on a sheet of paper   121


where the crack runs, is this: for every list of starting candidates, every run, and
every actual start in the list, the index bits the observer gains (log2 of the candidates
before minus log2 of the candidates after, both rounded up) are at most what the
run was charged. On four dots that sentence is false.

Definition 5.1 (What an observer knows). Fix a window w from states to what can
be seen. Given a list Ω of candidate starting states, a run t, and the actual start
s0 ∈ Ω, the observer’s knowledge K (Ω, t, s0 ) is the list of candidates s ∈ Ω whose
run shows the same thing through the window at every step as the actual run does.

   If that definition looks familiar, it should. It’s the standard way logicians of
knowledge set it up: what you know is whatever holds of every case you can’t tell
apart from the actual one, given everything you’ve seen (Fagin, Halpern, Moses
and Vardi’s Reasoning About Knowledge, 1995, builds a whole subject on it, runs
and observations included). And it’s the logically omniscient kind, the kind where
knowing some facts means knowing everything that follows from them, at no extra
cost (Section 14 comes back to that flaw). I’m using it on purpose, flaw and all.
This section is about learning, and learning in that sense is exactly the thing that
doesn’t have to merge. Settling, making a result stay so it can’t be handed back, is
the separate act with a price, and nothing in this definition settles anything.


Theorem 5.2 (An observer can learn with no merge). There is a four-state machine
(the demon), a window (the display), a cost satisfying the halving price, a run of cost
0, and candidates with |Ω| = 2, for which |K (Ω, t, s0 )| = 1. So the claim “for every
Ω with no repeats, every t, and every s0 in Ω: ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ − ⌈log2 |K (Ω, t, s0 )|⌉ ≤
cost(t)” is false for that machine and that cost. In the same machine, every cost
satisfying the halving price charges WIPE at least one.

Proof. The machine and run are the four dots above: MEASURE is a bijection, so cost
0 satisfies the halving price; the observer’s two candidates show different displays
after MEASURE; WIPE sends two pairs of states to one each, so the halving price
needs its cost ≥ 1.
   The demon is the picture, and the smallest case is smaller than it. The claim as
written already fails on a machine with two states that the window tells apart and
every move priced at zero, because the observer’s very first look tells the two apart,
and it never fails on a machine with one state. That’s why the interesting version is
learning after the first look, which is where the three states of Theorem 5.3 come in.
And WIPE’s price needs less than the halving rule: merge pricing alone charges it at
least one.
122   5 Learning borrows, committing pays


                   There is one thing to be exact about. The halving rule is a floor: it says merges
               cost at least this much, and it doesn’t say anything costs zero. So the theorem
               exhibits one price schedule that meets the halving rule and charges MEASURE
               nothing. A different schedule could meet the rule and still charge MEASURE;
               nothing in counting forbids overcharging. The claim is that learning is not forced to
               cost a unit. That’s what “borrows” in the section’s title means: the look takes a page
               and pays nothing, and the unit, like the floor, comes due at the wipe.
                   The physicists had this freedom on the books long before me. Paul Fahn (1996),
               doing the entropy accounting of Szilard’s one-molecule engine step by step, argued
               for a symmetry between the measuring step and the erasing step: on his account,
               which of the two you charge is partly a choice of bookkeeping, and the total is
               what’s fixed. Sagawa and Ueda (2009) derived a bound on that total, with the
               split depending on the memory. So, on their accounts, “a schedule could charge
               MEASURE instead” is a known freedom in how the books are kept, and I didn’t find
               a loophole. The other reading is very much alive too. Ruth Kastner (2025) argues
               that Brillouin was essentially right after all: once the physics of a real measurement
               is put back in, it’s measurement that pays and foils the demon, erasure drops out of
               the dissipation, and Bennett’s floorless copy fails as physics. The theorem above is
               about price lists, so it stands either way. What hangs on her is whether a real demon
               can look without a floor, which is the same question the next paragraph’s doubter
               presses on.
                   And the doubter from the last chapter cuts this side too, so I owe it to you,
               since I leaned on him there. In 2013 John Norton argued for a no-go result: at
               the scale of molecules, thermal jiggling keeps any process that’s supposed to be
               thermodynamically reversible from ever actually finishing, and finishing it takes
               more entropy than Landauer’s amount. If he’s right, Bennett’s measurement has a
               floor in practice after all, because it’s one of those processes. The theorem above
               survives that, because it’s about price lists: a schedule that meets the halving rule
               isn’t forced to charge the copy, whatever a real device spends. What wouldn’t survive
               is the physics I’ve been hanging on it, that a real demon’s look owes no floor, only
               the dissipation of happening that going slowly shrinks. If Norton is right, the line
               between learning and committing keeps its counting and loses its physics. I can’t
               referee that one either.


               5.4 Who holds the pen changes who pays

               Now comes the part that I think is the most beautiful fact in here, and you find it
               by playing with the four dots rather than by thinking about them. Run MEASURE
               twice. The first copies the hidden bit onto the display. The second adds the hidden
               bit in again, and adding a bit twice with a light-switch add gets you back where you
                            5.5 The smallest machine that teaches with no merge, and the one that can’t   123


were: the display is blank again. Check the arrows: 10 to 11 to 10. The display
went full and then blank, and nothing merged, and the price on the ledger was zero
both times. So a display that was blank before the first MEASURE can be put back to
blank with no merge and no floor, by a second MEASURE, though not by WIPE. This
is the borrowed page being handed back: while the original is still there to check
against, the copy can be un-copied. Each MEASURE still dissipates by happening,
and going slowly shrinks it.
    What’s the difference? MEASURE consults the hidden bit when it clears the display.
It knows what’s written there, because it has access to the thing it was copied from,
and so it can undo the copy. Nothing gets erased. WIPE doesn’t look. It sets the
display to 0 regardless, and “regardless” is exactly the many-to-one. Bennett has
the general form of this in the 2003 notes: he lists the “erasure of one of two copies
of data known to be identical” among the logically reversible operations, because
you’re removing a duplicate, and no information is destroyed. And it goes further
than Bennett in work that came after him: the quantum physicist Lídia del Rio and
colleagues argued in 2011 that the floor on erasing a system depends on how much
the eraser already knows about it, dropping to zero, and in the quantum case below
zero. The heat of clearing a record falls on whoever clears it, and its floor is lower
the more they know. Try it with a red or blue card under a cup and a note that
is blank or marked. Start with the note blank. Lift the cup: for red, toggle the
note (blank to marked, marked to blank); for blue, leave it alone. The note now
reports the colour. Repeat that same rule while the card is still available, and the
note returns to blank. Check all four card-and-note combinations: the rule undoes
itself, so no two land together. Erase the note regardless of the card instead, and
for either card both note values land on blank. That rule merges on the full set
of combinations. On the matched pairs you actually prepared, the card still has
the information, so nothing is lost there; the merge is in what the rule has to do
to every combination it might be handed, which is what a rule that doesn’t look
has to answer for. Cards and paper don’t measure heat. What they show is which
information each rule gets to use.


5.5 The smallest machine that teaches with no merge, and the one that can’t

There are two more small facts, and then the point. The demon measures what you
learn by comparing the start to the end, but an observer’s very first look already
rules things out before any step runs, so the fairer question is: after that first look,
can a step teach you more, at zero cost? Yes, and the demon still does it. And the
smallest machine that can is three states in a ring: U goes to V, V goes to W, W goes
to U, and the window shows “true” only at W. Start with candidates {U, V}; both
show false. Take one step. From U you now see false; from V you now see true. One
124   5 Learning borrows, committing pays


               step told them apart, and a ring forgets nothing, so a zero price meets the halving
               rule and is the price chosen here.
                  Two states can’t do it, ever, with any arrows, and this is the one that needs no
               price premise at all. If a machine has only two states and you can’t tell them apart at
               the first look, then the window shows the same thing on both, and those two are all
               the states there are, so the window shows the same thing everywhere, forever, and
               you never learn anything. Try to draw a counterexample. You’ll draw the same two
               dots a few times and give up, and the giving up is the proof. Three is the smallest
               number of states on which two states that look alike at the first look can come apart
               at a later look, and that’s what teaching is.


               Theorem 5.3 (Three states are the minimum for teaching at zero cost). Call a
               machine a zero-cost teacher when it has a cost satisfying the halving price, a list of
               candidates with no repeats containing the actual start, and a run of cost 0 after
               which the observer knows strictly more than after the first look, |K (Ω, t, s0 )| <
               |K (Ω, [ ], s0 )|. There is a zero-cost teacher with exactly three states, and there is
               none with two or fewer.

               Proof. Three: the ring U → V → W → U with the window true only at W,
               candidates {U, V }, one step, cost 0 (a ring is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies the
               halving price). Two or fewer: the actual start is always in the observer’s knowledge,
               so knowing strictly more after the run needs at least two candidates still left after
               the first look, which agree there. On a machine with two or fewer states those two
               are all the states there are, so the window takes one value everywhere and no later
               look can separate them. This half never uses the price at all.

               Finish together, for the first time
               Run the machine from N different starts and photograph its full configuration at
               every tick. Put the photographs in rows, one row per start, one column per tick.
               Every run finishes for the first time at tick T. Through that finish, two different
               states in the same column must have different successors.
                   The sheet has N ( T + 1) photographs, including the starts and finishes. Could two
               of them show the same full configuration? In the same column, cancel backwards
               and the starts would have to agree. In different columns, give both configurations
               the same remaining steps. One run would finish before its promised first finish.
               Every photograph has to show a different configuration.
                                                                                      5.6 The certainty bound   125




Theorem 5.4 (Room for synchronized first completion). Let F be a total rule, A
a set of N distinct starts, and H a completion reading. For every a ∈ A, suppose
F T ( a) ∈ H and F t ( a) ∈
                          / H for t < T. Suppose F is injective on { F t ( a) : a ∈ A} for
each t < T. Then all states F t ( a), with a ∈ A and 0 ≤ t ≤ T, are distinct. Any
carrier containing these runs therefore has at least N ( T + 1) configurations.

Proof. First compare photographs in the same column. If two showed the same state,
look one column back. The rule keeps different sources in that column apart, so
their predecessors must already have been the same. Repeat until the first column:
the starts agree. Thus different starts cannot give the same photograph at the same
time.
    Now compare different columns. Suppose run a at time i shows what run b
shows later, at time j, with i < j ≤ T. Run b has T − j ticks left before its first finish.
Starting from the identical state, run a must follow those same remaining steps and
finish too. Its time would then be i + ( T − j), earlier than T because i < j. That
contradicts the first-finish promise for run a.
    No two places on the sheet can therefore show the same full configuration. There
are N rows and T + 1 columns, counting time zero, so the machine needs at least
N ( T + 1) different configurations to hold the sheet.
    That is the room required by the whole sheet of possible runs. The photographs
can come from separate executions of one machine. What keeps different columns
apart is the common first finish: a cycle with no such finish can put the same state
in several columns. 2


5.6 The certainty bound

Now I can put the whole path from not knowing to knowing on one page, with
what it costs. You don’t know which state the machine started in. There are a few
it could have been, each with its chance; that’s your uncertainty. Run the machine.
Every one of those possible starting states goes somewhere, and only two things can
happen to a pair of them. Either they land on one state, and the difference between
them is gone from the machine: a merge, and the halving price charges for it, at
most one bit a unit. Or they land on two states, and the difference is still in the
machine, sitting in its state, kept as two states held apart. There’s no third thing a
pair of possibilities can do. So the uncertainty about where it started splits exactly
  2 The count is of full configurations, rather than simultaneously running machines or newly allocated

memory cells.
126   5 Learning borrows, committing pays


               in two: the part the merges destroyed, paid for in cost, and the part the end state
               still holds, paid for by the states it keeps apart.
                   Now put an observer at the window. Whatever they see is fixed by where the
               machine started, so whatever they learn is a fact about the start. And the same split
               holds for it: what they learned is either still held in the machine’s end state, or it’s
               gone from the machine and a merge paid for losing it. A run that costs nothing
               leaves every bit the observer learned still held in the machine. This is the precise
               sense of “learning borrows”: the observer’s copy is a copy, and the machine still
               holds the original. When the machine lets go of the original, a merge happens, and
               the cost comes due.
                   Said exactly, then: take a spread p over starting states and a run t, and write q
               for the spread of where the run ends. For an end state z with q(z) > 0, the starts
               that end at z have chances p( x )/q(z) between them; call that the spread of the start
               given z, and average its entropy over the ends:

                                                         ∑ q(z) H start given z .
                                                                                 
                                   H (start | end) =
                                                         z: q(z)>0

               This is how many bits you’d still be missing about the start if someone told you the
               end. Do the same for anything v that’s fixed by the start, like the whole film of what
               the window showed: H (v | end) is what you’d still be missing about v once you
               knew the end.



               Theorem 5.5 (The certainty bound). On a finite deterministic machine with an
               entropy-priced cost (Definition 3.6), take any spread p over starting states, any run
               t, and anything v that the start fixes. Then (1) H ( p) = H (start | end) + H (q): the
               uncertainty about the start is the part the run destroyed plus the part the end state
               still holds; (2) H (start | end) ≤ cost(t): the destroyed part was paid for, at most
               one bit a unit; (3) H (v | end) ≤ H (start | end) ≤ cost(t): whatever the end state
               can’t tell you about what an observer saw was paid for in cost, and everything else
               the observer learned is still held in the end state. In particular, after a run that costs
               nothing, the end state fixes everything the window showed, for every start with a
               positive chance.

               Proof. (1) Treat the whole run as one map from starts to ends; the proof of The-
                                                                                           q(z )
               orem 3.18 works for any map, so H ( p) − H (q) = ∑ x p( x ) log2 p( xx) , where z x
               is where x ends. Group the starts by where they end: for each z the terms
                                      p( x )   q(z)
               add up to q(z) ∑ x→z q(z) log2 p( x) = q(z) H (start given z). Adding over z gives
               H (start | end). (2) Let the run’s moves be i1 , . . . , in , and let q0 = p, q1 , . . . , qn = q
               be the spreads after each step. Entropy pricing says step k removes at most its own

cost: H (qk−1 ) − H (qk ) ≤ cost(ik ). Add over the steps: H ( p) − H (q) ≤ cost(t),
and by (1) the left side is H (start | end). (3) Fix an end z. Given z, the value of
v is a function of the start, so its spread given z is the spread of the start given z
pushed through that function, and by Theorem 3.18 (again for any map) a push
never adds bits. So H (v given z) ≤ H (start given z) for every z, and averaging
with weights q(z) gives the first inequality; (2) gives the second. With cost(t) = 0,
H (v | end) = 0, so each end state with a chance leaves one value of v.
    Entropy pricing and the halving price are the same premise (Theorem 3.16), so
the theorem holds under either. There are three things it doesn’t say. It doesn’t say
how much heat; that’s Landauer’s premise, applied to the destroyed part, H (start |
end), which is the uncertainty the run really removed. It doesn’t say the observer’s
own notes cost nothing: they need somewhere to be stored, such as a blank page.
Supplying that page is an initial condition; resetting an uncertain page for reuse
is a separate operation. And with a known start, p on one state, every term is
zero: nothing to learn, nothing destroyed, no positive floor from this premise. To
ask what heat the step or the observer actually produces, give its physical process
and preparation. The entropy calculation has not already charged somebody for
knowing.
    So the path between uncertainty and certainty runs both ways round. Going
in, certainty is got by narrowing what’s possible, and the deterministic calculation
separates distinctions lost from distinctions retained. A copy can put a retained
distinction in an observer’s memory. It need not allocate a fresh cell at every step,
and an initially held distinction needs no new crossing. The theorem counts entropy
lost under its pricing premise; it does not put every act of knowing on a heat ledger.


5.7 What the toll prices, said at last

Now I can say, more precisely than I could two chapters ago, what the unit of cost
in Section 2 is charged for. It is not charged for learning. What you know can be
narrowed with nothing merged, and an honest price list that charges merges can
leave it at zero; the demon is one machine where that happens. It is not charged
for looking, or for copying, or for finding out. Their physical dissipation depends
on the implementation. In the copying examples here they use a supplied blank:
the demon’s blank pad, the watcher’s own notes, a page somewhere that was blank
and now isn’t. But they borrow that page, and while the original is still there to
check against, the copy can be handed back. The unit is charged for the one thing in
Section 3 that couldn’t be done without merging, on a machine with finitely many
states: raising a flag that stays up, a record nothing hands back. Learning is the
demon writing on a blank pad, which merges nothing. What the demon pays for
is the wipe, a step where two states land on one. The unit in Section 2 is charged
128   5 Learning borrows, committing pays


               for the same reason, because raising a flag that stays up also lands two states on
               one, but it’s a different step: the demon machine has no flag, and its price list prices
               merges; commitments never appear in it. It is the same kind of landing in a different
               step: learning borrows, and committing pays.
                   So this is exactly what “No Free Insight,” the name I gave the toll before I
               understood it, covers, because I don’t want the name doing work it hasn’t earned.
               Insight in the sense of finding out can come with no merge and no cost; it borrows a
               page. The insight the toll prices is the kind made to stay, written into a record the
               machine can’t silently revise. Whether that narrower thing deserves the name is a
               fair thing to argue about; I kept the name because it’s the question I started with,
               and because the narrowing is the finding. I don’t count it as a retreat.
                   It also tells you how to read a bound that’s coming. Section 9 counts what it takes
               to narrow a list of candidates down to a shorter one: at least as many yes-or-no
               questions as it takes to point at the survivors among their rivals, a counting fact
               that holds for anything with a list in it. Turning that count into a cost, saying a run
               actually paid that many units, is a different claim, and when the book makes it, for
               any Thiele machine in Section 9, the payment goes in as a hypothesis, in one of two
               ways: a decision tree (a branching chart of yes-or-no questions, which Section 9
               builds) no deeper than the number of paid steps the run took is handed in, along
               with the lists themselves and the fact that the tree’s leaves cover the narrowing; or
               the run makes the narrowing itself, with every test step charged at least one and
               each test it passes keeping at least a set share of the candidates. This section is the
               reason it has to go in that way. The narrowing alone doesn’t force anyone to pay; the
               demon just showed you a narrowing charged nothing at all. So wherever narrowing
               gets a price in this book, the payment is a premise, and I’ll keep calling it one.
                   There is one more boundary. This whole section is about a machine that’s
               finite and deterministic and a watcher who crosses candidates off a list. There’s
               no quantum anything in it. This narrowing has nothing to do with “observation
               collapses the state”: the narrowing here is bookkeeping in the watcher’s list, the
               machine never notices, and the result would be the same if the watcher were a filing
               cabinet. In 2010 a group in Tokyo (Toyabe, Sagawa, Ueda, Muneyuki and Sano) did
               run a real demon, a tiny particle walked up a staircase of potential by feedback on
               what a camera saw, and the energy it gained was paid for by the information the
               camera took, with no violation of anything. The demon is real, it works, and it pays.
               Where it pays is the part that took a century.
                   What I still owe: everything so far says “costs at least one” and I’ve been keeping
               the cost on the side of the page, a running total you tally as you go. Part II first
               says what structure is; then comes the next question (Section 7). What happens
               when the machine keeps that total itself, inside its own state, where a step could in
                                                               5.7 What the toll prices, said at last   129


principle reach in and change it? That’s the counter, and it’s the next thing I have to
build.

          Part I found what keeping takes on a single cell and wrote it into a step. Part II
      is step three: the rest of structure is the same thing at a bigger size. It starts with
      the word itself, structure, and what the people who wrestled with it left behind,
      and comes out where Part I started, at a sorting of a pile into groups, a distinction
      held. Then it asks what follows, on any machine, once a distinction is kept and the
      keeping is charged, before I build one. The counter is the ledger, and it uses up
      states too: a number that only climbs takes a fresh value for every unit of cost. A
      window is what’s left when you stop looking at some parts of the state, and it can
      hide the very distinction that was paid for. Entitlement and insight ask what a later
      step may do because a distinction stayed. The latch is the blank cell’s no-to-yes over
      any machine at all, a reading the machine’s own steps turn on and nothing turns off,
      and a row of latches is a direction that only goes one way. The diagonal is the wall
      no level gets past: no state codes every question about the states (Part I proved that
      much), and no machine that can hand a program its own code, and can run the flip
      of a verdict as one of its own programs, can sort all its programs, from inside, by a
      question about what they do that some pass and some fail.
CHAPTER 6




What structure is

Part I put a charge beside a new permanent reading under explicit pricing rules.
This chapter starts with one yes-or-no question, states the ruler under which it is the
smallest way to sort, and goes after the rest of it. This whole section is about one
word, and I’ll give it to you now, so you can decide whether to stay: structure.
    I used that word for most of my life without once looking at it, which I suspect is
true of most people and most words, and it’s fine, right up until you do something
stupid. The stupid thing I did was build a machine that keeps a running total of
its costs, and the total has one rule I couldn’t talk it out of. You can arrange things
however you like, and the ledger lets you put any price on the arranging, including
none; the arranging has whatever physical cost its implementation imposes. But
the moment an arrangement has to stay, the moment you ask the machine to keep
it, or to vouch for it, to put its own name on the claim that these things belong
together, there’s a charge, and it isn’t zero. Charged in what? Physical changes have
costs determined by the implementation and protocol; keeping something takes
more on top, a merge or fresh states. Section 3 showed there is no other way for
a machine that picks its own next step to pay; when the moves are picked from
outside, whoever picks them is holding the difference. How much, why I picked the
one I did, and whether I had any business picking it at all: Part I went through all of
that. What was in front of me, standing there with the thing built, was a model that
charges for keeping structure, and I could not have told you what structure was. It
didn’t care. It can’t nod along the way a person does. It needed the word to hold
still, and the word had never held still for anyone, least of all me. (The model is
already on the page: five parts and one rule, which you met in Section 2. Part III
builds one small machine (Section 15) that meets it, so you can see a complete
example. Until then the rule is all that matters.)
    So I went looking at the people who’d wrestled it before me. Some of them have
been dead two thousand years and are still, I’d bet money, better at this than I am. I
used everything I had: language models, more than one, books, libraries, my own
gut, anything in reach. I don’t know if I found enough. I never do. There’s always
another shelf behind the one I was reading. And being dead and famous is not the


                                                 133
134   6 What structure is


               same as being right, so I pushed on each of them, and what follows is what I could
               reach, pushed on as hard as I know how. The one thing I’m asking is that you push
               on it with me, out loud, at your own kitchen table, because the first time through I
               was the only one checking, and that’s not enough people.
                   What they left me, pushed on, comes to a few sentences, and I’ll set them down
               here rather than walk you through everyone who said them. The relation came first;
               the number, when there is one, is a name for the relation, and sometimes there isn’t
               a name. Structure is something laid in, and the stuff it’s laid into doesn’t carry it by
               itself; the structure of a collection is not one more member of the collection, and the
               plan isn’t a brick. Sameness is coinciding under a move. Once you can say when
               two things count as the same, you’ve earned the right to name the thing they share:
               you sort a pile. Structure is what survives a chosen set of changes, and “chosen”
               is doing real work in that sentence; there’s no structure of a thing from nowhere.
               What a thing is is how it maps: structure lives in the maps. And the charge this book
               opened with is on one step a machine takes; how long anybody’s description of a
               thing is doesn’t enter it. Here is where mathematical logic eventually put the word
               down, which is also where it holds still.


               6.1 A set with some named relations

               What mathematical logic eventually settled on, with the logician Alfred Tarski giving
               the field its name, “the theory of models,” in 1954, is almost boring, and the boring
               ones are the ones that last. A structure is a set, called the domain, plus whatever
               relations and functions a chosen vocabulary names on it. Pick the vocabulary (Klein
               again: you choose), and a structure is anything that gives those names a meaning.
               Now I want to say “the smallest one,” and the word “smallest” has no meaning until
               I say what I’m measuring, so here is the ruler: count the names in the vocabulary
               first; when that ties, count how many things each name takes at once; when that
               ties too, count how many answers each name can give. The bottom of that ruler, for
               anything that takes things at all, is one name, taking one thing at a time, with two
               possible answers, which is a domain with one yes-or-no property named on it: one
               question, put to each thing. A single two-place relation (“these two go together”)
               can sort a pile too, and so can a single function that sends each thing to a label,
               but the first takes two things at once, and the second can give a different answer
               for every thing, more than two on any pile of three or more, so the ruler puts both
               above one question. There are two limits, and I’ll give them to you now, so you
               don’t have to find them. A vocabulary with one named constant (“this one, here”)
               takes no things at all, so it sits even lower on my ruler, and by itself it doesn’t sort
               anything, so the claim is “smallest that sorts.” Comparing things with the constant
               takes equality, and I count equality as a name when a structure uses it, one that
                                                                        6.2 Laying them all down   135


takes two things at once. Leave it uncounted, as first-order logic does, and the
constant sorts below one question: “is it this one?” splits a pile into that thing and
the rest, which is still a split in two, one question whose yes is a single thing. Plain
“smallest” would be false. And one question only splits the domain into two groups
when some things answer yes and some answer no; if they all agree there’s one
group and nothing was sorted. With those limits said, and with the ruler said: by the
count of names, the smallest structure that sorts anything is one question. Someone
with a different ruler might land somewhere else, and I’d want to see where. Least
information lands one bit lower, on the partition this section ends up starting from:
on a nonempty pile of n things a question can come out 2n ways, and a split into
at most two groups with neither one called yes can come out half as many. The bit
between them is the label, which group says yes. Keep it. It’s about to turn into the
whole section.


6.2 Laying them all down

Now lay those sentences on top of each other and see what shows through. I see
seven things. They’re my overlay, the places where I see the people who said them
agreeing. They never proved it together; some of them never met, and some of them
disagree (Eilenberg and Mac Lane put maps and their composition at the centre;
Shannon’s structure and Tarski’s are two different words). You’re in a position to
tell me if I’m seeing things.
    A list of seven slogans would be easy to nod at and impossible to check, so I’m
going to carry one thing through all seven and let you watch each one add to the
one before it. The thing is a square, side, diagonal and all: draw one. Draw a few
more on the same sheet: one small, one big, the small one again but tilted, and one
stretched out into a long rectangle. You’ll want a pile.
    Structure is about relations among things, and the things themselves aren’t it.
You see that in the diagonal, the bronze, Leibniz’s room, Bourbaki’s unspecified
elements, Tarski’s named relations and the arrows. On your sheet, what makes a
square a square was never the ink. It’s that the four sides match and the corners are
square, and that the diagonal stands to the side the way it does whether or not any
number names it. Every one of those is a relation among parts. But on its own this
first thing is too loose to use, because a sheet of paper is drowning in relations: this
square is left of that one, this one is nearer the coffee ring. Which relations count?
    Structure is what stays the same under a chosen set of changes. You see that
in Euclid’s triangles laid together, Klein’s allowed moves, Noether’s symmetry, and
Frege’s direction that every parallel line shares. This second thing gives the answer
the first thing was missing: the relations that count are the ones that survive the
moves you’ve decided to allow. Slide the small square across the sheet, turn it, and
136   6 What structure is


               the diagonal still stands to the side exactly as before; “left of the coffee ring” doesn’t
               make it across. The second thing is a filter on the first.
                   The same structure can be carried by different stuff: the statue in marble, or two
               sets that answer the same vocabulary the same way. The third thing is the second
               again with one more change allowed, which is to swap the material. Cut the square
               out of cardboard, or lay it out in string on the table, and if the relations survive, it’s
               the same square in every way you agreed to care about. Aristotle’s bronze is one
               more thing you agreed not to look at, and the wooden sandwich is what happens
               when the material was never on that list.
                   The first act of structure is a sameness that sorts a pile you were already given.
               It’s there in Euclid’s first common notion, Frege’s direction, Tarski’s one question,
               and Russell’s letter, with Zermelo’s repair that you must start from a pile. At this
               point the overlay stopped being a list for me and turned into a shape, so slow down
               here with me. Look at your pile of drawings and say: two of them count as the same
               when an allowed move, for now a slide or a turn, carries one exactly onto the other.
               Watch what happens to the pile. It falls into groups. The small square and its tilted
               twin go together; the big one sits on its own; the rectangle sits on its own. And it
               falls cleanly, nothing half in one group and half in another, for a reason you can
               check. Klein’s allowed moves always come with three guarantees: doing nothing
               counts as a move, every move can be undone, and two moves in a row is again a
               move. Those three are, in different clothes, “everything is the same as itself,” “if this
               matches that, then that matches this,” and “if this matches that and that matches a
               third, then this matches the third.” Put the last two together and you get Euclid’s
               first common notion, “things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to
               one another.” So the second thing, sameness under chosen moves, is a sorting of the
               pile the moment you ask which drawings it calls the same. Frege did it with lines
               and parallels. Tarski’s one question does it in the crudest way there is, by cutting
               the pile in two. And the pile has to be there first, because a sameness has to be a
               sameness among something; that’s Russell’s letter, and Zermelo’s repair.
                   Adding structure rules possibilities out. Every one of Euclid’s postulates rules one
               out. Half of English is already decided. A conserved quantity limits where a system
               can go. On your sheet: once the small square and its tilted twin are in one group,
               you’ve given up the right to answer any question the moves respect differently for
               the two of them. Tell me the side of one and the diagonal of the other isn’t an open
               question any more. A sorting rules out a whole bundle of possibilities at once.
                   Held structure gets used without re-deriving it. You see that in Shannon’s
               saving in time, Rissanen’s compression, Parnas’s one-module-at-a-time, and Leibniz’s
               analysis of situation (reasoning about where things are straight from their relations,
               with no coordinates laid down first). The fifth thing pays off here: the possibilities
               you ruled out are ones you never have to check again. Know which group a drawing
                                                                            6.3 The smallest piece   137


is in and you know everything the group shares without getting the ruler out, the
same way the row of 01 never needed writing out. There’s one catch, and I’ll need a
whole section for it: it only pays if you kept the sorting somewhere you can read it
back.
    And structure is always relative to a chosen frame, whether that frame is Klein’s
group, the vocabulary, the code you compress against, or Parnas’s criteria. Nobody
gets to say “the” structure of a thing without saying from where, and I do it constantly,
so watch me for it. On your sheet: allow stretching as one of the moves and the
rectangle walks over and joins the squares; allow only slides and turns and it doesn’t.
Same pile, same ink, different groups, because I chose different moves. The groups
were never in the paper. They were in the paper and the choice, together.
    I think the seven hang together this way. Relations are what structure is made
of. The chosen moves pick which relations count, and a change of material is just
one more move. Asking which things the moves call the same sorts the pile. The
sorting rules possibilities out, and what’s ruled out is what you get to skip later. And
because the moves were chosen, all of it is relative. Read that way, the fourth thing
sits in the middle: it’s where the first three turn into something you can write down,
and where the last three get their start.
    That’s my reason for starting the next subsection with a sorting, and I want to be
exact about what kind of reason it is, because it’s mine. None of these people said
“start with a partition.” Klein would tell you to start with the moves, Eilenberg and
Mac Lane with the arrows, Shannon with the probabilities. What I can actually point
at is narrower. In the framings about when two things are the same shape or the
same kind (Euclid laying one triangle on another, Klein’s moves, Frege’s directions,
Tarski’s question) there’s a moment where somebody decides what counts as the
same, and that decision, written down, is a sorting of a pile. In Shannon, Rissanen
and Noether I can’t find that moment as cleanly, and I’m not going to bend them
until I do. So the overlay doesn’t prove that a sorting comes first. It shows me where
the framings I trust most keep putting their first foot down, and I’m putting mine
there too.
    I looked for a framing that denies any of the seven and didn’t find one, which
could mean there isn’t one or could mean I didn’t look where it lives. If you know of
one, I’d like to see it.


6.3 The smallest piece

Now the sentence I wanted to say at the top and had no right to until here, and even
here I have to split it in two, because half of it is a textbook fact and the other half
is me. The piece of structure I’m going to start from is a partition.
138   6 What structure is


                  The textbook half: a partition and an equivalence relation are the same object.
               That’s Paul Halmos, Naive Set Theory, 1960, section seven, and you could read that
               section before dinner. I’ll say it in words first. Take any pile of things. An equivalence
               relation on it is a way of saying “these two count as the same” that behaves the way
               sameness should: everything is the same as itself; if a is the same as b then b is the
               same as a; and if a is the same as b and b the same as c, then a is the same as c.
               Every such relation sorts the pile into groups, the things that count as the same go
               together, and every sorting into groups hands you back a relation, “same group.” Do
               one and then the other and you land where you started, in both directions. So a
               partition and an equivalence relation are one object seen from two sides, and that’s
               the fourth thing on the overlay, the sorting of a given pile, now with a name and a
               page number.
                  I’ll give it in the exact form too, since this is the first place the book uses one.
               A set is a pile, x ∈ X means “x is in the pile X,” and a relation on X is any rule ∼
               that, for each pair of things, says whether x ∼ y holds. A few more symbols show
               up below, and each is a word in disguise. The buckets are written S j , with j saying
               which bucket (finitely many buckets in every example here, though nothing below
               needs that). A cap, S j ∩ Sl , is “what the two buckets share,” and ∅ is the empty pile.
               And curly braces with a colon, { y ∈ X : y ∼ x }, mean “the pile of every y in X for
               which y ∼ x holds”; the theorem writes that pile [ x ], the things that count as the
               same as x.

               Definition 6.1 (Equivalence relation, partition). A relation ∼ on a set X is an
               equivalence relation when it is reflexive (x ∼ x), symmetric (x ∼ y implies y ∼ x),
               and transitive (x ∼ y and y ∼ z imply x ∼ z). A partition of X is a collection of
               non-empty subsets of X, the blocks, such that every member of X lies in exactly one
               block. Spelled out, with the blocks written S j : each S j is non-empty, no two share
               a member (S j ∩ Sl = ∅ when j ̸= l), and together they cover everything (every
