               member of X lies in some S j ).



               Theorem 6.1 (Sameness and sorting are one object). Every equivalence relation
               on X determines a partition, whose blocks are the classes [ x ] = { y ∈ X : y ∼ x };
               every partition determines an equivalence relation, “x and y lie in the same block”;
               and the two constructions undo each other.

               Proof. The classes are non-empty (x ∈ [ x ] by reflexivity) and cover X. If z lies in
               [ x ] and in [y], then z ∼ x and z ∼ y, so x ∼ y by symmetry and transitivity, and
               then [ x ] = [y] by symmetry and transitivity again (anything the same as x is the
               same as y, and the other way round); so two classes either coincide or don’t overlap.
                                                                                      6.4 Buckets   139


Going the other way, take a partition and say two things match when they share
a block. Each thing shares its block with itself. If one shares a block with another,
the other shares it with the first. And if x shares with y and y shares with z, both
blocks contain y. A partition puts y in only one block, so all three share that block.
These are exactly reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. Going relation to partition
to relation returns “x and y share a class,” which holds exactly when x ∼ y (if x ∼ y
then x and y both lie in [y]; if both lie in [z] then x ∼ z and, by symmetry, z ∼ y, so
x ∼ y), so it is the original relation. Going partition to relation to partition returns
the original blocks, because the class of x under “same block” is exactly the block
that contains x.
    All of this is textbook mathematics (Halmos, section 7), and the book uses it as a
foundation. I’m claiming nothing new in it.
    And the smallest structure that sorts, by my ruler in Tarski’s setup, the one
question, is the same object a third time. Put a yes-or-no question to every thing in
the pile. The ones that say yes are one group and the ones that say no are the other.
Going the other way, a two-group partition becomes a question the moment you
point at one group and call it “yes.” The only thing a question has that the partition
doesn’t is which group got the label. So the set theorist’s first step and the logician’s
first step are the same step, and nobody has to pick a side, which is a relief, because
it’s an argument you can lose with yourself for a long time.
    So much for the textbook half. The other half is mine, so hold it looser, because
Halmos says nothing about “smallest” or “first” and I’d be lying if I let his page
number carry my sentence. In what I’m going to build, the order goes: a pile, then
groups in the pile, then whatever connects one group to another, and the groups
come first because a question needs something to be about and a connection needs
somewhere to land. That’s an order for my construction. It is not a law that every
account of structure has to start by sorting. You could start with an ordering instead
(“this one comes before that one”), or with arrows between the things themselves
and no groups at all, and people do, and nothing I’ve shown you rules that out. So
the honest sentence is: a partition is where I chose to start, it is the smallest start by
the ruler I gave you, and I chose it because it’s the first thing that can be right or
wrong about a pile and the last thing I could take away without everything I build
on it coming down. If you have a smaller start by a ruler you can state, I want to see
it. It would change this book.


6.4 Buckets

So I’ll do the smallest piece once, for real. Take everything in front of you and sort it
into buckets, with nothing in two buckets and nothing left on the floor, and that’s
the whole of the definition. It’s the thing you do with a kindergartner and a pile
140   6 What structure is


               of blocks, and I am aware that I’ve just marched you past two thousand years of
               people to arrive at a pile of blocks. Keep the blocks anyway. They’re about to cost
               you something.
                   Take ten blocks, and put the red ones in one bucket, the square ones in another
               and everything else in a third. Now a red square turns up, as they do, and you’ve
               got your first crisis: it belongs in two buckets and the rule says one. So this isn’t
               a partition yet, and you have to decide which bucket wins. That decision is the
               whole thing, because a partition is a pile of small rulings like that one, and once
               you’ve made them all, the pile is holding a fact it wasn’t holding a minute ago. The
               formal version says the same thing with fewer words and more squiggles, and you’ve
               already seen it: it’s the definition of a partition in the last subsection (Definition 6.1),
               which asks for non-empty buckets, with nothing in two and nothing on the floor.
                   The next part isn’t kindergarten. Why would that fact cost anything? Watch
               what it does to one question. Before the buckets, “are these two in the same group?”
               means working it out: go find the first one, go find the second one, apply the rule
               to each, and compare. After the buckets, it’s a glance: read the first one’s bucket,
               read the second one’s bucket, and you’re done. With each block’s address already in
               hand, and a table that retrieves a label in one operation, that is two lookups whether
               the pile has ten blocks or a billion. Those are access and cost assumptions. A pile
               with no addresses, or an index that must be searched, has not been given that same
               two-lookup rule. What you’re looking at is Shannon’s saving in time and Parnas’s
               one-module-at-a-time, the sixth thing on the overlay, showing up in a kindergarten.
                   Look at what makes that glance possible: a table, with a written-down line for
               each block saying which bucket it went in. The partition is the fact; the table is one
               way of holding the fact so it can be read back fast, and you had to build the table,
               and you have to store it, and it has to be the kind of thing you can read in one look
               (a bucket number, say; a list of every block in the bucket would have you searching
               through it again). Anybody who’s used a database has met this table; it’s what an
               index is, and an index is a thing you build, store, and keep up to date, and every
               part of that takes something. Take the table away and keep the partition and you’re
               back to working it out. And sometimes there was never a search to save: if the rule
               is “evens here, odds there,” you can answer “same group?” by looking at the last
               digit of each, no buckets needed. What survives is that holding a sorting in a form
               you can read back is worth something, and building that form cost something, and
               those are already two different events. Building the table, storing it, checking that
               it’s right, and deciding to rely on it are four different things. The first cost question
               I want to put to that structure lives in the gap between the third and the fourth.
               Nothing in the kindergarten has shown a charge in that gap. It has separated the
               acts well enough to ask.
                                                                                   6.4 Buckets   141


    So who, in everything I read, says what has to be paid? I found three answers that
come close, and I’ll be exact about how close, because this is the edge of what I know.
Rolf Landauer, in 1961, and Charles Bennett after him, say that any step which takes
two possible situations and makes them one, erasing a bit or merging two paths a
computation could have taken, has a heat floor when it removes uncertainty under
their thermodynamic assumptions. That is a physical claim about how the device
and its surroundings are prepared, Landauer’s principle, and in this book it is always
a premise, never something I prove. It’s the place, of all I’ve found, where a fact
about information turns into a fact about heat, though at room temperature the
amount for one bit is far too small to show up on anybody’s electricity bill. In 2012
a lab in Lyon erased one bit, held in a single tiny bead, and measured the average
heat it gave off coming down toward Landauer’s floor as the erasing was slowed,
and other labs have found the same since. Not everyone accepts the principle in
general, and I’ll come back to the people who don’t. Is sending blocks to buckets
a step of that kind? Push on it, because the answer depends on what you keep. If
you keep each block and write its bucket next to it on a spot you knew was blank,
you’ve merged nothing; you can read the block right back off the pair. You have
spent something, though: the blank spot the label now sits on, which the machine
hadn’t used before, and any heat from the writing depends on its implementation.
Bennett’s whole point in his 1973 paper was that a computation which keeps its
inputs, and keeps enough of its working to retrace its steps, can be run without
any merging step at all, and it pays for that by taking fresh states. If instead you
throw the block away and keep only the bucket label, then two different blocks
can leave the same label behind, and that is a many-to-one step, the kind Landauer
charges for. Both are things people call “sorting into buckets.” Only the second
loses a distinction. So the bucket by itself doesn’t hand you Landauer’s heat. The
forgetting does, when there is forgetting, and keeping instead is paid for with fresh
states. Whether a given machine forgets is a question about that machine. It has to
be answered on the page, and I won’t wave at it here. Rissanen says a model is paid
for in the bits it takes to state, and Grünwald says the price depends on the code.
Parnas says a bad cut is paid for later, at two in the morning. And that’s where it
stops. Rovelli, back in Section 5, prices a choice that sticks, and his choice is one
nobody could predict, which that section showed is a different act. I couldn’t find
anyone who says that the moment you vouch for a grouping, the moment you stand
behind “these belong together,” has a price of its own. Just arranging them that way
is a different act. That could mean nobody says it. It could mean I didn’t find the
person who does. I honestly can’t tell you which.
    So that’s where I am at the end of one word. A grouping, the act of making it, the
information kept about it, and a commitment to rely on it are different things. The
blocks let you separate them with your hands. Now take them down to the smallest
142   6 What structure is


               case there is, a bucket with two sides, one block, and a ruling that sticks, which is a
               cell going from blank to 0, the case Part I started from and showed what keeping
               it takes. The construction I will study keeps selected distinctions in a state. Some
               are there from the start. Some are newly recorded. Those are different cases: a box
               that already says YES can sit there forever under a do-nothing rule, with neither a
               merge nor fresh states. Part I’s count starts with NO and follows a new YES that
               stays under a fixed total rule. That is the case to which its merge-or-fresh conclusion
               applies. A grouping by itself does not supply that run or its price.
CHAPTER 7




The counter

Everything so far has kept the count of cost on the side of the page. You played
Section 2’s toy, you made a tally as you went, and the tally lived in your hand. The
machine never saw it. A tally takes a state it has never used for each unit it records
and never goes back to an old one, and putting it inside the machine doesn’t change
that; it only makes the machine the one paying with those fresh states. That’s fine
for a toy. For anything that’s going to run on its own, with nobody tallying, the total
has to live somewhere the machine can reach, which means the machine can, in
principle, write it. So this section is about what a counter has to be before you’re
allowed to call it a receipt. I mean the counter of any machine whose state carries
a running total that every step bumps by whatever a price list says that step costs.
Section 2’s five parts don’t need one (there the total was a sum you did on the side),
so this is one piece added to the five, and the facts below are about anything that
has it. I’ll give you the answer first, because it’s short, and then spend the section on
why each word is there: a receipt is a total that lives in the state, that only climbs,
that equals the sum of what was charged, and that nothing else could have been.


7.1 A stick, split down the middle

The oldest receipt I could find that you can still hold is a piece of wood. From about
1100, under Henry the First, until 1826, the English treasury recorded what it was
owed on tally sticks: a strip of hazel, notched across with cuts of set widths (the
treasury’s own handbook from around 1180, the Dialogue of the Exchequer, gives
them: a thumb’s width for a hundred pounds, a swollen barleycorn for a pound,
a bare cut for a penny), then split lengthwise so that each half carried the same
notches. The payer kept one half, called the stock, which is one story for where the
word stockholder comes from. The treasury kept the other. When the time came to
settle, you laid the two halves together, and only the two original halves fit, because
wood splits along a grain nobody can copy. Add a notch to your half and the other
half shows a gap where the partner should be. Try to remove a notch and you find
that wood can’t be uncut. When they finally stopped using them, the clerks burned
centuries of old tallies in the furnaces under the House of Lords, overheated the flue,

                                                  143
144   7 The counter


              and burned down the Palace of Westminster, which I mention because it’s the best
              fact I picked up for this book and because it tells you how many of them there were.
                  Do it: draw a border round a strip of card, notch it once for every coin you hand
              a friend, then split it lengthwise through the notches and keep half each. Don’t trim
              the edge or swap in a fresh strip. Now add a notch to one half and put them back
              together. You’ll see the mismatch straight away. And you can’t put a cut back: a
              patch is just one more thing to look at. The total is the notches, one per coin, and
              under that rule the count only climbs. Both halves started with the same count, so if
              they disagree now, somebody changed one. The mismatch won’t tell you who. What
              the stick gives you is a comparison you can make, not an object nobody can forge
              and not a verdict on who cheated.
                  Economists read the same stick another way, and they’re not wrong either. Alfred
              Mitchell-Innes (1913) made the exchequer tally his star witness that money is credit:
              the crown paid the people it owed by “raising a tally” on some branch of its revenue,
              a wooden acknowledgment of debt. A receipt to me, money to him, and it’s the same
              piece of wood. Narayana Kocherlakota (1998) later proved a version of his point: in
              a wide class of economies where nobody can be held to a promise, anything money
              lets people do, a memory of everyone’s past dealings lets them do too. His title says
              it in three words: money is memory.


              7.2 Why it has to climb
              Start with the second property, because it’s the one that does the most work and the
              one people fight hardest. Why can’t the counter ever go down?
                  The answer is in what the toll is for. The floor it buys, back in Section 2, says
              a run from NO to YES costs at least one. That sentence is a floor: it says the run
              paid at least this much. If the counter could come back down, a run could pay the
              toll, get its flag, and then take the payment back, and the floor would be a floor
              on nothing; “this run cost at least one” would be true of a run that ended having
              cost nothing. So a counter that can fall is an accountant you can lean on to revise
              the books, and a floor stated in terms of it isn’t a floor. The counter only climbing
              is not a flourish; it’s what makes “at least” mean something. This ledger records
              cumulative charges, each a whole number of units and none negative, so it never
              decreases. A refundable balance, one that pays money back, would be a different
              accounting object with a different invariant, and the floor here says nothing about it.
              (In Section 2’s abstract theorem the total is a sum of whole numbers and climbing is
              automatic; this paragraph is about why a total stored in the state, where a step could
              in principle write it, has to be designed so that no step ever lowers it.)
                  The same rule turns up in two places that have nothing to do with each other,
              pointing in opposite directions, and that’s a big part of why I trust it. In 1978 Leslie
                                                                                7.2 Why it has to climb   145


Lamport asked how a set of computers that pass each other messages, with no shared
clock, could ever agree on what happened before what. His answer is a counter
per machine with two rules: add one before you do anything, and when a message
arrives carrying the sender’s count, jump your own counter above it (never below
your own). Those counters, he showed, respect cause and effect: if this caused that,
this has the smaller number. And they do it “with no actual timing mechanism,” his
words; they’re clocks only in name. Try it with three people passing notes and you’ll
see it work in two minutes, and then let one of them reset their counter to zero after
reading a note, and watch a reply come out numbered before the note it replies to.
A counter that goes down can’t be leaned on for order.
                                           message
                    Alice sends                               Bob receives
                     stamp 2                                    stamp 3


                                                    next local act


                   Alice receives                             Bob replies
                      stamp 5                                  stamp 4
                                            reply



                     Elsewhere, Carol numbers an unrelated act 1.
               A smaller stamp alone does not prove a causal connection.

Start Bob at zero and Alice just after her local act 1. On receipt, each raises the local count
                     above both its old value and the incoming stamp.
    Where did Lamport get it? In the notes he keeps on his own papers, he says the
timestamps came from an earlier note by Paul Johnson and Bob Thomas on keeping
copies of a database in step, whose algorithm wasn’t quite right: it let things happen
in an order that broke cause and effect. What let him see the fix, he says, was special
relativity, which teaches that the one order of events everybody agrees on is the
order of what could have caused what. And he passes on a line from Jim Gray, the
database pioneer whose commit comes back in Section 14: Gray had heard two
opinions of the paper, that it was trivial and that it was brilliant. Lamport’s answer
is that he can’t argue with the first and isn’t inclined to argue with the second. His
account stops at relativity, so the chase does too. It leaves a good picture behind:
these update rules put a smaller number on every cause than on its later effect,
without a shared clock. The converse fails: two people can number unrelated local
acts 1 and 2. The numbers alone do not say that the first caused the second.
    Now the other direction. In 1949 Alan Turing, and in 1967 Robert Floyd, each
asked how you prove a program stops. Both times the answer was to find a quantity
146   7 The counter


              that goes down on every step and can’t go down forever (a whole number that
              can’t go below zero, say). If every step lowers it and it can’t fall forever, the steps
              can’t go on forever. Up-only gives you order, and down-only gives you stopping.
              They’re different rules (one needs the jump-above-the-message step, the other needs
              a floor it can’t fall below), but they have the same shape, seen from the two ends:
              a one-way quantity is something you can build on, and a two-way quantity is a
              number that happens to be written down somewhere.
                  There’s also a real-world case where a counter was allowed to go down and got
              gamed exactly there. Ethereum, one of the largest blockchains, charges “gas” for
              every step of a program, and for years it refunded gas when a program freed up
              storage. Someone noticed you could fill storage when gas was cheap, hold it, and
              cash the refunds when gas was dear, and a token was built to do exactly that, and
              the real work in a block could reach nearly twice the block’s stated limit. In 2021 a
              change called EIP-3529 cut the refunds sharply (none for self-destruct, a smaller one
              for clearing storage, and a cap of one fifth of the gas used). The written reasons are
              the gas token and those overfull blocks. I read both as the same lesson: a counter
              that goes down was being leaned on at the place where it went down. Ethereum’s
              gas comes back in Section 17 as one of five small models of systems people actually
              run, and it’s the only one of the five that takes a fee at the moment of the write, and
              it’s instructive that the part they had to fix was the part that could fall.


              7.3 Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else

              The third property is the plainest one. The counter after a step is the counter before
              plus what that step was charged. Add up a whole run and the middle values cancel
              out, the way a sum of differences collapses to last minus first, and the total is the
              sum of the per-step charges. Why state it?
                  I state it because it’s the property that fails quietly. Say a machine charges one for
              raising a flag, and also, somewhere in its error handling, forgets to add the charge
              when the step fails halfway through. Or it charges two in one code path and one
              in another for the same move. Or it has one step that writes the counter directly.
              Then the counter is mostly the sum of the charges, and “mostly” is the whole gap
              between a receipt and a note that says “trust me, about this much.” Conservation is
              the sentence that there is no “mostly”: every step, every outcome, every error, adds
              exactly its charge, and a step that fails is charged the same as one that succeeds,
              because the charge is on the attempt. For a machine built the way I’m describing,
              that sentence is the rule the counter is updated by, so it can’t fail by definition. What
              can fail is the claim that a real machine is built that way, and checking that means
              going through every move it has, the failure branches included, one at a time, which
              is dull and is the whole job. The run-long form, counter at the end equals counter
                                           7.3 Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else   147


at the start plus the sum of the charges, then follows from the one-step rule by the
cancelling sum; it’s below. It’s the kind of theorem that looks boring and is the one
you’d most want if you were going to rely on the number. One thing it doesn’t say
is that every unit of cost bought something. The ledger is exact about what was
spent. What the spending was worth is another question, and whether a unit of cost
bought a real narrowing is Section 9’s question, and it needs a witness on top of the
ledger entry.

Which mergers does this counter cover?
Draw the arrows of one run and put a receipt beside each departure. Charge on
entry into a parked state and let the parked state idle free. The charge now depends
on where the step begins. You can check exactly which mergers those receipts cover.
    This paragraph changes the accounting interface explicitly. The basic Thiele
definition uses a fixed instruction price c(i ) ∈ N. Here one autonomous step F has a
source charge a(s) ∈ N; with supplied instructions the broader signature would be
ce(s, i ). Its bill must be summed along the actual run. The same instruction can now
cost differently at entry and at idle. The theorem below states its own charge and
coverage premises; it does not change the instruction-cost definition used elsewhere.
    Start at u and follow L steps. The source positions are u, F (u), . . . , F L−1 (u).
Mark a landing state if two different sources in that stretch lead to it. Count each
marked landing once and call the total Merge( L). Walking past the same source
twice still gives one source. The bill, meanwhile, adds the charge for every step
taken.
    The pricing rule is this: whenever two different observed sources share a succes-
sor, at least one of them pays. Give each source its charge a(s) and let the ledger
add exactly that charge. Now every marked landing has a receipt behind it.


Theorem 7.1 (Receipts covering the observed mergers). Let a(s) ∈ N be a source
charge and let µ( F (s)) = µ(s) + a(s). Suppose every pair of distinct observed
sources with the same successor has a positive charge on at least one member. Then
                                 L −1
                   Merge( L) ≤ ∑ a( F t (u)) = µ( F L (u)) − µ(u).
                                 t =0

Proof. Every counted landing state has a paid predecessor. One predecessor cannot
belong to two different landing states, since its successor is fixed. Thus there are at
least as many paid source occurrences as counted landing states, and each costs at
least one. The ledger equality follows by adding its updates.
148   7 The counter


                 Try it with no going to yes and yes going to itself. Charge one at no and zero at
              yes. Give those states ledger values zero and one. Entry adds the one; every later
              idle step adds zero. The collision is covered and the parked machine can stay parked
              for free.
                 Now ask that parked yes-state how many mergers your observation has exposed.
              After one step you have seen only no as a source: no merger yet. After two steps
              you have seen no and yes, both leading to yes: one merger. The endpoint in your
              hand is yes both times. It cannot tell you which observation you made.
                 Add a clock and you can keep that difference. The endpoints become (yes, 1)
              and (yes, 2). You can read the clock and recover the count for the old graph. Draw
              the new full graph, though, and those clock values keep its states apart. Keep both
              drawings on the bench so you can see which arrows you are counting. An external
              record of the observation length can keep the same missing information.


              7.4 Only one honest count

              The next property surprised me by being provable at all. Suppose you fixed the
              schedule: this move costs one, that move costs zero, and so on, for every move. And
              suppose someone else keeps their own books: their own function from states to
              totals, which starts at zero and, on every step, goes up by exactly what the schedule
              says. Could their books disagree with the machine’s counter, somewhere, on some
              state you can actually get to?
                 No, and the proof is the tally stick. Both totals start at zero. On every step both
              go up by the same amount. So on every state you can reach by steps from the start,
              they’re equal. Nothing more is needed. Agreement at the start survives the first
              move, then the second, then every move after it. This way of proving a statement
              for any finite number of moves is called induction. The mathematician’s word for
              this is initiality: the counter is the one bookkeeping that all the others, if they’re
              honest about the schedule, turn out to be. Given the schedule, the count is forced.
              There are two things about that sentence I had to be careful with, and they’re worth
              saying before the symbols. It doesn’t assume the other books climb: climbing follows
              from the schedule, since the schedule never charges a negative amount, so “only
              one honest count” and “it only climbs” aren’t two separate demands on the other
              bookkeeper. And it holds on reachable states only. A state you can’t get to from the
              start is one where it says nothing about whether the other books agree, which is the
              right thing for a receipt to say.
                 I’ll state the properties exactly now: first the piece being added to Section 2’s
              five, a counter and a price list, and then the two facts about it. A counter machine
              here means a machine that keeps this ledger. It isn’t Minsky’s counter machine, the
              two-counter base Part I mentioned; the word is the same and the thing is different,
                                                                         7.4 Only one honest count   149


and Section 15 keeps the two apart. The counter gets the Greek letter µ (mu), which
is the letter the machine in Part III uses for it (Theorem 15.6).

Definition 7.1 (A counter kept by a price list). A counter machine has a set of states,
a set of moves, a step function apply that takes a state and a move, a start state sinit ,
a schedule c giving each move a cost in N, and a counter µ from states to N, such
that µ(sinit ) = 0 and µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + c(i ) for every state s and move i, with
no exceptions. A run of a list t of moves from s applies them in order, and c(t) is
the sum of their costs. A state is reachable when it is the start or is apply(s, i ) for a
reachable s and some i.



Theorem 7.2 (Conservation). In a counter machine, for every state s and every
list t, µ at the end of the run of t from s equals µ(s) + c(t). In particular µ never
decreases along a run.

Proof. Write the starting counter at the top of a column. Under it write the charge
for the first move, then the charge for the second, and continue to the end of the
run. After the first move the counter is the sum of the first two entries, because that
is its one-step rule. After the second it is that subtotal plus the next charge. Every
further move adds exactly the next entry. With no moves there is only the starting
entry. With any number of moves, the final counter is therefore the starting value
plus their charges, which is µ(s) + c(t). Every entry added is nonnegative, so no
subtotal is smaller than the one before.



Theorem 7.3 (Only one honest count). In a counter machine, let B (for “books”)
be any function from states to N with B(sinit ) = 0 and B(apply(s, i )) = B(s) + c(i )
for all s and i. Then B(s) = µ(s) for every reachable state s.

Proof. Choose a run that reaches s from the start; such a run exists because s is
reachable. At the start both books say zero. At the first move both add the same
charge, so they still agree. Whenever they agree before a move, adding that move’s
charge to both keeps them equal afterward. Carry this comparison along the chosen
run. The two books agree at its last state, which is s.
    One thing follows that’s easy to miss. If a run comes back to a state it has already
visited, the counter is the same both times, so the moves on that loop cost nothing
in total. A machine that keeps its counter inside its state can go round a loop only
when the loop costs nothing, and every paid move lands on a state the run has never
150   7 The counter


              been in, because the counter is higher there than anywhere before. So a counter
              that only climbs is itself paid for in fresh states: it needs a fresh number for every
              unit of cost, and it never gets one back. On finitely many states that leaves no paid
              move at all: play any move over and over from any state, the states come round,
              and a loop costs nothing, so its price is zero. One move priced above zero takes
              infinitely many states.
                  Those two proofs are the whole of it, and they’re about any counter machine.
              They’re on the page, where you can check every line. The machine I build later
              is one of these, and on it the run form is a theorem: the ledger after any list of
              instructions is the start plus the sum of their costs (Theorem 15.6). The uniqueness
              half holds even with the books’ rule asked only of reachable states.
                  I want to say plainly what initiality does not do, because the fact is smaller than
              the word. It doesn’t pick the prices. The schedule is an input: somebody decided
              that raising the flag costs one and adding two numbers costs zero, and nothing here
              says that decision was right (Section 3 is where I argued the floor isn’t arbitrary; the
              rest of a schedule has to be defended by whoever writes it). It doesn’t turn units
              of cost into anything physical. And it isn’t the category theorist’s “initial object,”
              though the word is borrowed for a related reason.
                  Try the same instruction list on another machine that understands those instruc-
              tions. Choose its start. The empty list leaves it there. Append one instruction and
              its own rule tells you the next state. Append another and the rule tells you again.
              There is only one answer at each stage. So there is only one way to assign a target
              state to every instruction list while respecting the chosen start and each appended
              move. This walking through a list is often called a fold. Nothing in the argument
              used a certificate or a price.
                  Now ask a different question. Can you assign a target state to each state of the
              first machine, instead of to each instruction list? Two different lists may leave the
              first machine at the same state. If those lists leave the target at different states, the
              assignment would have to give two answers at that one state. It cannot.
                  That is the only obstruction. Suppose every pair of lists that agree at the first
              machine also agree at the target. To assign an answer to a reachable state, take any
              list reaching it and run that list on the target. Choosing another reaching list gives
              the same answer, by the supposition. Appending a move respects both machines’
              steps because it extends those very runs. The assignment is fixed on every reachable
              state, since each comes with a reaching list. This is the descent condition: the
              assignment can come down from histories to states precisely when the target does
              not distinguish histories the first machine has already identified.
                  A toll does not force that condition. Take a one-bit machine whose set costs
              one and whose reset costs zero. Setting its bit once leaves it up. Resetting and
              then setting also leaves it up. But a target that keeps the whole instruction list
                                                         7.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name   151


distinguishes “set” from “reset, set.” Both lists reach the same bit state, and they
reach different history states. The instruction-list assignment still works; the state
assignment fails. That is where the word “initial” has to stop.
    And the borrowed word has a home. I didn’t build it, so I’ll point at it. That lists
of moves are the starting object, and that a machine’s behaviour factors through
its reachable states exactly when a condition like descent holds, is the theory of
minimal realization. Joseph Goguen put it as a universal property in 1972, in a
paper whose title says it outright, “Realization is universal,” and Thomas Colcombet
and Daniela Petrişan redid automata minimization in the same functorial terms in
2020. Their machines can have any output at all, which is the honest point: the fold
and the descent condition never use the record, so the toll is doing nothing here,
just as I said.
    The nearest classical parallel to “only one honest count” is in thermodynamics.
The mathematical physicists Elliott Lieb and Jakob Yngvason showed in 1999 that
once you fix which states of a system can be reached from which by adiabatic
processes, and that relation meets a short list of axioms, there is an entropy, a
function that goes up exactly along the relation, and it is unique once its zero and its
unit are chosen. Their uniqueness, like this one, comes after the fixing: the order is
the input there, the price list is the input here, and in both the count is forced by it.


7.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name
Now for something I first took as a let-down. It would be nice to have a new kind of
cost argument, and this isn’t one. The toll is a case of a technique that algorithm
people have used since 1985 and that a mathematician studying the stability of
motion had, in a different form, in 1892. I’m telling you it’s old so you don’t think I
invented it.
    The trick is called the potential method, and it works like this. Give every state a
number, call it the potential, that measures how much “owing” is stored up in that
state. Then look at each step and ask: does the cost of the step, plus the change in
potential it causes, ever come out negative? If it never does, you’ve got a bound: any
run costs at least the amount the potential dropped from start to finish, because the
drop had to be paid for by the steps along the way. The computer scientist Robert
Tarjan set it out in 1985, crediting the potential view to Daniel Sleator. Tarjan’s use
goes the other way (potential as prepaid credit, to bound a run from above): he used
it to analyse data structures that are occasionally expensive and usually cheap; and
the decreasing-function idea underneath it is the one the Russian mathematician
Aleksandr Lyapunov used in 1892 to prove that a system settles down. Do the coin
version, which runs Tarjan’s way, as a ceiling: a stack of coins, PUSH adds one and
costs one, POP-ALL removes them all and costs as many as it removed, potential
152   7 The counter


              equals the number of coins. PUSH costs one plus one potential; POP-ALL of k coins
              costs k and drops the potential by k, net zero. So any sequence from an empty stack
              costs at most twice the number of pushes, however many expensive pops are in it.
              The whole method takes three lines.
                  Push on that 1892 for a second, because a date like that hides a lot. Lyapunov
              wrote the idea up as his doctoral thesis, in Russian. A French translation came
              out in 1907, made by a French naval engineer, Édouard Davaux, and corrected by
              Lyapunov himself. The English one came out in 1992, a hundred years after the
              original, and it was translated from the French: a translation of a translation. So for
              most of the twentieth century a reader with only English met the idea secondhand
              or not at all. Did the algorithm people of 1985 get it from him? I can’t tell you, and
              nothing here needs them to have. Whether anybody walked from one to the other
              on purpose is a question I’d like answered. What I do have is a picture: the same
              idea, a number that only goes one way along a run, turned up in a thesis about
              whether a moving system settles down and in a paper about data structures, close
              to a century apart.
                  Now point it at the record. Give each place in the record’s order a number that
              falls as the record climbs, so that a step that climbs drops the potential by at least
              one. For every step to have non-negative amortized cost, the step that climbs has to
              cost at least one, which is the toll; a potential like that proves the toll wherever it
              exists. On two places there’s only one such potential, up to a constant: one if the
              flag is down, zero if it’s up. A step from down to up drops it by one, so for the step’s
              cost plus potential change to be non-negative, the step has to cost at least one. That
              requirement is the toll exactly, and on two places the two are the same statement:
              the toll holds for a machine if and only if every step has non-negative amortized cost
              under the flag potential (“amortized cost” is just that sum, the step’s cost plus the
              change in potential). Then the universal floor from Section 2, “any run from NO to
              YES paid at least one,” is just the potential method’s standard conclusion, the drop
              in potential from one to zero, and every system with the five parts that obeys the
              toll is an instance, which is exactly what a Thiele machine is. Two more facts fall out
              of the same picture. Under the toll, a run raises the flag at most as many times as its
              total cost; each raise uses up a unit and a unit isn’t used twice. And if you demand
              the upper-bound version too, that the potential before a step covers its cost plus the
              potential after, then the two together say every step’s cost is exactly the potential
              it drops. Go through the four cases. Down to down and up to up drop nothing, so
              they cost zero. Down to up drops one, so it costs exactly one. Up to down would
              have to cost minus one, and no step costs less than nothing, so the flag never comes
              down. So the two together hold exactly when raising the flag costs exactly one,
              everything else costs zero, and the flag never comes down. Those prices, a cost of
              one per raise and nothing on any other step, are rise-only pricing in its tightest form,
                                                        7.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name   153


and I’ll call them the exact schedule. The flag staying up comes from this ceiling, not
from the prices: a ceiling that counts raises instead, which Section 8 uses, leaves
the same prices and lets the flag come down at cost zero. Notice that Section 2’s
two-move illustration doesn’t meet it: its VOUCH move, played from YES, costs one
unit although it raises nothing, which the floor allows and the exact schedule forbids.
Part III’s example (Section 15) doesn’t meet it either, and can’t; both are still Thiele
machines, since the toll is all the model asks. The reason: its CHECK and COMMIT,
the check and the commitment that must come before its flag goes up, raise no flag,
and each sends two states with the same counters and line to one (a COMMIT lands
an empty channel with one already naming its claim, and a CHECK that fails lands
with the same state already trapped), so pricing the merges in the record’s part of
the state charges each of them one. It charges every instruction a fixed listed price,
which is a different job for the word exact (instruction-exact pricing), and it breaks
no rule. (These two facts hold even if the price depends on the state as well as the
move’s name, which is wider than Section 2’s per-name cost; a per-name cost is a
special case, and there the floor and the ceiling together are out of reach for any
system whose flag ever goes up.) Two older tools sit beside these. Run a list of moves
in a “writer,” a wrapper that adds up a number as it goes, and you get back the final
state and the run’s cost; and a per-move schedule is a “grade,” fixed before the run.
I’m borrowing those two and no more: neither brings along the full type systems
they come from. The writer is the move the programming-language researchers
Norman Danner and Daniel Licata make in their cost semantics, a translation that
carries a cost alongside a program’s result (Danner, Licata and Ramyaa, ICFP 2015;
Danner and Licata, Journal of Functional Programming, 2022). The grade is Shin-ya
Katsumata’s: a computation carries its resource as a grade, and the grades compose
as the computations do (“Parametric effect monads and semantics of effect systems,”
POPL 2014). Dominic Orchard, Vilem Liepelt and Harley Eades put grades into the
types of a working language (“Quantitative program reasoning with graded modal
types,” ICFP 2019). And the potential method went into types before any of those:
the computer scientists Martin Hofmann and Steffen Jost (POPL 2003) gave a type
system that attaches potential to data and predicts, before a first-order functional
program runs, how much heap it can use, which is where type-based amortized
analysis begins; the multivariate work of Jan Hoffmann, Klaus Aehlig and Hofmann
(2011) carried it further. Read against them, the counter is a grade carried in the
state by the step rule, and no type carries it. And what does that difference even
mean? A cost that lives in a type gets checked before the program runs, by whoever
checks the types; a cost that lives in the state gets written during the run, by the
step itself. The number is the same, and the moment of truth is different.
    So is mine an embedding of their frameworks, or something weaker? Half of it is
exactly theirs, and the other half is left out on purpose. The counter is their writer:
154   7 The counter


              a step that moves the rest of the state without looking at the counter, hands back its
              cost, and has the cost added on is a computation in the writer over whole numbers
              with addition, and running a list of moves in that writer gives back the final state
              and the total cost, nothing more and nothing less. Every system in this book whose
              step never reads its own counter has that shape. What doesn’t come along is the
              part of their frameworks that works before anything runs: the type systems that
              carry grades, Danner and Licata’s bounding relation and the recurrences they extract
              for a program’s cost. That isn’t a gap left to be filled later; it’s the moment-of-truth
              difference I just named. Putting the count in the step is choosing the other moment,
              so the grade here is written by the step at run time and never checked ahead of it.
                  How close do the two moments come? Close enough to say exactly, in a limited
              form. Take a small structured language over a machine with this kind of counter:
              sequencing, branches whose two arms carry the same grade, and paid acts each
              graded with their charge, and grade every program the way Katsumata’s discipline
              does, adding grades along the program. On loop-free programs the two agree on
              the nose: on every run that doesn’t trap, the counter rises by exactly the grade.
              The argument is conservation set beside the grade rule; the counter’s rise is the
              sum of the charges along the run, and the grade rule adds the same charges in the
              same order. Loops break the agreement, and in one direction only. A loop that
              runs a paid check once for every unit in some register, where the check always
              passes and is charged one, costs that register’s value on entry, and no fixed whole
              number is an exact grade for it; an input-dependent grade can express its exact cost
              if the corresponding proof is supplied. Cost-aware type theories such as calf (Niu,
              Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022) support such reasoning; this is not an automatic
              exact-cost inference procedure for arbitrary loops. So the counter is their writer
              exactly, agrees with fixed grades wherever a fixed grade can be exact, and where a
              run’s cost depends on its data it holds the exact number, which a fixed grade can
              at best bound, and can’t bound at all when the data has no ceiling. What has no
              counterpart in the step is the checking ahead of time: a type checker turning a
              program away before it runs.
                  There’s one more neighbour, closer than any of those, and I’ll name it before
              somebody names it at me. A number the step keeps up to date and nothing else
              ever reads is what program-proof people call an auxiliary variable, or ghost state.
              Susan Owicki and David Gries added auxiliary variables to parallel programs in
              1976, because some true facts about such a program can’t be proved without one,
              under the rule that an auxiliary variable never steers the program. Jean-Christophe
              Filliâtre, Léon Gondelman and Andrei Paskevich, in 2014, worked out when ghost
              code can be erased without changing what the program computes. By that test this
              section’s counter is ghost whenever no step consults it, and Section 11’s base-driven
              records are built exactly that way: the base moves the same whatever the ledger
                                                         7.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name   155


and the record say. So what does putting it in the step buy, if the number is ghost
anyway? Two things, as far as I can see. The number is there while the machine
runs, where a window can show it (Section 8), and not only inside a proof somebody
wrote afterwards. The rule that keeps it covers every permitted instruction and
therefore every run. A proof using ghost state can also establish such a machine-wide
invariant, and static cost proofs can coexist with a runtime ledger. The difference
here is that the defined runtime state includes the count. Whether a record stays
ghost depends on what else the step does with it; the machine in Part III has a part
that isn’t ghost, its table of checked facts, because the step reads it and refuses on it,
as the opening section said. One last relative, from the graph side: Section 2’s floor
is a cheapest-path bound in a system with weights on its moves. Every path from the
no-states to the yes-states crosses the line between them, and every edge across that
line weighs at least one. Weighted automata go back to Marcel-Paul Schützenberger
in 1961, and priced timed automata, which add clocks, were set out in 2001. The
floor is about the smallest case of what they compute.
    Exactly, for any Thiele machine with states S, moves I, step, per-name cost, and
reading:

Definition 7.2 (Potential, amortized cost). A potential is a function Φ : S → N. A
step has non-negative amortized cost under Φ when cost(i ) + Φ(step(s, i )) ≥ Φ(s).
The flag potential is Φcert (s) = 1 if cert(s) = no and 0 if it reads yes.



Theorem 7.4 (The toll is the potential method). (1) The toll holds exactly when
every step has non-negative amortized cost under Φcert . (2) For any Φ with non-
negative amortized cost and any run t from s, cost(t) + Φ(run(t, s)) ≥ Φ(s). (3)
So, under the toll, a run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least 1 − 0 = 1.

Proof. (1) Put the before and after flags side by side. Down-to-down and up-to-up
leave the potential unchanged, so any nonnegative charge meets the inequality. Up-
to-down adds one to the potential, so that case meets it too. Down-to-up removes
one: only there must the charge supply at least one to make up the drop. That is
exactly the toll.
   (2) Write one inequality for each step: its charge plus the potential after it is at
least the potential before it. Add the lines. Every interior potential appears once as
an after and once as the next before, so those equal terms cancel. Only the starting
potential, the final potential, and all the charges remain. Thus the charges plus the
final potential cover the starting potential. For an empty run the start and finish
agree and there are no charges, giving equality.
156   7 The counter


                  (3) The flag potential starts at one when the flag is down and ends at zero when
              it is up. The charges must cover that drop of one.
                  So what’s new, if the method isn’t? Only where it’s pointed. The potential method
              is a way of proving things about costs. What this book adds is a claim about which
              potential, one that falls as the record climbs, the flag on two places, and about what
              happens to that claim when you can only see a window of the state. The method is
              Tarjan’s and Sleator’s. Pointing it at the flag is mine, and I’m about to find out what
              that can and can’t survive.
                  The flag potential has relatives in physics-flavoured mathematics too, which I
              found after the fact. Resource theories study what you can turn into what when
              some operations are free: Bob Coecke, Tobias Fritz and Robert Spekkens gave the
              general definition in 2016, Fritz worked out its algebra in 2017, and Tomáš Gonda
              and Spekkens catalogued the numbers that never go up under free operations, which
              they call monotones, in 2023. Read with the raised flag as the resource and one unit
              of cost as the currency, the flag potential is the kind of cost monotone they build,
              measured in that currency, and the floor is its simplest case. Does that make the toll
              a resource theory? Only as the smallest example of one: it says a run from no to yes
              costs at least one. To say yes costs exactly one you’d also need a run that gets there
              for one. It’s a neighbour to know about, and I don’t count it as a result.


              7.6 What the counter is, said once
              A receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges
              on every path including the failures, and is the only such total, on the states a run
              from the start reaches, for its schedule. Each of those had a home before this book:
              the stick for a total that lives in the state, Lamport’s clocks for climbing, Turing’s and
              Floyd’s ranking functions for the same one-way rule run downward, the telescoping
              sum for conservation, the induction for the single honest count. None of them is
              physics, and none of them says what the charges should be. What they say is that
              once you’ve chosen the charges, the counter is the arithmetic and not a second
              opinion. And the toll on top of it is the potential method with the flag as potential,
              which is to say a trick from 1985 applied to the question from Section 6.
                 There’s one thing the counter can’t do just by existing: if you can only see part of
              the state, can you tell what the counter is? Can you even tell, from outside, which
              step paid? The stick works because you can lay the two halves together. What if
              you’re only ever shown one half, through a window, and the window doesn’t show
              the notches?
                 One piece of that has a short answer, and I’ll give it now so the next section can
              start from it. A window, for now, is just the part of the state an outside observer is
              shown (Section 5’s display was one, and Section 8 is about windows in general).
                                                               7.6 What the counter is, said once   157


Call a window counter-complete when some rule, applied to what the window shows,
returns the counter on every state; flag-complete likewise for the flag. Say a window
forgets the counter when changing the counter and nothing else never changes what
the window shows, and likewise for the flag.
   For a full product state in which the counter and flag can be set independently, a
window that forgets either field cannot recover that field on all states. Take a state
and make two copies of it, one with the counter set to 1 and one with it set to 2,
everything else held still. The window shows the same thing for both, so any rule
gives the same answer for both, and one of the two answers is wrong. The flag is the
same argument with yes and no. On the stick, a window that shows you the wood’s
colour and its length, and hides the notches, can’t tell you what’s owed, and staring
harder at the colour won’t help. (The argument builds its second state by hand, so it
may be one no run reaches, and counter-complete asks for every state. On the states
a run reaches, forgetting isn’t enough: a machine whose one paid move also moves
a position the window shows reads its counter off that position everywhere it goes.
What blinds a window on reached states is two runs that end on the same view with
different counters. The machine I build later has such a pair, written out move by
move: two runs with the same window, one paid and one not (Theorem 15.15).)
   Be careful what that says. Neither part can be dropped, and nothing else is
needed. Call one window bigger than another when what it shows decides what
the other shows. A window that gives back both the counter and the flag has a rule
for each, so what it shows decides both, and the window that shows those two and
nothing more is the smallest that works. And it’s about reading the counter back.
Which step paid is the harder question, and it’s the next section’s.
CHAPTER 8




Windows and shadows

Every state a machine keeps is a distinction, and a look from outside can show some
of them and drop the rest. I’ll call that look a window. I left you with the stick split
in half and asked what happens if you can only ever see one half through a window
that doesn’t show the notches, and with a harder question under that one: can you
tell, from outside, which step paid? This section is about windows. It’s a section
where the mathematics is so small that I’m going to state it in full and then spend
most of the pages on what it’s not, because the smallness is what catches people:
the fact is a one-liner and it’s tempting to climb over it with cleverness, and you
can’t, and seeing why you can’t is the content.


8.1 A cave, and the people who got good at it

This one is Plato’s, and the part I need is near the end. In the seventh book of the
Republic, Plato has Socrates, the main speaker of the dialogue, describe prisoners
chained in a cave since childhood, facing a wall, with a fire behind them and people
carrying objects along a walkway between the fire and their backs. All the prisoners
have ever seen is the shadows on the wall. To them, Socrates says, the truth would
be nothing but those shadows. Further on, Socrates reads the story out himself: the
cave is the world of sight, and the climb out of it is the soul’s climb toward what’s
really there. So a real world hidden from anyone who only looks is in the story on
purpose, and Plato put it there. It still isn’t the part I need.
   What I need comes a little before that reading, when one prisoner, freed and
taken up into the daylight, thinks back to the cave. The prisoners, Socrates says,
hand out honours to whoever is quickest at spotting the shadows as they pass
and best at guessing which comes next. The part worth reading twice is that the
prisoners get good at it. They build a whole science of shadows, with experts and
prizes, and it works, on shadows. What they can’t do is say anything about a carried
object that leaves no mark on the wall, and that isn’t because they’re stupid; it’s
because the information isn’t on the wall. Skill inside a window doesn’t reach past
the window, no matter how much skill. Plato dressed that fact as a lesson about


                                 158
                                                                           8.2 The shadow of a cube   159


education, and it is one, but take the dressing off and it’s a sentence about functions,
and it’s going to be the whole section.


8.2 The shadow of a cube
Do this one tonight with a lamp and a flat wall. Keep the lamp well back, hold a
cube face-on with its face parallel to the wall, and mark the outline of its shadow.
Replace it with square card and adjust the card’s size or distance until the outlines
match as closely as you can judge. Show your partner only that outline. It does not
tell them whether the object has thickness. For the exact mathematical version, take
parallel light rays and let the window report only the silhouette: an aligned cube
and a square face of the same size then give exactly the same square. Ask them, and
they’ll tell you, truthfully, that they can’t know, and if they’re honest they’ll also tell
you that no amount of staring at that square will change it.
    Now turn each a quarter turn about its vertical centre line. The card’s shadow
becomes a narrow edge; the cube still casts a broad face. With ideal parallel rays
and zero-thickness card, those are exactly a line and a square. Now the wall-watcher
knows, and what changed isn’t their cleverness but the window. A second look from
a different angle is a bigger window than one look, and what bought it was the turn.
Edwin Abbott wrote a novel about a window like this in 1884, Flatland. A Flatlander
never sees a shape. Abbott’s narrator says it in his first section: nothing was visible
to them, or could be, except straight lines. Put a coin flat on a table and lower your
eye to the table’s edge, and the coin turns into a line, which is all the view there
is. What gives a Flatlander anything more is fog. A line that’s near is bright and a
line that runs off into the fog goes dim, so a trained eye can read a triangle or a
pentagon off how fast the brightness fades toward the ends. The training takes time
and money, and in the story only people with money get it. The window got bigger,
and it was paid for in time.
    Then a sphere comes through the narrator’s plane. What his eye gets is a line
whose ends fade too fast for any flat figure he knows, changing size in a way no flat
figure could. He only settles that it’s a circle by feeling it, and the circle grows from
a point to its widest and shrinks back to nothing as the sphere rises through. From
one slice he can’t put a sphere together. From the slices one after another, seen and
felt and argued over, he starts to. The escape from a window is never “think harder.”
It’s always “a different window,” and a different window that answers the question
always has to show apart two states the old one showed alike; that’s Theorem 8.1
below, applied to the new window. In every story here, getting that window cost
something: a turn, a second look, training, time. What a change of window costs in
general is a separate question, and no theorem in this section prices it.
160   8 Windows and shadows


                  Who was Edwin Abbott? Not a mathematician by trade. He was headmaster of
              the City of London School for twenty-four years, a clergyman, and the author of
              more than forty books, a Shakespeare grammar among them. He put Flatland out
              under the name “A Square.” His full name was Edwin Abbott Abbott, two A’s, and
              the pen name may be a joke on that, A squared; nice if true, but take it as a lead. The
              part I like best comes from a sketch of his life on the geometer Thomas Banchoff’s
              pages: Flatland, by far the most read thing he wrote, isn’t mentioned at all in his
              obituary in the London Times or in his entry in the Dictionary of National Biography.
              The official record of the man was a window too: it showed the headmaster and
              the grammarian and left out the one book people still read. That changes nothing
              in the argument; it’s the argument, acted out by an obituary. (Flatland comes back
              later: Section 14 retells the sphere’s visit, and the Afterword, Section 24, says how
              the hunch behind this book started with it.)


              8.3 The whole fact, in one paragraph

             I’ll give the mathematics now, and I promise it’s all of it. You have a set of states, the
             real things. You have a window, which is a function that takes a state and gives you
             what you can see of it: the shadow, the slice, the half-stick without notches. And
             you have a question about the state, which is also a function: it takes a state and
             gives an answer. The thing you want is a decoder: a rule that takes what you can see
             and gives the right answer to the question, every time. When does one exist?
                  Think about two states that cast the same shadow. The decoder sees the same
             shadow for both, so it gives the same answer for both. So if the question has
             different answers on those two states, the decoder is wrong on at least one of them,
             and there’s nothing it can do about it, because it never saw the difference. That
             argument is the whole fact. If a decoder exists, then the question must already give
             the same answer on every pair of states that look the same through the window.
             Mathematicians call the set of states that cast one particular shadow the fibre over
             that shadow (think of the shadow as a point on the wall and the fibre as the bundle
             of all the things that could have cast it), and the sentence is: a decoder exists only if
             the question is constant on every fibre. The theorem just below says that, and the
             “only if” is the direction that bites. The other direction, “if the question is constant
             on fibres then a decoder exists,” is true too: send each shadow to the answer at any
             state that casts it, and constancy makes it not matter which one. A shadow nothing
             casts can get any answer, since no state shows it. But a decoder existing isn’t the
             same as being able to work it out: to compute its answer for a shadow you still have
             to find a state that casts it, and that search takes effort, and on some windows it
             can’t be done at all.
                                                               8.3 The whole fact, in one paragraph   161


    To say it exactly, let S be any set of states, V any set of views, w : S → V a
window, and q : S → A a question with answers in any set A. A decoder is a function
d : V → A with d(w(s)) = q(s) for every state s. The question is constant on fibres
when w(s) = w(s′ ) implies q(s) = q(s′ ).


Theorem 8.1 (Decoders need constant fibres). If a decoder exists, the question is
constant on fibres. Conversely, if the question is constant on fibres and there is at
least one answer, a decoder exists: send each view that some state shows to the
answer at any state showing it, and any other view to any answer at all.

Proof. If w(s) = w(s′ ) then q(s) = d(w(s)) = d(w(s′ )) = q(s′ ). Conversely, the
rule is well defined, because two states showing the same view have the same
answer by constancy, so it doesn’t matter which one is picked; and at any state s it
gives the answer at a state showing w(s), which is q(s).
   Nothing in the theorem cares what the states or the views are.
   Try the smallest case, by hand, because it’ll keep coming back. A state is a pair:
a position, 0 or 1, and a hidden flag, up or down. The window shows the position
only. Two moves from (0, down): one sets the position to 1 and raises the flag; the
other sets the position to 1 and leaves the flag alone. Both land on position 1. Now
write down every possible decoder from “what I see” to “is the flag up”: there are
exactly four functions from two positions to two answers. Check each against both
results. None of the four gets both right, because both results show position 1 and
one has the flag up and one doesn’t. That exhaustive check is the theorem on this
example; the general statement is the one-line argument above, and that’s the one
that carries the weight. There’s no fifth function hiding somewhere.
                      Position 1                        Position 1
                       Flag up                          Flag down




                                    The photograph
                                       Position 1
                                    Flag not shown



                                       One input
                                      One answer
 Answer yes and the bottom state is misread. Answer no and the top state is misread. The
                     photograph needs to carry another distinction.
