              8.4 The clerk with two photographs
              Now point it at the counter, because that’s why this section is here. Suppose you
              want to charge for raising the flag, exactly: at least one unit for every step that raises
              it, and nothing for a step that doesn’t. And suppose the person doing the charging
              is a clerk who sees only a window on the state, a photograph before the step and a
              photograph after. The clerk’s charge is a function of the two photographs. Can the
              clerk charge exactly?
                  The clerk can’t if the window has the wrong kind of blind spot, and the reason
              is the cube again. Suppose there are two steps that give the clerk the same before-
              photo and the same after-photo, and one of them raised the flag and the other
              didn’t. (The two-move toy above is exactly such a pair; so are “a stamp goes onto
              a document inside a closed drawer” and “someone opens and closes the drawer.”)
              The clerk has one charge for that pair of photographs. If the charge is at least one, it
              overcharges the step that didn’t raise the flag. If it’s zero, it undercharges the step
              that did. Any charge that never misses a raise charges something that wasn’t a raise,
              and no charge from those photographs is exact. The fix is the plain one: put the flag
              in the photograph. If the window shows the reading, then “one when the reading
              goes from down to up, zero otherwise” is exact, and such a window has no pair like
              the one above. Showing the flag is enough. It isn’t the only way: a window can hide
              the flag and still have no colliding pair, and then a charge from the photographs is
              exact, as the observation below says. And “exact” here means rise-only pricing: at
              least one on every step that raises the flag, nothing on any step that doesn’t. That’s
              all the clerk’s problem needs, and the charge “one for a raise, zero otherwise” meets
              it. So it’s exact about which steps get charged. It isn’t exact about how much, and it
              doesn’t pick out one charge: “two for a raise, zero otherwise” meets it too. Pinning
              the charge down takes one more demand, a ceiling: over any run, the total never
              exceeds the number of raises. With the floor and that ceiling there’s exactly one
              charge left, one per raise and zero otherwise, which is the exact schedule from the
              last section; that’s an if and only if for any system whose charge is decided step
              by step, from the state and the move: apply the ceiling to a one-step run. These
              charges look at where the step starts, not only at the move’s name, and they have to.
              A move that raises the flag from NO raises nothing when it’s played again from YES,
              so with Section 2’s price, one price per move name wherever you stand, nothing
              priced that way charges the raise and leaves the replay alone, and no system whose
              flag ever goes up meets the floor and the ceiling together. The clerk’s charge, read
              off the photographs, depends on the state from the start. All of this holds for any
              states and any steps. The window version, the cube theorem with a price in place of
              a decoder, comes next.
                                                                 8.4 The clerk with two photographs   163


    Same clerk, now in symbols, so you can check every word I just used. Take
the five parts of Section 2 with a window w : S → V, and say a step (s, i ) raises
the flag when cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A price is any function
that gives a state and a move a whole number of units, zero or more (wider
than Section 2’s per-name cost, which is the case that ignores the state). It meets
the floor when every raise costs at least one, and never overcharges when every
non-raise costs zero; together, it is exact, which is rise-only pricing (exact about
which steps are charged; the amount is pinned only by the whole-run ceiling
above, and pinned it is the exact schedule). A window price is one computed
from the two photographs only: price(s, i ) = b(w(s), w(step(s, i ))) for some charge
b : V × V → N. A collision is two steps (s1 , i1 ) and (s2 , i2 ) with w(s1 ) = w(s2 ) and
w(step(s1 , i1 )) = w(step(s2 , i2 )), the first a raise and the second not.
Observation 8.2 (No exact window price across a collision). If the window has a
collision, every window price that meets the floor charges at least one on some step that
is not a raise; so no window price is exact. If it has none, the window price “one on any
pair of photographs some raise casts, zero otherwise” is exact; in particular when the
reading is a function of the view, cert(s) = r (w(s)) for some r, there is no collision.
Proof. Across a collision both steps get the same charge b(v, v′ ). The floor makes
it at least one because the first step is a raise; the second step, not a raise, pays it.
With no collision, a step that casts a pair some raise casts is itself a raise, so that
price charges one on every raise and nothing on any other step. If the reading is r of
the view, two steps with the same photographs either both raise or both don’t, so
there’s no collision.
   So the exact price of raising the flag lives in the step itself, or in a window with
no colliding pair, and a window that shows the flag is the plainest such window.
A window that contains a pair like that one can’t carry it. Whether a particular
machine has such a pair, for a particular window, has to be checked machine by
machine and window by window; the observation tells you a window prices exactly
just when it has no such pair.
   You can also find the best cautious prices the clerk could use. Put all the steps that
give one pair of photographs in a tray. For this calculation restrict the clerk to zero-
or-one charges: each step ought to cost one if it raises the flag and zero otherwise.
Without that restriction an all-raising tray would allow charges of two, three and
higher, and there would be no largest price that avoids charging non-raises.
   To miss no raise, the clerk must charge one whenever the tray contains even one
raising step. That is the cheapest price that never undercharges. To charge no non-
raise, the clerk must charge zero whenever the tray contains even one non-raising
step. That leaves one only when every step in the tray raises the flag, and it is the
largest price that never overcharges. In a mixed tray the two demands disagree. In
164   8 Windows and shadows


              a tray of all raises, or all non-raises, they agree. That is the collision test again, now
              giving both best cautious prices.
                      Steps with these photographs       Miss no raise     Charge no non-raise
                      All raise                                 1                    1
                      None raises                               0                    0
                      Some raise, some do not                   1                    0
               The entries are the best cautious zero-or-one charges in each direction. The mixed tray is
                                          where the two requirements disagree.
                  The two tests are “some member” and “every member” applied to the same
              tray. F. William Lawvere studied this movement of logical questions along maps
              in “Adjointness in foundations” (1969). Robin Cockett, Isabelle Geng, Carlo Maria
              Scandolo and Priyaa Srinivasan (2023) use the same kind of construction to extend
              resource measures along a map. Here you can see the whole calculation in the tray:
              take its highest required charge or its lowest. Exact pricing is possible precisely
              when those two numbers agree for every attainable pair of photographs.
                  Control engineers have been hunting pairs like that for a long time, under other
              names. Discrete-event systems is the field of machines that jump from state to state
              on events, some of which an outside observer sees and some of which it doesn’t.
              In 1995 five engineers, Meera Sampath, Raja Sengupta, Stéphane Lafortune and
              Demosthenis Teneketzis of the University of Michigan and Kasim Sinnamohideen of
              Johnson Controls, asked when such an observer can always work out, from what it
              sees, that a hidden fault event has happened, within a bounded number of further
              steps. They called that diagnosability and gave a test for it on finite machines.
              Anooshiravan Saboori, then a doctoral student at the University of Illinois, and
              Christoforos Hadjicostis, the engineer who supervised his doctorate there, asked
              in 2007 the question the other way round, for secrets: a system is opaque when
              an observer can never be sure it’s in a secret state, because some run outside the
              secret always looks the same. Read the raise as the hidden event and the window as
              what the observer sees. An ambiguous pair of current views prevents an immediate
              answer from that view alone; a retained observation history might still distinguish
              the runs. One ambiguous pair is enough to defeat a decoder of the current view
              that must always answer correctly. Opacity asks more: every secret run in its scope
              must have a non-secret alternative with the same observation. The small machine’s
              no-oracle theorem below supplies an ambiguous pair; it does not by itself establish
              that stronger claim about all secret runs. That’s my reading; they don’t put it that
              way. Their versions are richer than mine: they allow delays, look at whole runs,
              and come with algorithms. What this section adds is only the price: what a charge
              computed through the window does across one such pair.
                                                      8.5 The three escapes, and what each one costs   165


   Why can’t the clerk just watch the step itself? A clerk who does, who sees the
whole state before and the move, charges exactly with no trouble at all: “one for a
raise” is a function of exactly those two things, and it’s the step price above. So the
collision bites an observer who doesn’t see the step, or who’s handed an account
of the step and can’t trust the account. That second kind is the trace problem,
which Section 14 takes up. If the names of the moves arrive in a log the program
wrote, the program can write whatever names it likes, and a clerk reading that log is
reading one more window, one the program painted. Seeing the move means being
underneath the program, where the step is.


8.5 The three escapes, and what each one costs
Suppose you’re the person outside, and you want to be convinced that a run paid.
The window you’ve got doesn’t show the counter. To see how bad that is, I’ll take
the smallest setting I can build. Take a counter machine from Section 7, give its
states a position and a flag as well, and give it a window that shows the position
and nothing else. Now take two runs from the same start, with the position at 0,
the flag down and the counter at 0. Run A makes one move that raises the flag,
costs one, and lands at position 1; its counter reads 1. Run B makes one move that
does nothing but step to position 1, at cost zero; its counter reads 0. Call the pair of
photographs, position 0 then position 1, the transcript. Both runs leave exactly that
transcript. A verifier is a rule that takes a transcript and says accept or reject. It is
sound when every transcript it accepts comes only from states where the claim holds,
and complete when every transcript from a state where the claim holds is accepted.
The claim is “the counter is 1.”
    No verifier on these transcripts is both, and the proof is three lines. Suppose
one were both. Run A ends with the counter at 1 and leaves the transcript, so
completeness says the verifier accepts it. Now soundness, on that same accepted
transcript: every state that leaves it satisfies the claim, and run B’s end state leaves
it. So run B’s counter is 1, and it is 0. The cube comes back here, with a verdict in
place of an answer: a verifier sees only what the window kept, and two states that
the window can’t tell apart get one verdict between them.
    Now dress the transcript up. Take any richer kind of transcript, with a way to
squash one down to its bare photographs, and say a verifier on the rich ones only
looks at the bare part when two rich transcripts that squash to the same photographs
always get the same verdict. If some rich transcript left by run A and some rich
transcript left by run B squash to the same photographs, then no verifier that only
looks at the bare part is sound and complete either: it gives those two the same
verdict, completeness makes that verdict accept, and soundness then lies about run
B. Notice what that needs: the pair has to survive into the richer kind of transcript. A
166   8 Windows and shadows


             design whose extra part tells A from B doesn’t meet the premise, and the argument
             says nothing about it. So it doesn’t classify every transcript design. What it says is
             that a verifier that only reads what the bare window keeps fails on that pair.
                 Economists got to the same wall by another road. Jerry Green and Jean-Jacques
             Laffont (1986) asked what a mechanism can do when people can claim about
             themselves only what their situation lets them back up, and Jesse Bull and Joel
             Watson (2007) built that into mechanism design as hard evidence. In their terms,
             an audit can tell apart only the cases the evidence on offer tells apart, which is the
             cube again, set in accounting.
                 What can you do? I know three things that work, and nothing says they’re the
             only ones; as far as I can tell, cryptography uses all three. What any of them needs
             is the cube’s own condition: no evidence the outsider can be handed may come both
             from a state where the claim holds and from one where it doesn’t. I’ll call them
             escapes, and be clear what from: from the window, not from the cost. Run A paid
             its one unit of cost whatever anybody outside can see. An escape is a way for the
             outsider to see that it did. Each rests on something you have to trust, and I’ll say
             what, because “a price” in the counter’s sense is not what any of them costs.
                 You can be shown the whole state. Then there’s nothing to decode; you read
             the counter off the state. The price is trust: you have to believe the state you were
             shown is the state there was.
                 You can be shown a commitment: the ordinary window plus one extra bit that
             is set when, and only when, the claim holds (here, that the counter reads exactly
             one). Reading that bit gives a verifier that is sound and complete for that claim
             exactly when the bit is binding (set only when the claim holds) and honest (set
             whenever it holds). The trust is in those two conditions, which are a contract about
             who can set the bit. The contract can be met, and a bit anyone can set breaks
             it, which is the one-line version of why an unsigned log is just another window.
             Nothing in that picture has a hardness assumption in it; whether a real commitment
             scheme meets the contract is a question for cryptography, and this book doesn’t take
             it up. (A clash of words I should own: “commitment” here is the cryptographers’
             word, something bound to a claim, which in their schemes also hides the claim
             until it’s opened, and this bit doesn’t bother hiding anything. The book’s commit
             (Section 14) is a different act, the closing of a question. It’s the same word doing
             two jobs. The sealed envelope, a commitment that hides its claim, has an exact
             theory of its own. Three information theorists, Andreas Winter, then at Bristol, and
             Anderson Nascimento and Hideki Imai, then at Tokyo, found in 2003 the best rate
             at which a noisy channel can carry commitments, and the cryptographers Claude
             Crépeau, Rafael Dowsley and Nascimento (2020) worked out how that rate drops as
             the committer gets some control over the noise, which is “take the pen away from
             the program,” Section 14’s fix for a log a program writes about itself, with a formula
                                                       8.5 The three escapes, and what each one costs   167


on it.) In 1999 the cryptographers Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey worked out how
to make a log that an intruder who takes over the machine can’t quietly rewrite,
and the honest scope in their paper is the honest scope here: it protects what was
written before the break-in, through keys, and nothing after. Two cryptographers at
the University of California, San Diego, Mihir Bellare and Bennet Yee, had named
that property forward integrity in a 1997 report and proved their scheme has it.
Point it at an AI agent that keeps its own log of what it did, and the line moves to the
very start: an agent that writes the wrong thing from its first step is on the far side
of the break-in for the whole log. A 2026 preprint on tamper-evident audit trails for
such agents, built from hashes anchored on a public blockchain, is even called Agent
Flight Recorder (by Laurent Bindschaedler, of the Max Planck Institute for Software
Systems, and Quentin Botha and Christoph Siebenbrunner, of the Vienna University
of Economics and Business), which is a word Section 14 uses too, and that section’s
fingerprint paragraph is the part of this book that applies to it.
    Or you can ask, which is interaction: the outside party gets to put a question and
gets an answer that pins the thing down. The price is the honesty of the answerer;
a liar’s answer is another shadow. Moore’s experimenter chose inputs; the zero-
knowledge proofs of the cryptographers Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali and Charles
Rackoff in 1985 are the refined form, where a verifier is convinced by a conversation
designed to cut exactly the line between true and false and nothing else, with a
mathematical guarantee against a cheating prover. I mention zero-knowledge to
say what I’m not claiming: the asking in this section is one round, with one fixed
question (“tell me your counter”), and nothing in it models a cheating prover; the
honesty is assumed, and nothing enforces it. My one round of asking is a toy of
the real thing, and I’m not going to let the real thing’s reputation stand behind
the toy. (Joseph Halpern, Yoram Moses and Mark Tuttle, computer scientists who
work on reasoning about knowledge in distributed systems, gave zero knowledge a
knowledge-based analysis in 1988, which is where I’d start for the logic of it.)
    The real thing even has a cave in it, which after Plato I can’t resist. In a paper for
the 1989 CRYPTO conference called “How to Explain Zero-Knowledge Protocols to
Your Children,” two cryptographers, Jean-Jacques Quisquater of Philips Research
and Louis Guillou of the French telecommunications lab CCETT, with their families
and Tom Berson of Anagram Laboratories on the byline, told it as Ali Baba’s cave: a
ring-shaped tunnel with a magic door at the back that opens only for a secret word.
Peggy goes in down one side while Victor waits outside; then Victor walks to the
fork and shouts which side she should come out of. If she knows the word, she
always can. If she doesn’t, she gets away with it only when Victor happens to call
the side she went in. Play it at the table with a coin for Victor’s shout: one round, a
cheat gets through half the time; twenty rounds, about one time in a million. The
part of the story that belongs in this section is that Victor ends up convinced, but a
168   8 Windows and shadows


              video of the whole thing convinces nobody else, because a staged run, where the
              two agreed beforehand which sides he’d shout, makes exactly the same recording.
              The recording is a window, and the real run and the fake one cast the same shadow.
              That’s the cube in the cryptographers’ favourite bedtime story, The cave protocol
              gets its bound from fresh, independent coin tosses made after Peggy has entered.
              That timing is what the staged video lacks. Other zero-knowledge protocols use
              different setups, including noninteractive ones; the cave does not prove that every
              proof must be a live conversation.
                  Each escape is a window with something added: the whole state, a bound bit, an
              honest answer. None of them is “a smarter verifier on the old window”: cleverness
              sits on the wrong side of the projection, and what’s true of any machine is the cube.
                  I’ll write the three constructions out exactly, for the pair above, with the relations
              written down. The relation matters: it says which state a transcript is allowed to
              describe. If it quietly assumes a truthful answer, then a verifier sound for it is sound
              only against honest answerers, and it says nothing about a liar. Write A and B for
              the states runs A and B end at, µ for the counter, and τ for their shared transcript.
                  The letter E below names a rule about which state may explain which transcript.
              Think of writing an allowed state beside each piece of evidence. E(s, t) says that
              state s is allowed beside transcript t. The little ∧ means both conditions must hold;
              ∨ means either is enough; ⇐⇒ means each side holds exactly when the other does.
              In the bare case, the only evidence is τ, and either endpoint may stand beside it.
              The three richer cases change that pairing rule, which is where their extra guarantee
              enters.

              Definition 8.1 (Three richer transcripts and their explanations). Keep the states
              A, B and their shared bare transcript τ, with µ( A) = 1 and µ( B) = 0. Write E0 (s, t)
              for t = τ ∧ (s = A ∨ s = B). The claim is µ(s) = 1.
                 A full-state transcript is a finite list t of states. Define ES (s, t) to mean that t is
              nonempty and its last entry is s. The verifier rejects the empty list; otherwise it
              accepts exactly when the last entry’s counter is 1.
                 A commitment transcript is a pair (t, b) of a bare transcript and a Boolean. For any
              chosen explanation relation EC , the commitment contract is the pair of implications,
              for all s, t, b:
                                      EC (s, (t, b)) ∧ b = true =⇒ µ(s) = 1,

                                      EC (s, (t, b)) ∧ µ(s) = 1 =⇒ b = true.

              These are binding and honesty, respectively. The verifier accepts exactly when b
              is true. One relation meeting the contract is EH (s, (t, b)) ⇐⇒ E0 (s, t) ∧ (b =
              true ⇐⇒ µ(s) = 1).
                                                       8.5 The three escapes, and what each one costs   169


    A response transcript is a pair (t, r ) of a bare transcript and a natural number.
Define E I (s, (t, r )) ⇐⇒ µ(s) = r. The verifier accepts exactly when r = 1. This
relation imposes no condition on the bare component t; the response alone carries
its entire truth condition.
    Each construction assigns verification the constant abstract cost 1.



Theorem 8.3 (Three conditional escapes). The full-state verifier is sound and
complete relative to ES . For every EC , the commitment verifier is sound and
complete relative to EC exactly when EC satisfies the commitment contract. The
response verifier is sound and complete relative to E I . Each has cost 1 under
the stipulated cost assignment. The honest relation EH satisfies the commitment
contract; the unchecked relation EU (s, (t, b)) ⇐⇒ E0 (s, t) does not.

Proof. For the full-state verifier, an explaining state is precisely the last entry. Read-
ing that entry’s counter accepts exactly when the explaining state’s counter is 1. An
empty transcript is rejected and has no explaining state.
   For the commitment verifier, acceptance says b is true. Binding then gives the
claim for every explaining state, which is soundness. Conversely, honesty says that
any explaining state satisfying the claim has a true bit, which the verifier accepts.
Read backwards, soundness for an accepted transcript is binding and completeness is
honesty. The equivalence in EH gives both implications directly. Under EU , however,
B explains (τ, true) even though µ( B) = 0. That violates binding.
   For the response verifier, explanation gives µ(s) = r. Acceptance adds r = 1, so
µ(s) = 1. Conversely, µ(s) = 1 and explanation give r = 1, so it accepts. The three
cost claims follow from the assigned constant.
    None of that leans on what A and B are. It uses only that one has the claim, one
doesn’t, and they share a bare transcript, so it holds for any pair like them, whatever
the states, claims, transcripts and explanation relations. Once two transcripts with
the same bare part are explained, one by a state with the claim and one by a state
without it, a verifier that’s sound and complete for the claim can’t be one that looks
only at the bare part. The three escapes get past that by adding full states, a bit that
keeps the contract, or a truthful answer.
    On the small machine of Part III (Section 15) the collision is a theorem too, and
it doesn’t depend on the two-move illustration. On that machine computing costs
nothing and never touches the record, and from a clean start the record goes up
only on an earned check, commitment and certificate. Give a run from a loaded
start (Part III’s word for a start at line 1 with the two counters set to a and b, written
(1, a, b)) the bare transcript made of a, b and the window on the counters the run
170   8 Windows and shadows


              ends with, and say a state explains a bare transcript when some run from that start
              ends at it showing that window.


             Theorem 8.4 (No bare verifier on the small machine). On the small machine: (1)
             No function from bare transcripts to Booleans is both sound and complete, under
             that explanation relation, for the claim “the record is up.” (2) There is a clean
             loaded state such that no function from bare transcripts to Booleans is both sound
             and complete for the claim “the ledger is at least 3 above what it was at that start.”
             (3) For the small machine of Part III, whose moves CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY
             and whose counter move DEC are defined there: a run CHECK is zero A, COMMIT
             is zero A, CERTIFY from the loaded start (1, 0, 0), which ends with the ledger at 3,
             and three DECs of a zero counter from the same start, which end with the ledger
             at 0, end with the same window, and no function on bare transcripts is sound and
             complete for “the ledger reads 3.”

              Proof. Theorem 15.15 gives a clean loaded state and two runs from it that end
              with the same window, one with the record up and one with it down, one whose
              ledger rose by at least 3 and one made of counter moves at no cost that leaves the
              ledger where it started. Both end states explain the same bare transcript. A verifier
              complete for the claim accepts that transcript, since a state where the claim holds
              explains it; a verifier sound for the claim then makes the claim true of every state
              that explains it, including the one where it’s false. That’s (1), and (2) is the same
              with the ledger: the paid run’s end state satisfies the claim, and the unpaid run’s
              doesn’t. For (3) the two runs are written out in the statement: three moves land
              on line 4 in both runs with both counters at 0, and the same two-state argument
              applies.
                  Parts (1) and (2), with a loaded state for a clean one and “at least 1” for “at least
              3”, hold of any machine whose flat moves cost nothing, can reach every window
              and can’t touch a record that some run raises, by the same argument; certification is
              what raises the gap to three.
                  Put with the three escapes, the whole picture holds for the small machine: the
              bare-transcript verifier doesn’t exist; the collision survives into any richer transcript
              that keeps it, so no verifier that only reads its bare part works either; a verifier on
              full states exists; one on the bare transcript with a committed bit exists, sound and
              complete when the bit is honest, and the unchecked bit breaks the contract; and one
              on a truthful response exists.
                  In the three escapes the collision is gone, and no trick did it: the extra information
              pulls A and B apart. The full-state transcript shows the counter outright. The honest
              commitment for A carries a true bit and the one for B a false bit. The honest
                                                      8.5 The three escapes, and what each one costs   171


responses are 1 and 0. In none of the three is the verifier asked to tell identical
inputs apart, which was the impossible job.
    Now for the limit, which I’d rather say before you find it. A list of states has
no authentication built into it, so nothing in it stops a liar from handing over
whatever the verifier wants to see. The commitment contract is assumed, and the
unchecked bit above is what happens when the assumption is dropped. The response
relation only allows a truthful counter value, so asking a question here does not buy
resistance to a cheating prover. And the cost 1 is an abstract price I wrote down. It
doesn’t measure what it takes to authenticate a state, check a cryptographic proof or
send a response. What these three show is which extra distinctions a verifier can
use. They are not an adversary model, a security parameter or a hardness reduction.
    So what would it take to make that commitment bit binding for real, against
somebody who wants to cheat? Cryptographers had to face that one in the open,
and the place I’d point is a short paper the computer scientist Manuel Blum, whose
Turing Award was for complexity theory and its use in cryptography, presented at
the CRYPTO meeting in 1981, “Coin Flipping by Telephone.” His setup: Alice and
Bob have just divorced, they live in different cities, and they want to flip a coin over
the phone for who gets the car, with nobody they both trust to do the flipping. If
Alice flips and announces, Bob has to take her word. If Bob calls it first, Alice can lie
about how it landed. Blum’s way out is for one side to commit first: send something
that fixes the choice without showing it, and open it only after the other side has
called. And what keeps that commitment binding isn’t anybody’s promise. It’s a bet
that a certain kind of big number is hard to factor. Push on that and you’re standing
on the honest edge of this subsection. In Blum’s protocol, binding is earned, on the
condition that factoring is hard. Here it’s written into the contract and assumed
outright, and the unchecked bit above shows what’s left without it. That’s why I
won’t say these escapes beat a cheater. Blum’s paper is the kind of thing it would
take, and nothing like it is in this chapter.
    Now point the three escapes back at the record I’ve been building, because
that’s where they bite hardest. A record kept in a machine’s state is bits too. Hand
someone outside a copy of those bits with a note saying “the flag is up,” and they’re
reading a window: the run that really raised the flag and a box built to print that
it did cast the same shadow. So putting the record in the step answers “was this
earned?” for whoever can see the state and trusts the step that wrote it. For anybody
else it moves the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust the box that says it
ran?” Crossing that line takes an escape, a window with more in it, and the three I
have are these: the whole state, from a box you already trust; a bit backed by an
authenticated and trusted source. A signature authenticates who signed the record;
it does not prove that the signer told the truth. A quote from measured hardware
likewise needs its connection to the claim (and Section 17 shows a quote vouches
172   8 Windows and shadows


              only for what was measured); or asking, against a box that might lie, which is
              the cryptographers’ business. One more relative deserves its name here, verifiable
              computation: the box hands back its answer with a short proof that the answer
              is right, which a checker can verify without redoing the work (Pinocchio, built in
              2013 by the computer scientists Bryan Parno, Jon Howell, Craig Gentry and Mariana
              Raykova), and proof-carrying data passes proofs like that along a whole chain of
              parties who don’t trust each other (the computer scientists Alessandro Chiesa and
              Eran Tromer, 2010). That’s the strongest export there is, and what it exports is the
              claim; the history stays behind. The proof establishes its stated relation about the
              input and output. Unless identity or timing is part of that relation and supported
              by the setup, it does not identify the physical machine or when it ran. Producing a
              proof may require a witness and substantial computation; possession of the public
              input alone need not suffice. Nothing in this book supplies any of these escapes. The
              model’s record is local to the machine that keeps it. The example of Part III keeps its
              record in its state with no signature on it at all, as a bare example would.


              8.6 What the window keeps
              Put the two boxes back under the camera. Their tops agree and their side stamps
              differ. The photograph answers questions about the tiles. To answer the stamp
              question, turn the camera far enough to include the side. The full state was there all
              along; what changed was which part reached the reader.
                  Taking more photographs from the same position only helps if something different
              eventually comes into view. When the two runs give the same picture at every step,
              a longer album keeps the same ambiguity. Kalman’s unobservable states give that
              situation for an entire trajectory. The question is which window you have, and which
              distinctions it keeps.
                  Rice’s theorem asks a different question about programs. Henry Rice proved
              in 1953 that no program can decide every instance of a nontrivial property of the
              partial function another program computes. Here you can use a box with just two
              states. Hand the reader one identical picture for both, and a question whose answers
              differ: the reader has one input and would need two answers. That argument
              finishes before any question about an algorithm’s time or computability arises.
                  The counter lives in the state, and whether anyone outside can read it depends
              entirely on what they’re shown, and a window with a pair like that in it can’t price
              the flag exactly, with any rule, ever. That raises the question I’ve been pushing in
              front of me since the buckets. Fine, the flag went up and was paid for and I can see
              it in the right window. What does that entitle me to? A paid flag is a paid flag, so
              what’s the claim behind it, and when am I allowed to lean on it?
CHAPTER 9




Structural entitlement

I keep writing the word “vouch” and then taking it back. Let me stop doing that
and say what it would take. A reading went from NO to YES, the toll charged the
move that did it (Section 2), maybe the reading stays up (Section 3 says what it
takes to make it stay), and the right window shows it (Section 8). Now: what is a
later step allowed to do because of that? It’s a different question from “is the thing
true,” and the gap between those two is the subject of this section, and I’d argue it’s
the subject of most of the arguments people have about evidence, so give me the
long way round.


9.1 The coin that moved

There’s an experiment you can run on a friend, and I’d ask you to actually run it,
because the feeling of it is the point. Put a coin under one of three cups while they
watch; say it’s cup one. Send them out of the room. Move the coin to cup three.
Then, and this is the trick, put a second coin under cup one. Bring them back and
ask: “Is there a coin under cup one?”
    Suppose they say yes because they trust that the coin they saw has stayed put.
There is a coin there, so their answer is true. Grant that their original look and
ordinary expectation of no interference justify the belief. The Gettier-style difficulty
is then visible: the reason follows the first coin, while the replacement makes the
answer true by luck. A suspicious friend who refuses the retention assumption has
not entered this particular trap.
    The experiment is Gettier’s trap, done with cups (Section 14 tells his own cases):
Edmund Gettier’s three-page paper from 1963, “Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?”,
which broke a definition of knowledge in about the time it takes to read it. The
definition was that you know something when it’s true, you believe it, and you’ve
got good reasons. Gettier took it from two philosophers of the 1950s, Roderick
Chisholm and A. J. Ayer, and the only place he mentions Plato is a footnote saying
Plato “seems to be considering” something like it in the Theaetetus. I’d assumed
people had leaned on that definition since Plato. As far as I can find, they hadn’t.
The Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on the analysis of knowledge calls the idea that it

                                                  173
174   9 Structural entitlement


               was ever widely held “a bit of a convenient fiction,” and Julien Dutant, a philosopher
               at King’s College London, wrote a 2015 paper called “The Legend of the Justified
               True Belief Analysis” arguing that the older tradition asked for something stronger:
               a mark on the belief that can’t be wrong. I’ve read only summaries of Dutant’s paper,
               so take that last part as his, secondhand. Gettier’s two cases, and the cups, show a
               belief that passes all three tests and still isn’t knowledge, because the reasons and
               the fact aren’t connected; they just happen to agree. Bertrand Russell had a related
               case in 1948: somebody looks at a stopped clock at the one moment it happens to
               be right, and they’re right about the time, and they know nothing.
                   Is 1963 the bottom? It isn’t even close, and 1948 isn’t either. The Stanford
               Encyclopedia’s entry on the analysis of knowledge, which is where I’d send you to
               check me, gives a case from the eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara:
               you’re looking for water on a hot day, you see water ahead, it’s a mirage, and when
               you get there you happen to find water under a rock. And one from Peter of Mantua,
               a logician of the late fourteenth century who died in 1400 and whose Logica survives
               in manuscript: Plato is running right next to you, you take him for Socrates, so you
               believe Socrates is running, and Socrates is in fact running, in Rome, where you
               can’t see him. Are there older cases still? Maybe, and this is where the trail goes
               cold, which isn’t the same as where it ends. What it changes is how much I trust
               the shape. People in different centuries, languages and traditions kept building the
               same trap by hand: a reason that points at one thing, and a truth that happens to be
               sitting on another.
                   What would repair this particular reason? Lift cup one again. Now there is a new
               look at the coin currently there. Under the ordinary assumptions about seeing the
               cup and coin, that gives current evidence instead of a memory about the coin that
               left. It does not make perception infallible or promise the coin will remain after the
               cup goes down. The demonstration isolates the missing connection; it is not a proof
               settling every account of knowledge.


               9.2 Plato nearly had it
               Who was Theaetetus, though? The dialogue is named for a real person, and I wanted
               to know who. He was a mathematician. In the dialogue he’s a teenager, and he
               tells Socrates that his teacher Theodorus had been showing them, one case at a
               time, that the side of a square of area three, or five, and so on up to seventeen, can’t
               be named by any fraction: the Pythagoreans’ diagonal from Section 6, done again
               case by case. The young man’s idea was to stop going one case at a time and find
               one word for all of them. Euclid’s tenth book, on lengths that share no common
               measure, is thought to be largely his work, and he’s credited with being the first
               to study the eight-faced and twenty-faced solids, the two Plato assigned to air and
                                                                           9.3 The shape, said once   175


water in the Timaeus. The dialogue opens with him being carried home to Athens
from the army at Corinth, badly wounded and sick with the dysentery going round
the camp, barely alive; the usual date is 369 BC. And the conversation itself has
come down as a record. Euclid of Megara (not the geometer) says he took notes as
soon as he got home, filled them out later, and had Socrates correct them whenever
he came to Athens, and he has the result read aloud. So the dialogue about what
turns a true belief into knowledge survives as a record Socrates himself corrected.
That changes nothing in the argument. I just like that the book about knowledge is
named for the man who took the diagonal and made it general.
    I want to be fair to the Theaetetus here, because it’s easy to be quick with the
ancients and they deserve better. Socrates, in that dialogue, doesn’t just say “true
belief plus reasons.” He tries three different senses of what the “account” behind a
true belief could be: a statement you can say aloud; a list of the thing’s parts; and,
third, the mark that sets this thing apart from everything else it could be confused
with. He tries each, and each fails, and the dialogue ends with nobody knowing
what knowledge is, which is one of the more honest endings in philosophy. But
the third sense is the one I’d underline: an account as the thing that distinguishes,
the test that gives the real case a value no rival gives. He couldn’t make it work
because he had no way to say what the account had to be attached to. Two and a
half thousand years later, this book’s guess is that the thing it has to be attached
to is a state, and the account is an object sitting in it. I’m not claiming that settles
Plato. I’m claiming he was pointing at the right thing, and that’s my reading of the
dialogue, which you can check against it in an afternoon.
    Push on that once more, because Socrates gives his own reason for dropping the
third account, and it isn’t the one I just gave. If the account means knowing the
mark that sets the thing apart, then knowledge has been defined as true belief plus
knowledge of something, and the word you were trying to define is back inside its
own definition, which is a circle. Does a check get out of it? It gets the word out: a
test that ran and found the mark isn’t defined in terms of knowing. Whether the test
was any good is still a real question, and it’s the question the rest of this section puts
a price on. So I’d say the circle moves rather than vanishing. It moves somewhere
you can look at it, which is the most I’d claim.


9.3 The shape, said once
What I mean by entitlement has three parts, and I’ll try to earn each.
   A run is entitled to a claim when three things are present. First, an object,
carried in the state: a grouping, a relation between groups, a counter, a package of
constraints. The object is a thing you could print; a belief doesn’t count. Second,
a checked relation between that object and the claim: a test that was actually run,
176   9 Structural entitlement


               with its result on hand; “a test exists” doesn’t count. Third, an event on the record
               that says this object was put there and paid for, so that anyone auditing the run can
               point back at the moment the claim was marked.
                  I’ll say it as a definition, so the rest of the section has something to point at:

               Definition 9.1 (Entitlement). A run is entitled to a claim when three things are on
               hand: an object carried in the run’s states; a checked relation between that object
               and the claim, meaning a test that was run and whose result is on the record; and a
               paid event, a move of the run at which the object was put in place and which the
               price list charged at least one. In a Thiele machine (Definition 2.2) a move that
               takes the reading from no to yes is a paid move, because the toll charges it; whether
               the object went in at that move is a separate question. This is the book’s word.
                   The first part comes with the third: a move of the run that put the object in place
               leaves it in the run’s next state. I name the object on its own anyway, because the
               checked relation is about it. Keep the second and third parts separate. A note saying
               “coin under cup one, checked” can be written without anyone lifting a cup. That
               gives an object, but no checked relation. Now actually lift the cup, find the coin
               and write the result. Suppose that move costs nothing: the note is on the sheet, the
               check really happened, but the NO box stays NO and the tally line stays blank. This
               time the object and the checked relation are both there. What is missing is the paid
               event. The run isn’t entitled in this definition’s sense; that doesn’t make the result of
               the check false.
                   The reverse distinction matters too. A move from NO to YES puts one unit of
               cost on the tally line, but the bare toll says nothing about what that move looked at.
               Payment alone supplies neither a check nor its correctness. The later machine will
               bind those acts together in its step rule; the five parts of a Thiele machine do not do
               that by themselves.
                   The part to hold on to is that nothing in the five parts makes a later move read the
               reading. The step function is handed the state and a move name, and it’s allowed
               to ignore the YES box completely; plenty of systems will. So when I say a run is
               entitled, I mean what someone auditing the run may conclude from the reading and
               the receipt. The system doesn’t have to enforce it, and unless somebody builds it to,
               it won’t.
                   This is a good place to line up the three things the word established has had to
               mean so far, because they blur easily, and a blur here would make the book look like
               it proves more than it does. The yardstick is the four conditions Section 14 sets for
               a check being about this very claim: the same property, the same thing, the same
               edition, and an honest check.

    After the column of questions, the first column is Section 2’s bare toll: a paid
crossing, and nothing says a check happened at all (Section 10 has a remark saying
exactly that, Remark 10.2). The second is this section’s entitlement. The third is
the small machine of Part III, whose step won’t let a commit through without a
passing check of the same property, on the same thing, at the same edition, for
every program from a clean start (Theorem 15.10, and Theorem 15.11 for a run
that ends certified), whose checker comes with a proof that it says what it means
(Lemma 15.2, Theorem 15.13), and whose certified runs from a clean start cost at
least three (Observation 15.19). Even there two things are missing, and the first is
in the table, where you’ll see it. The step doesn’t police whether a check could have
failed: a property every value has is a perfectly legal check, sound and useless. And
in all three columns the status belongs to whoever reads the record. The machine
doesn’t know anything. What its flag means is assigned from outside, by whoever
says what each property means.
    Why does the honest check carry so much? The philosopher Linda Zagzebski,
who works on knowledge and the virtues of a careful mind, argued in 1994 that any
account of knowledge whose justification leaves even a small gap between having
good reasons and being right lets a Gettier case through: take a case where bad
luck makes the reasons point the wrong way, then add a stroke of good luck that
makes the belief true anyway. The first three conditions plus an honest check close
that gap by construction, and only one half of honesty is needed for it, the half that
says no when the property is false. Saying yes whenever it’s true is extra. A check
178   9 Structural entitlement


               that can be wrong, a test suite that sometimes passes broken code, puts you straight
               back in her gap, and then the record certifies something smaller and still true: this
               procedure said yes.
                   And who certifies that the check is honest? The record doesn’t. Honesty is a fact
               about what the check does on every input, and a finished state holds the run’s values,
               not that. A proof of it can sit in a state and be checked there, but the checking
               is a check too, with its own honesty to vouch for, and somewhere the chain stops
               at a proof somebody accepts; in this book that proof is read outside every run,
               and nothing on the record pays for it. So an established claim is two things stuck
               together: a run property the record carries and a program property a proof carries,
               and the proof is entitlement for the auditor. The machine gets none from it. On
               the machine of Part III the chain stops at the first step, the checker’s own proof, by
               choice; Section 15 says why.
                   The engineering version of this was already built, in 1996 and 1997. The
               computer scientist George Necula, then at Carnegie Mellon, called it proof-carrying
               code: when you ship a program to a host that doesn’t trust you, you ship a proof
               with it that the program obeys the host’s safety rules, and the host checks the proof
               that arrived before running anything: not your reputation, and not “a proof exists
               somewhere,” but the one in the box. A quarter century earlier Stephen Cook’s
               certificates had the same bones, from Section 2: a claim comes with a witness that’s
               cheap to check, and the checker checks that witness. And the Scottish philosopher
               David Hume, in 1748, arguing about miracles in his Enquiry Concerning Human
               Understanding, laid out the thing the receipt replaces. He weighed testimony against
               evidence, and wrote that “a wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the
               evidence.” The way I read him, the whole of his argument is a method for how
               much to trust a witness when you have no receipt. The move in this book is to stop
               weighing. A claim on the record is either backed by its object and its paid event,
               or it’s testimony from outside, and a run that leans on testimony hasn’t earned it
               itself. It can inherit it, but only as far as the copy it leans on is genuine, which is
               Section 8’s problem of a record shown from outside.
                   Robert Brandom, a philosopher at the University of Pittsburgh, built a whole
               account of language on two words this book leans on, commitment and entitlement,
               and his Making It Explicit (1994) is where I’d send anyone who suspects I invented
               the pair. In his picture, as I read it and as his reviewers describe it, people talking
               keep score on each other: what each speaker is committed to, what they’ve put
               themselves on the hook for, and what each is entitled to, what they’re licensed to
               claim. You can be committed without being entitled (a reckless assertion), many
               claims count as entitled by default until someone challenges them, and entitlement
               can be borrowed: I can claim a thing on your say-so and defer to you when I’m
               challenged. Lay mine beside his and the differences are the content. His score is
                                                                          9.3 The shape, said once   179


kept by the other people in the room; here it’s a reading in the state. His entitlement
often comes by default; here it’s an event that has to happen and is charged. And
his deferral is my testimony, which I’ve just let back in on a leash: borrowed
entitlement is only as good as the copy is genuine. The leash has an older formal
cousin, the jurisdiction rule of Burrows, Abadi and Needham’s logic of authentication
(Section 8), where you take a statement on an authority’s word only if you already
believe the authority has jurisdiction over it. It came first, presented in 1989 and
printed in 1990, years ahead of Brandom’s book of 1994, and its words are believes
and jurisdiction where his are commitment and entitlement.
    There’s a whole field that would want a word here too, the logic of belief revision,
which asks how a reasonable mind should change what it believes when something
new comes in. Its nearest neighbours are worth naming, and I couldn’t keep them
apart until I put them back on the table with the cups. Your friend believes the coin
is under cup one. They can learn something that doesn’t clash with that, say cup two
is empty, and just add it. They can lift cup one, find nothing, and have to change
their mind about a table nobody touched. Or you can tell them you moved the coin.
The last two felt alike to me at first, but they aren’t: in one the friend was wrong,
and in the other the friend was right, and then the table changed.
    Krister Segerberg, a Swedish logician at Uppsala, built a logic of irrevocable
revision in 1998: accepting something so that it can’t be given up, which is the
firmness question taken to its end. Isaac Levi, a philosopher at Columbia who spent
a career on how beliefs get fixed and unfixed, split adding a belief into a deliberate
kind and a routine kind (I cite his 1991 book; the split goes back to his 1980 one).
Deliberate is reasoning your way there. Routine is where you take on whatever a
procedure you committed to in advance hands you, the way you’d accept a reading
off a thermometer you’ve already decided to trust, or what’s under a cup when you
lift it. What I think the split rests on is when the trust goes in: once, before the
data comes. A passing CHECK, the test move of the small machine in Section 15, is
routine in exactly that sense, with a checker proved honest once, outside every run.
    Neil Tennant, a logician at Ohio State, and Gösta Grahne, a computer scientist
trained at Helsinki, I first filed as two separate complaints. They’re one move
made from opposite sides. The target is the best-known impossibility in that field,
the Swedish philosopher Peter Gärdenfors’s 1986 theorem that a natural rule for
conditionals, the one his paper calls the Ramsey test, can’t live with rational revision.
Tennant argued in 2008 that it goes through only by treating some additions as
revisions: the friend who learned cup two was empty gets counted as having changed
their mind. Grahne, working on updates and counterfactuals, argued in 1998 that
Gärdenfors’s theorem bites only revising, so the friend whose coin was moved is out
of its reach. Side by side, they squeeze the theorem from both ends into one case:
being wrong about a table nobody touched.
180   9 Structural entitlement


                   The line this book leans on hardest is between two kinds of change. Revising is
               changing what you believe about a world that stayed put. Updating is changing it
               because the world moved. Two computer scientists, Hirofumi Katsuno and Alberto
               Mendelzon, drew that line for knowledge bases in a 1991 paper on the difference
               between updating a knowledge base and revising it; database researchers had
               been working on updates with incomplete information since the mid-1980s, Arthur
               Keller and Marianne Winslett among them. Grahne’s result stands on it. And look
               at what the friend sees: an empty cup one is the same empty cup whether they
               misremembered or you moved the coin. The evidence alone can’t tell revising from
               updating; that’s a fibre. What tells them apart is a count of how often the cups were
               touched. The machine in Part III keeps that count as an edition number for each
               thing, and its version rule treats every write as an update: a write moves the edition
               number, so every fact about the old edition stops counting for the new one.
                   And Alexandru Baltag, Bryan Renne and Sonja Smets, three logicians at Am-
               sterdam, gave a logic in 2014 that keeps apart three things Gettier’s cases blur:
               justified belief, explicit knowledge and conclusive evidence. The friend who watched
               has justified belief; the friend who lifted the cup has conclusive evidence. Explicit
               knowledge I read as knowing with the justification written out beside it, the way the
               record keeps its check, and I’m less sure of that one. Put them together and they say
               something exact about this book’s record. A record that’s never wrong and never
               corrected would be a dogmatist’s dream if its sentences were about the present, but
               they aren’t: each says a property held of a thing at one edition, and that sentence
               stays true after the edition number moves on. The record can be infallible and never
               corrected only because its sentences are edition-stamped. Strip the stamps, and the
               first write would turn it into a liar that can’t take anything back.
                   Push on that and it gives twice. The record is Segerberg’s irrevocable acceptance
               every time, with no revising in it. If a check was dishonest, the only fix that fits a
               record like this is a second record on top saying “withdrawn,” the way a revocation
               list works, so the infallibility leans on the checker, proved once, outside. And the
               record is never wrong partly because it only talks about past editions. Whoever
               reads it wants now, and getting from “held at that edition” to “holds now” crosses
               every update since. The record doesn’t make that step for you.
                   That leaves the logicians who taught the logic of knowing to count, whom
               Section 14 names again in passing. This time I take them properly, and I want to
               see what each price rests on. Ho Ngoc Duc, in 1997, gave the logic of knowing
               an operator for “true after some train of thought”: an agent doesn’t know every
               consequence of what it knows now. It can come to know any of them by taking
               steps of reasoning. I took that at first for the thing I was after, until I saw which way
               it points. His operator points forward, at what the agent could come to know. A
               record points back, at what was checked. His operator and a record are one arrow,
                                                         9.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals   181


read from opposite ends. And Sergei Artemov and Roman Kuznets, in 2014, turned
logical omniscience into a question of cost: a logic escapes it when every valid claim
that something is known comes with a proof whose size is bounded by a polynomial
in the size of the claim. The usual modal logics of knowledge can’t pass that test
unless NP equals coNP, which most people would bet against, and justification logic
passes it for knowledge stated together with its justification, because the size of the
justification pays for the search. That last clause took me a few reads. What I think
it means is Cook’s certificate from the proof-carrying-code paragraph above: put the
justification inside the claim, and the hard part, finding it, was paid before the claim
was written. Their price rests on an open bet, and it’s a price on looking, which is a
price of a sort. Steps and a price are both there, then, in their own form. What I
still don’t find in them is the one I care about: a single act that closes a question for
good and is charged as that act. Their steps are steps of reasoning, and their price is
on finding a proof. Neither is on settling. I couldn’t get past the journal’s paywall
to Artemov and Kuznets’s paper, so my account of it comes from how other people
describe it.
    Push on mine the same way and it gives. A check is one of Duc’s trains of thought,
so my act is the last step of his train, where the walking stops. What I’ve added is a
direction and a charge on stopping. Where the charge sits follows from one choice:
I want it to bind every program the machine runs, and a charge that does that has
to sit inside the step, since a program can skip any charge kept where it can write.
    There are three things entitlement is not. It isn’t permission: an access control
system says who may write to what, and that’s granted from outside and says nothing
about truth; a process with permission to write the note still has no entitlement.
It isn’t “it’s true, so I can use it”: that’s the cups. And it isn’t “sound by luck”: a
shortcut that gives the right answer because the inputs happened to cooperate is the
stopped clock. The count below has one condition aimed at it, and I’ll tell you what
the condition says and how much it actually catches.


9.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals
Now I need the number, because a book about what keeping costs has to say how
much, and the idea fits in a game you can play with three playing cards. Shuffle
cards marked 1, 2, 3 face down. Sort them using only questions of the form “is this
one bigger than that one?”, and count the questions. There are six orders the cards
could be in. Each question has two answers, so after one question you’ve split the
six into at most two piles, after two questions at most four, and you need to get
down to one. Four is less than six, so two questions can’t always do it, and three
can, and you can draw the tree of questions on paper and see it: six leaves, three
deep. The number of questions you need is at least the base-two logarithm of the
182   9 Structural entitlement


               number of possibilities you started with, rounded up: that’s log2 of 6, which is a
               bit under 3, rounded to 3. Donald Knuth, a computer scientist at Stanford, gives
               this, in the volume on sorting of his The Art of Computer Programming, as the lower
               bound for all comparison sorting, and the shape of the argument is just: a tree f
               questions deep has at most 2 f leaves, so it can’t tell apart more than 2 f cases.
                   And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards.
               There are 120 orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven
               questions, and seven is enough, though not by the obvious method. Finding the
               way is a good evening with a deck of cards (Knuth has it, under the name merge
               insertion, from the mathematicians Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in 1959). Now
               take twelve cards. They can be in 479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8,
               so the count says at least 29. Ford and Johnson’s method takes 30, and in 1965
               Mark Wells, a mathematician at Los Alamos who built a programming language for
               exactly this kind of combinatorial search, showed by a computer search that nothing
               does better: twelve cards need 30. The floor was 29 and the price is 30, so the count
               is a floor and only a floor; it never promises the floor can be reached, and the bound
               later in this section has to be read exactly the same way.
                   Ralph Hartley, an electronics researcher at Bell Labs, writing in the Bell System
               Technical Journal in 1928, before Shannon, measured information exactly this way:
               the logarithm of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count. I use that
               measure here, and I’ll say plainly it’s Hartley’s. Shannon’s would need a distribution
               over the list, and there isn’t one; there’s just the list’s length.
                   The same count works with something you can hold. Put three coins under three
               cups. Each coin is heads or tails, so there are eight possible rows under the cups.
               Someone hands you two answers: heads under the first cup, tails under the second.
               Lift the first cup and compare, and a matching answer leaves four possible rows. Lift
               the second and compare, and a match leaves two. The last coin can still be either
               way. The list really shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that count needed a claim
               about which way the last coin faces.
                                                               9.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals   183


                                Three coins under cups
                                   8 possible rows

                                                Lift first cup:
                                                find heads.

                                      First is heads
                                     4 possible rows

                                                Lift second cup:
                                                find tails.

                                First heads, second tails
                                     2 possible rows


                             The third coin could be either:
                                     heads or tails.
These observations halve the candidate list. A price on those observations is a separate rule;
                           the shrinking list alone supplies none.
     This is a parlour game, and an old one. In A Christmas Carol, in 1843, Scrooge’s
nephew Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks
of something, and everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no.
He’s thinking of an animal, a disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and
lives in London, and the answer is Uncle Scrooge. Most people know the game as
twenty questions, and twenty is a good number for it: a balanced question splits
the remaining field in half, and twenty such questions can guarantee identification
among 220 = 1,048,576 possibilities. A lucky answer to “is it this one?” can finish
immediately; the count is about handling every possible answer. Push on that,
though. The halving only happens because Fred answers truthfully about what’s
actually in his head. Lie once and the count still shrinks; it shrinks around the wrong
animal. The cups showed the same thing: the four and the two are real because
you lifted the cup and compared. Being told what was under it wouldn’t have made
them real.
     Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are “still on the
table,” the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior
and the second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as a list you could print.
They aren’t “the space of possible worlds.” Picture the ruling-out as observations,
each observation that ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like the
card tree. The bound says that if that tree is no deeper than the number of paid
steps the run took, and the tree has enough leaves to cover the narrowing in a way
I’ll spell out in a moment, then the counter rose by at least log2 of the prior’s length,
rounded up, minus log2 of the posterior’s length, rounded up. Put another way, the
184   9 Structural entitlement


               counter rose by at least one unit for each of the index bits the list lost, where the
               index bits of a list are the yes/no questions it takes to point at one entry of it, the
               card count again.
                   “Paid step” needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least
               one for. In a Thiele machine the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading is
               one; a price list may put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send, a check),
               and the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape, branches
               and leaves with nothing written on them, and “no deeper than the number of paid
               steps” is a count along the run that happened, not a walk down the tree. A paid step
               doesn’t have to have asked any question at all.
                   Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn’t say about the run. It takes the two
               lists, the tree and the covering as given. It doesn’t say the run produced the posterior
               from the prior; nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given
               lists, a tree and a covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover
               the rounded drop in list length. Here Section 5’s warning comes due: watching can
               narrow without costing anything, so the payment can’t be dug out of the narrowing.
               It goes in as a premise, the tree’s depth against the paid steps, and I’ll keep calling it
               one. There is a version where the run makes the posterior itself, from a prior and
               the tests it passed, and there the premise is a share each test keeps.


               9.5 What “narrower” buys: a stronger test
               Before the count, one link that’s pure logic, and Plato’s third account is the whole
               of it. Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each
               candidate looks like from outside. The list’s membership test accepts an observation
               when some candidate on the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get
               pickier: anything the short list’s test accepts, the long list’s accepts too. The word
               for that, and it runs backward from English, is stronger: the stronger test is the one
               that lets fewer things through.
                   Pickier, though, isn’t the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap. Take
               all six orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left of card
               2: 1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: “is 1 left of 2?” Every survivor says yes,
               and the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior’s test accepts yes and no, the posterior’s
               only yes, and the posterior’s test is strictly stronger. Second observation, same two
               lists: “is the first card a 3?” Now 3-1-2 says yes and the other two survivors say no,
               and among the removed orders 3-2-1 says yes and 2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept
               yes and no, so they have the same strength, even though three orders are gone.
               What made the difference is a removed candidate whose observation no survivor
               shares. Such a candidate is Plato’s mark, the thing that sets this case apart from
               everything it could be confused with, turned into a function. Narrow the list and
                                                                            9.6 What you’ve got   185


keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and the test is strictly stronger; narrow
it without one, and the test may not have moved at all.


9.6 What you’ve got
A paid flag is not a true claim; Section 8 left it at “a paid flag is a paid flag,” and
Section 10 will say it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation
behind it gives you is entitlement: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as
established, and can point at the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing
in the five parts makes the system itself read the flag; I said that above and I’m
saying it again because it’s the sentence most likely to get lost.) Entitlement costs
at least the index bits of narrowing it commits to, given lists, a tree and a covering
somebody supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree’s depth. The cups say why
entitlement and truth are different. Plato says what the checked relation has to do,
which is to distinguish. Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.
    Put the three pieces on one hypothesis list (narrow the list with a test that
separates, find the paid event, count the charges against a tree the run paid for) and
you get a single statement, structural entitlement, once over any Thiele machine
and once more on the small machine of Part III, where the run starts clean and the
paid steps are its own record moves, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY, at a cost of
exactly one each. The first one reads as follows.


Theorem 9.1 (Structural entitlement, over any Thiele machine). Take a Thiele
machine (Definition 2.2), a state s that reads no, and a run t from s that ends in a
state that reads yes. Take a type of candidates, a type of observations with an exact
equality test, an observation obs of each candidate, and a decoder d that turns a run
into an observation (what its record shows). Take lists Ω and Ω′ of candidates and
a decision tree T such that: (H1) Ω′ strictly narrows Ω: every member of Ω′ is in Ω,
and some member of Ω isn’t in Ω′ ; (H2) some dropped candidate w, in Ω and not
in Ω′ , shows an observation different from every survivor’s; (H3) the decoded run
d(t) is shown by some survivor; (H4) |Ω′ | > 0 and |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |; (H5) at least
depth( T ) steps of the run are charged at least one each. Then (1) the membership
test of Ω′ is strictly stronger than the membership test of Ω; (2) some step of the
run took the reading from no to yes, and that step was charged at least one; and (3)
the sum of the charges of the run’s steps is at least ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉.

Proof. (1) is the cards’ argument: the dropped w shows something no survivor
shows, so the posterior test says no where the prior test says yes, and every survivor
was in the prior, so nothing the posterior accepts is refused by the prior. (2) The
186   9 Structural entitlement


               run starts at no and ends at yes, so at some step the reading goes from no to yes,
               and the toll charges that step at least one. (3) is a count: the covering puts every
               survivor at a leaf of T, a tree of depth depth( T ) has at most 2depth(T ) leaves, so the
               index bits are at most depth( T ), and the sum of the charges is at least the number
               of steps charged at least one. On a system that obeys conservation the sum of the
               charges is the counter’s rise.
                   With the counter’s rise in place of the sum of the charges it’s the same count,
               so for a system that obeys conservation it’s the special case. Three things in the
               hypotheses feed nothing, and I’m naming them here so you don’t have to find them:
               (H3) isn’t used by any of the three conclusions; from (H1) only the inclusion is used,
               and the gap goes unused; and in (H2) the words “not in Ω′ ” go unused, since a
               candidate whose observation differs from every survivor’s can’t be a survivor itself.
               And (H4)’s |Ω′ | > 0 is used in that proof but can be dropped too: the covering
               forces it once the prior has a member.
                   A statement like that is true by packaging: it takes the hypotheses in and hands
               the conclusions back, and the right word for it is a checklist, a checklist for leaning
               on a claim. It discovers nothing about leaning.
                   And a checklist isn’t nothing. On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field, northeast of
               Dayton, Ohio, the Army was evaluating Boeing’s new four-engine bomber, the Model
               299. Shortly after take-off it plunged back onto the field and caught fire; that’s how
               the wire report of that day has it, and the later histories add that it pitched up and
               stalled first, which is what elevators locked in a raised position would do. Two men
               died of their injuries, the Army’s pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and Boeing’s chief test pilot,
               Leslie Tower. The airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks on, a locking
               mechanism worked from inside the cockpit that holds the control surfaces still while
               the plane sits on the ground. There’s a famous line that a newspaper called it too
