               much airplane for one man to fly. I couldn’t find that line in any paper from 1935;
               the earliest place I could find it is a New Yorker article from December 2007 by Atul
               Gawande, a surgeon who writes about how people get complicated work right, and
               he names no newspaper, so take it as a lead. What I can find is what came after. The
               answer was a card: a list of things to check, in order, every time, and the crews of
               the airplane worked through written checklists for each phase of flight. The most
               careful history of it I found is by Walter Boyne, a retired Air Force colonel and a
               former director of the National Air and Space Museum. By his account it wasn’t
               the first written routine for a pilot; those go back before the First World War. And
               it’s this crash, he says, that made the checklist the way a crew flew. The airplane
               went on to be the B-17. Nothing on that card was a discovery. Every item on it was
               something the pilots already knew. What the card did was make sure none of it
               got left out when it mattered. Putting entitlement’s hypotheses on one list does the
                                                             9.7 A grouping, checked and committed   187


same: it finds nothing new about leaning on a claim, and it makes the hypotheses
impossible to drop quietly.


9.7 A grouping, checked and committed
Section 6 ended on buckets, and the toll of Part I never needed them: it prices any
yes-or-no reading. In this subsection the word in this section’s title gets attached to
a partition in a theorem. Take a pile, a finite list of items, and a grouping, a bucket
label for each item. Its partition is “same label,” and the classes of that relation are a
partition in the sense of Definition 6.1. The data is a key for each item, drawn from
any type with at least two values (a grouping’s own labels can serve as a key), and a
grouping is sound for a key when any two items it puts in one bucket have the same
key. The grouping says “these belong together,” and the key says whether they do.
One grouping refines another when every bucket of the first sits inside a bucket of
the second.
   Put two red buttons and two blue buttons on the table, numbered 1 through
4, with 1 and 2 red. Let the key be colour. Circles round {1, 2} and {3, 4} give a
sound grouping: every pair inside a circle has the same colour. Split the red circle
into two singletons and it stays sound; splitting cannot introduce a mismatched pair.
Join 1 and 3 instead and it fails. Changing the circles’ names from A and B to North
and South changes none of these checks. That is why the reading below uses the
partition, not the spelling of its labels.
   Now comes the rule for the record. Put a tick beside a grouping only after
comparing the colours within each circle. Copy that ticked grouping onto a separate
commitment card, then place the card in a record envelope; charge one tally for
each of those three acts. Change a button’s colour between the check and the copy,
and the old tick must no longer authorize the copy. The machine’s SET rule below
does that by clearing the current table and channel. A record already kept remains
about the old colours, which it keeps with the grouping.
   Here is one example machine that meets the model, the smallest I know that
makes a record from a checked claim. It is an illustration; the theorem above holds
of any Thiele machine. The bucket machine holds a key, a table of checked groupings,
a channel, a record, a trap latch and a ledger. SET costs nothing; it replaces the key
and throws away the table and the channel, which were checked against the old key.
CHECK g costs one and passes when g is sound for the current key, and, when it
passes, writes g in the table. COMMIT g costs one and passes when the table holds
a grouping with the same partition as g, and puts g in the channel. CERTIFY costs
one and passes when the channel holds a grouping; if the record is still down it
then keeps that grouping with the current key, the key a grouping with its partition
was checked against, and a record already kept is left as it is. A CHECK, COMMIT
188   9 Structural entitlement


               or CERTIFY that fails traps, and a trapped machine only pays. The reading for a
               grouping g is: the record holds a grouping with g’s partition. In words, that reading
               says “this grouping has been checked and committed.”


               Theorem 9.2 (A committed grouping entitles exactly its refinements). (1) The
               classes of “same label” under any grouping form a partition. (2) Two groupings with
               the same partition of the pile have the same reading at every state of the bucket
               machine. (3) For groupings g and h of the pile, soundness of g for a key gives
               soundness of h for that key, for every key, exactly when h refines g. (4) On every run
               from a clean state (table and channel empty, record down), if the reading for g is up,
               the record holds a grouping and a key for which g is sound, and so is every grouping
               that refines g; and for every grouping h that doesn’t refine g there is a key for which
               g is sound and h isn’t. (5) The bucket machine obeys the toll, and a run from a clean
               state that ends with the record up has raised the ledger by at least three.

               Proof. (1) Every item has its own label, exchanging two items does not change
               whether their labels agree, and two agreements through a third label give agreement
               with each other. Thus “same label” has the three sameness rules, and its classes form
               the partition already constructed in Theorem 6.1.
                   (2) The reading asks which items were put together, not what the buckets were
               called. Replacing one grouping by another with exactly the same buckets therefore
               changes no answer to that reading.
                   (3) If h only cuts g’s buckets smaller, every pair h keeps together was already
               together under g. Soundness of g gives that pair equal keys, so h is sound too. If h
               does anything else, it puts some two items together that g kept in separate buckets.
               Give every item in the first item’s g-bucket one key value and every other item a
               second key value. Each g-bucket has a single key, so g is sound. The chosen h-bucket
               contains both key values, so h is not. This is why the key type needs two values.
                   (4) Follow the table, channel and record through the commands. They begin
               empty. CHECK inserts only a grouping it has found sound for the current key.
               COMMIT takes the partition of a grouping already in that table, so the selected
               grouping is sound for the same key. CERTIFY keeps that grouping and that key
               together; later commands do not replace an existing record. SET changes the
               key but empties both the table and the channel, so no old unchecked carry-over
               remains there. A failed command traps instead of inserting an unsound grouping,
               and trapped commands leave those fields alone. These are all the ways those
               fields change. Their promised soundness therefore survives every command of any
               run from the clean start. Apply (3) to the grouping and key in the record: every
                                                           9.7 A grouping, checked and committed   189


refinement is sound, and every non-refinement has the counterexample key just
constructed.
   (5) Only CERTIFY raises the record, and its price is one, giving the toll. A
successful CERTIFY needs a grouping in the channel. From an empty channel only a
successful COMMIT could have supplied it. From an empty table that COMMIT in
turn needs a successful CHECK. These are three distinct earlier acts in order, each
charged one. The run’s nonnegative bill is at least three.
    So “structural” has a theorem under it. The reading sees a grouping only through
its partition, which is item (2). If the recorded circles are sound, so is any way of
cutting them smaller, whatever the key is. A grouping that isn’t a cutting-smaller can
still happen to be sound for this key (paint all four buttons red and every grouping
is sound), but nothing in the record promises it: for some key it fails. Item (3) and
item (4) say exactly that much, and that’s all the record buys. It’s the three parts
of entitlement from the start of this section in their smallest case: the object is the
grouping, the checked relation is soundness for the key, and the paid event is the
CERTIFY, on top of a CHECK and a COMMIT at a cost of one each. What it doesn’t
do is make a later move act on the record. The only move that reads it is CERTIFY,
and only to leave a kept grouping alone. Like everything in this section, it says what
someone auditing the run may conclude.
    Before the machine of Part III, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the
“insight” in “No Free Insight” (Section 5), because I’ve been using it as if it meant
one thing.
CHAPTER 10




What insight is

I named the rule in this book “No Free Insight,” and the name ran ahead of any
careful account of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not
learning (Section 5), not looking, not copying. Part I already says where to look:
learning borrows and committing pays, so the part of insight a toll can price is the
part that stays. It’s time to say what that is, and to say it in a way that someone who
studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn’t laugh at. So who are those people,
and what did they find? I’ll go through what I ran into and push on each piece as I
go. Where a story reached me secondhand, I treat it as a lead to check.


10.1 Sultan and the sticks

In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station
with a colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until
1920, five years longer than planned, with the chimpanzees to watch. The famous
one is Sultan. Food is outside the cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each
too short, but one fits into the end of the other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks,
plays with the sticks, and then, by Köhler’s account, at a moment you can see, joins
them and reaches the food. Köhler’s words were Einsicht and einsichtig, which came
into English as “insight,” and the whole school of psychology he belonged to, the
Gestalt school, said that’s what thinking is: a restructuring, the moment two sticks
stop being two sticks and become one tool. Stacking up tries until one works was,
for them, something else. Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935
and in English in 1945, five years after he died at thirty-seven; he’d spent his last
years working with Köhler at Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a
box of tacks, matches, and the task of fixing the candle to the wall. The obstacle is
seeing the box as a possible shelf while it is presented as the container for the tacks.
And then he found that if you hand people the box empty, with the tacks poured out
beside it, they solve it far more readily. The objects were the same; what changed
was which relation among them was on the table.
   I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn’t add an object. Sultan
had both sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived

                                  190
                                                                            10.2 It isn’t a feeling   191


was a relation, which is to say a piece of structure in Section 6’s sense, and the
arrival was sudden. Hold that, because the thing the toll prices also arrives in one
step, and at its best it’s also a relation.


10.2 It isn’t a feeling
A feeling of getting closer is a different thing to measure from solving the problem.
Janet Metcalfe’s experiments help separate them. In the 1980s the psychologist
Janet Metcalfe asked people to solve problems while rating, every fifteen seconds,
how “warm” they felt, how close to the answer. On ordinary problems, algebra for
instance, the warmth climbs steadily and peaks at the answer, which is what you’d
expect. On insight problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the warmth stays flat,
flat, flat, and then the answer arrives, and if anything the people who felt warmest
beforehand were more likely to be wrong. She put that last finding in the title of a
1986 paper: premonitions of insight predict impending error. Those results concern
the predictive value of warmth ratings in those tasks. They do not show that a
solution has no accompanying feeling, or that every person follows the same curve.
Try it yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen seconds while doing
a long sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.
    And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well.
Archimedes, a mathematician who died in 212 BC, asked by Hiero, the king of
Syracuse, whether a goldsmith had cheated him on a crown, gets into a bath, sees
the water rise, and runs home naked shouting “eureka,” I’ve found it. That comes
from Vitruvius, a Roman writer on architecture, writing about two centuries later. Is
it true? Galileo Galilei, then a young Italian mathematician, at twenty-two, in 1586,
took it as known that Archimedes caught the goldsmith. What he didn’t buy was the
method. Water spilling over the side, as Vitruvius tells it, was to him “a crude thing,
far from scientific precision,” and he guessed some writer had set down a rumour.
So he wrote a little tract, La Bilancetta, proposing a balance weighed in air and in
water instead, which he thought was probably what Archimedes actually did, since
it rests on Archimedes’s own results. Whether there was ever a bath, or a shout,
nobody can check now. What survives is a story two centuries late, wrapped around
a real man and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept: the bath, the
shout, the running home naked, which is to say the feeling. What it left shaky is the
part that would count as the check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith.
The bit everybody remembers is the bit that tells you least.
    So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the “aha,” is keyed to
something that the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn’t the feeling of
having it. That’s a relief, because a system of states and moves doesn’t have feelings,
192   10 What insight is


               and a word that only meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The
               version this book can price has to be keyed to an event, and the question is which.


               10.3 What happens when a computation learns
              I’ll lay out the split first, then say what the toll does with each part, and then say
              who decided the split. Keep Section 2’s sheet of paper in front of you: the NO box,
              the YES box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and VOUCH.
                   The first thing: raw observation. Something comes in and gets written down. A
              counter ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting
              on it, and the reading doesn’t move because of it. Later moves can read what it
              wrote, but that reading is a move of its own. The demon’s pad in Section 5 was raw
              observation, and raw observation is what the statistician Dennis Lindley measured
              in 1956 as the information provided by an experiment, the words of his title, and
              defined as the expected drop in your uncertainty: a real quantity, and a quantity
              about what was seen. It can cost nothing on the ledger. The toll says nothing at all
              about a move that doesn’t cross from NO to YES, so a price list may charge it zero:
              on the paper, STAY and WORK cost nothing, and Section 5’s watcher narrowed a
              whole row of candidates without paying anything. “Can” is the word that matters.
              A price list is allowed to charge for looking anyway. And in the physical world a
              look takes something too: copied onto a blank page it merges nothing and owes no
              floor under Landauer’s premise, but it can dissipate under the stated thermal-model
              assumptions, and it uses up the page, which means taking states the machine hasn’t
              used, borrowed until the page is wiped (Section 5).
                   Lindley’s measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good,
              who was Alan Turing’s main statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in
              1979 that Turing had worked out the expected weight of evidence an experiment
              would give, to judge one of the codebreaking procedures before running it, and so
              partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work that stayed secret. Turing
              measured evidence in bans, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth of one called a
              deciban, and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of
              the sheets used in that procedure were printed. It’s the same base-ten unit other
              people call the hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that
              Turing didn’t know the logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in a
              paper by Charles Sanders Peirce, the same Peirce from Section 6, who’d called it the
              weight of evidence. Peirce is as far back as Good takes it. It changes nothing in the
              argument, but it shows how well trodden this first kind of thing is. For a century and
              a half careful people have measured what an observation tells you, and every one of
              those measures is about what was seen. The toll leaves that side of the line alone.
                                                     10.3 What happens when a computation learns   193


     The second thing: the raise. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES, and
that move is where the toll applies. In any system with the five parts that obeys
the toll, that move costs at least one, and every run that starts at NO and ends at
YES pays at least one somewhere along the way, which is Section 2’s universal floor.
What’s being charged for, at its best, is exactly the Gestalt thing, a relation committed
to: one tool, claimed, out of two sticks. I say “at its best” because Section 2 was
careful about what YES means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A crossing that
writes down which relation it’s committing to carries Sultan’s tool with it. A bare
crossing, VOUCH on the paper, commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the
same.
     The third thing isn’t a kind of event. It’s an observation about the floor: it’s the
same, whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep
relation, a result nobody could have guessed, Sultan’s two sticks become one tool.
The toll charges the crossing at least one. It doesn’t charge the striking crossing
more, because the floor’s proof never looks at anything but the reading before and
after. On the paper, VOUCH from NO makes one mark whether you were thinking
of Duncker’s box or of lunch. This toy charges one either way. The general toll
supplies the same lower bound for both; an actual price schedule can charge them
differently.
     The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In
1962 the psychologist Sam Glucksberg ran Duncker’s problem with money on it:
some people were told they could win five or twenty dollars depending on how
fast they solved it. With the tacks in the box, the people chasing the money did
worse than the people who weren’t. With the box empty the problem was easier for
everybody, and the accounts I’ve read don’t agree on what the money did there, so
I’ll leave that half alone. Paying more didn’t buy the insight, and on the hard version
it got in the way. That’s a fact about heads. It says nothing about records, and I
won’t push it further than that. But it makes a nice parallel to the paper. On the
paper a deeper crossing isn’t charged more, and in Glucksberg’s room a bigger prize
didn’t bring the crossing sooner. In neither place does the price measure the depth.
     I’ll state them exactly now, for any Thiele machine (Definition 2.2). A run is still
just a list of moves, carried out in the order written. The question is which of those
moves crosses from no to yes, and what that crossing lets you conclude about the
total charge.

Definition 10.1 (Raise, non-raising move). In a Thiele machine, a step from state s
by move i is a raise when it turns the reading on: cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) =
yes. A move i is a non-raising move when no step by it, from any state, is a raise.
Raw observation, the first thing above, is one kind.
194   10 What insight is


               Remark 10.1 (What the toll prices, and what it doesn’t). All three read straight off
               Definition 2.2 and Observation 2.2, with Section 2’s board as the example. (1) The
               toll puts no bound on the cost of a non-raising move; on Section 2’s board STAY
               and WORK are non-raising moves and cost 0. (2) Every raise is charged at least 1,
               by the toll, and every run from a state reading no to one reading yes has total cost
               at least 1, by the universal floor. (3) The floor is the same: the floor’s proof uses
               nothing about the end state but its reading, so it gives the same floor of 1 whatever
               else the end state shows. A higher floor needs more hypotheses than the toll, and
               those hypotheses do the work. A system that wants to charge more for a deeper
               certification has to write that into its price list, move by move; the toll doesn’t do it
               for anyone.
                  So the account comes down to two facts and a warning: looking can stay off the
               ledger, turning the reading on can’t, and the toll alone does not charge more for a
               remarkable claim, though another pricing rule or an additional requirement could.
                  Who decided the split? The costs alone didn’t. The toll prices exactly one thing,
               the crossing. A price list is allowed to put a floor under more moves than that (a
               look, a send, a check) and allowed to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into
               non-raising moves and raises is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is
               this book’s. The part that’s forced is the floor under the crossing, once you grant a
               reading that stays up, finitely many states that read yes, and a price on every merge;
               Section 3 is the argument; anything a price list charges beyond that is a choice,
               and any concrete machine owes you its whole table so you can see which choices it
               made.


               10.4 Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first

               The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being exposed: you
               make a conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for
               something, where “real” means the test could have failed. His word for that earned
               credit is corroboration. I lean on that idea all through this book (Section 14 gives it
               its full due), and this subsection shows where a Thiele machine has a version of it
               and where that version is weaker than Popper, which I have to say plainly.
                   Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin
               under a cup, a formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail,
               and it doesn’t move the box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt,
               pass or fail, fits Popper, because what made his test count was that it was really run
               and could have failed. CHECK is the test, and it’s a non-raising move in the sense
               above, because it never turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest
                                                                       10.5 What the word means   195


protocol is two moves: test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the
checking work and one for the crossing.
    But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step
is handed the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the
reading crossed. Play VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you
land in YES and make one mark, the same box and the same mark as the player who
checked first. The two tally lines differ by exactly what the CHECK was charged,
and if you charged it nothing they don’t differ at all. The mark for the crossing is the
same mark either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid for; it does not say
the commitment was earned. Popper’s corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn’t.
    You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in
the state when it passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark
is there. Making VOUCH wait like that is a design, written into the step function,
and it’s a perfectly good one. Nothing in the five parts or the toll asks for it. The
gap between the word and the bare system is real, and I’m leaving it in plain sight:
the toll prices the commit, and whether the commit was preceded by a test is a fact
about the run, or about a design somebody chose. The five parts don’t guarantee it.

Remark 10.2 (Nothing makes the crossing wait). Read off Definition 2.2. The toll
constrains cost(i ) for moves that cross, and nothing else; the step function is any
function of the current state and the move. So a Thiele machine may have a move
that crosses from a state no check has touched, and the toll still holds. On Section 2’s
board extended with CHECK, the run [VOUCH] from NO crosses with one mark, and
[CHECK, VOUCH] crosses with one mark for the crossing plus whatever CHECK was
charged, one mark in all if CHECK is priced at zero. Making a crossing depend on
an earlier check is a condition on the step function, which a particular system can
impose and the definition does not.


10.5 What the word means

Insight, in the sense this book prices, is a distinction made to stay: a move that flips
a reading from off to on, for good, and that move costs at least one, in any system
with the toll, whatever the reading is about and whatever its depth. At its best the
reading is a relation committed to, a claim checked and closed; a bare crossing that
commits to nothing pays the same, and the toll doesn’t tell the two apart. Part III’s
certified machine is one way to make sure a crossing is the first kind. There are
three boundaries, each from a different place. From Metcalfe: it isn’t a feeling, and a
system’s version has to be an event. From the proof: the floor is the same; a shallow
commit and a deep one both cost at least one, and cost is not depth. A system can
pay heavily to check a trivial claim, and Duncker’s box, a real insight, is still one
196   10 What insight is


               small commit. And from the two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing on its
               own. Price and correctness are separate books.
                   Which leaves a suspicion I’d have in your place. Everything so far has been one
               reading on one sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the
               shape of that record something I picked, or is it what any base-driven record has
               to look like, on any machine at all? The next section answers it: take any machine
               that steps, bolt a record onto it, and see what shape it’s forced into. How a concrete
               machine hangs actual claims on its parts, a checked property of one counter at one
               edition, and where those sit in the state, comes in Part III (Section 15).
CHAPTER 11




Records over any base: the latch

The blank cell comes back here, over any machine: a reading that goes from no to
yes because the machine did something, and stays. For the whole book so far I’ve
been building up a thing with a flag and a counter, and you’d be right to suspect that
the whole apparatus is special pleading for one machine, the one I keep promising
to build. So this section answers the suspicion with no particular machine in it at
all, and sees what’s left. Take any machine that steps deterministically, anything at
all with states and one next state for each. Call it the base: the part of the state the
record watches. Now put a record over it, under rules I’ll state, and ask: what can
the record be?
    The answer is one shape, and I’ll show you the shape first because it’s a thing
you can build from a cup and a die.


11.1 A cup and a die

Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule is that the first time a coin lands in
front of it, you turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now
roll a die, and put a coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. If a six appears, the
cup turns over on the first one and stays turned over. Write down which roll did it.
That number is where the record happened, and the cup afterward is the record. If
no six appears, the cup stays down; a reachable event need not occur on every trial.
    For the deterministic base in the theorem, write the rolls down first and replay
them. The base state is the fixed list and a finger pointing to its next entry; a step
moves the finger one place, regardless of the cup. The event asks whether that entry
is six. Nothing about the cup changes which entry comes next.
    The cup is a latch. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when two
British physicists teaching engineering in London, William Eccles, a radio pioneer,
and Frank Jordan, applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds
whichever state you last put it in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and
caches in the device you’re reading this on descend from it. Cut its reset wire and
what’s left has one input, “set,” and the rule new state = old state or set: once set, it
stays set. The cup is that circuit: a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

                                                  197
198   11 Records over any base: the latch


                    (Eccles and Jordan didn’t call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a trigger
               relay. Where the newer, sillier name came from I can’t source, so I’ll leave it at that.)
                    Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build
               one on purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that’s very close to this book’s. In
               the mid-1950s Wen Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American
               Bosch Arma Corporation in Garden City, New York, was asked by the United States
               Air Force, in the accounts of his career I could find, for a more flexible and secure
               way to hold the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer
               of the Atlas missile. What he and his Arma colleague William Henrich patented
               (filed in 1957, granted in 1962, under the plain title “Storage matrix”) was a grid
               with a connection at every crossing, where you set the numbers by taking out the
               connections you didn’t want, physically or by burning them out with too much
               current. The word burn is right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a
               chip. The descendants are called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and
               a fuse blown in one stays blown: there’s no current you can send to grow it back.
               The grid was a whole memory built out of cups with no reset wire, made because
               somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly change later. That doesn’t prove
               anything here, because the theorem below doesn’t care what a cup is made of. But
               it’s good to know the shape wasn’t invented for a sheet of paper. Somebody needed
               it, for stakes a good deal higher than a die.
                    Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: every base-driven record, over any
               base, is a cup with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.


               11.2 What “base-driven” has to mean
               The content is in the definition, and I’ll give you all five rules, because the theorem
               is only as strong as they are.
                   A machine extends a base when there’s a map from the bigger machine’s states
               down to the base’s, and that map starts in the base’s start states, reaches every one of
               them, moves in step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through
               the map), and agrees about halting. The bigger machine may carry as much hidden
               state as it likes beyond the base, and that’s what the words “any base” are about:
               the base doesn’t get to see the extension, and the extension doesn’t get to change
               what the base does.
                   The extension carries a record, a yes/no reading, and a ledger, a counter. It’s
               a base-driven record when five things hold. One: the record’s next value depends
               only on the base’s current state and the record’s current value. (I’ll call this driven
               by the computation. It says the record answers to what the machine is doing. A
               clock on the wall or someone’s hand doesn’t get a say.) Two: the ledger never
               goes down (Section 7). Three: the step that turns the record on costs at least one;
                                                               11.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   199


that’s the toll (Section 2). Four: once on, the record stays on; that’s permanence
(Section 3). Distributed-systems people have a name for a predicate like that. The
computer scientists K. Mani Chandy and Leslie Lamport, in their 1985 paper on
taking a consistent snapshot of a distributed system, called a property stable when
once it holds it holds forever after, and stable properties are the ones a snapshot can
be trusted to detect. Five: some run from a start state actually reaches a step that
turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.
    I’ll write the rules out exactly. On/off is true/false, ∨ is “or” (on when either side
is on), and nextk is k steps.

Definition 11.1 (Base, record-carrying machine, cover). A base B is a set of states
with a step function nextB , a set of starting states, and a halting predicate. A record-
carrying machine M is a set of states with a step function next M , a set of starting
states, a record rec from states to Booleans, a ledger µ from states to whole numbers,
and a halting predicate. The cost of a step is cost(m) = µ(next M (m)) −̇ µ(m). A
cover of B by M is a map π from states of M to states of B that sends starting states
to starting states, has every starting state of B as the image of some starting state
of M, commutes with the steps, π (next M (m)) = nextB (π (m)), and agrees about
halting: m halts exactly when π (m) does.


Definition 11.2 (Base-driven record, latch). M with cover π is a base-driven record
over B when (R1, driven by the computation) there is one function f such that, for
every state m, rec(next M (m)) = f (π (m), rec(m)); for every state m, (R2, ledger)
µ(m) ≤ µ(next M (m)); (R3, toll) if rec(m) is off and rec(next M (m)) is on, then
cost(m) ≥ 1; (R4, permanence) if rec(m) is on, so is rec(next M (m)); and (R5, a
reachable write) some starting state m0 and some k have rec(nextkM (m0 )) off and
rec(nextkM+1 (m0 )) on. An event is a function h from base states to Booleans, and its
latch is the step (b, r ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b)). M factors as the latch of h when, for
every state m (reachable or not),

      (π (next M (m)), rec(next M (m))) = (nextB (π (m)), rec(m) ∨ h(π (m))).
   The theorem says that under those rules the base state and the record move
exactly as a latch: the record switches on at the first base state where some event
holds, if it started off, and never goes off, and the event is read off the extension’s
own rule by asking it what it does when the record is off (stated exactly below).
The theorem is about what the base and the record do together. The hidden state
the extension carries can’t push the record anywhere (R1) doesn’t allow, since the
record’s next value is a function of the base state and the record’s own value. The
theorem doesn’t say the whole extension is a bare latch machine, and it doesn’t
make hidden state show up anywhere in particular: an extension can carry a field
200   11 Records over any base: the latch


               that touches neither the record nor the ledger. And the event is pinned down only
               on base states that some state with the record off covers; on a base state with no
               such state above it, f (b, off) is whatever (R1)’s function says, and nothing in a run
               ever consults it.
                   I promised the content was in the definition, and the proof bears that out: it is
               a short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only two of the
               five rules, “driven by the computation” and “permanent.” The ledger, the toll, and
               the reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A latch is what you get from “answers
               only to the base” plus “never comes back down” alone. The other three rules matter
               for the converse: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that
               event, priced at one unit per write, is a base-driven record. The event can be one
               that holds everywhere, and then its latch is up after one step from every start and
               tells no two starts apart. It’s still a latch and still base-driven: the converse doesn’t
               ask the record to distinguish anything. A record that starts off and tells two starts
               apart at some step has to latch an event that has held along one run by then and
               not yet along the other, and the latch tells them apart for as long as that stays so.
               Put the two together and base-driven records are exactly latches: one shape, and no
               others, over any base.
               Observation 11.1 (The record is a latch). Let B be any base, π a cover of B by
               M, and suppose M’s record is driven by the computation (R1), through a function
               f , and permanent (R4). Then M factors as the latch of the event h(b) = f (b, off).
               In particular every base-driven record factors that way; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are not
               hypotheses.
               Proof. Ask the extension what it would do with the record off above each base state
               b. Call its answer h(b). Rule (R1) lets you ask that as one function of b: no other
               hidden field is allowed to change the answer.
                  Now take an actual state. If its record is off, (R1) gives exactly that answer h(b)
               for the next record. If its record is already on, permanence keeps it on, whatever
               h(b) says. Together those two cases say “keep an existing on, otherwise use h(b),”
               which is r ∨ h(b).
                  The cover already says that the base part takes its own next step. Put that base
               step beside the record rule just obtained and I have the stated latch equation. No
               charge or starting condition entered the argument.
                  The latch’s nearest neighbours are in verification, and they’re old. The computer
               scientists Martín Abadi and Leslie Lamport, then at Digital’s research lab in Palo
               Alto, added history variables to specifications in 1991: extra state that records what
               has happened and never steers the system, used to prove that one specification
               implements another. A history variable that only ever turns on is the cup. Temporal
               logic has the same record as an operator. In the past-time temporal logic that Orna
                                                               11.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   201


Lichtenstein, Amir Pnueli and Lenore Zuck set out in 1985, “once h” holds now
exactly when h has held at some point so far, and a runtime monitor keeps it in one
bit with the update r ′ = r ∨ h. Klaus Havelund and Grigore Roşu, two computer
scientists working on runtime verification, synthesized monitors of exactly that
kind for safety properties written in that logic in 2002. That update is the latch of
Definition 11.2, word for word. The observation adds the other direction: a record
driven by the computation that never comes down can’t be anything else.
    One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways: it
never asks what the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down
is base, and the record’s rule is allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is
extension, and (R1) keeps the record’s rule from reading it. Draw the line low, so
the base is only the computation’s own working state, and (R1) is a real demand.
Draw it high, put every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1) is easy
to meet, and the latch shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds
wherever you draw the line, and that’s exactly why it can’t tell you where a record’s
meaning lives. The meaning lives in what the event h reads, and that’s in the base
by construction. On the small machine of Part III (Section 15), the checks that give
the flag its meaning sit in the base its cover picks out. So when that machine arrives,
ask it first which parts it puts above the line.



Theorem 11.2 (Every reachable latch is a base-driven record). Let B be any base
and h any event. Let Latchh have states (b, r, x ), starting states (b, off, 0) with b
starting in B, step (b, r, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), x + δ) with δ = 1 when r is off
and h(b) is on and δ = 0 otherwise, record r, ledger x, halting as b halts, and cover
(b, r, x ) 7→ b. Suppose some starting b0 and some k bring Latchh from (b0 , off, 0), in
k steps, to a state whose record is still off and whose base state satisfies h. Then
Latchh is a base-driven record over B.

Proof. The construction keeps a base state, a flag and a tally. Looking only at the
base state gives the promised cover: a start lies over the chosen base start, every
base start has such a flag-down, tally-zero start above it, and each step advances the
base exactly once. Halting is read from that same base state.
    The next flag consults only the present flag and the base event, giving (R1). The
tally adds either zero or one and never falls, giving (R2). If the flag rises, it was off
and the event held, exactly the case that adds one, giving (R3). An on flag stays on
under the displayed rule, giving (R4). Finally the supplied run reaches a state with
the flag still off and the event true. Its next step raises the flag, giving the reachable
write (R5).
202   11 Records over any base: the latch


                  Whenever a base run reaches the event at all, use its first such visit. Before that
               visit the flag remains off, so this is the supplied kind of run.
                  What about a base that never merges, a reversible one? It can carry a record,
               and the next theorem says exactly what it pays. Keep every earlier record value in a
               history beside the latch, one more entry on every step, and the whole step merges
               nothing either. But that history needs a fresh slot at every step, forever, so the
               machine never comes back to a state it has been in, which puts it in the fresh-state
               column. On a finite state space there aren’t fresh states to go on taking forever, and
               a permanent record can’t be written by a step that merges nothing at all. A step that
               merges nothing is called injective: no two states go to the same next state. Keep
               the old readings on a strip, newest first. If the strip reads [off, off] and the current
               reading is on, the next strip reads [on, off, off]. The notation r :: H below means
               exactly that: put the old reading r at the front of the old strip H.


               Theorem 11.3 (Records on reversible machines). (1) Let B be a base whose step
               is injective. The machine with states (b, r, H, x ), step (b, r, H, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨
               h(b), r :: H, x + δ) (δ as in Theorem 11.2), starting states with r off, H empty and
               x = 0, has an injective step, never visits the same state twice on a run (the history
               gets one entry longer on every step), and under the supposition of Theorem 11.2 it
               is a base-driven record over B. (2) With finitely many states reading on, a single
               injective step with a permanent reading never turns that reading from off to on.

               Proof. (1) Suppose two full states have the same successor. Can you recover what
               they were? Their successor base states agree. The base keeps different sources apart,
               so their earlier base states agreed too. Their new history strips also agree. The first
               entry of each strip is the old record, so the old records agree; removing that first
               entry leaves the old histories, which therefore agree as well.
                   Those equal old base states and records determine the same charge δ. Subtract it
               from the equal new tallies and the old tallies agree. Every part of the two earlier
               full states agrees, so they were the same state. The step is one-to-one.
                   On a run the strip grows by one entry every tick. A full state cannot recur, because
               its strip would have to have two different lengths. Carrying that strip changes neither
               the base nor the flag nor the tally rules checked in the preceding construction, so
               all five base-driven record conditions still hold under the supplied reachable-event
               premise.
                   (2) Suppose instead there are only K on-states and an off-state enters them.
               Permanence sends all K on-states into that same collection, and the entrant lands
               there too. A one-to-one step would have to put K + 1 different sources into K places.
                                                            11.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   203


It cannot. Hence a permanent reading with finitely many on-states cannot rise under
a one-to-one step.
    So a base that never merges can carry a record without merging anywhere only
by paying in fresh states: once the record is up, the run never comes back to a state
it has been in (Proposition 3.5). A history that grows by one entry every step is one
way to supply them, and a base that never repeats a state, a counter, supplies them
already. A machine with finitely many states hasn’t got fresh states to go on taking,
so it can’t carry one without merging: on a finite machine an instruction that first
raises a permanent reading must merge some possible states. The entering state
need not belong to the colliding pair; Section 3 prices the instruction under merge
pricing.
    Process-calculus people ran into the same thing from the other side. Vincent
Danos and Jean Krivine, two theoretical computer scientists in Paris, wanted to pin
down what a transaction is. In 2004 they had built a reversible version of CCS,
Robin Milner’s calculus of processes that talk to each other, where every step can
be rolled back, and in 2005 they modelled a transaction in it as a process that
wanders freely through everything that can be undone until it performs an action
declared irreversible, which is the commit. The way I read it, they start from steps
that all come undone and ask what has to be added before anything sticks, and
the theorem above starts from a record and asks what the step under it must be.
In their calculus, as in the theorem, a permanent effect needs a step with no way
back, and the calculus has to say which steps those are. The word I tripped on was
declared. Theirs are labelled. Mine, I thought, are picked out by counting, since on a
finite machine the first write merges whatever anyone calls it. Push on that and it
gives. I choose the event h, and on a base that grows its history forever the write
merges nothing, because it pays in fresh states instead (Theorem 11.3), so there my
permanence is declared too.
    There’s an arrow of time in that theorem, and I should say where it came from,
because I put it there by hand. Every starting state has the record off. That’s the
only reason a raised record means the event happened: it was down at the start,
and only h lifts it. Turn the cup up before the first roll and it tells you nothing
about the die. So the clean start is an assumed ready state, a past hypothesis in
miniature. The past hypothesis is David Albert’s name for an assumed low-entropy
beginning of the universe, which several of the accounts below lean records on.
Whether every trusted record leans on it is their argument, and I’m not settling it.
Nothing in this book derives one; every theorem here that reads a raised record as
news that the event happened assumes its small version and starts from there. The
latch observation doesn’t need it, and that’s why on its own it can’t say the event
happened.
204   11 Records over any base: the latch


                   When I went looking for who else had found the arrow hiding in the start, I got
               five papers that read like five unrelated answers. They lined up once I asked each
               one the same thing: what does the cup being down at the start rest on? There are
               two places to put it. You can put it at the beginning, as a fact about how things
               started. Or you can put it in the structure of what causes what. David Wolpert, then
               a physicist at Los Alamos and the same Wolpert as the free-lunch theorem, sorted
               memory systems in 1992, and one of his kinds works only because it begins in a
               prepared state set up by a process that runs one way, which is how it leans on the
               second law. That’s the cup put down by somebody before the game, at the first place.
               Wolpert and Jens Kipper, a philosopher at Rochester, put in 2024 that sorting on a
               formal footing, and they say plainly that they have no formal proof this kind can
               only remember the past. I trust them more for that sentence. What I think they’re
               saying is that a prepared start buys you a memory, and getting its direction too takes
               something they can’t yet prove.
                   Aram Ebtekar, an independent researcher in Vancouver, and Marcus Hutter, who
               works on the theory of general artificial intelligence at Google DeepMind and the
               Australian National University, built in 2024 a reversible toy world, imposed a past
               hypothesis on it, coarse-grained it, and got records of the past and none of the
               future. As I read their route, the clean start doesn’t go straight to the records. It
               goes through a causal structure first, and the arrows come out of that. Thomas
               Blanchard, a philosopher of science at Cologne, got in 2024 the same lopsidedness
               of knowledge out of the causal Markov condition, a condition on causal structure.
               So Blanchard starts at the second place, which is the middle of Ebtekar and Hutter’s
               road. That took me a while to see, because one is a toy world and the other is
               philosophy of causation. They go from the start to causes to records; he goes from
               causes to records. The fit is my reading, and it’s mine to defend. And Carlo Rovelli,
               two years before his paper on the cost of choosing from Section 5, studied traces in
               “Memory and entropy” (2022) and concluded that a memory turns low entropy into
               available information. He’s at the first place, and he says what the beginning gets
               spent on. Read against the latch, that’s the blank the record uses up: the flag can
               say yes once because it started at no.
                   So does the latch explain why records point backwards? It doesn’t, and I’ll say
               that plainly so it doesn’t look like it does. The step runs forwards and the runs start
               clean, and a theorem built on those two can only hand the arrow back. Push further
               and it gives in a second place. The history that grows forever looked like a way
               around the clean start. It starts empty, so it leans on the same blank. Under a step
               that forgets nothing, on a finite set, no permanent record can ever be written, past
               or future, which is Zermelo again. On the map the book sits at the first place, with
               Wolpert and Rovelli, and it sits there by assumption. Ebtekar and Hutter at least
