imposed their start on a world with its own dynamics and watched what came out.
I wrote mine into the definition.
    Constructor theory, which Section 3 brings in as a neighbour of the counting
argument, has a paper on time (Deutsch and Marletto, 2025) saying that laws stated
as which transformations a device can and can’t bring about can’t mention time at
all, so duration has to come from relations between physical systems, clocks, that
have their own dynamics. What I think they’re saying is that whenever you want a
duration you point at a second system and count what it did. This book is in that
position by construction. The step count is the only time in it, and it comes from
the machine’s own steps. The next subsection has a record turned at the fifth tick
of a hidden clock, and (R1) throws it out, which read beside them is a rule about
which system may be the clock: the one being recorded. Push on it, though. Their
laws have no step in them, and the paper’s work is getting duration and dynamics
out of clocks and timers. I put a step, nextB , into the definition of a base. So I’m in
their position only at the far end of their argument, where a clock already exists.
The base is my clock, and I assumed it.
    Physicists have built this latch on paper too, in quantum mechanics, and it
behaves the way the last theorem says. The question that sorted them for me is
where the cup puts what it forgets, since a closed quantum system with separate
energy levels comes back (Bocchieri and Loinger, Section 3) and the theorem left
only two ways to pay for a record that stays: fresh states, which here mean a history
that never ends, or a merge. Klaus Hepp, a mathematical physicist at ETH Zurich,
wanted a measuring device inside quantum mechanics itself, and studied in 1972 a
particle that flips spins in a long chain as it passes, now called the Coleman-Hepp
model (I know Hepp’s paper only from accounts of it), and John Bell (1975) took it
apart: the record is exactly definite only for an infinitely long chain, which is the
fresh-state column above, a history that never ends, in quantum clothes. Jonathan
Halliwell, a theoretical physicist at Imperial College London, used in 1999 a two-
state detector that flips once when a particle crosses a point and is kept from flipping
back by a large environment, which is a latch with the environment holding the
history. His abstract calls it effectively irreversible, and I like that he puts the word
effectively right there where you can see it. And Murray Gell-Mann, the physicist
who named the quark, and James Hartle, of the University of California at Santa
Barbara, gave in 1995 the property a name inside their framework of decoherent
histories: the permanence of the past, past alternatives that stay settled as the story
is extended into the future. They name (R4) for whole histories and leave the cup to
others. So Hepp’s chain, as Bell read it, is exact and infinite, and Halliwell’s detector
is finite and only effectively permanent. Mine is finite, exact and permanent at once,
and it gets there by letting the first write merge. Push on that and it gives: I never
say where the merged state goes. Hepp’s chain had to be infinite. Halliwell had to
206   11 Records over any base: the latch


               put his in an environment. Mine just goes, and the toll writes a unit in a counter.
               That’s fine in a model of computation, and it’s exactly where this stops being physics.


               11.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp
               A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each
               hypothesis dropped, and it does, and they’re the two ways a record goes wrong in
               the world.
                   Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every
               step: on, off, on, off. It’s driven by the computation; it’s not permanent; and it’s not
               a latch of any event. Such a record is a toggle, a piece of working state. A record you
               can revoke is working state wearing a record’s clothes, and if a revocation has to stick,
               that’s a second latch (“revoked”), which is how certificate revocation lists actually
               work: you add an entry; you never delete the certificate. Alin Tomescu, a computer
               scientist then at MIT, and his coauthors (2019) built append-only authenticated
               sets and dictionaries for transparency logs, and revocation fits that shape exactly:
               a revocation goes in once and stays. The pair lemma (stated below) covers two
               latches that can each read the other; do it with two cups where the second only
               turns over on an even roll if the first is already up, and you’ll see the second can
               never turn before the first.
                   Dialogue theorists built a version of that two-latch rule for arguments. Give each
               speaker a row of cups, one for every claim they’ve made. Everybody I read in this
               field is answering two questions about those cups: whose hand turns them, and can
               they come back down. C. L. Hamblin, an Australian philosopher and logician who
               also came up with reverse Polish notation for early computers, wrote Fallacies (1970),
               and it has a chapter on formal dialectic where each speaker has a commitment store, a
               list of what they’re on the hook for, and the rules of the dialogue update it, while the
               speaker doesn’t. I know that chapter from other people’s accounts of it. Hamblin’s
               store is an answer to the first question, and it’s (R1) for arguments: the cup answers
               to what happened in the dialogue, and the speaker’s hand is kept off it. Henry
               Prakken, who works on AI and law at Utrecht, built in 2005 dialogue games for
               argumentation on stores like that and made commitments sticky: a claim can be
               retracted only when it has been challenged, and claims and backtracking carry a
               price. He also floats a convention that once a player has retracted a proposition,
               that player can’t take it on again, which is a revocation that stays revoked, the way
               an entry on a revocation list does. Prakken’s rules are an answer to the second
               question, and it took me a second pass to see that they’re two answers: a cup can
               come down, and coming down costs, and once it has, the taking-back is itself a cup
               that stays up. Erik Krabbe, an argumentation theorist at Groningen, names in 2001
               the awkward part of that: retraction is frowned on, and yet resolving a dispute takes
                                               11.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp   207


somebody retracting a doubt or a point of view, so the rules have to say when taking
a commitment back is allowed. As I read him, he’s standing between the two ends
of the second question. A store that never gives can’t settle a dispute, and a store
that gives whenever it’s asked isn’t a store. The part of all that I’d keep is Hamblin’s,
that the store belongs to the rules and doesn’t belong to the speaker. Take the pen
away from the program. And this book answers Krabbe with a price: a take-back is
a second cup, “revoked,” and turning it costs at least one like any other write, so a
retraction is allowed, permanent and paid for, which is Prakken’s convention with
the toll attached. Where mine gives is his first condition. He lets a claim come down
only when it’s been challenged, and nothing in my latch asks why the second cup
turned. The pair lemma lets the second cup’s event read the base and the first cup,
and nothing in it requires a challenge to be there.
    The same field has a notion that looks a lot like earning. In the abstract argumen-
tation of Phan Minh Dung, a computer scientist at the Asian Institute of Technology
in Bangkok (1995), arguments attack one another, and the grounded semantics starts
from the arguments nobody attacks and keeps adding the ones they defend. Look at
how it’s built: things go in and never come out, which is a row of cups turned one
at a time. Pietro Baroni and Massimiliano Giacomin, at Brescia, introduced in 2007,
and Martin Caminada, then at Aberdeen, revisited in 2014, strong admissibility: a
set is strongly admissible when every argument in it is defended by others in the
set that don’t lean back on it, so the support bottoms out. Strong admissibility is
the argumentation form of an earned claim. Above the bottom, nothing in it is
in by default, which puts it at the far end from Burge’s default on the testimony
map in Section 8. Caminada argues it plays a vital part in the dialogue games that
decide grounded acceptance. I’ve read Caminada’s paper; Dung’s and Baroni and
Giacomin’s I know through what later papers say about them. Notice the bottom,
though. An argument nobody attacks gets in on a check that can’t fail, and this book
says a check that can’t fail establishes nothing (Section 14). Now turn that on my
own cups, because it lands. My first write needs only that h holds, and what h reads
sits in the base, where the latch theorem doesn’t look. I charge a unit for it, and a
unit is a price, not a check. So my earned records bottom out the way Dung’s do, in
something let in without an argument, and the one difference is that mine pays to
get in. Whether a machine’s earned record certifies exactly the strongly admissible
sets is the kind of statement I’d have to prove before I said it, and I haven’t.
    A record that’s allowed to change its mind isn’t lawless, though; it’s somebody
else’s subject. Count how many times the cup may be turned. Once, from down
to up, is the latch. More than once and you’re somewhere else, and the people
who went there sort it two ways: by how many turns are allowed, and by how long
the game runs. The philosopher Hilary Putnam, then at MIT, and E. Mark Gold,
a computer scientist at a research lab in Santa Monica, in back-to-back papers in
208   11 Records over any base: the latch


               1965, looked at questions a machine answers by guessing and revising, where the
               answer is whatever the guesses finally settle on. Putnam’s paper says outright that
               you’re never sure you have the correct answer. That stopped me the first time. What
               kind of answer can’t you ever be sure you have? The way I came to read it: the
               cup’s position at any moment is the current guess, the answer is where it ends up,
               and nobody watching can tell when it’s done moving. Yuri Ershov, a logician in
               Novosibirsk, sorted those in 1968 by how many revisions they’re allowed (that’s
               how his hierarchy is described; I haven’t read his paper). Allow one, from no to yes,
               and you get exactly the sets a program can list. That level is in a modern account of
               the hierarchy by Rod Downey, Carl Jockusch, Timothy McNicholl and Paul Schupp,
               four computability theorists, and you don’t need their word for it. If a program lists
               the set, guess no for every number and flip the guess to yes when the number shows
               up on the list. Going back, if every guess flips at most once, from no to yes, run all
               the guessing side by side and write a number down the moment its guess says yes.
               Those listable sets are what a permanent record raised by a search catches. Allow
               two, three, and so on, and every extra change buys new sets: the rungs of the ladder
               are all different. A record that can come back down lives on that ladder. Now put
               Putnam’s worry on my cup, because it lands. On the bottom rung a yes is final the
               moment it appears, and a no never is, since down means not yet. A single cup of
               mine can certify that something happened and can never certify that it didn’t; a
               final no would take a second cup, turned by finding a reason, and that’s the pair of
               latches again. That’s what the bottom rung costs, and I’d rather name it. This book
               stays on the bottom rung; I’m pointing at the ladder, and I’m not climbing it.
                   The ladder doesn’t stop at finite time, and the people who followed it past infinity
               have names for the two kinds of record I just described. A definition that only ever
               adds, stage after stage, and keeps everything it has at each limit, is an inductive
               definition (the long treatment is a 1974 chapter by Wayne Richter and Peter Aczel,
               two recursion theorists). It’s the latch run through the infinite, a cup that goes up at
               some stage and is still up at every stage after. Let it take things back, and keep what
               stays put from some stage on, and you have what John Burgess, a philosopher and
               logician at Princeton, called in 1986 quasi-inductive definitions, which he met in the
               revision theories of truth that grew up beside the logician Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory
               of truth, which builds up the true sentences in stages. Burgess’s paper measures how
               complicated the truths of those theories get. I’ve read its abstract, but not the place
               where he names them. What took me a few reads is that Burgess’s rule at a limit
               is Putnam and Gold’s rule, keep whatever the guesses settled on, applied at every
               limit stage along the way. That’s my reading of how the two fit. If it’s right, the split
               between a cup that only goes up and a cup that settles is the same split at finite
               time and past it: a permanent record is the first kind, and a toggle that’s allowed to
               settle is the second. Joel Hamkins and Andy Lewis, two set theorists, let a Turing
                                               11.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp   209


machine keep running through the ordinals in 2000. At a limit a cell keeps its value
if it settled, and reads 1 if it kept flipping back and forth forever, and the trick they
use again and again is the toggle: flash a flag on and off every time a guess changes,
and at the limit the flag is on exactly when the guess changed infinitely often. A flag
that can come back down is how that machine learns what no finite run could tell it.
A permanent one can’t do that trick, because at a limit a cell that only ever goes up
just stays up. So past infinity the toggle is the clever one: a latch tells you a thing
happened at least once, and their flashing flag tells you it happened infinitely often.
I threw the toggle out a few paragraphs back anyway, and I’d do it again, because
before the limit its reading can’t be relied on, and nobody using a machine of mine
gets to wait for a limit. One finite-time fact belongs beside it, so nobody concludes
too much from permanence. Hao Wang, a logician then at Oxford, described in
1957 a machine whose only write is to mark a square and which can never erase
one, and it computes everything a Turing machine does. Permanence of a machine’s
own memory costs it no computing power, given an endless tape: each mark goes
on a square nobody marked before, which is the fresh-state column again. What
the book prices is a permanent reading raised by a step that has to work whether
or not the reading is already up, which is a different thing. So the cost I named a
paragraph ago is a cost in what a reading can claim, and computing power doesn’t
pay it.
     Drop “driven by the computation.” Take a base that counts, and a record that
switches on at the fifth tick of a hidden clock, whatever the base is doing. It’s
permanent, and the computation doesn’t drive it; such a record is a timestamp. A
timestamp is not evidence: it says when and doesn’t say what happened, and a record
switched by an outside party or a clock records that party or that clock and leaves
the computation out. Try it with the recorded die list. Keep a second tally hidden
beside it, and turn the cup when that tally reads five before a move; then advance
both the tally and the finger on the list. Run two trials from the same list entry with
the cup down, but start the hidden tally at five in one trial and zero in the other.
The next cup values disagree although everything the base shows agrees, which is
the failure of being driven by the base. If the tally always starts synchronized with
the list position, the position can predict the cup; the distinction matters below.
     The two examples do exactly what I said they do: the toggle is driven, isn’t
permanent and isn’t a latch; the timestamp is permanent and isn’t driven. That each
also keeps the other rules (the ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one,
a run reaches it) is true by inspection.
     Permanent but undriven is a timestamp, driven but impermanent is a toggle,
and a record is the thing that’s both. Undriven, for the timestamp, means that
along the runs that actually happen the base state doesn’t fix when the record turns;
Lemma 11.7 below says why that’s the condition, and what (R1) as written adds to
210   11 Records over any base: the latch


               it. That’s the whole discrimination, and I think it’s the most useful single sentence
               in this book for looking at systems other than the one I build, which is why it’s here.
                   I’ll now state the pair lemma and the two counterexamples exactly. The base for
               both counterexamples is the counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one,
               every state is a starting state, and nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: ¬r is r
               flipped, and a statement in square brackets, like [k = 5], reads on when it’s true and
               off when it isn’t.


               Lemma 11.4 (Two records are two latches). Let c1 , c2 be two records on
               M, with cover π onto a base B, such that: there is one function F with
               (c1 (next M (m)), c2 (next M (m))) = F (π (m), c1 (m), c2 (m)); the ledger never goes
               down; a step that turns either record on costs at least one; and each record is
               permanent. Then there are h1 , h2 with c1 (next M (m)) = c1 (m) ∨ h1 (π (m), c2 (m))
               and c2 (next M (m)) = c2 (m) ∨ h2 (π (m), c1 (m)) for every m.

               Proof. Hold the second record fixed and ask what the joint rule does to the first when
               the first is off. Call that answer h1 (b, r2 ); it is the first component of F (b, off, r2 ). At
               any actual state whose first record is off, that is its next value. At any state whose
               first record is on, permanence keeps it on. Thus its rule is r1 ∨ h1 (b, r2 ).
                   Now hold the first record fixed and ask the corresponding question with the
               second off. The answer is h2 (b, r1 ), the second component of F (b, r1 , off). The same
               off/on argument gives r2 ∨ h2 (b, r1 ). The records may affect each other’s raising
               condition, but neither can undo an on once it is there.



               Lemma 11.5 (The toggle). Let the toggle have states (n, r ), step (n, r ) 7→ (n +
               1, ¬r ), every state starting, record r, ledger n, cover (n, r ) 7→ n onto the counter. It
               is driven by the computation, with f (b, r ) = ¬r; it is not permanent; and it factors
               as the latch of no event.

               Proof. At (0, on) the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch
               gives on ∨ h(0) = on there.



               Lemma 11.6 (The timestamp). Let the timestamp have states (b, k, r ), step
               (b, k, r ) 7→ (b + 1, k + 1, r ∨ [k = 5]), every state starting, record r, ledger b, cover
               (b, k, r ) 7→ b onto the counter. It is permanent and not driven by the computation.
                                                11.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp   211


Proof. Permanence: on ∨ x is on. Not driven: the states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off)
have the same base state and the same record, and their next records are on and off,
so no f of the base state and the record can give both.
    “Driven” is a condition on every state. The timestamp makes every state a starting
state, so the two states the proof compares are both ones a run can begin at, even
though a timestamp started at (0, 0, off) would never reach (0, 5, off).
    That last sentence does more work than it looks, so I’ll state it as a lemma. Start
the same timestamp in sync, at (b, b, off) only. On every state its runs reach, the
hidden count equals the base, and the timestamp is exactly the latch of [b = 5].
(R1) still rejects it, because (R1) asks about every state, and (0, 5, off) is a state,
though no run from a synchronised start reaches it. So (R1) as written separates the
timestamp from a latch partly by how the cover is drawn and through states nobody
visits. The separation I mean is the one on reachable states: the timestamp with
every state a start fails (R1) even when only states some run reaches are counted,
since two starting states sit over the same base state with the same record and
disagree about the next one. And the latch theorem holds in that reachable form
too.


Lemma 11.7 (The timestamp, on the states runs reach). Say M’s record is driven on
reachable states when (R1) holds for every state reached from a starting state in some
number of steps. (1) If M’s record is driven on reachable states and permanent, then
on every reachable state M steps as the latch of some event. (2) The timestamp of
Lemma 11.6 isn’t driven on reachable states. (3) The timestamp started in sync, with
starting states (b, b, off) and the same step, record, ledger and cover, is permanent,
isn’t driven by the computation, is driven on reachable states, and on every reachable
state steps as the latch of [b = 5].

Proof. (1) is the proof of Observation 11.1, run on reachable states only. (2) The
states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off) are starting states, reached in no steps, and the proof
of Lemma 11.6 applies to them. (3) From (b, b, off) every step adds one to both
counts, so a reachable state has k = b and its next record is r ∨ [b = 5]. Over every
state, (R1) fails at the same pair as in Lemma 11.6.
    So “permanent but undriven is a timestamp” is a sentence about the timestamp
with every state a start, over the cover that hides its count, and it holds there in the
strong form: undriven on the very states its runs pass through. A timestamp started
in step with its base is a latch on the runs it has, and (R1) throws it out only because
(R1) also looks at states those runs never reach.
212   11 Records over any base: the latch


               11.4 Is there only one such machine? No: one structure, two unforced choices.
               I have to take apart the sentence “there’s only one way to carry a record,” because
               three different things get squeezed into it.
                   The first claim asks: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to
               keep the books, starting at zero and adding each move’s price? Yes, on every state
               reachable from the start; that’s Section 7’s initiality, and it assumes the price list.
                   The second claim asks: is every base-driven record over a base the same machine,
               charges and all? No, and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take
               any base-driven record, give it a new ledger that adds each step’s old cost and one
               unit more, whatever the step is, and then walk the five rules. The record still answers
               only to the base and its own value (R1); the cost never touches it. The ledger still
               never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything. The step that turns the record
               on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a floor and a surcharge only raises
               the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same run still reaches the
               write (R5). So the surcharged machine is base-driven, and it isn’t the machine you
               started with: wherever the original sat still at no charge, the surcharged one pays
               one unit a step for sitting still. Do it with the cup and the die, and charge one unit
               for every roll, six or not. The cup turns over on the same roll as before, so you’ve
               changed the cost and nothing about the record. A machine that charges for CPU
               time is base-driven and isn’t the one that doesn’t. The new ledger has to sit beside
               the old state and not be read off it. A step’s cost is the ledger after less the ledger
               before, so a ledger read off the state charges nothing for a step that leaves the state
               where it was, such as a halted machine stepping to itself, or for any step on a loop
               (Section 7). The surcharge is paid in fresh ledger values, the way every counter that
               climbs is paid for.
                   The same base computation and latch are visible after forgetting the new ledger.
               The full transition graph can be different: a free self-loop becomes an endless line
               of increasing ledger values. So the comparison preserves base, reading and the
               stipulated stopping convention, not every full-state distinction. If the ledger is also
               observed, these are different contracts. The construction allows a nonnegative
               surcharge depending on the current state in this broader accounting interface. Such
               a charge is not in general a price on instruction names alone. The price schedule
               remains an unforced choice after the base and event have been fixed.
                   And then there’s the second unforced choice, and this one still surprises me:
               which event is the record? Nothing in the five rules picks it, beyond (R5)’s demand
               that it hold somewhere a run reaches; on a base whose runs pass through only one
               state that leaves one record, and the choice opens as soon as a run passes two states
               an event can tell apart. The converse above already says so, if you read it twice:
               for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per
                           11.4 Is there only one such machine? No: one structure, two unforced choices.   213


write, is a base-driven record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on the first six,
and another turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire; both are
base-driven. Roll a one first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about
whether anything has been recorded. So which permanent reading counts as the
record is a second thing nobody forces on you. The price list is one unforced choice
and the event is the other, and that second choice is the question Section 18 is about:
what, if anything, makes certification the event worth recording. “The ledger passed
one” is an event only if the chosen base includes enough information to decide it.
An extension-only ledger is hidden from a base event, just as the hidden clock was.
The unforced choice is among functions of the chosen base.


Corollary 11.8 (The event is an unforced choice). Let B be any base and h1 , h2 two
events, each meeting the supposition of Theorem 11.2. Then Latchh1 and Latchh2
are both base-driven records over B. If some run from a start of B reaches a base
state b with h1 (b) on and h2 (b) off, and h2 holds nowhere earlier on that run, then
after the step from b the same run has the first record on and the second off.

Proof. That both are base-driven is Theorem 11.2 applied twice. Along that run the
second record is still off when it reaches b, since h2 hasn’t held, and the latch’s own
rule keeps it off, off ∨ h2 (b); the first is on after that step, whatever it was before,
since h1 (b) is on.
    Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and some-
times doesn’t, with odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix
the odds? No, and the counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and
differently loaded coins. I’ll set it up carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves
at random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive,
never empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at
least one. Call such a record a permanent probabilistic record. Call two such records
the same schedule when the same moves are possible and every move is charged the
same, and the same in probability when the weighted lists give every move the same
odds.


Theorem 11.9 (The schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities). (1) There are two
permanent probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in
probability. (2) There is a permanent probabilistic record that no deterministic latch
on its current value describes.
214   11 Records over any base: the latch


               Proof. (1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights 1 and 1, the other
               with weights 1 and 2; from on, both stay on with weight 1; both charge 1 for the
               write. Same possible moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record
               moves from off both to off and to on, while a latch r ∨ h(r ) gives one value.
                   These are finite-weight models on one bit with no base underneath; they say
               nothing about any particular machine.
                   The third claim asks: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every base-
               driven record-carrier has to have? No, because the extension may carry any hidden
               field it likes, so two carriers over one base can have state spaces of different sizes,
               and nothing needs them to match.


               11.5 Records with more than two values

               A cup has two positions, and some records have more: a counter of how many
               checks passed, or a level that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one
               threshold at a time. For each value a, “the record has reached a” is a yes/no reading,
               and each of those readings is a latch. What doesn’t go through is squeezing the
               whole record into one cup. “Rises” needs one word of explanation: the values come
               with an order ≤, “is at or below,” which needn’t compare every pair (that’s what
               makes it a partial order), and [ a ≤ x ] is the yes/no reading “x has reached a.
                   For example, keep separate records that an experiment was repeated and that
               its calculation was checked. “Repeated only” and “calculation checked only” are
               different places; neither includes the other. “Both” is above each. In this order,
               moving up means retaining what was already done and possibly adding another act.
               The order also has three rules: a place includes itself, inclusion carries through an
               intermediate place, and two places including each other are the same place. Those
               are the rules the proof below uses.”

               Definition 11.3 (A growing record). Let the record take values in a set A with
               a partial order ≤ decided by a Boolean test. A record ρ on M, with cover π
               onto a base B, is a base-driven growing record when: there is one function f with
               ρ(next M (m)) = f (π (m), ρ(m)); it grows, ρ(m) ≤ ρ(next M (m)); the ledger never
               goes down and every step that changes ρ costs at least one; and some run from a
               starting state reaches a step that changes it.



               Theorem 11.10 (Growing records are families of latches). (1) For every base-driven
               growing record there is an h with

                                [ a ≤ ρ(next M (m))] = [ a ≤ ρ(m)] ∨ h( a, π (m), ρ(m))
                                                            11.5 Records with more than two values   215


for every value a and state m: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read
the current value. (2) The thresholds determine the value: if [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y]
for every a, then x = y. (3) For a growing record, charging every change is the
same as charging every threshold that switches on. (4) One latch is not enough:
a three-valued record that climbs 0 → 1 → 2 over a one-state base, each climb
charged one, is base-driven, and no single Boolean latch with a decoding from the
base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct k-bit words, each
word’s set bits contained in the next one’s, has at most k + 1 members.

Proof. (1) Fix a threshold a. If the old record has already reached it, growth keeps
it reached. If it has not, the cup rises exactly when the next record f (b, x ) reaches
it. Define the event to say both things: “not reached at x, reached at f (b, x ),” or
h( a, b, x ) = [ a ̸≤ x ] ∧ [ a ≤ f (b, x )]. Keeping an existing yes and otherwise using
that event gives the stated latch equation.
    (2) Suppose x and y give the same answer at every threshold. Ask the threshold
named x itself. The record x has reached it, so y must have reached it too: x ≤ y.
Ask the threshold named y and get y ≤ x. The order’s third rule says those two
records are the same.
    (3) If the value stays put, every threshold gives the same answer before and after.
If it grows from x to a different y, look at the threshold y. It is reached afterwards.
It was not reached before: y ≤ x, together with growth x ≤ y, would force x = y.
Thus some threshold switches on exactly when the record changes. Charging those
steps is the same requirement in either wording.
    (4) Keep the base at its sole state and let the record move from zero to one, then
two, then stay at two. Add one to the tally at each climb. The record rule consults
only its present value, keeps it growing and pays for both changes, so it meets the
requirements. A single flag over that unchanging base offers a decoder only two
inputs, flag down and flag up. It cannot reproduce the three different record values
just visited.
    (5) Lay the distinct bit words out in their increasing order. At each move to the
next word, at least one bit that was zero must become one; no one may become
zero. Across the whole chain there are only k bits available for those changes. There
are therefore at most k moves between distinct words, or k + 1 words including the
first.
   I have two cautions about that. In (1) each threshold’s event may read the
record’s current value, so the events aren’t all functions of the base alone. And (3)
charges a step when it switches some threshold on: a step that switches on three
thresholds at once owes at least one, and nothing here makes the charges add up
per threshold.
   The order need not be finite; (5) is the finite-memory bound.
216   11 Records over any base: the latch


               11.6 What leaving the base open buys you
               The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record
               isn’t special pleading for one machine. Over any base that steps deterministically,
               under rules you can read, a record that answers to the computation and never comes
               down is a latch on an event, and the proof doesn’t care what the base is. What a
               particular machine adds on top of the latch is a choice of price list and a choice of
               event, and both are choices. That is why the permanent-flip theorem in Section 3
               never needed the word certify: it forces a merge in whatever stays. The surcharged
               cup shows the first: the cost can change and the record not notice. The two cups on
               one die show the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine that
               meets the model will have to make both choices, and whether its choice of event is
               the right one is a question I’ll get to (Section 18), and won’t claim to have settled.
               Before that, a record can have more than two positions. Earlier in this section a
               record that rises got cut into one cup per threshold; the next section asks how much
               of the rest of the book survives once a record has more places to be than up and
               down.
CHAPTER 12




The shadow, exactly

Section 8 put the machine behind a window and asked what an outsider could tell.
It found that two states can look the same through the window and differ in what
matters, and that a price computed from the window can’t be exact if the window
has a collision (Observation 8.2). That was for one cup. With a whole row of cups
in hand I can ask the sharper version of the same question, which is also the one I
actually care about. Take the ordinary machine, the one with no cups and no ledger,
and let it look at itself. What’s the shape of everything it can’t see, and what does
the toll cost in terms of that shape?


12.1 The ordinary machine is a shadow

Take any machine with a record and a ledger, and sweep both off the table, the
cups and the counter. What’s left is a machine that steps the same way and knows
nothing about either, provided the step’s effect on everything else never depends on
the cups or the counter: sweeping them off has to commute with the step. A system
whose control reads its record or its ledger has no shadow in this sense. Where the
premise holds, call what’s left the shadow. Over any one state of the shadow there’s
a pile of full states, all casting that same shadow and differing only in their record
and their ledger. Section 8 already called the pile over a point the fibre over it. The
shadow is one particular window, the one that shows everything except the cups
and the ledger.
   The shadow has its own fibres, and every move has piles of its own too: the states
a move sends to one landing spot. I’ll call those the move’s landing piles. A fibre is
everything that looks the same before anybody moves. A landing pile is everything
that ends up in the same spot after one move. Keep the two kinds apart, because
the whole section turns on how they meet.


12.2 Pricing from the shadow
First the window question, over a whole row. A window price charges each step from
what the window shows before and after it. It meets the floor if it charges at least

                                                 217
218   12 The shadow, exactly


              one for every step that turns a cup over, and it’s exact if it also charges nothing for
              any step that turns no cup over. A collision is two steps that look the same through
              the window, where one turns a cup over and the other doesn’t.
                  With one cup, the fix in Section 8 was to put the cup in the window. So my first
              guess for a row was that the window has to show some of the cups. Try the smallest
              version: a record in the whole numbers, and a window that shows only the first
              cup, the one that asks “at least one?” Let the record rise on some steps and hold
              still on others. Once it’s past one, that cup is up before and after both kinds of step,
              so a step that turned over a cup further along looks exactly like a step that turned
              over nothing, and the two make a collision. So then, I thought, the window has to
              show every cup. That’s wrong too, from the other side. Take a record in the whole
              numbers with two moves, one that adds one and one that leaves it alone, and a
              window that shows only whether the record is even, which on the row is whether an
              even number of cups are up. You can’t read the record off that window, and no flat
              charge is exact, since some steps turn a cup over and some don’t. But the evenness
              changes on exactly the steps that turn a cup over, so charging one exactly when the
              evenness changed is exact.


              Theorem 12.1 (Window prices over a direction). (1) If the window has a collision,
              every window price that meets the floor charges at least one for some step that turns
              no cup over, so no window price is exact. (2) An exact window price exists exactly
              when the window has no collision; on a machine with finitely many states and
              moves, whose views can be told apart by a yes-or-no test, it can also be computed.
              (3) Along any run, a window price that meets the floor charges at least the number
              of steps that turn no cup over but look, through the window, like a step that does.
              Some window price meets the floor and, among the steps that turn no cup over,
              charges one on exactly those, so that number is the least overcharge; when it can be
              decided, for each pair of views, whether some step showing them turns a cup over,
              that price can be computed. (4) A window can price exactly without showing where
              the record is: there’s a record in the whole numbers with a move that raises it and a
              move that leaves it alone, and a window that shows only whether the record is even;
              the evenness changes exactly on the rises, no charge that is the same for every step
              is exact, and charging one exactly when the evenness changes is exact, although no
              rule reads the record off the window. (5) There’s a record in the whole numbers
              and a window that shows only the one cup “at least one,” and that window has a
              collision.
                                                               12.3 What a priced move destroys   219


Proof. (1) The two colliding steps get the same charge. The floor makes it at least
one because of the step that turns a cup over, and the other step pays it too. (2)
Without a collision, “does some step that looks like this turn a cup over?” is a
question about what the window shows; charge one exactly when the answer is yes.
On a finite machine you can answer it for every pair of views. (3) A step that turns
no cup over but looks like one that does gets that step’s charge, which is at least
one by (1)’s argument; add along the run. For the other half, charge one exactly
when the answer to (2)’s question is yes, which needs that question to be decidable,
and count the overcharge. (4) A rise changes the evenness and the other move
doesn’t, so the window sees exactly the steps that turn a cup over; a flat charge
either charges nothing for a rise or charges something for a step that turns nothing
over; and 0 and 2 look the same through the window. (5) The first cup, as above.
   Item (4) changed how I think about this. I’d assumed a window had to see the
cups to price them. It doesn’t; it has to see them move. A window that cannot tell
you your exact place, but detects every rise and every pause, can charge the right
amount every time.


12.3 What a priced move destroys
Now the fibres. Part I showed that the move raising a permanent flag on a finite
machine lands two possible states on one state, and Theorem 4.4 showed the same
for a step that turns any cup over, once the cups only go up. Which two? It matters
a great deal. If they’re in different shadow fibres, then the ordinary machine lost
a distinction too; the record may also differ between them. If they’re in the same
fibre, the ordinary machine lost nothing, and what got destroyed was only ever off
the table: two states that cast one shadow, told apart by their cups or their ledger,
crushed into one.
    My first guess was that it’s always the second kind, because the cups are where
everything happens. It isn’t always. It depends on whether the ordinary machine
forgets anything on its own.


Theorem 12.2 (The toll prices a collapse inside a fibre). On a machine with finitely
many states and a growing record: (1) a move that turns a cup over somewhere
sends two different states to one landing spot; (2) if the shadow exists, so that
sweeping commutes with the step, and the shadow’s step for that move forgets
nothing, sending different shadow states to different shadow states, then those two
states are in the same shadow fibre, and every landing pile of the move lies inside
one fibre; (3) without that premise it can fail: there’s a two-state machine whose
two states sit in different fibres and whose shadow step forgets, so the merge at
220   12 The shadow, exactly


              the step that turns the cup over lands two states from different fibres and no fibre
              loses a point. (4) The halving price, which says a move of cost c shrinks any finite
              collection of states by at most a factor of 2c , holds exactly when every landing pile
              has at most 2c states, on a machine of any size.

              Proof. (1) is the counting argument of Theorem 4.4, with growth. (2) If two states
              land on one spot, their shadows land on one shadow spot, and the shadow’s step
              tells shadows apart, so the two states cast the same shadow to begin with. (3) The
              stamp of Theorem 4.5, with the record’s value also shown in the visible part, so each
              state is its own shadow: both states land on yes, and so do their shadows. (4) is
              the worst pile-up of Premise 3.4. Any 2c + 1 states of one landing pile would be a
              collection that lands on a single spot, which the premise caps at 2c , so no pile has
              more; and any finite collection is at most the number of spots it lands on times the
              biggest pile. Neither half needs the machine to be finite.
                 So on a machine with finitely many states and a record that only grows, when the
              ordinary machine forgets nothing, the toll is a price on crushing a fibre: on taking
              two states that cast one shadow, which only what’s off the table told apart, and
              making them one. The last of those premises is the one I just showed you failing.


              12.4 What the shadow is

              Put the two sections together and you get the shape I’ve been circling since the
              Flatland night (the night a video about Flatland gave me the hunch behind this book;
              Section 24 tells it). The ordinary machine is the shadow of a machine with a row of
              cups beside it. Over every shadow state there’s a whole fibre, a pile of states that
              differ only in their cups and their ledger, and the ordinary machine can’t tell them
              apart, on a machine whose step never looks at the cups. On a machine that obeys
              the toll, a step that turns a cup over costs, whichever cup it is and however many it
              turns, and on a machine with finitely many states whose record only grows, when
              the ordinary machine forgets nothing, what that cost pays for is exactly crushing
              two states of one fibre into one. A window can charge the right cost without seeing
              the cups, if it sees them move. And on a machine with the halving price, where each
              unit of cost pays for at most one halving, the cost in bits, times the weight of the
              spread, is never less than what got crushed on average.
                  What I haven’t shown is that any of this is out there in the world, that nature
              keeps a direction like this over its own shadows. That’s a belief of mine, and nothing
              in this book proves it. What I’ve shown, and you can check, comes with its premises
              showing. A machine whose record is driven by the computation and climbs a partial
              order is a row of cups, one latch for every line. If it also has finitely many states,
              never lets the record come down, and prices its merges, it has to pay this way. And
                                                                                12.5 Shortcuts   221


when its ordinary machine forgets nothing, what it pays for is exactly this. It’s less
than the Flatland night promised me. It’s also the part of it that held when I pushed.


12.5 Shortcuts
There’s a question every machine with a record runs into once its programs can
be handed their own code. A cup is worth turning over because something later
glances at it and doesn’t have to work the thing out again, the way Section 6’s glance
reads a block’s bucket off the table without applying the rule from scratch. Call any
move like that a shortcut, and call it sound when it gives the answer the long way
would have given. (That gloss is about cost, leaning on what was done so nothing
is redone, and the wall I’m about to show you doesn’t look at cost at all; the next
section says exactly what it does look at.) So can a machine like that decide, from
inside, whether its own shortcuts are sound? That question runs into a wall, the
same wall Kurt Gödel and Alan Turing hit, and I have to show you that it’s there
before I show you anything that pretends to be on the other side of it.
CHAPTER 13




The diagonal

In Section 6 I said you’d watch the same move get made again and again as the
book went on: somebody says “everything is X,” it’s true enough to do real work
with, and then somebody draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now,
because Sections 11 to 12 just handed a record, and a whole direction of them, to
any system that steps, and the next thing anyone wants from a system with a record
is for it to tell sound shortcuts from unsound ones by itself. Before I let anything
claim that, I have to show you the wall every such claim runs into, and then show
you exactly where a system with a record stands relative to the wall. It doesn’t stand
on the far side, because nobody’s on the far side. A record keeps a distinction and
pays for it. What it can’t do is the judging: no machine that can hand a program
its own code, and can run the flip of a verdict as one of its own programs, can sort
all its programs, from inside, by a question about what they do that some pass and
some fail. So the record carries a commitment, and somebody still has to make it.


13.1 Now point it at the record
The question Section 12 left open can be asked with nothing in it but what Parts I
and II have built. A system steps; a record rides along and latches on an event
(Section 11); when the event is a certification, Section 9 said the reading, with
its object and its paid event behind it, is what lets an auditor treat a claim as
established, and for a claim that a shortcut is sound, that’s what makes the shortcut
admissible. Can a system like that have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that
correctly decides, for every program, “does this program admit a sound shortcut”? A
procedure like that would be autopilot: hand it any program and it says yes or no,
and it’s always right.
    The exact statement is narrower than the question in plain words, so I’ll give it
before the proof. In the theorem, “admits a shortcut” is any property of programs
with two features: two programs that behave alike agree on it, and there’s one
program that has it and one that doesn’t. Those two features are all the argument
gets to look at. The diagonal doesn’t see soundness. Each system that wants the
wall picks its own property, and whether that property lines up with being entitled

                                 222
                                                                  13.1 Now point it at the record   223


to soundness in Section 9’s sense is a separate fact about that system, checked one
system at a time if it’s checked at all. A procedure that returns soundness records for
some programs, or only for restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not what
the wall rules out.
    So in the theorem “shortcut” is a label. The plain-words gloss at the end of
Section 12, leaning on a record so the thing isn’t worked out again, is about how a
program gets its answer, and how is exactly what extensionality throws away: the
theorem only gets to see what programs do, and it treats any two that do the same
as one. A question like “is there a cheaper program that gives the same answers?”
isn’t the theorem’s question, and a wall for it would need a different theorem. The
nearest thing I know of is Manuel Blum’s speedup theorem, from 1967, and it goes
somewhere stranger: there are computable functions with no fastest program at all,
where every program for the function has another that’s faster on all but finitely
many inputs. Blum’s theorem is a fact about cost, not a wall about deciding, and
nothing in this book proves anything in that territory. Each use of the wall also
names its sameness. In the substrate theorem it’s the substrate’s own ≃; on L it’s
what a term computes; on the host of the small machine Part III builds, it’s the
partial function a program computes. A particular notion of shortcut gets the wall
only after someone proves it behaves alike on programs that are the same in the
sense in use, and holds of one program and fails of another.
    The answer is no, under premises. The proof is the two index cards, and I’ll give
you the premises because they’re the whole content. Suppose there were such a
decider, one that says yes exactly when a program admits a shortcut. Build the flip:
“if the decider says yes about me, behave like a program that admits no shortcut;
if it says no, behave like one that does.” If the system has a recursion theorem (a
program can be handed its own code), and if that flip is one of the transformations
the system can carry out, and if “admits a shortcut” depends only on behaviour (two
programs that behave the same agree on it), and if there’s at least one program each
way, then there’s a program that behaves exactly like its own flip, and whatever
the decider says about it is wrong. Both cases close in a line each. This rules out a
decider that says yes if and only if a program admits a shortcut, for any substrate
with those parts. (A substrate here is the mathematical structure just described:
programs, a run that may fail to give back a state, a counter with a step relation it
never goes down along, an encoding of programs as data, a notion of “representable”
transformation, and the recursion theorem for those. It says nothing about what
the states are made of.) It’s Rice’s trick one floor over, and I should be careful with
that. Rice stated his theorem for classes of recursively enumerable sets, the sets
a program can list, and it’s usually taught now for the functions Turing machines
compute. This wall is the same diagonal with different premises: it carries its own
recursion theorem and its own list of representable transformations, and it picks the
224   13 The diagonal


              property. So it isn’t a corollary of Rice as Rice stated it, and it doesn’t show that any
              property is harder or easier to decide than classical halting. And I want you to have
              one thing about its proof: it never touches the counter, the toll, or the step relation.
              It uses the recursion theorem, representability of the flip, the two witnesses, and
              extensionality, and nothing else.
                  I’ll set out the setting and the wall now, with every word pinned down so you
              can poke at it.

              Definition 13.1 (Substrate). A substrate has a type of states, a type Prog of pro-
              grams, and a run map that takes a program and a state and either gives back a state
              or gives nothing. It has a counter µ on states and a step relation along which µ
              never decreases; an encoding enc of programs as states with a decoder dec such
              that dec(enc( p)) = p; and a predicate Rep on maps f : Prog → Prog, the transfor-
              mations the substrate counts as its own. Two programs are equivalent, p ≃ q, when
              run( p, s) = run(q, s) for every state s. The last condition is the recursion theorem:
              for every f with Rep( f ) there is a program p with p ≃ f ( p).


              Definition 13.2 (Shortcut predicate). A shortcut predicate on a substrate is a prop-
              erty A of programs with two programs y and n such that A(y) holds, A(n) fails,
              and A is extensional: p ≃ q implies A( p) ⇐⇒ A(q). For a Boolean function d on
              programs, its flip is f d ( p) = n if d( p) is true and f d ( p) = y if d( p) is false.



              Theorem 13.1 (No inside decider). Let a substrate carry a shortcut predicate A
              with witnesses y and n. Then for every Boolean function d on programs with Rep( f d )
              there is a program p with p ≃ f d ( p), and d( p) = true ⇐⇒ A( p) fails at that p. So
              no such d is right about A on every program.

              Proof. Hand the proposed judge d to the flip construction. The flip is an allowed
              program transformation, so the recursion theorem supplies a program p that behaves
              exactly as its own flip tells it to behave. Now ask the judge about that particular
              program.
                 If the judge says yes, the flip sends p to the no-example n. Thus p and n behave
              alike. The question depends only on behaviour, and n fails it, so p fails it too. The
              judge’s yes is wrong.
                 If the judge says no, the flip sends p to the yes-example y. Now p and y behave
              alike. Since y passes, p passes too. The judge’s no is wrong. Those are its only
              answers.
                                                                      13.2 What this does to the book   225


   I used the recursion theorem to obtain this one self-matching program, the two
examples to give the flip somewhere to go, and the rule that alike behaviour gets the
same verdict. The counter, the step relation and the encoding played no part. Any
setting supplying that same fixed point for the flip gives the same contradiction.
    So what’s ruled out is a d that says true exactly when A holds, and whose flip the
substrate can represent. Every part I named is a premise, and the theorem covers
every substrate that supplies them all.
    So the wall is there. The part I have to be honest about is who counts as a decider.
The theorem rules out a decider whose flip the substrate can itself represent. It says
nothing about a decider standing outside, and an outside decider can exist for the
very same property, correct on every program. The line between inside and outside
is the boundary of the sentence, and the boundary is Richard’s lesson: the language
you talk about a system in is a different language from the one it talks in.


13.2 What this does to the book

It does two things. It keeps me honest: nothing in what follows claims that a system
with a record can check its own shortcuts on autopilot, because that’s a wall, the
same wall, and I showed you the bricks. And it tells you what a record can do,
which is the thing Part II has been about since the counter: it can carry a shortcut
with its receipt, so that the question “was this earned” is answered by an event you
can point at. No decider has to exist for that, which is lucky, because on a system
with a recursion theorem no inside one can. The diagonal says such a system can’t
automate the judgement from inside, for any behavioural property with a yes and a
no. The latch says you can record the commitment. Those are different jobs, and a
record does the second.
     The diagonal has a famous cousin that looks as if it ought to bite a record too, so
let me walk right up to it. Gödel’s second theorem says a consistent system strong
enough for arithmetic can’t prove its own consistency, and Martin Löb, a logician
answering another logician’s question, sharpened that in 1955: if such a system
proves “if this is provable, it’s true,” it already proves the thing itself. So can a record
vouch for itself, and does Löb stop it? My first guess was that Löb stops it, since a
record looked like a system talking about itself. I landed somewhere else, and mostly
it’s a relief. Hold two things side by side: “there’s a receipt for this somewhere,” and
the receipt in your hand. Löb’s theorem is about provability, the bare claim that
some proof exists, the receipt somewhere. A raised Boolean flag is not, by itself,
the receipt in your hand. From a clean start the earned-history theorem says there
was a passing check, commitment and certification in that order. The flag does not
identify the claim or the steps, and it need not store a proof of the checked claim.
226   13 The diagonal


              The native table and channel carry more information; exporting a proof requires an
              interface that actually supplies one.
                   Sergei Artemov’s distinction between implicit provability and explicit proof terms
              is useful here, but neither a flag nor the word “receipt” turns one into the other. The
              guarantee in this book comes from an external proof about the checker, the clean
              start and every permitted operation. It is not an internal proof of the system’s own
              consistency, and does not evade Gödel’s or Löb’s hypotheses.
                   Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it.
              Its trust rests on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from
              outside the machine. That’s where I chose to stop this machine’s chain of reasons.
              Gödel’s second theorem does not forbid a machine from checking a proof about a
              checker. What it limits is a system’s ability to prove its own consistency, when the
              system is strong enough to do arithmetic and its axioms can be listed by a machine.
              Eliezer Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff’s 2013 draft on agents that trust their
              own rewrites describes a related problem, the Löbian obstacle: how an agent can
              justify trust in a successor’s proofs. That’s a cousin of this question, and it doesn’t
              settle it, and it doesn’t make my design the only one possible. So I didn’t get rid of
              the receipt somewhere. I moved it out of the machine and handed it to whoever
              reads the record.
                   One more thing follows from the same picture, by a short argument. Can a record
              rest on itself, the way the sentence “this sentence is certified” would like to? It can’t
              if it’s earned and permanent. The check behind the certificate that put the record up
              happened while the record was still down, because the record goes up only after that
              check passes, and once up it never comes back down, so it goes up only once. So
              no claim whose truth needs the record already up can be the claim the record went
              up on. (A later certificate, with the record already up, can stand on such a claim; it
              raises nothing.) Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory of truth calls a sentence like that, one that
              only ever leans on itself, ungrounded, and earned records are grounded in his sense:
              every one bottoms out in a check that didn’t lean on it. Caspar Oesterheld’s 2019
              work on programs that cooperate by simulating each other needed a grounding step
              of the same kind to stop an infinite regress. I haven’t written this argument out
              anywhere else; the claim is exactly what this paragraph says, and it’s short enough
              to check by hand.
                   I want to draw one last distinction, because the two are easy to conflate and
              conflating them is the easiest way to misread this book. There’s a second wall,
              nothing to do with the diagonal. It’s Section 8’s kind of wall, a window with a
              colliding pair in it. Two states that differ in their certification reading can look
              identical through a window that doesn’t show that reading, the stamp inside the
              closed drawer and the drawer opened and shut, and then no function of the window
              recovers the reading (Theorem 8.1: a decoder has to give one answer on everything
                                                                 13.2 What this does to the book   227


the window lumps together). This wall comes from missing information. Nothing
about it is undecidable; it holds for finite things with nothing to compute; and it
sits beside Rice. None of Rice is underneath it. The property the diagonal uses (any
behavioural property of programs with a yes and a no) is a different kind of thing
from the reading the window hides, and nothing here says the two are the same. So
there are two walls, on two different axes. The diagonal is about what no inside
procedure can decide. The window is about what no outside observer can see. I’ll
need both, and I’ll try not to call one by the other’s name again. The machine I build
later has a colliding pair of exactly that kind (Theorem 15.15).

          Part III is step four, the sharpest case. A record that a claim was checked and

CHAPTER 14




What established means

Parts I and II were about any kept distinction at all. This chapter picks one: the
distinction between an answer that was checked and the same answer that wasn’t.
It’s the case the first pages of the book called the sharpest, and it’s sharp because
the two answers are the same bits, and everything that differs is in what was kept.


14.1 Two computers that end up the same

You met these two computers in one paragraph at the start of the book. Now I’ll
take them slowly: what an ordinary computer does about what Part I found keeping
takes, and why that matters to anybody who isn’t a physicist.
    Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand
numbers.
    The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until
nothing is out of order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to
back and checks that every number is no bigger than the one after it. That check
could have failed. It passes. Then it tidies up after itself, wipes its scratch work,
and leaves the sorted list in memory. (That check compares neighbours, so what it
settles is that the output is in order. That the output holds your thousand numbers
and no others is a second claim, and it would take a second check comparing the
output with the input. When I say sorted below, I mean in order.)
    The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into
it earlier, same thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.
    Now wait until both are done and read the retained digital state we have chosen
to compare: the list, the working registers and the control position. Arrange for
both programs to finish at the same control point and clear the scratch fields. Those
endpoints can agree. The first compared the entries and checked their order. The
second loaded the same answer without doing either. Wheel the boxes out, swap
them and bring them back. From those fields alone, neither of us can tell which run
happened.
    That is a construction with a specified observation. It does not establish that
every microscopic state of two physical computers agrees: the room, heat, clocks or

                                                 231
232   14 What established means


              retained logs may carry other evidence. And ordinary computers can keep a checked
              flag or a protected log. These two programs were arranged to erase the distinction
              from the fields being read. That choice, and what it prevents the next reader from
              answering, is the example.
                   Who cares? Anybody who’s been handed a sheet that says “all tests passed.”
              Anybody who’s looked at an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the
              same whether somebody checked the brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit,
              a proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of itself: every one of them is a pile
              of bits that could have come out of either computer, and the question that matters
              is the one the bits can’t answer. Did something establish this, or did it just print it?
              I’ll come back to every one of those later in this chapter and say which of them this
              book actually helps with, and I’ll warn you now that it’s fewer than you’d hope.
                   I’m going to call the first run’s relation to that answer established: it checked the
              order of this list. The second run has the answer without that relation. The list’s
              order is there either way. What can a machine keep of the difference between the
              runs? The rest of this chapter takes that question apart.
                   It belongs in a book about a 0 because a record that the check ran would be a
              distinction that stays, a 0 in some cell that says “checked.” These two computers
              did not keep that record. A machine that does keep it gives you something more to
              inspect.


              14.2 Look harder

              The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don’t look at the end, look at everything.
              So make the computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of
              a warehouse, every wire a lamp that’s lit or dark, every switch something you can
              walk up to and touch. Nothing is hidden in a chip too small to see. Put both of them
              side by side and walk the floor.
                  While they run, sure, you’d see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting
              up, comparing and swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish, and the
              comparing wing goes dark. Now walk the floor and look at every single lamp.
              The sorted list is spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both, the same pattern, and
              everything else is dark in both, because both cleaned up.
                  There is no lamp anywhere that says “a check ran here and passed.” It isn’t
              hidden, and it isn’t encrypted; it just isn’t there. You can see every retained digital
              field in this drawing, and none records the earlier check. Looking harder doesn’t
              help, because the problem isn’t that you can’t see enough. It’s that nothing was kept.
                  The shape I want you to carry through the rest is that the problem was never
              visibility; it’s keeping.
                                                                            14.3 So keep the trace   233


14.3 So keep the trace
Then the fix is obvious, isn’t it? Don’t let the run go. Keep the trace: every
comparison, every swap, the check and its answer, written down as it happens.
Wheel the computers out on the cart and back, read the traces, and you’ll know
which one sorted. Problem solved?
    It’s the right instinct, and it gets most of the way to this book. But take it apart,
because “just keep the trace” has three things wrong with it, and each one is a piece
of what comes later.
    First, a trace is bits, and bits can be typed in. Whoever typed the sorted list into
the second machine can type a trace in too: “compared, swapped, checked, passed,”
a few thousand lines of it, every one of them plausible. A trace written by a program
is something the program produced, unless some enforced rule constrains how the
program can write that log. So keeping the trace doesn’t answer the question; it
moves it. Did something establish this trace, or did it just print it?
    Second, the way out of that is to take the pen away from the program. Don’t
let the program write its own trace. Have something underneath it write the trace,
one step at a time, as the steps actually happen, so nothing a program does can
add a line that didn’t happen or erase one that did. Airplanes do a version of this.
Flight recorders go back to a prototype David Warren built in Melbourne in the
1950s. He was an Australian scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories,
working on jet fuel, and after a string of unexplained airliner crashes he wanted
a box that would hold the instrument readings and the voices in the cockpit for
whoever came looking afterwards; I know his story from museum and encyclopedia
accounts, and I haven’t read his own report. The recorders that came out of that
idea preserve instrument data and cockpit sound. The sound can include a person’s
account, correct or mistaken. A recorded sensor reading can also be wrong about
the aircraft. What the recording supplies is evidence of what those channels carried,
subject to the recorder and sensors working as specified. Crash protection helps
that evidence survive. The flight recorder has the right shape, and that shape isn’t
mine. Later in this chapter it gets its name from computer security, a reference
monitor, and I’ll say outright that a machine built that way would be doing what
this book describes. What the book adds is narrower than a rulebook for everything
underneath. It’s about the records that go up and never come back down: what that
something has to keep for good, and what keeping it takes.
    Third, a fixed memory cannot retain every possible history of unbounded length
with exact recovery. Give the run one independent yes-or-no choice per tick: after n
ticks there are 2n histories to distinguish. A fixed number of bits eventually runs
out. A completed finite trace can fit, and a predictable trace can compress. The
obstruction needs unbounded independent possibilities, not just the word “trace.”
234   14 What established means


                  Flight recorders make a practical choice about the history to retain. A voice
              recorder loops, replacing older sound when its capacity is reached. Thirty minutes,
              two hours and twenty-five hours are different retention windows; the applicable
              requirement depends on the aircraft and rule. The FAA’s 2026 final rule extends
              twenty-five-hour recording to specified newly manufactured aircraft. Whatever
              window is chosen, it is a window. It does not imply that no other machine can store
              an entire finite run.
                  The fingerprint is the sharpest reply, so take it seriously. Fold every new line of
              the trace into a fixed-size scramble of everything before it, and you’ve got a hash
              chain. The timestamps of Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, two cryptographers at
              Bellcore whose story comes later in this chapter, work that way; so do the audit logs
              the cryptographers Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey designed in 1999; and so do
              the measurement registers in the security chip a lot of computers carry, the TPM.
              For the PCRs and lifecycle under discussion, an extend folds a measurement into
              the previous value. Reset permissions depend on the register, platform and locality;
              some PCRs are resettable during operation. A claim about an unbroken history must
              specify which resets and writers its policy permits. That really does keep something
              about the whole trace in a few dozen bytes. But look at what it keeps: it keeps a
              binding, and the content isn’t in it. To read the history you still need the trace stored
              somewhere, and the fingerprint only tells you whether a copy somebody hands you
              is the one that went in. The binding holds only because nobody knows how to find
              two traces with the same fingerprint, which is a bet on how hard a search is. No
              law of nature backs it. That part isn’t only my opinion. The computer scientists
              Moni Naor and Guy Rothblum proved a sharp version of it in 2005, and they even
              call the thing a fingerprint: keep a small private fingerprint of a big file somebody
              else stores, check the file by reading only a little of it, and against an opponent
              with unlimited computing the size of the fingerprint times the amount you read has
              to be on the order of the whole file. Do even slightly better than that against an
              opponent with limited computing, and you’ve shown that one-way functions exist,
              which is the hardness bet in its barest form. Their setting is a stored file. A growing
              trace is a different setting, but it’s the same bet, with its terms written down. And
              squeezing traces that keep growing into a fixed number of bits has to land many
              traces on one fingerprint, and that’s a merge, hidden behind how hard it is to find
              which traces land on the same fingerprint. It’s the same merge as in the example
              of Part I (Section 3) where four people have to sit in three chairs. Fingerprints are
              great, but they’re not a way out of forgetting; they’re a very clever way of forgetting.
                  So the real question was never “save everything.” The real question is: what’s the
              smallest thing worth keeping for good, and what does keeping it take? The answer
              this book ends up with is the commitment, in the database’s sense, a question closed,
              and the trace drops away. (The cryptographer’s sealed envelope also goes by the
                                                                14.4 Computed, stored, established   235


name commitment. It’s a different thing, and both come up later.) What’s kept for
good isn’t every comparison the sort made, just the one fact that a check of this very
claim passed and the question got closed. And the part that matters most is that
keeping even that one fact for good takes something on every machine. It’s paid by
forgetting something somewhere else or by taking fresh states the machine never
gets back, and on a finite machine the fresh states run out, so it’s the forgetting.
That’s Part I’s counting of states again, and Part I counted the fresh states.
    So the premise was never that computers can’t keep records. They keep records
all day. It’s that nothing in the rules of an ordinary computer makes the record paid
for, permanent, or earned, and those three come in at different places, so I’ll say
where. Paid for is the model’s one rule: in the Thiele Machine, the step that raises
the record has to cost something. Permanent is a premise, the one Part I’s counting
