                  At the end, the bits on both machines are still the same sorted list. Everything
              else differs. The sorter’s record is up and its counter reads 3. The copier’s record is
              down, and it’s paid 2 for two refusals, because on that machine a refused attempt
              still costs what it costs. (Read those as two separate attempts. Written as one stored
              program, the copier would stop at its first refusal and pay 1.) Nothing the copier can
              do raises its record without first running a passing check of the claim it then commits
              to. And no outside window that only shows the list can tell you which is which; the
              difference is all in the part the window doesn’t show. Walk that warehouse now and
              there’s finally a lamp that’s lit in one and dark in the other.
                  Now, how literally should you take that table? It’s a picture of the chain, and
              the chain is what’s proved. The small machine’s own checks are three questions
              about one counter: is it zero, is it even, is it at least some number. What its proofs
              need from the questions is a checker proved to say yes exactly when the answer is
                                                                 14.15 Two layers, and the names   257


yes, and an exact test for telling two questions apart. That’s enough for “sorted”: a
version of the machine that takes any questions with checkers like that proves the
same chain once for all of them, and with a list packed into one counter it certifies
a sorted list for a cost of three and refuses an unsorted one forever (Section 15).
Without a proved checker for “sorted,” the chain would be honest about a counter
and only by convention about your list, which is Gettier’s pocket again, one level
down.
    And a lamp for whom? The record is bits too. It’s a lamp on the machine, for
anybody walking that warehouse. Hand somebody a printout of it across a desk and
you’re back at the sticker on the windshield: they have to trust whoever hands it
over, or have some way to check the box that says it ran. That crossing is a different
problem with its own tools, signatures, attestation and proofs a stranger can check,
and this book doesn’t solve it. Section 8 says what those tools rest on, and the
small machine’s record, like any record kept in a machine’s state, carries nobody’s
signature. What the step changes is the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust
the box that says it ran?” That’s a smaller question, but it isn’t no question.
    So, back to the list from the start of this chapter: the test sheet, the sticker,
the audit, the ledger, the proof, the confident AI. I’ll give the straight answer on
which of those this helps. The sticker is a question of whether a piece of paper is
genuine, and nothing here touches it. The “all tests passed” sheet fits only if the
test is a checker proved to mean what it says, in the machine’s own language; a set
of tests that can miss a bug certifies “this procedure said yes,” which is true and
smaller. An audit and a ledger get the test sheet’s answer: kept by a program on an
ordinary computer, they’re bits the program wrote, and they fit only where the step
underneath keeps the record and refuses to raise it without the check. A proof is
one example: checking its steps is a procedure that can reject them. Whether its
statement says what you meant is still yours to read. The AI that talks as if it’s sure
of itself isn’t addressed at all. Section 22, under “Outward consequences,” says how
little of the outside world I’ve reached.
    Now comes the honest half. Take away the small machine’s rules and keep only
the bare toll, and the copier has an easier move: pay one unit, flip the record to
yes, and that’s the whole move. The toll is satisfied and the receipt is real, but it’s
a receipt for nothing. The bare toll prices the closing of the door, and the check
behind it goes unpriced.


14.15 Two layers, and the names

The layers, once. The core definition (Definition 2.1) is a Thiele machine: states,
moves, a step, a cost for each move, a record in an order, and the toll; the two-place
record (Definition 2.2) is its smallest case. Everything else is added on top, and each
258   14 What established means


              theorem names what it adds. First come extra structures and requirements: a ledger
              that sums the costs, a window, permanence of the reading, a price on merges. Then
              an earned implementation, the small machine of the next chapter, with a checker
              proved sound and a provenance theorem. Then a universal interpreter for a stated
              class of guests. The bare definition doesn’t ask the step to be computable, so when I
              say the record adds no computing power, I mean relative to a fixed flat part.
                 Substrate versus scaffolding. Two layers run through the book, and confusing
              them makes the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The substrate is the
              shape: a kind of state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape
              for different extra pieces, and the pieces aren’t the same. The universal floor (the
              “pays something” result of Section 2) asks for a record in an order and the toll on it.
              The counter’s uniqueness (only one count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a
              starting value and a schedule of increments; Section 7 gives the argument, a short
              induction that works for any system with those two pieces, and on the small machine
              of the next chapter the ledger is the sum of the charges by theorem (Section 15).
              The diagonal asks for a recursion theorem for the transformations the substrate can
              express, and needs no toll and no encoding at all. “Substrate-level” doesn’t mean
              one fixed set of parts that every theorem shares. A theorem only gets to use the
              parts it asks for. Ask it what it needs and it’ll tell you, and whatever else is lying
              around the workshop isn’t the theorem’s. So each result is stated over exactly the
              extension it uses. The substrate with the extension a theorem names is what I mean
              by the model, and the name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. The scaffolding is
              everything that holds the shape up so you can touch it, and when I say my machine,
              the small machine, the machine I build or the build, this is what I mean: the machine
              of the next chapter, with its two counters and their versions, its table of checked
              facts, its channel, trap, ledger and flag, its six instruction kinds and their prices, the
              host with a register for every whole number, and the universal programs that run on
              that host (Appendix C.1). The build fills in several extensions at once and borrows,
              for any one theorem, only the extension that theorem names. Let that line blur and
              a theorem stated over one extension starts reading as if it carried premises it never
              uses. “Substrate” never means the build, and it never means the side of a simulation
              doing the stepping; for that I say “the machine doing the stepping,” as against “the
              program it runs.”
                 So the book keeps the two apart: Parts I and II were about any system with
              the pieces each result names, and their pictures were small worked instances you
              could hold (two boxes on a sheet of paper, chairs in a room, a row of dots). The
              example machine wasn’t one of them; where they said something about it, they
              pointed ahead, and the next chapter builds it. Every Part II claim that has a machine
              instance gets that instance in the next chapter or in Appendix C.1, with its own
              theorem, and Part II said so in one sentence at most. When the origin story (the
                                                                 14.15 Two layers, and the names   259


afterword, Section 24) says the shape “was the substrate the entire time,” it means
this layer, the model’s shape. It doesn’t mean any piece of the build. The same goes
for two more of its words. When it says “the machine” about the thing it named
the Thiele Machine, or calls that thing a meta machine, it means the model; “my
machine” is the build of the next chapter. And when it lists what the model asks for
(a state, a step, a record, a ledger, a window), read the ledger and the window as
two of the extra pieces: a result asks for them only if it uses them.
    The build is one piece of scaffolding, and I’d rather you know up front that it is
one instance, chosen to be small enough to inspect. Section 15 builds the smallest
honest machine I could: two counters, six instructions, a table of checked facts, a
ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are proved there (a flag raised from a clean
start was checked, then committed, then certified, on the same edition, with nothing
touching that thing between the check and the commit), and so is universality, by
matching Minsky’s two-counter machines step for step. Then one fixed program,
on a host made of the same kinds of instruction with more counters, runs every
program of it, and with one paid move added, every computably presented Thiele
machine (Appendix C.1). None of that is the model. It shows the model fits in six
instruction kinds.
    The names again, with the certified one pinned down, because I’ll hold to them
for the rest of the book. A Thiele machine is any particular system that fits the
definition, its five parts and its toll (Definition 2.1); the toys on paper in Part I
count, a clock counts, and so does the small machine, with its toll proved. The
small machine is certified, which asks four things of it. The first is that the moves
of its flat part can’t touch the record, and that the record stays up once it’s up. The
second is a record that, from a clean start, rises only after a passing check of a
claim, then a commitment to that same claim with nothing it’s about changed in
between, then a certificate, with the checker proved to mean what it says. Over a
language fixed first, the claims and what they mean are that language’s, and the
proof is that the checker’s yes makes the claim true in its sense; every instance in
this book is stated that way. The third is exact prices: one unit for each of those
three acts and nothing for anything else. And the fourth is a claim whose check,
commit and certificate raise the record from a loaded start exactly when the claim
holds there, with the claim holding at some loaded starts and failing at others. A
machine that meets all four hides its record and its ledger from a window on its flat
part, by theorem (Theorem 15.15). That’s about an observer who sees only where
a run ended; one who also has the program and the start can work both out. The
small machine meets it, and so does the same machine over any properties with
an exact test for telling two of them apart and a checker proved to say yes exactly
when the property holds, as long as one of them can come out both ways, sorted
lists included. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed machine running one fixed
260   14 What established means


              program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with every step of the
              guest’s computing done by the host’s own counter moves and every rise of its record
              put where its program put it; a certified one also earns each guest’s record again by
              its own check, commit and certificate. Nothing is left to the guest’s good manners.
              Appendix C.1 builds one, U: a fixed program in the small machine’s own six kinds
              of instruction, on a host with more counters, with no step of any guest built in. Its
              guests are the small machine’s programs, so every computation runs on it under
              Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine, and it matches each guest’s halting,
              answer, flag and ledger exactly, raising its own flag by its own check, commit and
              certificate. Then UP , the same program with one more handler for a paid move that
              does nothing else, takes as its guests every computably presented Thiele machine,
              one whose next move (picked by a driver), step, prices and reading are computed
              by programs, with the reading decided on every state. It matches the guest’s halting,
              raises its own flag on its own earned chain exactly when the guest’s reading has
              said yes, and keeps the guest’s prices to within a surcharge of at most two when the
              guest’s reading starts at no, which no program on that host, run from a clean start,
              can avoid in general. And a computer that runs the small machine, your laptop say,
              isn’t the small machine. Read through the emulator’s prices and flag it’s a Thiele
              machine, a finite one, like the toys of Part I, and its counters stop somewhere. It
              implements the small machine, inside bounds, the way a laptop implements a Turing
              machine. Push on that comparison, because it’s loose, and the looseness is the point.
              Does a laptop implement a Turing machine? Not exactly. Turing’s tape never runs
              out, and a laptop’s memory does; strictly, a laptop is a very large machine with
              finitely many states, and it behaves like a Turing machine only on computations
              that fit. Nobody minds, because the bound is known and most computations people
              care about fit inside it. That’s the same deal any device running the small machine
              gets: its counters stop somewhere, and the theorems speak only for runs that fit.
              The bounds aren’t fine print. They’re the whole difference between implementing a
              model and being one.
                  How much can a difference in width matter? There’s a famous answer, and
              it’s worth the detour. On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket lifted off and
              broke apart about forty seconds after its engines lit. The inquiry board, chaired by
              the mathematician Jacques-Louis Lions, traced it to one conversion in the inertial
              reference software: a sixty-four-bit floating-point number, an alignment value called
              BH that’s tied to horizontal speed, squeezed into a sixteen-bit signed integer. On
              Ariane 4, where the software came from, that value could never get big enough to
              overflow, because of how that rocket flew in its first forty seconds. Ariane 5 flew
              differently. The value got too big, the backup unit failed on it, the main unit failed
              the same way one cycle of its software later, seventy-two thousandths of a second,
              and the function doing the converting didn’t even serve a purpose once the rocket
                                                              14.15 Two layers, and the names   261


had lifted off; it was kept for commonality with the old rocket. The board’s report
says the assumption that made the conversion safe had been agreed on and then,
not on purpose, kept out of sight of any outside review. A width premise that holds
on one machine is a fact about how that machine gets used. The code doesn’t carry
it, and yet it travels with the code without anybody noticing. The only defence I
know is the dull one: write the premise into every statement that needs it, where
the next person will trip over it.
CHAPTER 15




The earned-chain counter
example

The chapters before this one never built a machine you could program. They said
“any states, any steps,” and whenever a picture was needed, a board or some chairs
or a cup stood in. Now I have to build a machine, and the first question is about
the one I built before it. I built a big one first, on the way here (the Afterword,
Section 24, tells that story), with dozens of instructions, some picked for reasons
and some picked because I had to pick something, and theorems held of it. What
does that show? That the model works, or that I’m good at stacking instructions
until the proofs go through? A big machine is a wonderful place to hide a mistake.
It’s a garage so full of stuff that you could lose a car in it.
    So the example machine in this book is a small one. I want the state and every
way of changing it where you can inspect them. There are six instruction kinds, and
you can follow how a check stays tied to an object, how a change makes it stale,
and how the next move uses that relation. Each kind takes operands, a counter or a
property or a line to jump to, so there are unboundedly many instructions. It’s one
way of building the model, not the only one, and the theorems will say which facts
hang on these particular choices. I built it by throwing things out until nothing more
would go. I haven’t got a proof that nothing smaller works, and I’m not claiming
one.


15.1 What the model asks for, and the example that meets it

The model asks for states, moves, a step, a price on each move and a record in an
order, with the toll. Before any of its parts, I’ll give the example that meets it in
three sentences. Its record has two places, a flag that is the blank cell, and its flat
part is two counters and a jump, the part a window on the counters shows. Raising
the flag is the write of a 0, a merge in the record’s part of the state (flag down and
flag up land on the same state), which is why the step that raises it is charged once




                                 262
                                           15.1 What the model asks for, and the example that meets it   263


merges in that part are priced (Theorem 3.19, in Part I). And the order rule, check,
then commit, then certify, is what makes a raised flag mean something.
     Parts I and II define the model by five parts and one rule. The example meets
them with the smallest record there is, a flag that reads no or yes and, once yes,
stays, which on a machine is the blank cell’s 0. Here yes means “certified,” because
that’s the event I picked (Section 18, later in this part, asks whether anything outside
the rules picks it out). It adds a toll: the step that raises the flag costs something
(Section 2). And it adds a ledger, the running total of those costs, a whole number
that only climbs (Section 7). And Section 11 proved the thing this whole chapter
stands on: over any base at all, a base-driven record is a latch, a bit that switches on
at an event the base decides and never switches off (Observation 11.1). The record
watches the base. It doesn’t compute anything the base couldn’t compute without it.
     Push on that for a second, because it cuts the job in half. If the record adds
no computing power, then all the computing power comes from the base, and the
question “how small can the machine be” splits into two questions that don’t touch
each other. For the base: what’s the smallest thing that can compute everything
there is to compute? For the record: what’s the smallest set of pieces that makes the
flag mean something?
     There’s one honest asterisk on “don’t touch,” because the machine below makes
it matter. What’s blind is the flag and the ledger: the base never reads either of
them. But the pieces that make the flag mean something (a table of checked facts, a
slot for a commitment, a trap that stops a refused run) have to sit where the step
can read them, which is in the base, and they do steer the run: a failed check stops
a program dead. The latch theorem holds wherever you draw the line between base
and record, which is exactly why it can’t tell you where the meaning lives. On this
machine the meaning lives on the base side of that line, in the bookkeeping, and the
flag on top reports it. That line has to sit at the core: the step reads the table, the
channel and the trap, so a map that hid any of them wouldn’t move in step. The
record-layer merge of Part I draws a lower line, with only the line number and the
two counters below it, and what the premise charges moves with that line. Drawn
there, all three record acts merge in the record’s part and the premise charges each
of them; drawn at the core, it charges only CERTIFY.
     The record question, the second of those two, is the one Part II left to the
machine, on purpose. Section 10 said that testing a claim and committing to it are
two different acts, and that nothing in the five parts of the model makes the second
wait for the first. Read Section 2’s definition again with that in mind: a machine
where you pay one unit and raise the flag over nothing in particular obeys every
rule in it. That machine is honest about the price and silent about what was bought:
it’s a receipt for nothing. The toll alone can’t fix that, because the toll is a rule about
264   15 The earned-chain counter example


              cost, and “was this earned” is a question about order: did a check happen, of this
              claim, before the commitment, with nothing changing underneath in between?
                  This machine is my attempt to make the order part of the machine, in the smallest
              place I could find to do it. I’ll show you the pieces, then the proofs, then the places
              it falls short, which there are, and which I’d rather you hear from me.

              The blown fuse cannot be hidden from every future move
              Blow the fuse and pull the lever. Nothing moves. Replace the fuse, start from the
              same counter values, and that lever can turn the gears. The fuse decides what the
              next pull does, whether the camera can see it or not.
                 That is what a failed CHECK does here. It traps the core, and every free instruction
              then leaves the whole state alone. Suppose I hide the failed check from the camera
              and still demand that the next picture depend only on the present picture and the
              free move. The live and trapped pictures agree. The camera’s rule must give them
              the same next picture. Since the trapped box stays still, the projected live box has to
              stay still too.


              Theorem 15.1 (A globally check-silent native shadow is static). Let π be any
              projection from native full states, with any target type. Suppose every CHECK
              preserves π, and each zero-cost instruction i has an autonomous projected rule hi ,
              so π (exec(s, i )) = hi (π (s)) for every state. Then hi (π (s)) = π (s) for every s, i. If π
              is onto, each hi is identity everywhere. The conclusion also holds on the reachable
              states from a fixed start when those same laws hold throughout that reachable
              domain.

              Proof. Stand at any native state s and read counter A. Ask CHECK whether that
              counter is at least one greater than the number just read. It is not, so this check
              leaves a trapped state t. In symbols, the chosen question is A ≥ A(s) + 1.
                 By the proposed silence rule, the failed check has not changed the picture:
              π (t) = π (s). Now choose any free instruction i. At the trapped state it changes
              nothing at all. The camera’s rule hi must therefore leave that picture alone. But it is
              also the picture of s, and hi receives only the picture, not a choice between the two
              boxes. It must leave s’s picture alone too. Written as one chain,
                               hi (π (s)) = hi (π (t)) = π (exec(t, i )) = π (t) = π (s).

                  You could begin at any s and choose any free i, so every free projected move is
              still on the whole image. If every base picture occurs, that is the whole base. I did
              choose a different failing question for different counter values; the premise allows
              every CHECK at every state, so it allows each of those choices. Finally, if s was
                                                                    15.2 The example machine, piece by piece   265


reached from the fixed start, append this CHECK to that run to reach t. Both boxes
remain inside the reachable domain, and the same argument applies there.
    The fuse belongs with the gears that read it. The certificate and ledger can sit
beside them unread. The later slice follows the computing moves while the machine
is live; a failed check takes it out of that working domain. That is where the line
goes on this machine. 3


15.2 The example machine, piece by piece

I’ll go through the whole state a piece at a time, in words first.
• Two counters, A and B. Each holds a whole number, with no upper limit.
• A version for each counter, also a whole number with no limit. It starts at 0 and
  goes up by one every time its counter is written. Think of it as the counter’s
  edition number: a new value is a new edition.
• A line number, which instruction comes next, counting from 1 (more on that
  choice just below).
• A fact table: a list of facts. A fact is three things stuck together: a property, a
  counter, and a version. “A is even, as of edition 3” is a fact. The table has room
  for sixteen. Why sixteen? It’s a pick, with no derivation behind it, and what the
  pick gives up is set out in the subsection near the end of this chapter on what the
  machine doesn’t do.
• A channel: either empty, or holding one fact. This is where a commitment sits.
• A trap: one bit, down at the start. When it goes up, the machine has refused
  something, and it stays up.
    Counting lines from 1 looks like the least interesting choice in the chapter, and
it’s one of the oldest arguments in programming, with a famous referee. Edsger
Dijkstra was a Dutch computer scientist, one of the generation that founded the
field, and for over forty years he mailed numbered notes to a few dozen colleagues.
In 1982 he wrote one of them, EWD 831, titled “Why numbering should start at
zero.” His case goes through ranges first. Of the four ways to write “2 up to 12” with
less-than signs, he picks the one that takes the bottom in and leaves the top out,
2 ≤ i < 13: two ranges that meet end to end then share one number written once,
and the length is just the top minus the bottom. Start a sequence of N things at zero
and it’s 0 ≤ i < N, and each thing’s number is how many things came before it. He
reports that programmers on the language Mesa, which allowed all four conventions,
   3 A view that exposes refusal, or a machine with a different failure rule, would supply a different

interface. The obstruction concerns the native failure semantics and a globally CHECK-silent autonomous
projection.
266   15 The earned-chain counter example


              found the other three a steady source of clumsiness and mistakes, and he points
              out that FORTRAN starts at one. Does that settle it? It settles which convention is
              tidier, by an argument you can check. It doesn’t settle which convention somebody
              else’s work used, and that’s the catch: the two-counter machine used by Forster,
              Larchey-Wendling and coauthors numbers its lines from 1, and so does this machine,
              because matching it line for line is worth more here than tidiness. Is zero the right
              place to start counting? Dijkstra’s title says it is, and I can’t tell you more than that.
              What his note carries is an argument about which way makes fewer mistakes. That
              part you can check for yourself, and it’s the more useful thing to have.
                  Everything in that list is the core, the part the base moves. Outside the core sit
              the two pieces from the model: the ledger µ and the flag. The machine never reads
              either of them to decide what to do next. I’m not asking you to take that on trust:
              it’s how the step is written, and it shows up as a theorem below.
                  The properties a fact can name come from a tiny fixed language with three words:
              is zero; is even; and is at least n, for any whole number n you like. Each one comes
              in two forms. There’s the checker, a little program that computes yes or no: compare
              with 0, look at the last bit, compare with n. And there’s the meaning, the plain
              arithmetic statement the checker is supposed to be checking: the number is 0; the
              number is two times something; n is less than or equal to the number. Why both?
              Because a checker is code, and code can be wrong in ways that look right, and
              “the checker says yes” is only worth anything once somebody has proved it says yes
              exactly when the meaning is true. That proof is one line per property, and it’s the
              first block below.
                  Why can a machine check a claim at all? Because a claim with a precise meaning
              is something you evaluate: plug in the values and turn the crank. George Boole
              worked out in 1847 that you can do arithmetic on claims this way, treating “and”
              like multiplication and “or” like a kind of addition. Why multiplication? Try it at
              the table. Write 1 for true and 0 for false, and multiply: one times one is one, and
              anything times zero is zero. That’s “and” to the letter. Then comes the stranger thing
              Boole noticed. Say “x and x” and you’ve said nothing new; it’s just x. In numbers
              that’s x × x = x, and he made it a law of his system, and it’s a law ordinary numbers
              mostly break. Which numbers equal their own square? Two times two is four, no. A
              half times a half is a quarter, no. Zero, yes. One, yes. That’s the whole list. So when
              Boole wrote his bigger book in 1854, The Laws of Thought, he asked you to imagine
              an algebra whose letters take the values 0 and 1 and nothing else. Every checker on
              this machine answers in that algebra.
                  And the 1847 book has a backstory worth a detour, which I found in the Stanford
              Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on Boole. Boole was largely self-taught and spent
              about fifteen years as a schoolmaster, and what pulled him back to logic, early in
              1847, was a loud public quarrel between Augustus De Morgan and the Scottish
                                                         15.2 The example machine, piece by piece   267


philosopher Sir William Hamilton over who had first thought of a small technical
idea in the old logic of syllogisms. Two well-known men fighting over credit, and a
schoolmaster watching from the side picks up the subject and writes the little book
this paragraph is about. Few people remember what the quarrel was over. Every
checker in this chapter runs on what the bystander wrote.
    Then push on it, because Boole’s “or” isn’t quite the one a checker uses. His plus
only made sense for things that can’t both hold at once, so “x or y” with both of them
true had no meaning in his system. William Stanley Jevons, an English economist
who also worked on logic, read “or” as “either or both,” which gives “x or x is x,”
the same trick as before. He wrote to Boole in 1863 saying plus ought to work that
way, and in 1864 he put it in a book called Pure Logic. Boole wouldn’t have it, since
it broke the tie to ordinary algebra his whole system stood on. The “or” in every
programming language I know is the inclusive one Jevons argued for. Does that
change anything about the checker? No; the crank turns the same way. It changes
the picture: the “or” a checker uses is the one the man who invented the algebra
turned down.
    Hanging a checked claim on a point in a computation is an old move too. Tony
Hoare, in 1969, built a whole way of reasoning about programs out of it: attach a
claim to a point in a program (“whenever execution reaches here, this is true”), and
reason forward from claim to claim. Robert Floyd had done it two years earlier on
flowcharts. Their claims were checked on paper by the person writing the proof.
This machine’s version is a property of one counter at one edition, checked by a step
while it runs.
    And is two years earlier the bottom? Not even close, and the next step down is a
paper this book already leaned on. In June 1949, at a Cambridge conference held
for the new EDSAC computer, Alan Turing gave a talk three pages long, “Checking
a large routine,” the same note the counter chapter used for stopping (Section 7).
Stopping was the second half of it. The first half is this move, twenty years before
Hoare: the programmer should make “definite assertions which can be checked
individually,” and the correctness of the whole should follow from them. His example
program computes a factorial using nothing but addition, and his picture for why
you’d bother is one you can do on the back of an envelope. Add up a long column
of four-digit numbers and hand someone only the total, and they have to redo the
whole sum at one sitting, because the carries tie every column to the one before
it. Hand them the total of each column as well, and the job falls apart into small
checks they can do one at a time. Each column total is a claim hung on a point in
the middle of the work, so the person checking never has to hold all of it at once.
The paper got its due mostly later: in 1984 two computer scientists, F. L. Morris of
Syracuse University and C. B. Jones of Manchester University, who had worked on it
together at Oxford, republished it, with its misprints corrected, as an early program
268   15 The earned-chain counter example


              proof by Alan Turing. Theirs is the text I read, and the column of numbers is Turing’s
              own example in it. Does any of that change the machine? No. It changes the date
              on the idea, and it tells you something I like: the first person to ask how you’d check
              a program put the claims in the middle of it. He didn’t save them for the end.
                 The machine has six instruction kinds.

                Instruction            What it does, when the trap is Cost

                INC c                  Adds one to counter c, adds one      0

                  The first two are Minsky’s machine, and HALT lets a program say it’s done. It says
              it by doing nothing: HALT leaves the state where it is. If it put the trap up instead,
              it would land a live state on its trapped twin, a merge in the record’s part, and the
              record-layer merge would charge it. The last three are the record’s, and they read
              as a chain: you can only certify with a commitment in the channel, you can only
                                                         15.2 The example machine, piece by piece   269


commit to a fact in the table, and the only way into the table is a check that passed.
The chain has three links, and each one costs.
    One of what? One unit of µ, the same unit as Section 2’s toll. Why one? Why
would ten be worse? Because one is the least each of these three acts can cost once
a merge in the record’s own part of the state is priced, as the end of this paragraph
says, and Section 3 is where that pricing comes from. The argument for a whole
finite machine doesn’t reach this one: these counters have no top, and some of the
base moves merge states at a price of zero. What does reach it is the record-layer
merge named at the start of this chapter (Theorem 3.19, in Part I), which gives
the toll once you’ve agreed to price a merge in the record’s own part of the state.
Agreeing to that is my choice. Once I have, one unit on each of the three acts isn’t:
COMMIT and CERTIFY merge when they pass, and all three merge when they fail,
because a failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else, so the failed state lands
where the same state with the trap already up lands. What I pick is one rather than
more.
    The whole numbers have a history of their own. In 1888 the German mathe-
matician Richard Dedekind published a little book whose title asks what numbers
are and what they’re for, and in 1889 the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano
published a booklet, written in Latin, that set out the axioms for the whole numbers
in the form people still teach: there’s a first number, and every number has a next
one, and a few rules about how “next” behaves. I had the two of them down as
working independently. I went looking, and the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on
Dedekind says Peano acknowledged Dedekind’s priority, which is why the axioms
often go by both names. (Peano’s booklet is also where the sign ∈ that you met in
Section 6 comes from: he wrote it as a Greek epsilon, for the Latin est, “is.”) Start
from zero and take “the next one” three times, and you have three. Once prices are
whole numbers, one is the smallest price that isn’t nothing.
    The zeros matter just as much: computing costs nothing on this ledger. Plus one,
minus one and jumping around cost zero, with physical costs left to an implemen-
tation model. Only the three acts that make a claim cost, and each of them costs
whether it passes or traps. Failing is not a discount.
    The version rule. Some numbers show why versions exist. Start with A = 4,
version 0. CHECK is even A passes, and the table gets the fact (even, A, 0). Now INC
A: A becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT is even A. The machine
looks for (even, A, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only has (even,
A, 0). There’s no match, so the machine traps. The old fact is still sitting in the
table, still true about edition 0, and completely useless for committing to anything
about edition 1. A fact is about one edition of one counter, and an edition never
comes back, because versions only go up and never wrap. The version rule is the
whole trick against stale evidence: you can’t check a number, change it, and then
270   15 The earned-chain counter example


              commit to the check. And the never-wrap part isn’t a convenience. INC A, then
              DEC A back to the same line, puts the line and both counters exactly where they
              were, at no cost, and once record-layer merges are priced neither move may join
              two states that agree on those. If the record had only finitely many settings over one
              line and one pair of counters, enough round trips would bring the whole state back
              to where a CHECK left it, with A touched in between and its COMMIT still passing.
              Under those free-move, injectivity and continued-use requirements, the record fibre
              cannot be finite. This machine supplies fresh editions without a bound. A bounded
              implementation can instead stop before wraparound or change its invalidation and
              pricing rules; that changes the contract.
                  What the version rule stops is the time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug from Sec-
              tion 14, the file checked and then swapped, and the database answer to it is Kung
              and Robinson’s: at commit time, check that nothing you read was written in the
              meantime, and back out if something was. The version rule is that check, done by
              the step, on one counter. It also shows where the guarantee ends. It works because
              one step does every write and every write bumps a version. A second writer that
              changed a counter without bumping its version, a second processor or a device
              writing memory on its own, would walk right around it, and none of the theorems
              below are about a machine with one of those.
                  Processor designers put a cousin of this check in silicon. Jensen, Hagensen and
              Broughton, at Lawrence Livermore in 1987, described a pair of instructions now
              called load-linked and store-conditional: the load reads a word and the processor
              starts watching it, and the store goes through only if nothing has written that word
              since; otherwise it fails and the program tries again. It’s tempting to say CHECK
              is the load and COMMIT is the conditional store, and it’s wrong in two places.
              COMMIT doesn’t write the counter it checked, and the thing doing the watching,
              the fact, sits in a table the step keeps. No single processor holds it. The hardware
              version does cover the second writer, because the watching happens on the memory
              everyone shares, which is exactly the case the version rule leaves out.
                  The real kinship is older, and it’s somewhere else. Picture the table and the
              counters shared by many processors, with CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY each
              done as one indivisible step. Maurice Herlihy (1991), a computer scientist who has
              spent his career on how many processors can share memory safely, ranked shared
              objects by how many processors each one can bring to agree on a single value with
              nobody ever waiting on anybody. Test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and
              reports what was there, brings exactly two. A sticky bit, the idea of Serge Plotkin
              (1989), a Stanford computer scientist working on distributed algorithms, is a cell the
              first writer jams for good, with the first writer’s value, and everyone after can read
              it; it brings any number. I guessed that the shared object would sit at the top with
              the sticky bit, because a write that kills every fact about a counter, together with a
                                                         15.2 The example machine, piece by piece   271


commitment other processors can see, looks like a way to build one. Ranking the
object takes its operations, what each one returns, which steps are indivisible, how
it starts and which processes run it, and then a proof that every processor decides,
they all decide the same value, the value is one somebody proposed, and nobody
waits. That proof goes through with every instruction one indivisible step and the
whole state readable, and it puts the object at the top. The reason is the order of the
fact table. Start it clean, with counter A at zero and the trap down. Each processor
CHECKs a property that holds of A at zero, Zero to propose 0 and Even to propose
1, then reads the table and decides the bit of its oldest fact. Nobody touches A, so
the first CHECK of the run passes. The table never loses an entry or reorders the
ones it has, and a CHECK that finds it full trips the trap, after which nothing moves,
so the first CHECK of the run fixes the oldest fact for good. Every processor that
decides decides that bit, the bit is somebody’s proposal, and each one decides after
two of its own steps whatever the others do. The version rule and the commitment
play no part. The trap alone doesn’t do it: it records that something trapped, and it
doesn’t hand everyone the first writer’s value.
    Now take the version rule away, let failures change nothing, keep only the
properties “at least n” so that a checked property only ever turns true, drop the
decrement, and make the fact table (with no room limit), the commitments and
the flag sets and latches that only grow. I guessed that then the object drops to the
bottom rung, the level of plain memory, which is the shared-memory face of what
the database researchers Joseph Hellerstein and Peter Alvaro (2020), at Berkeley
and Santa Cruz, call CALM, where monotone means nobody has to coordinate. That
guess is proved too, by Herlihy’s own kind of argument. Let the updates return
nothing and let the whole state be readable. If at every state, of any two updates,
one leaves the state alone, or the two commute, or one overwrites the other, then no
protocol brings two processors to agreement with nobody waiting. To see why, give
one processor 0 and the other 1. At the start the answer isn’t settled, since either
one running alone has to decide its own bit. Nobody waits, so it can’t stay unsettled
forever, and there’s a last unsettled state: whichever processor moves next settles
it, one way if it’s the first and the other way if it’s the second. Look at those two
moves. If one is a read, or an update that leaves the state alone, the other processor
can’t tell whether it happened, and running alone it decides the same bit either
way. If the two commute, both orders end on the same state with both processors
in the same place. If one overwrites the other, the overwriter running alone can’t
tell whether the other move happened first. Each case contradicts the two ways the
answer was settled. The monotone object, with registers beside it, has that property.
An update that fails changes nothing. Two updates that both succeed still succeed in
either order, because an instruction that would succeed still succeeds after anything
else has run, and adding to sets and to counters gives the same result in either order.
272   15 The earned-chain counter example


              Two of the conditions do real work there. The table needs no room limit: a full table
              that turns away the latecomer is a first-writer-wins cell again, and that’s back at the
              top. And the ledger: it changes neither result as long as a failed act in the variant
              isn’t charged, or nobody reads the ledger. Charge a failed CHECK where everyone
              can read the total, and one processor INCs while the other CHECKs at least 1; the
              total and the table then tell each of them which act came first, and that’s enough
              for two to agree. Neither idea is mine: the top is Plotkin’s and the bottom is the
              monotone fact that field already knows.
                  Process-calculus people have a statement of the same split. Johannes Åman
              Pohjola and Joachim Parrow, computer scientists at Uppsala University (Parrow
              is one of the inventors of the pi-calculus, a mathematical model of processes that
              talk over channels), in 2016 proved that no model whose parallel composition is
              monotonic, where a neighbouring process can never stop a step, has a consensus
              process. One of their examples of a model that does is test-and-set. Test-and-set isn’t
              a sticky bit: in Herlihy’s ranking it brings two processors to agree, and a sticky bit
              brings any number.
                  Their setting is small enough to go through here whole. A model is any set of
              processes with a step relation and a way to compose two processes that doesn’t care
              about order or grouping. Composition is monotonic when whatever a process can
              reach alone, it can still reach with anything set beside it. A consensus process is one
              where any number of copies, run together, can end up agreeing on either of two
              outcomes; once a run has one outcome it can never show the other; and an outcome,
              once reached, survives having more copies, run any way you like, set beside it. Their
              theorem goes through in a few lines: run half the copies to one outcome and the
              other half to the other. If neither half can block the other, the whole crowd can
              reach the pair of end states set side by side, and since each outcome survives the
              company, both outcomes hold there, which is forbidden. Then the machine goes
              into it. A process is a shared machine state with a crowd of threads, each proposing
              a bit. Composing two processes pools their threads, each thread keeping whatever it
              has already decided, and settles the shared state like this: if one side is still at the
              fresh start, the composite takes the other side’s state; if both have already moved,
              the composite is jammed, a state where no thread can take a step. That composition
              doesn’t care about order or grouping: a fresh start is neutral, and any two moved
              states jam whichever way round you put them. One thread proposing each bit is
              a consensus process in exactly their sense, for the outcomes “some thread decided
              0” and “some thread decided 1”: copies started fresh can reach either outcome and
              never both, because the first passing check fixes the oldest fact and every later thread
              reads the same one; and an outcome survives company, because pooled threads
              keep their decisions. So by their theorem the composition isn’t monotonic, and
              the small machine sits on their non-monotonic side. That verdict is cheap, though:
                                                          15.2 The example machine, piece by piece   273


a composition that jams any two moved states makes every shared-state machine
non-monotonic, so the encoding puts it there, not the fact table. What does the
work in the run, making every thread read the same outcome, is the order of the
fact table, the same as above; a store that refuses a stale commit for good, as the
version rule does, refuses in the same spirit. The shared-memory version of their
split is the pair of results above: the small machine’s object reaches agreement for
any number of processors, and the monotone variant, with its table unbounded and
no charge for failing that anyone can see, doesn’t reach it even for two.
    Security people know the pattern by a third name. A check that blesses a value,
and a write that takes the blessing away, is close kin to dynamic taint tracking,
where a label rides along with the data and a sanitizing step changes it; the labels go
back to the computer-security researcher Dorothy Denning’s 1976 lattice model of
how information is allowed to flow. How much a monitor like that has to remember
is a studied question too: Chamseddine Talhi, Nadia Tawbi and Mourad Debbabi
(2008), three security researchers at universities in Quebec, worked out which rules
a monitor can still enforce when its memory is bounded. The version rule is one
small, specific member of that family, done by the step.
    Notice what isn’t a write. DEC on a counter that’s already 0 doesn’t change the
counter, so it doesn’t change the version. It’s a test that happens to move the line
number.
    The fact table. Facts go in and never come out. Nothing erases them and nothing
overwrites them. When the table is full, a seventeenth CHECK traps rather than
pushing an old fact out to make room. That choice has a downside, and I’ll set it out
in the subsection on what this machine doesn’t do.
    Traps. Any failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else in the core; the
ledger still takes the instruction’s cost. Once it’s up, every instruction leaves the
core alone. A stored program stops at a trap. But I also prove things about any list
of instructions, programs or otherwise, because an adversary doesn’t have to run
my programs; they can feed the machine whatever they want. For those lists, an
instruction after a trap is still charged its cost, and still changes nothing. That trap
keeps nothing of what tripped it, and the record-layer merge charges it for that.
Merely counting refusals does not remove the merge. A live state with count zero
and its already trapped twin with count zero can both become trapped with count
one. Keeping the entire previous state in a history would make each extended move
injective, but that is a different, unbounded state space. The counter alone is not
that history.
    The exact version comes next.
274   15 The earned-chain counter example


              Definition 15.1 (Properties, checker, meaning). A property is one of: Zero, Even,
              or Ge(n) for a whole number n. The checker eval( p, v) computes yes or no: v = 0
              by equality, evenness by the parity function, n ≤ v by comparison. The meaning
              holds( p, v) is the arithmetic statement: v = 0; there is an m with v = 2m; n ≤ v.



              Lemma 15.2 (The checker says what it means). For every property p and every
              whole number v, eval( p, v) = yes if and only if holds( p, v).

              Proof. Ask whether the number is zero: the equality test says yes at zero and no at
              every other number. Ask whether it is at least n: the comparison says yes precisely
              when n is no larger than it. Those two tests already answer the arithmetic questions
              they name.
                 For evenness, the checker says yes at zero, no at one, and adding two leaves its
              answer unchanged. Take any whole number and remove pairs until fewer than two
              remain. If none remain, the number was two times the number of pairs removed,
              and the checker gives zero’s answer, yes. If one remains, it was two times that many
              pairs plus one, and the checker gives one’s answer, no. Thus yes means exactly
              v = 2m for some whole number m. These are all three properties in the language.


              Definition 15.2 (Core, state, claim, start). A core k holds two counters A, B and
              their versions (whole numbers), a line number, a fact table (a list of facts, a fact
              being a triple of a property, a counter and a version), a channel (empty or one fact),
              and a trap bit. Write val(k, c) and ver(k, c) for counter c’s value and version. A state
              s is a core, written core(s), with a ledger µ(s) and a flag cert(s). The claim p of c in
              k is the fact ( p, c, ver(k, c)). The table’s room is 16. The start start( a, b) has counters
              a and b, versions 0, line 1, an empty table, an empty channel, the trap down, µ = 0
              and the flag down. A state is clean when its table and channel are empty and its flag
              is down.


              Definition 15.3 (Instructions, costs, the step). The instructions are INC c, DEC c j,
              HALT, CHECK p c, COMMIT p c and CERTIFY, with effects on a core with the trap
              down as in the table above. Passing any check, commitment or certification requires
              the trap to be down. With that condition, CHECK passes when eval( p, val(k, c)) =
              yes and the table holds fewer than 16 facts, COMMIT passes when the claim p of
              c is in the table, and CERTIFY passes when the channel holds a fact; a failing one
              sets the trap and changes nothing else. On a core with the trap up, every instruction
                                                           15.2 The example machine, piece by piece   275


changes nothing. Costs: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost 1, the rest 0. One step
on a state is
                                                                                   
    exec(s, i ) = cexec(core(s), i ), µ(s) + cost(i ), cert(s) ∨ fires(core(s), i ) ,

where cexec is the core’s step and fires(k, i ) is yes exactly when i is CERTIFY and
passes at k. For any list t of instructions (a trace), run(t, s) applies them in order
and cost(t) adds their costs. A program is a list of instructions numbered from 1; a
program run fetches the instruction at the line number and executes it, and stops
when the trap is up, the line holds HALT, or the line holds nothing.

    Read the step line slowly, because the rest of the chapter leans on its shape. The
core moves by its own rule and nothing else. The ledger adds the cost. The flag
becomes “it was up, or this is a CERTIFY that passed.” The core’s move doesn’t
mention µ or the flag anywhere. The base is blind to the record by construction.
    The shortest worked run there is uses the program CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is
zero A; CERTIFY. Start at start(0, b), for any b. Line 1: A is 0, the checker says yes,
the table is empty so there’s room, and the fact (zero, A, 0) goes in. µ = 1. Line 2:
the claim about A’s current edition is (zero, A, 0), and it’s right there, so it goes into
the channel, and µ = 2. Line 3: the channel holds a fact, the flag goes up. µ = 3.
Line 4 has no instruction, so the program stops. The run ends with three paid acts,
in order, a flag that’s up, and a channel that names the last earned commitment,
which here is (zero, A, 0).
    Now start the same program at start(5, b). Line 1: A is 5, the checker says no,
the trap goes up, µ = 1, and the program stops right there. The flag is down, and
you can run it as long as you like: it stays down. That second run is the point of the
first. The same three instructions certify from some starts and refuse from others,
because the check could have failed, and from most starts it does. A check like that
has a no pile, which is the only kind Section 14 counts as establishing anything.
    Could I have picked an even dumber claim? I could: CHECK at least 0 A passes
on every number there is, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for
3 from every start. The step doesn’t ask whether the question was worth asking,
and it shouldn’t. Worth is a count over the rivals a run narrows (Section 9), and a
step that sees one state has no list of rivals to count. What the step checks is order,
aboutness and that the checker tells the truth. What a check that can’t fail is worth,
the entitlement count says exactly: zero bits, for a cost of three. The price is for
standing behind the claim. What the claim bought is a separate number, one the
step doesn’t compute, and I keep the two apart. It’s on the list at the end of the
chapter.
    Others walked into the same line from communication. Three theoretical com-
puter scientists, Oded Goldreich, Brendan Juba and Madhu Sudan (2012), built a
276   15 The earned-chain counter example


              theory of communication with a partner you may not understand, in which getting
              a message across counts only as a way to reach a goal, and the central notion is
              sensing: being able to tell, from what you see, whether you’re making progress. They
              ask two things of it. It has to be safe: with any partner in the class, when there’s no
              progress it keeps saying so, so it can’t report a lasting success that didn’t happen.
              And it has to be viable: with a partner who could help if you spoke its language, the
              right way of speaking gets a yes from it within a known time, and keeps getting one.
              Either half alone is cheap. A sensor that always says no is safe, and one that always
              says yes is viable. Their main result, as I read it, is that the two together, with the
              ways of speaking listed one after another, are enough for one strategy that reaches
              the goal with every such partner. Their theorem, in their setting, is a check that can
              fail and never lies, standing in front of a verdict you can’t take back, and it’s the
              same shape.


              15.3 It computes everything two counters can

              First the flat part, because the example is meant to run every program, and that has
              to be shown. Put the ordinary two-counter program beside this machine’s program.
              Replace each “add one” by this machine’s INC, and each “subtract if possible and
              jump” by its DEC, keeping the named counter and jump destination. That is all the
              translation does.
                 Now cover the facts, versions, channel, flag and ledger with a sheet. Leave the
              two counters and line number visible. I want to show that the visible part follows the
              original program exactly. The hidden versions may change, but these instructions
              cannot raise the trap, so the sheet never hides a new refusal that would stop the
              comparison. Here are the two programs and the window written precisely.

              Definition 15.4 (Two-counter program, compile, window). A two-counter program
              M is a list of instructions, each either MINC c or MDEC c j. A configuration is a
              triple (line, a, b). One step of M: if the line holds no instruction, M has stopped;
              MINC adds one to c and goes to the next line; MDEC subtracts one from c and goes
              to line j if c is above 0, and goes to the next line if c is 0. mrun(n, M, x ) is n steps
              from x, staying put once stopped. The compile of M replaces each MINC c by INC c
              and each MDEC c j by DEC c j. The window of a core k is the triple (line number,
              val(k, A), val(k, B)).
                                                      15.3 It computes everything two counters can   277




Theorem 15.3 (Step for step). For every two-counter program M and every core
k with the trap down: M has stopped at window(k) if and only if the program
compile( M ) has halted at k; and if M steps from window(k ) to y, then one program
step of compile( M ) from k lands on a core with window y and the trap still down.
So for every n, n program steps of compile( M ) from k land on a core whose window
is mrun(n, M, window(k )), with the trap down.

Proof. Look up the instruction at the line. If there is none, both sides stop. If
it’s MINC c, the compiled INC c adds one to c and goes to the next line, which is
exactly the window’s move (the version also moves, but the window doesn’t show
versions). If it’s MDEC c j, split on whether c is 0, and both sides do the same
thing in each case. Neither instruction can trap. After that move the windows agree
again and the trap is still down. Those are exactly the conditions I began with, so
the next instruction can be compared in the same way. Repeat until the chosen n
steps have been counted; if either side stops earlier, both stay put for the remaining
comparisons.



Theorem 15.4 (Halting matches). For every two-counter program M and whole
numbers a, b: M stops after some number of steps from (1, a, b) if and only if the
program compile( M ) halts after some number of program steps from start( a, b).

Proof. The start has window (1, a, b) and its trap is down. Apply Theorem 15.3
after any number n of steps: the two configurations still have the same window, the
trap is still down, and one is stopped exactly when the other is halted. The same n
witnesses termination in either direction.
     Now comes the part that isn’t mine. Two-counter universality is Minsky’s, and
the constructions of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors connect it to
several other models. The counter convention matters: DEC at zero goes on to
the next instruction; otherwise it takes one off and jumps, the convention used
in Andrej Dudenhefner’s certified decision procedures for two-counter machines
(2022). Their route runs from a tape to counters and packs finitely many counters
into two. The remaining step here is to match that two-counter machine to this
machine’s INC/DEC fragment, instruction for instruction.
     I want to be exact about what “undecidable” means in the theorem below, because
it’s stated as a connection between two problems. Suppose you had a procedure that
answered the halting question for this machine. Then you could write a program
278   15 The earned-chain counter example


              that lists, one by one, every single-tape Turing machine that doesn’t halt. No such
              list can exist: the ones that do halt can already be listed (just run them all, a step at
              a time, and call out each one as it stops), and with both lists running side by side
              you’d have a halting decider. So the theorem says: a decider here would give you
              that impossible list.


              Theorem 15.5 (Halting is undecidable for this machine). The two-counter machine
              with the instruction convention just stated agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its
              step, its stop, and its termination match those of the compiled program, so its
              halting problem at ( M, a, b) has a positive answer if and only if compile( M) halts
              from start( a, b). Consequently, the question “does program P halt from start( a, b)?”
              is undecidable in the following reduction sense: a decider for it would make the
              complement of single-tape binary Turing machine halting enumerable.

              Proof. The agreement is a case split on the counter-machine instruction at the
              current line, and then induction along the run, ending in Theorem 15.4. Composing
              a proposed decider for the compiled program with the compile map would decide
              two-counter halting. The tape-to-counter reduction would then decide single-tape
              binary halting and so list its complement, as claimed.
                  What that buys is that the base of this machine is a universal machine in Minsky’s
              sense, and that no algorithm can predict in general what it’ll do. What it doesn’t
              buy is a fast machine, or one where your input arrives conveniently. The counters
              start holding a and b, given directly; there’s no encoding layer in this construction.
              Minsky’s prime-power packing is how you’d get from “any Turing machine” to “two
              counters,” and I use that construction as it stands.
                  Is “given directly” just a convenience, or does it bite? It bites, and somebody
              found exactly where. In 1972 Rich Schroeppel, then at the MIT AI Lab, wrote a
              ten-page memo titled “A Two Counter Machine Cannot Calculate 2 N .” He spells
              out the convention first: a counter machine computing a function starts with n
              in one counter and zero in the others. Then he gives a proof that a two-counter
              machine started that way can’t compute 2n . That’s his theorem, and I don’t reprove
              it. A cousin holds on this machine: no program multiplies every input by one large
              constant fixed by the program’s length. So the packing Minsky needs is precisely the
              thing two plain counters can’t do for themselves. Hand the small machine its inputs
              straight and there are functions of them it can’t compute; hand it the inputs already
              packed and it computes anything a Turing machine can. That’s no contradiction with
              the undecidability above, which ranges over every program and every starting pair,
              packed ones included. The base hides nothing; it just needs its input pre-chewed,
              and the chewing is somebody else’s.
                                                    15.4 It’s a Thiele machine, and the flag is a latch   279


15.4 It’s a Thiele machine, and the flag is a latch
Now it’s the record’s turn. There are three facts to state first, and all of them read
straight off the step line.


Theorem 15.6 (Ledger, toll, permanence). For every state s and instruction i,
µ(exec(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ), and for every trace t, µ(run(t, s)) = µ(s) + cost(t).
If cert(s) is down and cert(exec(s, i )) is up, then i is CERTIFY, it passes at core(s),
and cost(i ) ≥ 1. If cert(s) is up, so is cert(exec(s, i )).

Proof. Each instruction adds its listed charge to the ledger. Start at µ(s): after the
first instruction its charge has been added, after the second both charges have been
added, and every further instruction adds its own. An empty list adds nothing. Thus
any finite trace leaves exactly the starting ledger plus the sum of the charges.
    The flag has two ways to be up afterwards: it was already up, or this instruction
successfully certified. If it was down before and up afterwards, only the second way
is available. The instruction must be CERTIFY, its check of the channel must pass,
and its listed charge is one. If the flag was already up, the first way keeps it up
regardless of the next instruction.
   The middle clause of those three is Section 2’s toll, for this machine, which means
this machine is one of the things Section 2 was about, and Section 2’s universal floor
applies to it without my lifting a finger.


Theorem 15.7 (The small machine is a Thiele machine). The states, the instructions,
the step exec, the cost and the flag, with the toll of Theorem 15.6, form a Thiele
machine (Definition 2.2). So the universal floor (Observation 2.2) holds here: if
cert(s0 ) is down and cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 1.

Proof. Take the state and instruction sets of Definitions 15.2 and 15.3, their step and
cost, and the flag as the reading. These provide the five components of Definition 2.2.
Theorem 15.6 supplies its one required rule. Applying Observation 2.2 gives the
claimed bound.
   Section 11 comes next. Section 11 said: take any base, and any record that
answers only to the base and never comes back down, and the record is a latch.
This machine has a base: a program together with a core, stepping by the program
step. And it has a record, the flag, with the ledger riding along. So the question is
whether it’s a base-driven extension in Section 11’s five-rule sense (Definition 11.2),
and if it is, Section 11 does the rest.
280   15 The earned-chain counter example




              Theorem 15.8 (The flag is a latch of the base). Let the base have states (program,
              core), stepping by the program step, starting at start( a, b)’s core for any a, b, and
              halting when the program has halted. Map each (program, state) to (program, core).
              Then the machine, run as a closed machine on (program, state), is a base-driven
              record over that base, and so its flag factors as the latch (Observation 11.1) of the
              event “the next instruction is a CERTIFY that passes.”

              Proof. First the cover (Definition 11.1): the map sends starts onto starts, it commutes
              with the step because the core’s move never reads µ or the flag, and whether the
              program has halted is read off the core. Then the rules of Definition 11.2 one at a
              time. Driven by the computation: the next flag is the old flag or “the next instruction
              is a passing CERTIFY,” which is a function of the base state and the old flag (that’s
              the step line). Ledger: µ only adds. Toll: Theorem 15.6. Permanence: Theorem 15.6.
              A reachable write: the three-line program of the worked run raises the flag from a
              start. Section 11’s theorem then gives the factorization.
                  So far there’s nothing new. The toll, the floor and the latch are things Parts I and
              II already promised about any machine of this kind. The next subsection is the part
              neither of them could give.

              The lamp and the claims it does not name
              The lamp is on. Which claim turned it on? Did another claim get certified afterwards?
              Look at the lamp as long as you like. It still gives you one answer.
                 Put a file beside it. Every time CERTIFY succeeds, copy the fact from its channel
              into the file: the predicate, the counter it concerns, and that counter’s edition. Call
              the set of filed facts R. Publishing the same fact again leaves the same set. A later
              write can change the counters while the old receipt stays filed under its old edition.
                 Run this record alongside the native state. The native instructions keep doing
              exactly what they did before. Forget the file and you recover their run. Open the file
              and you can ask which claims were actually published.


              Theorem 15.9 (The native lamp is the archive’s Boolean reading). From a clean
              start with an empty added archive, after every finite native instruction word,
                                            cert(s) = true   ⇐⇒    R ̸= ∅.

              Membership in R means exactly that this fact was emitted by a successful CERTIFY
              earlier in that word. Already recorded facts persist, and zero-cost instructions cannot
              add a fact.
                                                                    15.5 Commitments are earned   281


Proof. Start with the empty archive and the flag down. Inspect the next instruction.
A successful CERTIFY inserts its channel fact into R and raises the flag. Whether
or not that fact was already present, the resulting set is nonempty and the flag is
up. Every other case leaves both the archive and the flag alone, including failed or
trapped instructions. This includes every horizontal move. It follows, one instruction
at a time, that a fact belongs to R exactly when some earlier successful CERTIFY
published it, that no later move removes it, and that the flag is up exactly when R is
nonempty. Forgetting R leaves the native updates untouched, so it also recovers the
native run.
    The lamp tells you whether that file is empty. The file tells you what is in it.
Below, I will make 65,535 different nonempty files leave the entire native machine in
one identical state. Before that, follow how a fact earns its place: CHECK establishes
it in the table, COMMIT selects it, and a successful CERTIFY publishes it. Each step
has a job.


15.5 Commitments are earned
The shape comes first, before the words. Pick any run from a clean start, any list of
instructions at all, chosen by somebody who’d love to cheat. Look at the moment
a COMMIT would pass. Then, somewhere earlier in that run, there’s a CHECK of
exactly the same claim that passed and paid, at the same edition of the counter, and
between that CHECK and now, nothing touched the counter. That holds on every
list of instructions anybody can write, not “probably” and not only “on the programs
I wrote.”
    To say “nothing touched it” exactly takes one word.

Definition 15.5 (Untouched). A list of instructions mid, run from a state s, leaves
counter c untouched when, for every way of splitting mid as t1 , then i, then t2 ,
executing i at the core reached by running t1 from s leaves both ver(·, c) and val(·, c)
as they were.



Theorem 15.10 (A commitment was checked first). Let s0 be clean and pre any
trace after which COMMIT p c would pass. Then pre splits as pre1 , then CHECK p c,
then mid, where: the CHECK passes at the core reached by pre1 ; CHECK p c and
COMMIT p c each cost 1; c’s version after pre1 equals its version after pre; and mid,
run from just after the CHECK, leaves c untouched.
282   15 The earned-chain counter example


              Proof. COMMIT passes, so the claim ( p, c, ver(c)) for the current version is in the
              table. By the no-forging invariant (Theorem 15.14 below), that fact was written by
              a passing CHECK p c at some point pre1 , with the version c had then; since it’s the
              current version too, the two versions are equal. Versions never go down, and any
              instruction that changes a counter’s value also raises its version, so an instruction in
              mid that touched c would have left c’s version higher at the end than at the CHECK.
              It isn’t. So nothing in mid touched c.



              Theorem 15.11 (A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified). Let s0
              be clean and t any trace with cert(run(t, s0 )) up. Then for some p and c, t is

                        pre1 , CHECK p c, mid1 , COMMIT p c, mid2 , CERTIFY, post,

              where the CHECK passes at its state, the COMMIT passes at its state, the CERTIFY
              passes at its state, c has the same version at the CHECK as at the COMMIT, and
              mid1 leaves c untouched. And when the CERTIFY runs, the channel holds exactly
              the claim that COMMIT made: the fact (p, c, c’s version at the CHECK). CERTIFY
              takes no operand; this is what ties it to the claim.

              Proof. The flag starts down, so some first instruction raised it, and by Theorem 15.6
              it’s a passing CERTIFY. A CERTIFY passes only with a fact in the channel, the channel
              starts empty, and only a passing COMMIT puts a fact there, so some earlier COMMIT
              p c passed. Take the last one before the CERTIFY: the fact in the channel is the one
              it wrote. Theorem 15.10 at that COMMIT gives the CHECK, the equal version, and
              the untouched stretch, and the equal version makes the committed fact (p, c, c’s
              version at the CHECK).
                  The failure side comes next, so you can see the refusals are clean, with nothing
              left half-done:


              Theorem 15.12 (Unearned steps trap and change no claim). If COMMIT p c would
              not pass at a core k, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the channel and the
              table as they were. If CERTIFY would not pass at a state s, executing it puts the trap
              up and leaves the flag as it was.

              Proof. If the trap is already up, the core is unchanged and its trap remains up.
              Otherwise, the failed COMMIT takes the failure branch of the instruction table: set
              the trap, leave every other core field alone. A failed CERTIFY takes the same branch,
                                                                      15.5 Commitments are earned   283


and its fires value is false. The flag update is then its old value or false, which leaves
it unchanged. The instruction’s charge still applies to the ledger.
    If that rings a bell, it should. It’s Milner’s move from Section 14: in LCF a
theorem is a value that only the rules of the logic can build, so nobody can just
print one (Milner and two colleagues on his Edinburgh project, Michael Gordon and
Christopher Wadsworth, wrote the system up in 1979, and Gordon, who went on to
build the HOL prover at Cambridge, told its history in 2000). Here the thing nobody
can print is one bit, and what guards it is one step rule. Milner’s guard was a type
checker. Same architecture, much lower down.
    A provenance theorem is also an itemised receipt, and the itemised receipt has
a history that’s exactly this gap. James Ritty ran a saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and
believed some of his staff were pocketing money. On a steamboat trip to Europe in
1878 he watched a mechanism that counted the turns of the ship’s propeller, and
wondered whether something like it could count the money instead. In 1879 he and
his brother John patented a “Cash Register and Indicator,” and they sold a version
under the wonderful name Ritty’s Incorruptible Cashier. The first model was this
book’s counter (Section 7) with brass on it: press a key, the amount goes onto a
dial showing the day’s running total. There was no drawer and no paper. At closing
