time you hold the dial up against the cash. And that’s all a total can do. It tells you
that the money is short. It can’t tell you which sale went missing or who rang it
up. The paper came later. The patents passed to other owners, first a Cincinnati
salesman named Jacob Eckert, and in 1884 to John H. Patterson, who renamed the
business the National Cash Register Company, and the story told about that company
is that it added a paper roll: one copy kept for the shop’s own books, one handed to
the customer. That last part I only have from histories of the company and of the
machine, so hold it the way you’d hold any company’s story about itself. The order
is right either way: first a total that can tell you something’s wrong, then a list that
tells you where. The ledger µ is the dial. Theorem 15.11 is the list: which CHECK,
of which claim, about which edition, before which COMMIT. The theorem supplies
that list about the run. The machine doesn’t keep it as data anyone can read back
from the end state, and nothing in the theorem gives a procedure for rebuilding it
from there. A fact in the table holds a property, a counter and a version number.
That’s neither the counter’s value back then nor a log of what happened in between.
    Read Theorem 15.11 once more for what it doesn’t say. Between the CHECK and
the COMMIT, the counter is untouched. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY,
it isn’t promised anything. You can check A is even, commit to it, add one to A,
and then certify. The flag goes up, and what it stands on is a commitment about
the edition that was current when you committed. The certificate is historical: it
says “this was checked and committed about this edition,” and it says nothing about
284   15 The earned-chain counter example


              whether that’s still true. I think that’s the right meaning for a certificate (a birth
              certificate doesn’t expire when the baby grows), but it’s a meaning, and you should
              know which one you’re getting. So a certificate doesn’t say the claim holds at the
              CERTIFY, and it doesn’t say the claim holds at the end of the run. A CERTIFY that
              rechecked the version would give a different guarantee. That’s a possible extension,
              and the historical theorem doesn’t need it.
                                                Start: counter 1, edition 0
                                            No fact, no commitment; flag down

                                                               CHECK: tally 1

                                                 Counter 1, edition 0
                                    Saved fact: this edition is at least 1; flag down

                                                               COMMIT: tally 2

                                                Counter 1, edition 0
                                       Channel commits to that fact; flag down

                                                               DEC: tally 2

                                                 Counter 0, edition 1
                                       Channel still names edition 0; flag down

                                                               CERTIFY: tally 3

                                                 Counter 0, edition 1
                                        The old commitment remains; flag up

                The checked claim was true of edition zero. The raised flag does not say that the current
                                              counter is still at least one.


              15.6 What a passing check means

              Provenance says a CHECK happened. It doesn’t yet say the CHECK was right, and
              that’s a separate question with a separate proof. A machine could have a perfectly
              ordered chain of check, commit, certify, all standing on a checker that says yes to
              everything. So what does a fact in the table actually tell you about the counter?


              Theorem 15.13 (Checker soundness). Let s0 be clean and t any trace, and let k
              be the core of run(t, s0 ). For every fact ( p, c, v) in k’s table with v = ver(k, c), the
                                                                   15.6 What a passing check means   285


property holds of the counter’s current value: holds( p, val(k, c)). In particular, if
COMMIT p c would pass at k, then holds( p, val(k, c)).

Proof. Carry one sentence through every instruction: every fact in the table has a
version no higher than its counter’s, and if its version equals its counter’s, its property
holds of its counter’s value. A clean start has an empty table, so the sentence holds
there. A passing CHECK adds a fact at the current version, and the checker said
yes, so by Lemma 15.2 the property holds. A write raises one counter’s version, so
every old fact about that counter falls strictly behind and the second half no longer
applies to it. Nothing else changes a value or a version. The sentence holds after
every instruction, so it holds at the end. The part about COMMIT is the case where
the claim is in the table at the current version.
    So, on a run from a clean start, a live fact means exactly that one of three
arithmetic properties holds of one counter’s current value. It doesn’t mean “the
program is correct,” and it doesn’t mean “the number is interesting”; it means the
property holds of the value, now. That’s all “checked” means on this machine, and
it’s enough to be true. Three events stay separate here. The property holding of the
value is one. A CHECK passing is another: a CHECK of a property that holds still
doesn’t pass when the table is full or the trap is already up. A certification is a third,
and it needs a COMMIT and a CERTIFY after the CHECK. So a CHECK that didn’t
pass says its property is false only when the trap was down and the table had room
before it.
    So who checked the checker? Nothing on the record did. From a clean start, the
record carries the run’s half of the story: a CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same
claim about the same edition, then a CERTIFY. The other half, that the checker says
yes exactly when the property holds, isn’t in any run. It’s Lemma 15.2, a proof
about the little program the step calls, priced by nothing on the ledger. So a claim
established here stands on two legs: a fact about this run, carried by the record, and
a fact about the checker, carried by a proof that whoever reads the record has to
accept. That’s the Münchhausen trilemma from Section 14 taking its third horn on
purpose: the chain of reasons stops at a proof, named and on the page, where you
can decide whether you’d have stopped there too. And the entitlement it gives is the
reader’s. The machine doesn’t know anything. It keeps the order.
    The question in that paragraph is older than any checker, and its most famous
wording isn’t about what you’d guess. “Who will guard the guardians?” gets
quoted about governments and police and the people checking mathematical proofs.
Where’s it from? Plato’s Republic has the worry, sort of: in Book III (at 403e),
Glaucon, Plato’s older brother and one of the people Socrates is talking with, says
it would be absurd for a guardian to need a guardian, which is close in words and
opposite in mood, a man calling the question silly. The Latin, quis custodiet ipsos
286   15 The earned-chain counter example


              custodes, is from the Roman satirist Juvenal’s sixth satire, and it’s a joke about a
              husband. His friends tell him to bolt his wife in and set guards on her; the line
              asks who’ll watch the guards, since she’ll start with them. And it gets better. In
              1899 an Oxford undergraduate, E. O. Winstedt, found extra lines of that satire in
              a medieval manuscript in the Bodleian Library, lines the other copies lack, partly
              overlapping the familiar ones, and the famous question sits in that tangle. Scholars
              have argued ever since about whether those lines are Juvenal’s at all. So the most
              quoted sentence about trusting the checker comes with a doubtful source of its own.
              Does that change anything here? It doesn’t. The answer used here is simple: you
              never get rid of the last guard, you make the last guard small enough to watch
              yourself. Lemma 15.2 is one line per property. Euclid had the instinct: five postulates
              you can hold in your head, and everything else meant to follow from them.
                  That split, a fixed checker proved sound from outside and a process that only
              gets to act when the checker says yes, has a name in the writing on self-improving
              programs. The AI researcher Jürgen Schmidhuber, at the IDSIA lab in Lugano,
              described a Gödel machine (2003) that rewrites its own code only after its built-in
              proof searcher has proved the rewrite useful, and Benja Fallenstein and Nate Soares
              (2015), researchers at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, survey
              agents that reason about their successors through formal proofs a fixed checker
              accepts. Same architecture, aimed at a different question: they want to know when
              a machine may trust a smarter version of itself, and this machine only wants to
              know whether a flag was earned. Keeping the checker’s proof outside the machine
              is my design choice. The nearest theorem, in Section 13, is narrower: no procedure
              whose flip the substrate can represent decides, for every program, a property that
              depends only on behaviour and holds of one program and fails of another. It doesn’t
              say a machine can’t check a proof about a checker, or verify a restricted part of itself.
                  Soundness rules out a lying checker. It doesn’t rule out a pointless question:
              at least 0 has a perfectly sound checker and an empty no pile, as the worked run
              showed.
                  Program checking has a theory of its own, and its founding paper asks for a
              checker that could have said no. The computer scientists Manuel Blum and Sampath
              Kannan (1989; journal version 1995) defined a checker for a computational problem:
              given a program and an input, it may run the program as it likes, and it must say
              “correct” with high probability when the program is right everywhere and “buggy”
              with high probability when its answer on that input is wrong. A checker that always
              says “correct” isn’t one. Here the checker is fixed, deterministic and proved sound
              once, and the part of their demand that survives is the fourth thing certified asks
              for: some claim whose check can fail.
                                                                           15.7 Nothing gets forged   287


15.7 Nothing gets forged
The proof of Theorem 15.10 leaned on an invariant I promised to show you, and this
subsection shows it. The fear it answers: could some clever sequence of instructions
get a fact into the table without a CHECK writing it? Could a DEC with a funny
jump target do it, or a COMMIT after a trap, or something I didn’t think of? I answer
it one instruction at a time, which is the only way I trust myself to answer it.

Definition 15.6 (Earned fact; no forgery). After a trace t from s0 , a fact f = ( p, c, v)
is earned when t is pre, then CHECK p c, then mid, where the CHECK passes at the
core reached by pre, f is exactly the claim p of c at that core, and, if f is live at the
end (v equals c’s version after t), mid leaves c untouched. The trace has no forgery
when every fact in the table after it is earned.



Theorem 15.14 (No forging). For every core k, instruction i and fact f in the table
after executing i at k: either f was already in k’s table, or i is CHECK of f ’s property
and counter, it passes at k, and f is the claim it writes. Consequently, if a trace has
no forgery, so does that trace followed by any one instruction; and from every clean
start, every trace has no forgery.

Proof. Inspect who can write to the table. INC and DEC change counters, versions
and the line; they leave the table alone. HALT leaves it alone. COMMIT reads it and
may write the channel, but cannot write the table. CERTIFY reads the channel and
cannot write the table either. CHECK is the only remaining instruction. On failure it
adds nothing; on success it adds exactly the property, counter and present edition it
just checked. A trapped instruction changes no core field. That exhausts the ways a
fact could appear after one instruction.
    Now suppose the table’s old entries already have their promised histories. A new
entry gets its history from the passing CHECK just performed. For an old entry, that
earlier CHECK still happened. If the entry is live after the new instruction, its saved
edition equals the counter’s edition now. The counter’s edition never goes down.
It therefore could not have risen away from the saved edition and then returned.
In particular, it was already live before this instruction and the instruction did not
change the edition or the value. Its untouched stretch extends by this one step. If the
entry is stale, only its earlier passing CHECK is required, and that history remains.
    At a clean start there are no entries to forge. The argument preserves that promise
after the first instruction, after the next, and after each further instruction in any
finite trace.
288   15 The earned-chain counter example


              15.8 The window can’t see the record
              Section 8 was about windows: a view of a state that shows some of it, and the
              theorem that a window which shows the same before-and-after pair for a raise and
              a non-raise cannot price both exactly (Observation 8.2). The two runs below are the
              smallest pair I could build where the window is Minsky’s view of the machine (line
              number and the two counters) and the record is everything else.
                  Run two traces from start(0, 0). The earned run is CHECK is zero A; COMMIT
              is zero A; CERTIFY. The idle run is DEC A 0, three times. In the idle run, A is 0
              every time, so each DEC just goes to the next line and writes nothing. Both runs
              end on line 4, with A = 0 and B = 0, both versions 0. Through the window they’re
              identical. One of them has paid 3, holds a fact, could commit again, and has its flag
              up. The other has paid nothing, holds nothing, can’t commit, and its flag is down.
              They’re like two photographs that show the same picture and are of different people.


              Theorem 15.15 (Same window, different record). The earned run and the idle run
              from start(0, 0) end at cores with the same window and the same versions of A and
              B, and with different ledgers, different flags, different tables, and different answers
              to “would COMMIT is zero A pass.”

              Proof. In the earned run, CHECK adds (Zero, A, 0), COMMIT puts that fact in the
              channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. The ledger is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. No counter
              is written. In the idle run each DEC sees zero, so it advances the line without
              writing a counter or raising a version. Its three costs are zero and it adds no fact or
              commitment. So both final windows are (4, 0, 0) with versions (0, 0). The earned
              table contains the current zero claim and the idle table is empty, giving the stated
              difference in whether another COMMIT would pass, as well as in the ledger and
              flag.



              Theorem 15.16 (No window oracle). There is no function g from windows to whole
              numbers with g(window) = µ at the end of every trace from start(0, 0). Likewise
              there is no function from windows to yes or no that gives the flag at the end of every
              such trace, and none that gives whether COMMIT is zero A would pass.

              Proof. Such a g would have to give both 3 and 0 on the one window the two runs
              of Theorem 15.15 share. The same for the flag and the commit right.
                The record lives off the window, and that’s Section 8’s shape, made of pebbles.
              Anybody who only watches the counters and the line number, which is everything
                                                               15.8 The window can’t see the record   289


Minsky’s machine is, can’t tell you what was paid, what was committed, or whether
the flag is up, and the reason isn’t that they looked carelessly; it’s that none of it is
there to see.
   Two things the same in everything you look at and still two things: philosophy
has an old fight about exactly that, and it’s worth a detour, because it tells you which
side of the fight these theorems stand on. Leibniz said that for real things it can’t
happen. There are no two individuals indiscernible from each other, he wrote in
1716 to Samuel Clarke, the English philosopher and theologian who was taking
Newton’s side against him in an exchange of letters, and he told a story to go with it.
A clever gentleman of his acquaintance, talking with him in front of the Electress
Sophia of Hanover, Leibniz’s friend and patron, in the garden at Herrenhausen she
had helped lay out, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. She dared him
to. He “ran all over the Garden a long time” looking, and it was “to no purpose.”
You can run his search tonight with a handful of anything, leaves or coins or grains
of rice: look hard enough and every pair differs somewhere. Then in 1952 Max
Black, a Russian-born philosopher teaching at Cornell, pushed back with a universe
you can’t build at the table. Nothing in it but two iron spheres, the same size, the
same colour, the same everything, some distance apart. Name a difference between
them. There isn’t one, and there are still two of them. People have argued about
Black’s spheres ever since, and I’m not going to settle it.
   I don’t have to, because Leibniz’s claim is about every property a thing has. The
theorems above are about three: the line and the two counters. The two runs aren’t
indiscernible in his sense at all: one has a fact in its table and its flag up, and the
other doesn’t. They’re indiscernible to a window, which is a much cheaper thing,
and it’s the thing that matters for a machine, because an observer of a machine only
ever gets a window. Leibniz’s gentleman would always find his difference if he could
look at everything. It doesn’t help him if all he’s allowed to look at is three things
about each leaf.
   There’s a horse in this, too, if you squint. In Germany in the early 1900s a
mathematics teacher named Wilhelm von Osten showed off a horse called Clever
Hans, who answered arithmetic questions by tapping a hoof, and got them right, in
front of crowds. Hans gave the same answers out as a horse that could count, and
that’s the idle run’s matching window. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst stopped
looking at the answers and started changing the conditions, and published what he
found in 1907. Put blinders on Hans, or have him asked by someone who didn’t
know the answer, and the arithmetic fell apart. Hans was reading the questioner:
tiny, unintended movements of the head and body as the hoof reached the right
number. That’s the probe. Pfungst didn’t argue with the answers. He asked a
question the answers couldn’t fake, one that needed the real thing to be there, the
way a COMMIT needs a checked fact to be in the table: run COMMIT is zero A after
290   15 The earned-chain counter example


              each of the two runs, and one passes and the other traps (Theorem 15.15). And
              the part of the story I like best: nobody was lying. Von Osten was never persuaded
              by Pfungst and kept showing his horse. A matching window doesn’t need a cheat
              behind it, which is why you want a probe. An accusation is the wrong tool for it.

              The rebar example, on the actual counters
              Put a one in counter A, leave B at zero, and give the machine these four instructions:

                         CHECK ( A ≥ 1);     COMMIT ( A ≥ 1);       CERTIFY;     DEC A 5.
              The check passes. The claim gets committed and certified. Then DEC takes the one
              away. Look at the counters now: zero and zero. The value that passed the check has
              gone.
                 Start again with both counters zero and give the same instructions. This time
              the first check fails and the machine traps. The zero stays where it was. Look at the
              counters at the end: zero and zero again. One run has its certificate up; the other
              has it down.


              Theorem 15.17 (Same final counters and bill, different certification). For those
              two clean starts and that word, both final counter pairs are (0, 0) and both ledgers
              are 3. The first certificate is true and the second false. No function of just the final
              counter pair can recover which of those starts passed the check.

              Proof. For the start A = 1, B = 0, CHECK sees 1 ≥ 1, writes the edition-zero fact,
              advances the line from 1 to 2 and makes the ledger 1. COMMIT finds that live fact,
              puts it in the channel, advances to line 3 and makes the ledger 2. CERTIFY sees the
              occupied channel, raises the flag, advances to line 4 and makes the ledger 3. DEC
              sees a positive A, changes it to zero, advances to line 5 and raises A’s version from
              0 to 1. Its price is zero. The final counters are (0, 0) and the flag is up.
                  For the start A = 0, B = 0, the first CHECK fails. It sets the trap, leaves the
              line at 1, leaves the table empty and charges one. The external word still supplies
              COMMIT and CERTIFY: on a trapped state they change no core field and cannot
              raise the flag, but each adds its unit to the ledger. DEC then changes nothing and
              charges zero. The final counters are again (0, 0), both versions stay zero and the
              flag is down. Both ledgers are 3. A function of the common counter pair would have
              to return both flag values, which is impossible.
                 The counters show the same surface. The record keeps the difference. Open the
              rest of the box and the trap, version and line number tell different parts of the story
              too: one run reached DEC, while the other stopped at the check.
                                                               15.8 The window can’t see the record   291


   Ask the successful run to CHECK A ≥ 1 once more. It fails; A is zero now. The
old certificate stays up because the earlier certification still happened. That receipt
keeps its past even while the workspace goes on to something else.

One clipboard, 65,535 different publication histories
Open the whole native box this time. Read the counters, versions, table, channel,
line number, trap, ledger and lamp. I can make all of them agree while the files of
published claims differ in 65,535 ways.
    Start clean at A = 16, B = 0. CHECK the sixteen claims A ≥ 0, . . . , A ≥ 15.
Those counter values are initial data, before any instruction: versions zero, line 1,
ledger 0, empty table and channel, and trap and flag down. Every one passes on
edition zero. The clipboard now has sixteen entries. The line number is 17, the bill
is 16, and the certificate is still down. I can choose which of those checked claims to
publish.
    Visit the claims in order. At each one, choose between these blocks:
              publish it:           COMMIT claim; CERTIFY,
              leave it unpublished: COMMIT claim; COMMIT claim.
Count the steps in either block: two. Count the charge: two. Look at the channel
when it finishes: the same claim. The counters and table stayed put. Once one
publication has raised the lamp, that lamp stays up whichever later blocks you
choose. CERTIFY reads the channel without consuming it; this is why the two blocks
leave the same channel as well as the same line and bill. The predicates overlap
logically; it is the choice to publish each checked claim that is independent.


Theorem 15.18 (The exact native publication-history fibre). In the extension re-
taining the set of published claim/edition facts, exactly 65,535 different nonempty
sets can lie above one reachable native endpoint. This is the maximum over clean
native runs with cert true. Sixteen additional fixed binary bits suffice to encode the
set relative to the native table, and fifteen do not suffice in the worst case.

Proof. First prepare the table. After the first j checks, for 0 ≤ j ≤ 16, its entries are
exactly A ≥ j − 1, . . . , A ≥ 0, newest first and all on edition zero (the table is empty
at j = 0). The line is 1 + j, the ledger is j, the counters and versions are unchanged,
the trap is down and the flag is down. This holds at j = 0. If j < 16, there is still
room and 16 ≥ j, so the next CHECK prepends precisely the next fact, advances one
line and charges one. That proves the preparation claim through j = 16.
    Now process the sixteen facts in order. Each COMMIT finds its fact in the
unchanged table at the current edition. Either block ends with that fact in the
292   15 The earned-chain counter example


              channel, advances two lines and charges two. The publishing block additionally
              raises the flag and inserts that fact into the archive; the other block changes neither.
              Inducting on the number j of blocks gives line 17 + 2j, ledger 16 + 2j, and exactly
              the chosen subset of the first j facts in the archive. The flag is up if and only if at least
              one publishing block has occurred. None of the blocks changes counters, versions,
              table order or trap. At j = 16 every nonempty choice therefore has the same native
              endpoint: A = 16, B = 0, versions zero, line 49, ledger 48, trap down, flag up, and
              channel ( A ≥ 15, A, 0). Its archive is precisely its chosen subset. There are two
              independent choices at each of sixteen positions, hence 216 subsets; excluding the
              empty one leaves 65,535 different archives above that endpoint.
                  For the upper bound, keep two invariants together: every published fact is in the
              table, and every occupied channel names a fact in the table. Both hold at a clean
              start. CHECK only prepends to the table. A successful COMMIT selects an entry
              already there. CERTIFY publishes only its occupied channel. Counter writes can
              make a fact stale; they preserve the channel and never remove table entries. Failed
              and trapped instructions do not introduce a new channel fact or publication. Thus
              both invariants survive every instruction, including later writes. Every final archive
              is a subset of the final table.
                  If that table has d distinct entries, it has at most 2d − 1 nonempty subsets. The
              table has at most sixteen entries, so d ≤ 16 and 2d − 1 ≤ 65,535. An explicit code
              puts beside each table entry one bit saying whether it belongs to the archive, and
              pads with zeros to sixteen positions. Duplicate entries receive matching bits. Read
              back the entries with bit one and you recover the set. Equal codes therefore give
              equal archives, and an archive above a flag-up state uses a nonzero code. Finally,
              fifteen fixed bits have only 215 = 32,768 values, fewer than the exhibited 65,535
              archives; sixteen bits have 65,536 values and the code just given suffices.
                 Put sixteen checkboxes beside the clipboard’s sixteen lines. A tick says that line’s
              claim was published at least once. The table already names the claims and editions;
              the extra marks say which ones made it into the publication file. The lamp gives
              the same yes for every nonempty selection. Open the checkboxes and all 65,535
              selections come apart. Each tick answers whether that claim was published at least
              once. Order and repeated publications leave these answers unchanged.
                 In Chapter 14 the camera showed the working value. Here I let it see the entire
              native machine and still found histories it could not recover. The map here forgets
              the added publication file; its fibre contains those different files above one native
              endpoint.
                 The sixteen-line clipboard eventually fills. Even sixteen repeated checks of one
              fact fill it, and the next CHECK traps. The unlimited-edition machine has a larger
              obligation: keep accepting independent publication choices across every finite
                                                                      15.9 The exact price is three   293


number of editions and keep them recoverable at the same working picture. Its fibre
has to keep growing. That is the count from Chapter 14, with its own camera and
its own task.


15.9 The exact price is three
Section 2 said a raised flag costs at least one. On this machine that’s true and too
modest. A raised flag needs a CERTIFY, a CERTIFY needs a COMMIT, a COMMIT
needs a CHECK, and each of those is its own instruction costing one. So a raised
flag costs at least three. One of what: three units of µ, one per paid act, each one
the least price a record-layer merge allows. And three is the number of links in the
chain, not a guess that happens to hold.
Observation 15.19 (The minimum price of a certificate). If s0 is clean and
cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 3 and µ(run(t, s0 )) ≥ µ(s0 ) + 3. For programs:
if the flag is up after n program steps from start( a, b), then µ ≥ 3 there.
Proof. Theorem 15.11 finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different
places in t, each costing 1, and every other instruction costs at least 0. The ledger
statement is Theorem 15.6. A program run is the run of the instructions it actually
executes, so the program form follows.
    The three is three independent units, one for each part of a clean start. A flag
that is down buys the first: a run that raises it costs at least one. An empty channel
buys the second: with the flag down and the channel empty, a run that raises the
flag costs at least two. An empty table buys the third, and that is the theorem above.
Leave out any one part and its floor fails, and a cheaper certificate is there: with the
flag already up it costs 0, with a commitment already in the channel 1, and with
a live fact already in the table 2. Every run from a state that ends with the flag
up costs at least three exactly when the flag is down and one of two things holds:
the trap is up, or the channel is empty and every fact in the table is about an older
version of its counter. And three is paid exactly from every clean start whose trap is
down.


Theorem 15.20 (Three is tight). For all whole numbers a and b, run the program
CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero A; CERTIFY for 4 program steps from start( a, b).
If a = 0, it ends with the flag up and µ = 3 exactly. If a ̸= 0, it ends with the flag
down and the trap up, and for every n, n program steps from start( a, b) leave the
flag down.
294   15 The earned-chain counter example


              Proof. If a = 0, the checker for Zero says yes at 0, so the first instruction adds
              (Zero, A, 0) to the empty table and charges 1. No counter changes, so the second
              instruction finds that same fact, puts it in the channel and charges 1. The third finds
              the channel occupied, raises the flag and charges 1. The line is now 4, beyond the
              three-instruction program, and the fourth program step adds no charge. The final
              ledger is exactly 3. If a ̸= 0, the checker says no, so the first instruction sets the trap
              and leaves the flag down. A program run takes no step once the trap is up, so every
              later program step leaves the state, flag included, exactly where it is.
                 Theorem 15.20 is the worked run from early in this chapter, now holding from
              every start.
                 The version whose check can’t fail, CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A;
              CERTIFY, certifies from every start for exactly 3. So the floor of three is reachable
              from every loaded start, and that’s the machine declining to police trivial checks.
              On that program the check distinguishes no inputs.
                 The floor is 3, and a run whose check could have failed pays exactly 3, so 3 is the
              price. The bound has no slack in it.
                 Don’t mistake that 3 for a measure of how hard a claim is to certify. It’s the
              same 3 for every claim, easy or hard, because only the three acts that make a
              claim are priced and the counters work out whatever the check needs at no charge
              on the ledger. A cost of certifying that grows with the claim would have to price
              the checking itself, and that’s a different question with its own literature. Four
              theoretical computer scientists, Guy Blanc, Caleb Koch, Jane Lange and Li-Yang
              Tan (2022), studied one version of it under the name the query complexity of
              certification: how many questions an algorithm has to ask a black-box function to
              hand back a small certificate for its answer. Their count moves with the function.
              Mine doesn’t move at all.
                 And that’s every piece of the machine, standing on six instruction kinds: a base
              that computes everything two counters can, a ledger that’s exact, a toll the universal
              floor applies to, a flag that’s a latch of the base, a window that can’t see the record,
              and, from a clean start, a commitment that can’t happen unless a check of the same
              claim, on the same edition, came first and was right.


              15.10 The machine versus the program it runs
              The three hosts of Appendix C (the simpler host, U and UP ) all come down to one
              distinction, and it’s worth saying on its own, because the two halves are easy to run
              together: the machine doing the stepping (what the machine is) and the program it
              runs (what runs on it). The toll of Section 2 is a property of the machine doing the
              stepping. A rule a program keeps holds as long as the program keeps it.
                                                      15.10 The machine versus the program it runs   295


    I keep a picture for it: play Monopoly on the counter of a real bank. The game
has a bank of its own, with its own rules, and one of them is printed in the rules
sheet: the Bank never goes broke, and if it runs out of money the Banker may issue
more by writing on any ordinary paper. Inside the game that’s fine; the players
agreed to it. The real bank’s teller, standing right there, has no opinion about any of
it. Push a thousand in Monopoly money across her counter and her ledger doesn’t
move, because her rules are about her own money. The game’s money is nothing
to them. The real bank is the machine doing the stepping. The game is a program
it happens to be hosting. A rule that lives in the game holds as long as the players
keep to it. A rule that lives in the bank holds whatever the players do.
    (And since the game is on the table: its box told an origin story for decades, that
an out-of-work salesman named Charles Darrow invented it during the Depression.
The board is older. Elizabeth Magie, an American writer and game designer with an
economic argument about land to make, patented The Landlord’s Game in 1904,
with a square track, railroads and a square that sends you to jail, and in 1902, in The
Single Tax Review, described it as “a practical demonstration of the present system
of land-grabbing with all its usual outcomes and consequences.” Darrow sold his
version to Parker Brothers in 1935, and the company bought Magie’s patent for
a few hundred dollars, five hundred by the accounts I found. A story told by the
company selling the product is a lead to check, every time. It changes nothing about
banks. It’s a good reminder of who writes the story on the box.)
    A fixed machine can enforce an invariant in its own transition table, and that
includes a Turing machine. Give its tape a ledger track and a certification cell, and
write a table that never sets the cell without bumping the ledger: that machine
keeps the invariant in its step relation. The ledger track is part of its state, though,
and a ledger kept in the state isn’t a price on the move. The toll of Definition 2.2
puts the price on the move, the same from every state, so what it charges depends
on what the machine’s moves are. Give it one move, the next step its table picks: if
the table sets the cell from any configuration at all, that move costs at least one, so
every step does, whatever the track says, and the machine is a clock. Give it a move
for each row of its table: every row that can set the cell costs at least one wherever
it’s taken, and a row that never sets it can cost nothing. Either way it’s the price on
its moves that meets the toll, and the track only simulates it. Priced that way, it’s a
Thiele machine itself, so it can’t be a counterexample to the model. What it doesn’t
do, built the ordinary way, is enforce the toll on the programs it runs. A universal
machine whose table was written only to interpret carries the simulated certification
bit as plain data on its tape. If the host is programmable, so that other code shares
that tape with the guest, any of that code can flip the bit without paying, because
the host’s step has no opinion about it. So an ordinary programmable computer, as
built, doesn’t enforce the toll for its programs; that comes from how it’s built, and
296   15 The earned-chain counter example


              it could be built to enforce it. A host whose own step mirrors the guest’s bit and
              charges for its crossing enforces it, and the universal programs U and UP are fixed
              tables that go one better: they earn their own flag, by their own check, commit and
              certificate, exactly when the guest’s would rise, and pay on their own ledger what
              the guest pays, U exactly and UP to within a surcharge of at most two when the
              guest’s reading starts at no (Theorems C.5, C.4, C.7 and C.8). That’s a statement
              about which reading a step rule prices, not a claim that Turing machines can’t price
              one.
                  Computing ran into this exact gap in hardware, and how it got out is worth the
              detour. In 1974 two computer scientists, Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, asked
              when a machine can run guests, a whole operating system inside another, efficiently
              and safely. Their answer is one sentence you could check against any instruction
              set. Call an instruction sensitive if it reads or changes the machine’s own settings,
              the things the host has to keep for itself, and privileged if running it outside the
              host’s own mode makes the machine stop and hand control to the host, which is
              called a trap. For the kind of machine they modelled: if every sensitive instruction is
              privileged, a host can be built. The guest runs at full speed, and whenever it touches
              something that matters, the machine itself stops it and lets the host decide, and a
              host like that is one whose step has an opinion.
                  Then the obvious next question: did the machines people actually bought pass
              the test? The most common one didn’t. In 2000 John Scott Robin, an Air Force
              officer, and Cynthia Irvine, a computer-security researcher at the Naval Postgraduate
              School, went through every instruction of Intel’s Pentium and found seventeen that
              are sensitive and not privileged; POPF, which loads the processor’s flags, is the one
              usually pointed at. A guest could run them and the host would never hear about
              it. The fixes came two ways: VMware rewrote the guest’s code on the fly so the
              troublesome instructions never ran as written, and in the middle of the 2000s Intel
              and AMD added hardware support so they’d trap. Does that change anything here?
              It doesn’t change the theorems. Popek and Goldberg were after speed and isolation.
              A record and a price weren’t their question, so their result isn’t mine and mine isn’t
              theirs. It changes the picture, though. The universal programs sit where they’d want
              a host to sit: the host’s own steps collect each guest’s toll and earn each guest’s
              record again. And an industry learned the same lesson the expensive way: a rule
              binds the guest only if it lives in the step underneath.
                  The smallest version of “a ledger beside an ordinary machine” is a Turing machine
              configuration with a counter next to it, where each step adds one, plus one more if
              it writes a nonblank symbol. The counter doesn’t disturb the machine.
                                                                15.11 The small machine’s merges   297




Theorem 15.21 (A counter beside a Turing machine changes nothing). Let a Turing
machine with transition table δ step a configuration c to tmn (δ, c) after at most n
steps (stopping when δ has no entry). Pair each configuration with a counter, and
step the pair by stepping the configuration and adding the step’s charge. Then for
every n, δ and pair (c, m), the configuration part after at most n steps of the pair is
tmn (δ, c). In particular this holds from (c, 0).

Proof. Put the ordinary run and the run with the counter side by side. Both start
with configuration c. Whenever their configurations agree, they look up the same
entry in the same transition table. If the entry is absent, both stop. If it is present,
both take the same next configuration; only the paired run also changes its counter.
Their configurations therefore agree again, ready for the next comparison. This
covers every step up to the chosen limit n, as well as a stop before that limit. The
counter’s value never enters a lookup.
   The pair is a Turing configuration with a number riding beside it, and nothing
more. Its counter is kept in the state, and a ledger kept in the state isn’t a price on
the move: Definition 2.2 puts the cost on the move’s name, and this counter’s charge
depends on what the step writes. This theorem therefore does not supply exact
accounting for the basic instruction-price signature, or a reading with an earned-
history meaning. It does not rule out equipping the same state space with other
instruction prices and a Boolean reading satisfying the basic toll. The projection
claim is simply that this additional count leaves the tape computation alone.
   One limit on all of this needs saying, so it isn’t read as more. Certification is one
event. If you wanted a machine to carry some other kind of reading, you’d need an
event for it, evidence for it and a price law for it, and nothing here supplies any of
those.


15.11 The small machine’s merges

And the whole small machine isn’t the eight-state piece it runs. It merges some
states without adding anything to the ledger.


Theorem 15.22 (The small machine’s merges). (1) A move of the small machine
that takes the flag from down to up is CERTIFY; CERTIFY merges two different full
states into one (a state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up land
on the same state), and it costs at least one. (2) DEC A 2 also merges two different
298   15 The earned-chain counter example


              full states, and it costs nothing. So it is false of the small machine that every move
              that merges is priced.

              Proof. (1) Only CERTIFY changes the flag, and it costs one. The two states with
              the flag down and up, and a committed claim, are the same state after CERTIFY.
              (2) Take a core at line 1 with A at 1 at version 0, and the same core with A at 0 at
              version 1. DEC A 2 takes the first to A = 0 at version 1, line 2, a write; it takes the
              second to line 2 with A still 0 at version 1, because DEC on zero is no write. Same
              state, zero cost.
                 The theorem puts names to the last item on the list of what this machine doesn’t
              do, near the end of this chapter. Part I’s counting of states wants a finite machine that
              puts a price on every merge. This machine has counters with no top, and it prices
              the three record acts and leaves its counting merges at a price of zero, so Part I’s
              counting of states doesn’t reach it whole, and that’s why the eight-state piece is a
              piece. The record’s part of the state closes the rest: asked only of merges between
              states with the same line and counters, the merge premise holds for this machine’s
              own prices and forces the toll on it with no finiteness premise (Theorem 3.19).


              15.12 Reading the instruction rules
              The instruction rules settle some concrete questions about running this machine.
              Follow them through a check, a zero decrement and a trapped trace.
               • The check price is flat. CHECK costs 1 whether it’s asking “is this 0” or “is
                 this at least a billion.” The property language is fixed and each property is one
                 evaluation, so “pays for its work” here means that flat price, the same however
                 hard the question was. A machine that charged by the difficulty of the check
                 would be a different machine, and I haven’t built it.
               • DEC on zero isn’t a write. It doesn’t change the counter, so it doesn’t change
                 the version. That’s the right call for versions (nothing changed), but it means
                 DEC on zero is a way to move the line number that adds nothing to the ledger
                 and leaves no trace in the record. The idle run in the subsection on the window,
                 earlier in this chapter, uses exactly that.
               • After a trap, a trace still pays. On programs, a trap stops the run. On arbitrary
                 traces, instructions after a trap are each charged their cost and none of them
                 changes the core. That isn’t a separate choice. A price belongs to the instruction,
                 the same from every state (Definition 2.2), so a CERTIFY on a trapped machine
                 costs what every CERTIFY costs, and the ledger adds it; Theorem 15.6 has no
                 exceptions for that reason. The choice is one level up, in putting the price on the
                                                               15.12 Reading the instruction rules   299


  instruction and not on the instruction at a state, and what it brings with it is that
  a trapped machine is still charged for instructions that change nothing.
• “Checked” means what the property language can say. On this machine that’s
  is zero, is even and is at least n, and a live fact means one of those holds of one
  counter’s current value. It doesn’t mean the program is correct, or that anything
  follows from the property, or that the property was worth checking. So can a
  proved machine of this kind check “sorted,” the claim the sorter-and-copier table
  of Section 14 runs on? It can, through an encoding. A copy of this machine,
  instruction for instruction, with its property language left open, has provenance,
  checker soundness, no forging and the floor of three proved once for every
  property language that comes with an exact equality test and a checker proved
  equal to its meaning. Give it “the list this counter encodes is sorted” as a property
  and it certifies a sorted list for three and refuses an unsorted one forever. The
  instruction rules are those already given, with the chosen property language in
  place of the three original properties. For sorted lists, decode 0 as the empty list
  and 2h (2t + 1) as the list with head h and tail decoded from t. Every positive
  code has t smaller than itself, so decoding terminates. The checker returns yes on
  an empty list or singleton, and on a, b, . . . exactly when a ≤ b and it returns yes
  on b, . . .. Induction on the list proves that this is exactly adjacent nondecreasing
  order. The provenance proof uses only equality of properties, and soundness
  only that the checker’s yes means the property holds, so the same instruction-by-
  instruction argument applies. What makes that a check of the list is the proof that
  the checker means sortedness. Without that proof, “sorted” would be a number
  some unconstrained code wrote into a counter, and the record would be honest
  about the counter and silent about the list.
• The certificate is historical. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, the counter
  can change, and the flag still goes up. The flag says a claim was checked and
  committed about an edition. It says nothing about whether the claim is still true.
• One latch, and a channel that moves on. The flag records that an earned chain
  happened, once. After that it stays up, and later CERTIFYs change nothing. The
  channel is the part that names a fact: with the flag up from a clean start, it names
  a fact that some earlier passing COMMIT committed. But a later commitment
  replaces it, so at the end it names the last earned commitment, which needn’t
  be the one the flag rose on. Two runs from start(0, 0) show it, worked from
  the instruction table. First run: CHECK is zero A; CHECK is zero B; COMMIT
  is zero A; CERTIFY; COMMIT is zero B. Second run: the same five instructions
  with the last two swapped, so COMMIT is zero B comes before CERTIFY. Both
  end in the same state: both counters 0 at version 0, both facts in the table, the
  channel holding (zero, B, 0), the trap down, a ledger of five and the flag up. In
300   15 The earned-chain counter example


                  the first run the flag rose at step four, on the commitment about A. In the second
                  it rose at step five, on the commitment about B. So the flag is an ever-certified
                  latch: it says an earned chain happened at some step, and the end state doesn’t
                  say which claim or which step. A receipt naming the claim the flag first rose
                  on would need that claim kept where nothing can overwrite it; a receipt with
                  a time on it would also need the step number kept; and several certifications
                  that each last would need a record richer than one flag. The publication file
                  constructed earlier in this chapter keeps the set of claims certified at least once.
                  That extension shows exactly what the native state left out. It still does not record
                  which certification came first or at what step; those questions would need their
                  own retained answers.
               • Sixteen checks per run, ever. Facts never leave and the table holds sixteen, so a
                 run gets at most sixteen passing CHECKs in its whole life, and the seventeenth
                 traps. A certificate needs only one, so this costs nothing for the theorems, but
                 it’s a hard wall for any program that wants to keep checking forever, and it’s this
                 machine’s small version of “you can’t keep all of it” from Section 14. A CHECK
                 that repeats a claim already in the table, same property, same counter, same
                 edition, passes again and takes another entry. So the wall is sixteen passing
                 CHECKs, and sixteen different claims is a different count. Removing duplicates,
                 evicting old facts or collecting dead ones would each be a different design, and
                 each would need its own invariants proved.
               • The clean start matters. Provenance, soundness, no forging and the price of
                 three are all stated from a clean start. Hand the machine a table pre-loaded with
                 facts nobody checked, and of course none of that follows. The theorems are about
                 what the machine produces. What you smuggle in at the door is outside them.
                 The door is narrower than clean for some of them: a commitment’s provenance
                 and checker soundness use only the table, and hold from any start whose table
                 holds nothing but facts about older editions; the empty channel and the lowered
                 flag come in for the flag’s provenance and the price of three. Spell the door out
                 once: the theorems cover any list of instructions anybody can issue, from a clean
                 start, on a step that runs as written, with nothing else writing to the machine.
                 They say nothing about whoever sets or restores the start, about a reset, about a
                 device that misbehaves, or about whoever carries the flag’s value to you.
               • The universal programs have stated guests. U (Appendix C.1) runs every
                 one of this machine’s programs from every clean start start( x, y), with halting,
                 answers, flag and ledger matched (the flag over the whole run, the ledger at
                 matching points). UP (Appendix C.2) runs every computably presented Thiele
                 machine, with its reading decided by a program, its record carried as a latch, and
                 its ledger matched to within a surcharge of at most two when its reading starts
                                                               15.12 Reading the instruction rules   301


  at no, and of three when it starts at yes. When the guest certifies with a ledger
  below three, no program on that host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger
  exactly. A machine outside that class, with a reading no program decides, isn’t
  covered by either. The host with a guest step built in, charging one per guest step
  whatever the step was, would have a ledger at least the guest’s and usually more;
  U’s is exact, and UP ’s is exact up to the surcharge.
• Encoding and running time. The universality result takes its inputs already
  packed into the counters. Getting there from an arbitrary Turing machine goes
  through Minsky’s exponential packing, and that packing is what it takes to reach
  two counters this way. Anyone who wanted this to run fast would have to start
  the analysis over.
• The step charges for the act, not for what the claim is worth. CHECK at least
  0 passes on every value, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for
  three from any fresh loaded start (the note after Theorem 15.20), and that’s by
  design. The step checks order, aboutness and an honest checker. What a claim is
  worth is the entitlement count of Section 9, a number computed over the rivals a
  run narrows. A step sees one state, so it cannot compute that count. A check that
  cannot fail narrows nothing and costs three, and the book keeps both numbers,
  apart.
• The toll on this machine comes from the record’s part of the state, with no
  finiteness premise on the whole machine. Section 3’s counting of states forces
  a toll on a finite machine that prices every merge. This machine is neither. Its
  counters have no ceiling, as a machine that runs every program has to have, and
  its editions can’t have one either (the version rule says why), so it’s infinite. And,
  by design, its unpriced instructions merge states: take a core at line ℓ with c at 1
  and version w, and a core at line j − 1 with c at 0 and version w + 1, everything
  else alike, and DEC c j sends both to line j with c at 0 and version w + 1, at
  a price of zero. A price of zero doesn’t mean the hardware pays nothing. Any
  physical heat belongs to the implementation’s account. A positive floor requires
  the thermal premises and an input distribution with entropy loss; merely taking
  a step establishes neither. This ledger does not measure that heat. The ledger
  leaves those merges out on purpose. It counts the keeping in the record, not what
  computing spends. Computing doesn’t have to merge; a reversible base computes
  by paying in fresh states. On this machine full merge pricing would charge DEC,
  an ordinary step, and clause (c) asks for computing to cost nothing. Charging
  every move would instead give a clock’s schedule. Its total counts moves, rather
  than isolating record acts. The machine can still retain a record; this total alone
  does not say which acts established it. So merge pricing on this machine applies
  to the record’s part of the state only: a move that sends two different states with
302   15 The earned-chain counter example


                  the same line and counters to one state costs at least one. This machine’s own
                  prices meet it. The endless counters would allow a raise that merges nothing,
                  and the flag doesn’t take it: CERTIFY lands a state with the flag down and the
                  same state with the flag up on one state, a merge of exactly that kind, in plain
                  view. So every price list that meets the premise charges the flag-raising step
                  at least one, with no finiteness premise, and through the trap it charges every
                  CHECK and COMMIT at least one too, so a certificate from a clean start costs at
                  least three on every such list (Theorem 3.19). That’s a price I assume for losing
                  distinctions in the record, and assuming it is all it is. Turning it into heat takes
                  the physical conditions of Section 3; a unit on a ledger isn’t heat on its own. The
                  exact price of one, the least the premise allows on each of the three acts, is still a
                  design choice.


              15.13 What this chapter adds up to
              So this chapter has one machine, and it isn’t the model. It’s a Thiele machine in
              the opening’s sense, a Thiele machine with the toll proved (Theorem 15.7), and its
              toll charges the blank cell’s 0: raising its flag is a merge in the record’s part of its
              state (Theorem 3.19). Its flat part computes whatever a Turing machine can, under
              Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine, its computing adds nothing to the
              ledger and can’t touch the record, and, from a clean start, its record is earned.
                  If you ever find yourself wondering whether a property of this machine is the
              model’s or just the machine’s, hold it up against Section 2’s definition of a Thiele ma-
              chine, the latch of Section 11, and the four things certified asks for (Section 14.15).
              What follows from those holds of every machine that meets them; the rest (a table
              of sixteen facts, three properties) is this machine’s choice. The flat price of one is
              the third of the four, and at least one of it is what the record’s merge premise asks of
              each act on this machine. There are six instruction kinds, and a seventh, PAY, for a
              host that has to charge somebody else’s prices (Appendix C.2). If the model needs
              more than the five parts and the toll, this is where it will show.
CHAPTER 16




How far it reaches

The small machine earns its flag, and pays for it, on its own programs. Everything
in this chapter asks how far that carries. Every statement in it is proved, and the
runs are reported as runs. I give each statement here and leave the constructions to
the appendices, because they’re about the reach of the case, not the case.
    Other machines as guests. One fixed program, U, written in the small machine’s
own six kinds of instruction on a host with more counters, runs every program of
the small machine as a guest, from every clean start. It fetches, decodes and carries
out each guest instruction itself, the way Turing’s universal machine does; nothing
in the host means “run one guest step.” It halts exactly when its guest halts, with
the guest’s answer in its counters; its flag goes up during its run exactly when the
guest’s goes up during the guest’s, by its own check, its own commitment and its
own certificate; and its ledger equals the guest’s at every point where the two runs
match. The host is a certified Thiele machine, and whether U halts is undecidable.
Add one move, PAY, that costs one and does nothing else, and the same kind of
program, UP , runs every Thiele machine whose next move, step, prices and reading
are computed by programs that always answer: it halts when the guest’s run stops,
its flag goes up exactly when the guest’s reading is yes at some state of its run, on
a chain whose check is the guest’s own reading, and its ledger is the guest’s prices
plus a surcharge of at most two at the raise when the guest’s reading starts at no,
and exactly three when it starts at yes, a surcharge that no program on that host,
run from a clean start, can always avoid. Appendix C has both.
    Other flat cases. Lay the toll over a register machine, a Turing machine or the
lambda calculus and none of them computes one function more; what each gains is
a record and a cost. Each is the flat case with its price column put back (Section 11).
    Machines from parts. Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a
Thiele machine stays a Thiele machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What
breaks, breaks for reasons you could name in advance: a single flag for two claims
costs two claims’ worth, a clock is still a clock, a shared value without a version can’t
be trusted, and a hand-off that costs nothing can’t be allowed to carry a certificate
(Appendix D).


                                                  303
CHAPTER 17




Five small models

So far there’s been a toll, a counter, two kinds of wall and a latch, every one of them
shown on paper, on cups and cards and dice I made up, and then a small machine to
run them on. That is the model on paper and on one small example. It’s time to go
and look at what people actually do. I picked five systems that keep records other
people rely on, with real money or real security behind them, and asked each the
pricing question from the paper models: is there a price on the moment the record is
written? The question isn’t about the work around the write; it’s about the write,
the moment the 0 goes on the page and stays. I’ll tell you the answer first, because
it’s a single sentence and it surprised me: of the five specifications, read through the
transcriptions I made of them, only one takes a fee at the moment of the write, and
that one has a leak at exactly the place Section 7 said a counter leaks, where it goes
down.
     “Price” needs one meaning for all five, or the answer is whatever I want it to be,
so I’ll fix it here, and every system below gets classified by it. A specification prices
an event when it attaches one of three costs to it. A fee: something taken at the
event itself, whatever happens afterward. A bond: value put at risk by the event
and lost only if some later event happens, a contradiction, say. A budget: a finite
allowance the event draws down, so that only so many such events can ever happen.
A wall isn’t a price under this definition. Nobody pays a hash; reversing one is just
infeasible. Neither is work a protocol needs and never charges for. The table at the
end of the section has a column for each of the three kinds, and what it shows is a
finding about the five, because the definition came first.
     Three things are easy to blur in a section like this, so I’ll name them now and
keep them apart all the way through. There’s the real specification: the document
real money and real security run on. There’s my transcription: one mechanism
copied out of that document into a mathematical model, small enough to examine.
And for some of the five there’s a wrapper: a tiny abstract model that takes one
premise as given and says what follows from it. A claim proved at one level isn’t a
claim at the level above it. Near the end I’ll walk one system, gas, through all three,
so you can see exactly where each claim stops.


                                  304
                                                17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back   305


    For each system I isolate the mechanism the question concerns: a fragment with
its own states and operations, transcribed from the system’s specification where one
was available. I will put that mechanism on the page, state the guarantee it carries,
and show how the argument follows its rules.


17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back

Ethereum and chains like it decide which blocks are final by having validators,
people who’ve locked up money (their stake), vote on checkpoints: blocks picked out
at regular numbered rounds called epochs. A vote isn’t for one checkpoint. It’s a link
from a checkpoint the validator already trusts, the source, to a later one, the target,
and every chain starts from one first block, its genesis, which counts as trusted from
the start. In the design Vitalik Buterin and Virgil Griffith published in 2017, called
Casper, a checkpoint is justified when validators holding two thirds of the stake vote
a link to it from a justified source, and finalized when it is justified and a two-thirds
link runs from it to its direct child. The record is “this checkpoint is final.”
    Two rules carry the price: don’t vote for two different targets in the same epoch,
and don’t cast a vote whose span, source to target, surrounds the span of another of
your votes. Break either and your deposit can be destroyed, which is called slashing.
The theorem they prove, called accountable safety, says that if two conflicting
checkpoints are ever both finalized, at least a third of the stake broke a rule and
can be slashed. So the price is on reversal, on making the record contradict itself.
The write itself, finalizing, need not incur a slashing penalty. This is not a claim that
running validators has no operating costs or other protocol charges. In the terms
from the start of the section, Casper’s price is a bond. The deposit stands behind
every vote, the finalizing votes included, and it’s taken only from a validator whose
own votes contradict each other, which is what making the record contradict itself
takes from a third of the stake.
    Do it with three validators of equal stake. Draw genesis at epoch 0, two competing
children at epoch 1, and one child of each at epoch 2. Let A and B vote both links
on the left branch, from genesis to its first child and from that child to the next. Let
B and C do the same on the right. Each link has two of the three votes.
306   17 Five small models


                                                      genesis
                                                      epoch 0

                                               A, B             B, C

                                          left                     right
                                        epoch 1                   epoch 1
                                       A, B                            B, C
                                        left child               right child
                                         epoch 2                   epoch 2

              B appears on both branches at each target epoch. A and C do not. The diagram
              records votes; it has no step deducting a balance. Both epoch-1 blocks are justified
              and have the required link to their child, so both finalize. B voted for different
              targets at the same epoch, which makes B’s third of the stake slashable, while A and
              C have broken neither voting rule. The votes supply evidence for a penalty; this
              example does not execute the transaction that collects it, and Theorem 17.2 below
              has exactly this instance, so the theorem’s premise isn’t vacuous: forks of that kind
              can be built, and the theorem fires on them.
                  The fragment is a reconstruction of the published casper-proofs argument from
              Runtime Verification and the University of Texas at Austin, based on Yoichi Hirai’s
              proof, with validator sets and quorum intersection as a premise. A quorum is a set
              of validators big enough to act, here two thirds of the stake, and quorum intersection
              is the arithmetic of the three-validator example: two thirds plus two thirds is four
              thirds, so any two quorums share at least a third. The fragment takes the overlap as
              given; it doesn’t do that arithmetic. It has no deposits, no rewards, no fork choice
              (the rule for picking a branch to build on), and no connection to anything else in this
              book. A finalization fork implies that a set of validators the size of that overlap, at
              least a third of the stake, has committed a slashable offence. A one-validator chain
              finalizes without any such offence, which is the “write costs no stake” sentence,
              proved here in a degenerate setting.
                  The fragment is small enough to read in one sitting, and every name below is
              from the transcription.

              Definition 17.1 (Casper setting and votes). A setting has a type of validators, a
              type of block hashes with a parent relation and a genesis hash, and two classes of
              validator sets, the “two-thirds” sets Q1 and the “one-third” sets Q2 . It carries two
              premises: quorum intersection, for any two sets in Q1 some set in Q2 lies inside
              both; and at most one parent per hash. A state says, for each validator, target hash h,
              target epoch t and source epoch u, whether that validator voted the link (h, t, u). A
              link from p at epoch u to h at epoch t is justified by q when q ∈ Q1 , every member of
              q voted (h, t, u), h is the (t − u)-th descendant of p, and t > u. Genesis is justified
                                                 17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back   307


at epoch 0, and a block reached from a justified block by a justified link landing
at epoch t is justified at t. Block h is finalized at epoch v with child c when c is a
child of h, h is justified at v, and the link from h at v to c at v + 1 is justified. A
finalization fork is two finalized blocks h1 ̸= h2 , neither an ancestor of the other.
The transcription calls a validator slashed when it voted two different targets with
the same target epoch (a double vote), or voted links (h1 , t1 , u1 ) and (h2 , t2 , u2 )
with t1 > t2 and u2 > u1 (a surround vote). The state is quorum-slashed when some
set in Q2 consists of such validators. These names describe offending votes, not a
balance deduction: there are no account balances in this state.



Theorem 17.1 (Accountable safety). In every setting, every state with a finalization
fork is quorum-slashed.

Proof. Let the fork be h1 finalized at v1 and h2 at v2 . If v1 = v2 , the epoch is above
0, since genesis is the only block justified at 0, so the links that justified h1 and
h2 there are each voted by a set in Q1 ; quorum intersection gives a set in Q2 that
voted both, and their targets h1 and h2 differ. That set double-voted. If v1 ̸= v2 , say
v1 < v2 , walk down the chain of justified links that justifies h2 . Every block on that
chain is an ancestor of h2 , so none descends from h1 . (So v1 > 0: the only block
justified at epoch 0 is genesis, an ancestor of every justified block.) Some link in
the chain starts at or below v1 and lands above v1 . If it lands at v1 + 1, it and the
finalization link of h1 have distinct targets at that epoch, and the intersection set
double-voted. If it starts at v1 , its source is a justified block at v1 other than h1 , and
the links that justified those two blocks give a double vote the same way. Otherwise
it starts below v1 and lands above v1 + 1, so it surrounds the finalization link of h1 ,
and the intersection set made a surround vote.
   Everything the fragment promises stands on the overlap, and with the overlap
taken away it promises nothing. The one parent is in the setting because the original
proof uses it, and the proof above never does.


Theorem 17.2 (The premise can hold, and the write costs no stake). (1) In the
three-validator setting where each validator has stake 1, Q1 is the sets of stake at
least two thirds and Q2 the sets of at least one third, the state where A and B vote
one branch and B and C the other has a finalization fork; B is slashed, A and C
are not, and { B} is in Q2 . (2) In the one-validator chain setting, one vote finalizes
genesis and no validator is slashed.
308   17 Five small models


              Proof. Both are computations on fixed finite data. In (1) every link carries two of
              the three votes, so stake two thirds, so both epoch-1 blocks are justified and each has
              a justified link to its child at epoch 2: both are finalized, and as siblings neither is an
              ancestor of the other. B voted two different targets at epoch 1, which is the double
              vote; A’s and C’s votes are one link at epoch 1 from source 0 and one at epoch 2
              from source 1, which neither double-vote nor surround. In (2) the one validator’s
              vote from genesis at 0 to its child at 1 is a justified link, so genesis is finalized, and a
              single vote can neither double-vote nor surround.
                  For the record itself, one thing that means is that finality is revocable at a price,
              the price is named, and a final block can hold a false statement.
                  The obvious next question is whether the 2017 design is what Ethereum actually
              runs. The answer is partly, and the paper’s own title is the clue. It’s called Casper the
              Friendly Finality Gadget, and its first sentence says it’s a finality system that overlays
              a chain still choosing its blocks by proof of work, so it’s a gadget, bolted on top. In
              2020 a larger group, Buterin among them, wrote up Gasper, which joins Casper’s
              finality to a fork-choice rule called LMD GHOST, and on 15 September 2022, in the
              switch people called the Merge, Ethereum stopped choosing blocks by proof of work
              at all and went over to proof of stake. So the checkpoints and the two slashing rules
              above are one part of a system that holds real money today, and the transcription
              is of that part’s safety proof as the 2017 design states it. Everything between the
              two, the fork choice and the rest of the running protocol, is the gap between my
              transcription and the running system, which I walk through near the end of this
              section with a photocopied recipe and a kitchen. None of that moves the price:
              finalizing still costs an honest validator no stake, and what costs is contradicting
              yourself.


              17.2 Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write
              Every operation on Ethereum costs gas, paid in ether by whoever sent the transaction.
              The yellow paper, Ethereum’s formal specification, gives the reason in one line: every
              computation is fee-bearing so the network can’t be abused and halting questions are
              sidestepped. The record I care about is a nonzero slot in the shared storage, which
              every full node in the world (every computer keeping its own complete copy of the
              chain) has to keep until it’s cleared. Clearing a slot is allowed, and the refund rules
              below exist to reward it.
                 Writing a fresh storage slot from zero to nonzero costs twenty thousand gas, by
              the table in the paper’s appendix, plus twenty-one hundred for touching a cold slot,
              one the transaction hasn’t touched yet (after the first touch it’s warm). As I read it,
              the point is to discourage storage growth, since storage grows every node’s database.
              That charge is a fee on the write, at the moment of the write, and it’s the only fee in
                                                     17.2 Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write   309


the five. Gas has a budget too, in the sense from the start of the section: every block
has a gas limit, and the gas its transactions use can’t exceed it, so only so many
writes fit in a block.
    Where does a number like twenty-one hundred come from? Somebody picked
it, so the obvious next question is who, and why, and the answer has a date on it.
In September 2016, just as Ethereum’s developers were gathering in Shanghai for
Devcon 2, their developer conference (the third one, since they started counting
at zero), attackers started filling blocks with an operation that was cheap in gas
and expensive in fact: it sent every node off to read data from its disk, and nodes
fell behind the chain. The first repair, a fork that October called Tangerine Whistle,
raised the prices of the operations the attack had leaned on. The cold-slot charge
came later, in a proposal by Vitalik Buterin and Martin Swende called EIP-2929,
switched on in the Berlin upgrade of April 2021, and the motivation it gives is still
those 2016 attacks. So twenty-one hundred isn’t a law of nature or a measurement
of anything deep. It’s a scar: a price set after somebody found the place where the
old price was wrong. That doesn’t change the argument; the write is still priced at
the moment of the write. It does change how I read the rest of that table: some of
its numbers, at least, are somebody’s answer to “what did this cost last time,” which
is a record of a different kind.
    Now for the leak, which is Section 7’s leak. Set a slot and then clear it in the same
transaction and you get a refund. Count it through: first write twenty-two thousand
one hundred; clearing it costs a hundred and credits a refund of nineteen thousand
