nine hundred; net, twenty-three hundred. The other half is that if you leave it set,
you pay at least twenty thousand. The write is priced, and the revoked write nearly
isn’t. But I have to add what the fragment leaves out, because twenty-three hundred
on its own misleads: the realized refund is capped at one fifth of the gas the whole
transaction used (that’s the 2021 change from Section 7, the one that ended the
refund-hoarding token’s advantage). So a real set-then-clear pays a lot more than
twenty-three hundred. As for how much more, the cap is a fifth of everything the
transaction used, and that includes the twenty-one thousand every transaction pays
just for existing. Take a transaction that does nothing but set and clear the slot, and
count only that base and the two stores (the instructions that load their arguments
add about a dozen more): it uses 43,200 gas, so the cap is 8,640, so it pays 34,560,
which is 13,560 on top of the base. (Look at the slot alone and forget the base, which
the rule doesn’t do, and you’d get 17,760.) Either way it’s far above twenty-three
hundred. The counter-level net is twenty-three hundred, and what the transaction
pays is not.
    The arithmetic below is the way the specification has it, so you can redo it with a
pencil.
310   17 Five small models


              Definition 17.2 (One slot in one transaction). A slot run records the slot’s value at
              the start of the transaction (original), its current value, whether it has been touched
              (warm), the gas charged so far, and the refund counter. A store of a new value
              charges 2100 if the slot is cold, plus 20000 if the slot still holds its original value,
              the new value differs, and the original is 0 (2900 if the original is nonzero), and
              otherwise 100. If the value is unchanged, the refund does not change. Otherwise
              add together these applicable adjustments: add 4800 when the original and current
              values are nonzero and the new value is zero; subtract 4800 when the original is
              nonzero and the current value is zero; and, when the new value restores the original,
              add 19900 if that original is zero, or 2800 if it is nonzero. Store the new current
              value, mark the slot warm, and keep the original value unchanged. The run starts
              fresh: original and current 0, cold, gas and refund 0. The net charge is gas minus
              refund.



              Theorem 17.3 (Pricing the persistent write and the revoked one). (1) For every list
              of stores from a slot whose original and current values are 0, warm or cold, with
              gas and refund 0, if the slot ends nonzero then the net charge is at least 20000, and
              from a fresh slot, which is cold, at least 22100. (2) Storing 1 then 0 leaves the slot
              at 0 with net charge 2300; storing 1 alone has net charge 22100.

              Proof. (1) Keep two lines on the sheet: “current value zero: net at least zero,” and
              “current value nonzero: net at least 20000.” The starting slot meets the first line. I
              will check that every store leaves it meeting whichever line describes its new value.
              The original value remains zero throughout, so there are only four changes to check.
              Zero to zero adds 100 to net; zero to nonzero adds 20000; nonzero to nonzero adds
              100; and nonzero to zero adds 100 − 19900 = −19800. The last case starts with
              net at least 20000 and so ends at least 200, still nonnegative. So every store leaves
              the appropriate line true. Carry the two-line test through the list of stores: if the
              final value is nonzero, the net charge is at least 20000. A cold access adds another
              2100, once, on the first store. Keep that extra charge in a separate column; later
              updates are exactly the ones just checked and do not depend on the accumulated
              total. A nonempty run from a cold slot therefore pays that 2100 on top of the
              bound, giving at least 20000 + 2100 when it ends nonzero. (2) Direct computation:
              2100 + 20000 = 22100 for the first store, 100 for the second, refund 19900, and
              22200 − 19900 = 2300.
                The fragment covers one slot in one transaction, with the gas and refund arith-
              metic copied out of the Ethereum execution specification’s storage instruction and
                                                     17.2 Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write   311


gas table, at a named commit. It has no stack, no call context, no other slots, and no
refund cap, the one-fifth rule applied at the end of a transaction.
    Then comes the wrapper, which is a different kind of object, and the walk near
the end is about exactly that difference. It’s a gas schedule in the abstract: any states,
any steps, a cost per step, a yes/no commitment flag, and a charge predicate saying
which steps get charged. It formalises no EVM (the Ethereum virtual machine) at
all. It is Section 8’s result with the whole-run ceiling, the one that pins the amount
as well as which steps pay, under a new name. Its two halves are worth reading
separately. Leave one committing step uncharged, and a one-step run commits at no
charge, so the floor fails outright; one missed commit is enough. Charge one step
that doesn’t commit, and the schedule charges more than the number of commits
on that one-step run, so the ceiling fails. And the class isn’t empty: in any system,
the price that charges one exactly on a step that raises the flag and nothing on any
other meets both halves (Section 8’s step price).
    The wrapper itself is the cleanest thing in this section and has the least Ethereum
in it.

Definition 17.3 (A gas schedule). A gas schedule has states, instructions, a step,
a cost c(s, i ) ∈ N that may depend on the state, a Boolean commitment flag on
states, and a Boolean charge predicate χ(s, i ), with two premises: a charged step
costs at least 1, and an uncharged step costs 0. A step commits when it takes the flag
from false to true. For a run t from s, let c(t) be its total cost and n(t) its number of
committing steps. The schedule has the floor when c(t) ≥ n(t) for every run, and
no overcharge when c(t) ≤ n(t) for every run. It has unit pricing when c(s, i ) = 1 if
χ(s, i ) and 0 otherwise.



Theorem 17.4 (Gas schedule exactness). For every gas schedule: it has the floor
and no overcharge if and only if χ(s, i ) holds exactly when the step from s by i
commits, and it has unit pricing. Moreover, (1) if some committing step from an
uncommitted state is uncharged, that one-step run costs 0 and the schedule fails the
floor; (2) if some charged step does not commit, the schedule overcharges.

Proof. The equivalence is Section 8’s characterization with the whole-run ceiling,
under another name. From right to left, each step’s cost is 1 on a committing step
and 0 otherwise, so a run’s cost counts its commitments. From left to right, apply
the floor and no overcharge to one-step runs: a committing step must cost at least 1,
so it is charged; a charged step costs at least 1 and may not exceed its commitment
count, so it commits and costs exactly 1. Parts (1) and (2) are those one-step runs
read the other way.
312   17 Five small models


                 Gas prices storage growth and computation. It says nothing about whether what’s
              stored is true.


              17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past
              A trusted platform module keeps platform configuration registers, or PCRs. An
              extension hashes the old value together with a new measurement digest. A quote
              signs selected PCR values and challenge data supplied by the asker; the verifier must
              check the signature, challenge and expected measurements. That can establish a
              fresh report of those values. It does not establish that every relevant fact about the
              machine was measured.
                  PCR reset permissions depend on the register, locality and platform rules. Some
              reset at startup; some support permitted resets during a boot. Thus “you can only
              extend” describes an interval with those resets excluded. Intel SGX uses enclave
              measurements and attestation reports for a related purpose, but it does not use this
              PCR-extension interface.
                  What does the specification price on the registers? Nothing: no fee, no bond,
              no budget. Within the stated reset and access restrictions, forging a different
              measurement history that passes verification relies on defeating the cryptographic
              assumptions or trusted components. Authorized resets are a separate operation,
              not an attack that requires breaking a hash. Expensive against infeasible is the
              difference between a price and a wall, and it’s easy to blur, which is why the
              definition at the start of the section leaves walls out. What stands behind a cost can
              come in three currencies. It can be economic, a fee or a deposit the protocol takes
              (Casper and gas are here). It can be cryptographic, a reversal made infeasible by a
              hardness assumption, which makes it a wall with no exact price on it (attestation
              and transparency are here). Or it can be physical, energy spent or hardware worn,
              which none of these five specifications charges as a fee or a bond; the nearest thing
              is the chip’s write budget, below. And the record’s permanence is only as long as the
              register lives: a register’s continuity lasts only through the interval allowed by its
              reset rules, not necessarily an entire boot.
                  Why the registers, then, when something that lasts would make a better record?
              Because the quote is what a remote asker reads, and the registers are what it signs.
              The same chip has longer-lived records, and they’re closer to the latch than anything
              else in this section. Version 2.0 of its specification has storage slots of a kind it
              calls a bit field, changed only by a command that ORs new bits into the old value.
              During that index’s lifetime the command can set a bit and cannot clear one, the
              OR rule from Section 11. Deleting and redefining an index is governed by separate
              authorization and policy; it must be included in any claim about persistence across
              that lifetime. It also has counters advanced by an increment command. On first use,
                                            17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past   313


a new counter starts above the values previously held by counters on that TPM, so
deleting an index and making a new one does not restart the count at zero. This is a
guarantee of the specified chip, not protection against replacing it with another chip.
And those slots are rationed. Bryan Parno and his coauthors, building a system called
Memoir in 2011, noted that the specification of the day only required a counter to
be able to tick once every five seconds, and that the chip’s storage was expected
to survive about a hundred thousand writes in its whole life, so writing once a
second would wear it out in under twenty-eight hours. Memoir writes to it twice
per boot. Those figures describe the hardware assumptions discussed in Memoir,
not a universal write quota for every TPM. Endurance and throttling constrain real
use, but an expected endurance figure is not itself an enforced protocol budget.
The quoted PCR interface supplies no such numerical price. On the bit field it’s
the budget of Theorem 11.10’s chain of k-bit words, which can only climb k times.
Phones and small controllers go one floor further down, to fuses like the PROMs
in Section 11: a version number kept as a row of fuses, one more blown at each
security update, and boot code that refuses anything older. An industry guide on
it, Rob Smart’s 2021 explainer for PSA Certified, a security certification scheme for
chips and devices, tells designers to make sure there are enough fuse bits to last
the number of updates expected over the device’s lifetime, which is part (5) of that
same theorem, written as a design rule.
    What all of this is for is rollback. Memoir’s example is a password checker restored
to an old saved state to undo a user’s password change, and in 2017 a system called
ROTE did the same job for Intel’s enclaves by having several machines vouch for
each other’s counters, with the stated result that the only way left to break it is to
reset every one of them to its start. In 2016 Raoul Strackx and Frank Piessens’s
Ariadne got that job down to flipping a single bit of non-volatile memory per state
update, which they call the theoretical lower limit. Notice who the attacker is in
every one of these: whoever gets to put an old state back. A bad program doesn’t
come into it. A record kept by the step can’t see that attacker. Every guarantee the
small machine gives about a record’s earned history (Section 15) is stated from a
clean start; put back a state the machine really reached and each one still holds
of it, through the run that reached it first, and none of them can say that nothing
came after it. The per-step toll still holds after a restore; it just can’t tell you what
happened before it.
    Replicated services put the same kind of record somewhere else: inside each
replica, where a replica that’s been taken over still can’t make it say two different
things. Byung-Gon Chun and coauthors’ attested append-only memory (A2M, 2007)
is a log a replica can only add to; Dave Levin and coauthors’ TrInc (2009) shrinks
that to a trusted counter; MinBFT (Giuliana Veronese and coauthors, 2013) uses
a trusted counter to reach agreement with 2 f + 1 replicas when f of them can lie,
314   17 Five small models


              where the usual count is 3 f + 1; and Damysus (Jérémie Decouchant, David Kozhaya,
              Vincent Rahli and Jiangshan Yu, 2022) has a small trusted service, the Checker,
              that keeps a monotonic counter of where the protocol is. Allen Clement, Flavio
              Junqueira, Aniket Kate and Rodrigo Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what
              such a record buys, and as I read their result it’s a good warning for this book. On
              its own, stopping a replica from saying two different things doesn’t lower the 3 f + 1
              bound in an asynchronous network at all. Add signatures that a third party can
              check, and it turns any protocol that survives crashes into one that survives liars,
              with no extra replicas. The way I read it, a record helps the others only as far as
              they can check what it says, which is Section 8’s point from the other side.
                  There’s a fourth currency under those three, the logical kind, and it’s the one
              every permanent record on a finite chip pays in: Section 3’s counting of used and
              fresh states applies to any of these records. With only finitely many states holding
              the record on, a step that switches it on somewhere, and never switches it off
              anywhere, forgets something. Forgetting alone doesn’t single out a record write:
              any step that overwrites a field able to hold two values forgets something too. What
              singles it out is where the forgetting lands. Take the states the record already reads
              yes on, together with the one the step switches on. The step sends every one of
              them to a yes state, and it can’t keep them apart, so what it destroys is a distinction
              on the record’s own yes side: two states it already vouched for, or the state it just
              raised and one that was up already. Any overwrite merges states somewhere; a
              permanent write is forced to merge them on that side. That needs no premise about
              money, keys or heat. The economic, cryptographic and physical payments each
              need a premise of their own about their kind (a fee rule, a hardness assumption,
              Landauer’s principle), and they hold exactly where that premise holds.


              Theorem 17.5 (A permanent write forgets on its own yes side). For any states S,
              instructions I, step and Boolean reading: suppose a duplicate-free list names every
              state, the instruction i never turns the reading from on to off, and i turns it on at
              some state s. Then the step by i is not injective. More: the step by i sends every
              state that reads on, and s, to a state that reads on, and it is not injective even on
              those states.

                 Count the on-states and call their number K. The list of all states is finite, so this
              count is finite too. The instruction keeps each of those K sources on, and it also
              sends the additional off-state s to on. That gives K + 1 distinct sources with only K
              on-states available as landing places. Two sources must land together. Both came
              from the stated collection, so the failure to keep sources apart already occurs there.
              Permanence of any other instruction was never needed.
                                           17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past   315


    What the quote can do is say what was measured. It can’t say the measured
code is correct, and it can’t say anything about runtime state that was never folded
in. A correctly measured buggy program attests beautifully. The fragment proves
that exact limit: one register, a hash about which nothing is assumed, a quote as a
pair, and no function of the quote decides a runtime flag the quote ignores, which
is Section 8’s cube again. And a second small result shows that a sign-and-verify
interface alone gives no authenticity (a scheme where verify always says yes passes
the interface), so a cryptographic premise has to be added; the fragment doesn’t
model signatures, formats, or a freshness check (the nonce is just a field the verifier
fixes).
    The same limit, turned outward, is the honest edge of the four conditions of
Section 14. Every one of them is about a thing the machine holds: same property,
same thing, same edition, honest check. For a claim about the world (the oven is
hot, the parcel arrived) there’s no edition the machine controls. Whatever reads
the world is a window onto it, and “nothing changed between the check and the
commit” stops being something a step can enforce and becomes a premise about the
sensor. So a record can establish claims about the machine’s own state, and claims
about the world only through named premises about whatever measured them. A
correctly recorded sensor reading establishes what the sensor reported. Whether
the oven was hot still depends on the sensor and the connection between its report
and the world.

Definition 17.4 (Platform and quote). Fix any functions H : N × N → N (the
extend hash) and δ : N → N (the digest); nothing is assumed about either. A
platform is a measurement log (a list of numbers) and a Boolean runtime flag.
Its register is the log folded from 0 by H. The quote with nonce n is the pair
(δ(register), n).



Theorem 17.6 (The quote cannot attest unmeasured state). For every nonce n
there is no function D from quotes to Booleans with D (quoten ( P)) = flag( P) for
every platform P.

Proof. Take two platforms with the empty log, one flagged true and one false. Their
quotes are equal, since the quote never reads the flag, so D would have to return
both values on one input.
    Anything that depends only on δ(register), the quote can answer; that’s what it’s
for. And the second result is the one I mentioned: a “signature” scheme whose check
316   17 Five small models


              always says yes fits the sign-and-verify interface perfectly and accepts a signature
              no key ever made, so the interface on its own promises nothing.


              17.4 Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced
              The certificates that make your browser show a padlock are issued by hundreds
              of authorities, and a bad or compromised one can issue a certificate for a domain
              it shouldn’t. Certificate Transparency puts certificates in public append-only logs
              built as Merkle trees. An inclusion check ties a certificate to a particular root; a
              consistency check ties a later root to one the reader already has. It was specified in
              RFC 6962 in 2013 and revised as RFC 9162 in 2021. I went looking for which one
              the running logs follow, and it’s still 6962: Mozilla’s reference for web developers
              says browser implementations are based on 6962, and as late as November 2025
              Chrome’s team was only proposing to drop its rule that every certificate carry a
              timestamp from at least one 6962 log. The fragment I transcribe is 9162’s. A Merkle
              tree is Section 2’s hash chain folded into a tree: hash each certificate (those are
              the leaves), hash the leaf hashes in pairs, hash those in pairs, and so on up to one
              root hash. To prove one leaf is in, the log hands you only the few hashes sitting
              beside the climb from that leaf to the root, the path, and you redo the climb yourself.
              A second check, consistency, shows that a bigger tree is a smaller one with leaves
              added on the end and nothing rewritten. The record is a leaf in the tree.
                  The data structure has a history of its own in security. The computer scientists
              Scott Crosby and Dan Wallach, at Rice University, built tamper-evident logs on the
              same kind of tree in 2009, with a proof that an entry is in the log and a proof that a
              later version of the log extends an earlier one, each a logarithmic number of hashes.
              A rewrite that fails to extend a previously witnessed root is caught by the consistency
              check.
                  The RFC prices nothing, and it says in its first section that logs let interested
              parties detect misissuance afterward. They don’t prevent it. And a log that shows
              different views to different people (a split view) can defeat the auditing, so logs are
              still trusted parties. What it buys is visibility.
                  Which raises the obvious question: if the specification prices nothing, why does
              any authority bother logging? Nothing in the RFC makes it. The answer is a browser.
              Chrome’s team set the rule, enforced from Chrome 68 in July 2018, that every
              certificate issued after 30 April 2018 had to meet its transparency policy, and a
              publicly trusted certificate that doesn’t is simply not trusted by Chrome: the visitor
              gets a full-page warning in front of the site. So there is a price after all, though it
              isn’t anywhere in the specification: it lives in one vendor’s browser, and it’s the price
              of being shown to that browser’s users at all. Is that the bottom? Not quite, because
              it means the strongest lever on this record is a policy one company can change,
                                                       17.4 Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced   317


which is a fact about who holds the stamp. The tree has nothing to do with it. That
policy changes nothing in the table at the end of this section, which asks what each
specification prices. But it’s worth keeping two sentences apart: “the specification
prices nothing” and “nothing is priced.”
    Do the inclusion proof by hand. Lay out seven cards d0 through d6 , each standing
for one leaf hash. Join neighbours with paper brackets: a = ν(d0 , d1 ), b = ν(d2 , d3 )
and c = ν(d4 , d5 ). The last card stands alone. Next join a to b, giving L = ν( a, b),
and c to d6 , giving R = ν(c, d6 ). The root is ν( L, R). Here ν means “put these two
expressions, in this order, inside one labelled bracket.” Equal symbolic hashes must
have exactly the same bracket structure.
    To check d3 , keep only that card and the three siblings d2 , a, R. Combine d2 on
its left to recover b, then a on the left to recover L, then R on the right to recover
the root. You never needed to open the cards inside a or R. Those three siblings are
the inclusion path.
                     Step    What is supplied   What is rebuilt
                     Start   card d3            starting leaf hash d3
                       1     d2 on the left     b = ν ( d2 , d3 )
                       2     a on the left      L = ν( a, b)
                       3     R on the right     root = ν( L, R)
Swapping left and right changes the bracket. The path has to carry the correct order
as well as the correct siblings. The hashes here are brackets, not numbers, so what
you just checked is how the tree is put together; a real log uses short hashes, and
“two different trees can’t give the same root” is then a separate promise from the
cryptography. Nothing in this fragment signs anything, no auditors talk to each
other, and no log misbehaves.

Definition 17.5 (Inclusion check, RFC 9162 section 2.1.3.2). Given a leaf index
m, a tree size N, a leaf hash, a root hash and a path, the check rejects unless
m < N. Otherwise start counters f = m, s = N − 1 and an accumulated hash r
equal to the leaf hash. For each path element p, reject if s = 0. If f is odd or f = s,
replace r by ν( p, r ); in this branch, while f is positive and even, halve both counters
with rounding down. In the other branch replace r by ν(r, p). After either branch
halve both counters once more. At the end accept exactly when s = 0 and r is
the claimed root. A symbolic hash makes a leaf hash ℓ( x ) and a node hash ν( a, b)
distinct constructors: two hashes are equal only when their entire constructions
agree.
   The consistency check used here takes old and new sizes M, N, roots u, v and a
path, and rejects unless 0 < M < N. If M is a power of two, prepend u to the path.
Reject an empty resulting path; otherwise its first element seeds two accumulated
hashes rold , rnew . Start f = M − 1, s = N − 1, and halve both while f is odd.
Process each remaining path element p: reject if s = 0; when f is odd or f = s, put
318   17 Five small models


              p on the left of both accumulated hashes and halve both counters while f is positive
              and even; otherwise leave rold alone and put p on the right of rnew . After either
              branch halve both counters once. Accept exactly when s = 0, rold = u and rnew = v.
              All halvings round down.



              Theorem 17.7 (The RFC’s own examples pass). With the symbolic hash, in the
              RFC’s seven-leaf tree with leaves d0 , . . . , d6 (writing dk also for its leaf hash ℓ(dk )),
              the inclusion check accepts leaf 3 with path [d2 , ν(d0 , d1 ), ν(ν(d4 , d5 ), d6 )], and
              likewise leaves 0, 4 and 6 with their paths; the consistency check from size 4 to size
              7 accepts. For every input with m = N, the inclusion check rejects.

              Proof. Use the brackets a, b, c, L, R built above. For leaf 3, the counters start at
              (3, 6): put d2 on the left, leaving (1, 3); put a on the left, leaving (0, 1); put R on
              the right, leaving (0, 0) and root ν( L, R). Leaf 0 has path [d1 , b, R] and three right
              combinations. Leaf 4 has path [d5 , d6 , L]: right, right, left. Leaf 6 has path [c, L]: left,
              then left; its first branch shifts (6, 6) to (3, 3) before the ordinary halving, which
              accounts for the unpaired last leaf. Each reconstructs the same root. For consistency
              from 4 to 7, the old root is L and the supplied path is [ R]. Prepending L seeds both
              hashes with L; shifting the initial (3, 6) gives (0, 1), so the sole remaining element
              leaves the old root alone and makes the new root ν( L, R), with final counters (0, 0).
              The boundary case m = N fails the first test m < N.
                  And the append-only part of the fragment is as plain as it sounds: the history is a
              list, and adding to the end of a list leaves every old entry where it was.


              17.5 Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence

              Necula’s idea, from Section 9, is to ship untrusted code with a proof that it obeys the
              host’s policy; the host computes what would need to be true and checks the proof
              with a small checker. The record is the checked proof or the result of checking it. An
              implementation may retain either. Proof-carrying code does not by itself require a
              permanent latch or assign an abstract toll to acceptance. Producing and checking
              the proof both take computational work; that work has not been identified with the
              unit charge in this book.


              17.6 The same table, five ways

              Lay them out by the one definition of price from the start of the section. Casper puts
              a bond behind the write and takes it on reversal (slashing). Gas takes a fee at the

on its longer-lived slots and counters. Transparency prices nothing. Attestation and
transparency make reversal infeasible or visible. Proof-carrying code prices nothing
and keeps nothing.

   Each row proves what its own transcription says, and no more. To read a row
as a claim about the running system you’d need evidence from that system, and no
row shows that certification is the one event every model has to price.
   So the thing the toll charges for, the moment the record is written, is charged
a fee in one of the five specifications I read, and in that one the designers had
to patch the place where the charge could be clawed back. I find that neither a
vindication nor a refutation. It’s a fact about what people built, and what they built
was mostly walls (hash chains, signatures) and penalties for contradiction. Tolls
on commitment were rare. Whether a toll on commitment is a better design than a
wall is not something I can prove, and I won’t pretend the five say so. What I read

              in them, and it’s a reading of five fragments I chose, is that each has a condition
              treated as a record, though the conditions differ in durability, and that the price axis
              is mostly empty. With one definition of price fixed before the survey, that last part is
              a count: of fifteen cells in the table, four are filled (one fee, one bond, two budgets),
              and only gas takes a payment at the moment of the write.
                 That leaves the question Section 11 raised and Section 18 has to face. The five
              systems have five different events chosen as “the record”: finalized, committed,
              attested, logged, checked. Is there anything that picks out one event as the one
              worth recording, or is it an unforced choice every time? The pointer thesis is my
              proposed answer, and the next section gives the evidence it asks for.
CHAPTER 18




The pointer thesis

Everything so far leaves one choice open. A permanent record driven by the machine
is a latch on an event, and the event is yours to pick (Section 11, the two cups on one
die). Five real systems each picked a different one (Section 17), and for the machine
in this book I picked certification. So I owe you an answer to the obvious question:
is that just my choice, or is there something about how people and machines lean
on records that picks this event out?
    What I have is a thesis, in the sense the Church-Turing thesis is one (Section 6):
a claim tying defined things to the world, which no proof can settle. Whether it
stands or falls is what decides whether the choice of event has a reason behind it.
Nothing before it depends on it; the latch, the windows and the counting arguments
hold whichever event a system records. What follows is the claim, where I got it,
and how its terms apply to the systems being described.


18.1 The claim

Of all the events a machine could put on its ledger, the ones its price list charges
for and its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records get copied and
relied on by parties who didn’t produce them: checked, stored, and acted on across
independent places that share no other state. Copying alone can’t be the test. A
replicated system copies everything it holds to every node, the gas used in a block
header as faithfully as the word final, so rival events get copied too. Reliance does
not automatically separate them either. In Ethereum, the previous block’s gas use
helps determine the next block’s base fee: another party reads it and acts on it. That
is an explicit rule in EIP-1559.
    So the examples cannot establish that certification alone is copied and acted on.
The thesis asks whether a separately justified class of reliance selects it, and whether
that selection gives a reason to charge its establishment. The formal toy below fixes
its readers and actions in advance. It can test those choices, but it cannot choose the
real readers for us. Both the claimed selection and its connection to prices remain
to be justified.


                                                  321
322   18 The pointer thesis


                   There’s a second handle on the same question, and it comes from Section 3.
               The permanent-certificate theorem (Theorem 3.1) never uses the word certification
               for anything special: given Section 3’s rule that forgetting is charged, it prices any
               reading that, once up, stays up, on a machine with finite memory. So it points at
               a narrower candidate: the events to price are the ones that write a record no later
               step can take back. Certification is one of them. As an exact answer that candidate is
               false, because a merging step can also revoke (Section 3’s three cards). Whether the
               records that are copied and relied on are the permanent ones, and whether being
               copied and relied on picks out anything the merge criterion doesn’t, is what the two
               handles have to settle between them.
                   I can see two holes in that from here, so you don’t have to find them for me. The
               first is a missing premise. Even if the world copies certification records more than
               any other kind, “copied” doesn’t give you “priced” on its own. Something has to
               connect them, and the best candidate I have is a premise about incentives: a record
               that many independent parties copy and lean on is exactly the record worth forging,
               so it’s the one where a price buys the most protection. That’s a reasonable premise,
               but it’s still a premise. The thesis’s second half states the connection as a claim to
               be tested; it doesn’t explain it, and nothing in this book supplies the explanation.
               The second hole is a circle. If “certification” just means “the record other people rely
               on,” then of course it’s the one that gets relied on and copied, and the claim says
               nothing. So the event has to be picked out without mentioning reliance: here it’s a
               reading going up for good right after a check of the same claim passed, which you
               can find in a run without asking who reads it. Whether the world copies that event
               more than its rivals is then a real question, and it could come out no.
                   The thesis says no more than that, and what’s left is the rest of what a thesis
               owes you.


               Thesis 18.1 (The pointer thesis). Let C be the class of ecosystems with reliance
               that faithfully model deployed record-keeping disciplines, each with its reachable
               states, its observers reading independent carriers, its certification event, and the
               records its discipline prices. Then for every member of C: (1) the certification event
               is the pointer on the reachable states, so it is copied and relied on by parties who
               didn’t produce it, and every event copied and relied on in that sense holds wherever
               certification does; and (2) every record the discipline prices is copied and relied on
               by parties who didn’t produce it.

                   The thesis leans on two notions with no precise mathematical definition: what
               it is to “faithfully model” a system, and which systems count as “deployed.” Those
               two tie the definitions to the world, the way “computable in the plain-English sense”
                                                                          18.2 The end of the logic   323


does in the Church-Turing thesis, and no definition can do that job, so the claim is a
thesis. The other term it needs, independent carriers, has an exact definition: each
observer’s view depends only on its own part of the world, and any two observers’
parts can be set independently of each other. The schema takes the class, the
reachable states, the certification event and the priced records as inputs; it proves
nothing about which real systems satisfy them.


18.2 The end of the logic
The logic that started in Part I ends here. Part I found what keeping takes: anything
kept is paid in a merge or in fresh states, alongside the model-dependent thermal
bounds (Section 1), and a toll on raising a flag is forced by three premises (Section 3).
Learning doesn’t have to merge anything, so it owes no floor; it borrows a blank
page, which is a supply of fresh states, and can hand it back. Committing on a finite
supply of fresh states has to merge (Section 5). Part II earned the rest. The counter
is arithmetic once the schedule is fixed (Section 7). A window with a colliding pair
in it can’t price the flag exactly (Section 8). Entitlement is an object, a check, and
a paid event, and, given lists, a tree and a covering that someone supplies, and
a run that paid for the tree’s depth, it costs at least the index bits it commits to
(Section 9). Insight is a distinction made to stay, and a committed relation is that
at its best (Section 10). A feeling doesn’t qualify. Over any base a record that is
driven by the computation and never comes down is a latch, with two unforced
choices, the price list and the event (Section 11). With more than two places, a
record that is driven by the computation and climbs a partial order is a row of cups,
each one a latch; the toll over the whole row charges at least one on any step that
turns up some cup, and a straight line of stages needs exactly one cup fewer than it
has stages, cups that only turn up (Section 4). When the machine has finitely many
states, its record only grows, and the ordinary machine forgets nothing, the toll
prices crushing two states of one fibre, and a window can price exactly by seeing the
cups move (Section 12). No inside procedure whose flip a substrate can represent
decides a shortcut property, given a recursion theorem. What a record can do is
carry the commitment (Section 13). This part made “established” a record that a
check of the claim passed (Section 14), and the small machine earns one by a check,
a commitment and a certificate, one unit each (Section 15). Of five specifications,
read through my transcriptions, one charges a fee at the write (Section 17). For the
choice of event, the pointer thesis proposes certification and lists how that proposal
could fail (Section 18).
    One question about the price itself is still open: do the requirements I’ve put on a
price pick out the toll and nothing else? If a short list of them left only one price
standing, that would settle it. The lists I tried don’t, and the no is small enough
324   18 The pointer thesis


               to check on three states. Call them blank, once and twice, with once and twice
               reading yes. The flip takes blank to once and leaves the other two where they are.
               The smooth takes both once and twice to twice and leaves blank alone. The smooth
               forgets something, so the price on merging from Section 3 charges it one unit. (The
               flip forgets too, blank and once both land on once, so the price on merging charges
               it as well, as the list requires.) It raises nothing, so the toll charges it nothing. Now
               try requirements that name no reading: no charge on a move that changes nothing,
               none on a move that forgets nothing, the same cost when you rename the states,
               a total that adds up along a run, a cost that looks only at the step, and a cost of
               one on the flip from blank. The toll, read as the price that charges the flip from
               blank and nothing else, meets every one of them on this machine. So does the price
               on merging. They disagree on the smooth, so that list doesn’t pick between them.
               What picks the toll is a requirement that names the record: over any run the total
               is never more than the number of times the reading went up. With the floor, that
               leaves exactly one price, one unit per raise and nothing else (Section 8), and it
               rules the price on merging out, because the smooth costs that price one unit and
               raises nothing. The only renaming of the three states that respects the moves is
               the identity, so the renaming requirement asks nothing there. So the uniqueness is
               real and it’s small. It holds once you’ve said which reading you’re charging for, and
               which reading deserves the charge is the pointer thesis, which is still a thesis.
                   The uniqueness theorems that do exist are about pricing information loss, and
               they’re worth a look because they say what kind of charge the price on merging
               is. John Baez, Tobias Fritz and Tom Leinster (2011), mathematicians who work in
               category theory, the mathematics Lawvere’s diagonal theorem came from, asked
               what a measure of information loss has to look like. As I read their paper, they
               proved that, for maps that preserve a probability measure, Shannon entropy is
               up to a constant factor the only measure of information loss that is functorial,
               convex-linear and continuous. János Aczél and Bruno Forte, mathematicians at
               the University of Waterloo who worked on functional equations, and C. T. Ng,
               who had taken his doctorate there under Aczél in 1971, asked in a paper of 1974
               which entropies deserve to be called natural, and proved, by their account, that the
               entropies with a short list of natural properties are exactly the linear combinations of
               Shannon’s and Hartley’s, where Hartley’s is the log of the count, so even for merges
               the choice between the average and the worst case is a real choice. Both price
               merges. Neither prices raises, so neither picks out the toll, and that’s the three-state
               example again, at a larger size. On the other side of the fence, Luciano Pomatto,
               Philipp Strack and Omer Tamuz (2023), economists at Caltech and Yale who asked
               what learning something should cost, proved, by their account, a uniqueness result
               for what it costs to acquire information, with constant marginal costs. That result
                                                                     18.2 The end of the logic   325


prices producing a signal, which is a different matter from what Section 5 reads off
a copy onto a blank page; the copy owes no floor and borrows fresh states.
    Most of that isn’t a machine. The theorems of Parts I and II quantify over “any
states, any steps,” and the five models are small copies of somebody else’s systems.
The example machine is the small one of Section 15, the least I could make that
still shows the whole model, with every part named and every price written down,
and the program that runs every program of it and, with one paid move added,
every Thiele machine whose workings a program can compute, is in Appendix C.
That’s where everything above has something to bump into. If a statement up there
doesn’t mean what I think it means, that’s where it shows, and Part IV is how you’d
go looking.
CHAPTER 19




The counter against physics

Section 3 did the physics argument once: on a finite machine a permanent flag
merges states, a price list that charges merges (a named premise, with Landauer’s
principle, another named premise, as the physics behind it) charges the flag, and
the toll follows. I’m not going to do it again. This section is about what a machine’s
counter, the small machine’s µ included, has to do with any of that. The counter is
a count in the machine’s own unit. Heat is a separate premise, and here is exactly
where the two touch and where they don’t.


19.1 The premises have to be able to hold together
The one piece of this section that I think is good physics discipline is a consistency
test. Suppose you want to claim the counter tracks dissipation. You need two
premises: that every step you’ve chosen to count dissipates at least one unit, and
an upper calibration that bounds dissipation by the charge. Can those two hold
at once? There’s a theorem saying exactly when: a model satisfying both exists
precisely when every operation you’ve chosen to count (the statement below calls
those eligible) costs at least one. I should say how little that shows. The model the
proof builds takes the dissipation to be the cost itself, so the theorem shows the two
premises don’t contradict each other. It doesn’t show that the counter tracks any
dissipation. Still, it does bite on a schedule: if you count a zero-cost step, no such
model can exist. One example where the premises hold is a one-bit restore, where
restoring the bit to one costs one and idling costs nothing; the small machine’s
flag-raising steps, below, are another.
   Now point the test at the small machine of Section 15, counting every step that
collapses some yes-or-no property, and it fails. Read without the last clause of the
floor, it would fail at a step that forgets nothing: INC A raises “A ≥ 1” one way, is
one-to-one, and costs zero. With the clause in place the failure sits at a merge. Its
unpriced instructions merge states (the last item of the list at the end of that chapter
has the pair: two cores that one DEC sends to the same core, at zero cost), so DEC
A 2, which collapses the property “A is zero or the line number is 2” by sending a
state where it’s false and a state where it’s true to the same state, costs zero there,

                                 326
                                                   19.1 The premises have to be able to hold together   327


and (1) below says no dissipation can charge it one and stay under its cost. The
machine prices the certifying chain and leaves its other merges unpriced, so the
premise pair holds for the steps the toll is about and fails for the whole instruction
set. That follows from computing at no cost on a base that keeps no history, and the
base is the part that’s by design. The hardware pays for those unpriced merges in
heat, off the ledger. The ledger counts the record only. A unit of cost is not a joule.


Theorem 19.1 (When the premises can hold together). (1) For any set of operations,
any predicate “eligible” on them, and any cost, a dissipation with δ(i ) ≥ 1 on every
eligible i and δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ) on every i exists if and only if every eligible operation
costs at least one. (2) On a one-bit machine with a reset of cost 1 and an idle of cost
0, taking “eligible” to mean “sends two different states to one”, such a dissipation
exists.

Proof. (1) If such a δ exists, 1 ≤ δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ). Conversely, take δ = cost. (2) The
reset is the only operation that sends two states to one, and it costs 1; apply (1).
    Three statements are in play, and each points its own way. Energy at a scale, µ · c,
is a conversion and points nowhere. The calibration, δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ), puts the charge
above the dissipation: an upper bound. Landauer’s principle puts the heat above
an entropy loss: a lower bound. The theorem above says the assumptions can hold
together, which is compatibility, and it isn’t evidence. It doesn’t make the ledger the
least energy anything needs, and it doesn’t make it the heat anything gives off.
    Now point the first way out of Section 3, keep everything and pay by taking
fresh states, at a machine. Keep the previous state in a history list (push it onto
the front each step; below, s :: h is the list h with s put on the front) and every
fixed-instruction step becomes injective, while the step you can see stays the same;
the line number can collapse to one place while the bigger state keeps its past. The
unpriced merge, lifted to a machine with history, isn’t a merge. It still pays, though:
the list gets one state longer every step, so the run never comes back to a state it has
been in, and that’s the fresh-state column of what keeping takes. On any memory
you can build the list fills it, and then the merge is back. So “this step merged,
so it dissipated” can’t be said of the visible step alone. It’s a sentence about the
whole state including whatever history is retained, and a physical model has to say
what’s retained. The permanent-certificate theorem in Section 3 supplies that for
the certifying step on finite memory. For the rest of a machine’s steps it’s unsaid.
328   19 The counter against physics




               Theorem 19.2 (Keeping history makes every step injective). Let the history step
               send a pair (s, h), a state and a list of past states, to (apply(s, i ), s :: h). For any step
               function, the history step with a fixed instruction is injective, and its first component
               is the original step. Each step makes the list one longer, so a run of history steps
               never visits the same pair twice.

               Proof. Undoing the history step, by popping the list, returns the old pair, so two
               pairs with the same image are equal. The list after n steps has n more entries than
               at the start, so two pairs at different times of one run differ in the length of their
               lists.


               19.2 Permanence and the heat premise
               Is there a heat prediction the permanent-certificate theorems make that Landauer’s
               principle alone doesn’t? No, and the reason is short. The smallest case, one certified
               state and one flipping in, is “set a bit to one whatever it held,” which is the reset
               Landauer described and Bérut measured; Landauer’s own name for it is “restore
               to one,” and Section 2 put it beside the toll. The general bound, the larger of kT
               ln((m plus k) over m) and 2k over (m plus k) times kT ln 2, for squeezing m plus k
               equally likely states into m, is what Landauer’s principle gives for that squeeze, at
               kT ln 2 for each bit removed. What the permanence theorems add is the structural
               half: finiteness and a permanent reading force any flag-raising instruction to merge
               some full states. They don’t say the newly certified state is one of the states that
               collide, and they don’t supply the spread over inputs or the physical conditions a
               heat bound needs. Supply those and Landauer’s premise prices the uncertainty that
               was actually removed. The machine result and the physical premise do different
               jobs, and neither does the other’s.


               19.3 At the bottom: what I suspect and can’t prove

               This is underneath the proofs, so read it with the lights on. None of it is a theorem,
               and I’m not going to dress it up as one. It’s why I care, and I’m putting it here, after
               the main text’s proofs and apart from them, so you can check that none of it got into
               them.
                  Physics has a word for the moment a question closes: measurement. And the
               people who thought hardest about it keep describing it in this book’s shape. They
               ran together for me until I put them on one picture. Flip a coin in a crowded room.
               Before it lands, it could go either way. After, it’s settled, somebody chalks it on a
                                                  19.3 At the bottom: what I suspect and can’t prove   329


board, and the result gets copied out into the world, the light and the air, so many
times that it can’t be taken back and everybody who looks agrees. There are five
pieces: the question, the landing, the chalk mark, the copies, the agreeing. Each
person leans on a different one. Zurek, in Section 18, leans on the copies. Rovelli’s
coin has to hit the ground, so his piece is the landing.
     Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist whose institute in Copenhagen was where
quantum mechanics got argued into shape, leans on the mark. In a 1954 talk he
said seeing anything at that scale depends on an apparatus that works irreversibly,
like permanent marks on a photographic plate: a door that swings one way. I found
that line quoted in a recent paper and haven’t seen the page in Bohr’s book myself.
John Wheeler, the Princeton physicist who made the name “black hole” stick, went
further in a 1989 talk in Tokyo and leaned on the question: every physical thing
gets its existence from yes-or-no questions answered and registered, boiled down to
“it from bit.” As I read him, the coin has no face until something asks and something
writes the answer down. How literally he meant that, I can’t tell. And Peirce, way
before any of them, leans on the agreeing: the kind of settling worth trusting is the
kind that has to answer to everybody. Laid out like that, they pair up. Bohr and
Rovelli lean on a step that only goes one way, in the plate and in the coin. Zurek
and Peirce lean on many onlookers who agree, one with light and one with people.
     Lay that next to everything in this book and the parts line up: a check that could
have come out either way, a result that’s now settled, a price paid in forgetting
or in fresh states, a record that stays. I suspect that isn’t a coincidence. I suspect
the event this book prices on a machine is the same kind of event physics calls a
measurement, showing up in a different place. The forgetting is my step. Bohr only
says irreversible, and getting from a record that stays to a merge or to fresh states is
Part I’s counting of states. Push on it and it gives at Zurek, for the reason Section 18
gave: copying onto fresh light merges nothing and uses up fresh states, which is
Bennett’s measurement that owes no floor. So physics’ own word lands on both sides
of the line between Bennett and Rovelli: the chalk on the paying side, the copies on
the borrowing side. The landing I’d put with the chalk, and when Section 5 pushes
on Rovelli’s paper it slides toward the borrowing side, the side of finding out. So two
pieces already stick out, and I’ll leave them sticking out. Which picture a settling on
a machine matches is part of the suspicion, and the suspicion doesn’t settle it. That’s
as far as I’ll take it here: a suspicion.
     John Bell asks for precision in those words. He was the Northern Irish physicist
at CERN whose 1964 theorem is behind the CHSH game. In 1990 Bell wrote a
short, furious essay against the word “measurement,” with a list of words he said
have no place in a physics that wants to be precise. On the list: system, apparatus,
environment, irreversible, information, and measurement, which he called the
worst of all. I used half of them in the last few paragraphs. To turn that suspicion
330   19 The counter against physics


               into a physical claim, each of those words would need a specified meaning and a
               connection to the device. The proofs here work with the models and machines I
               have defined; the physical applications state the further premises they use.

The claims and their conditions

Start with a box holding an answer. I need to know which full states count as
holding it, which moves keep it there, and whether the box has finitely many such
states. Those choices make the counting argument possible. Add a price on merging
and the same count gives a charge. Give a reader only the tabletop picture and there
is another question: how much of that event reaches the reader?
    Here I put the connections in one place. The statements and their proofs stay in
the chapters where I built them; this is a way to follow what each piece contributes
to the next.


20.1 Keeping a distinction

One next state. Follow one deterministic rule from a start. Until the first repeated
state, every visit is new. At the first repeat, either you have returned to the start,
or two different predecessors have reached the same state. From then on the rule
repeats the same successors. Those are the three columns of the step law (Section 1).
A choice between several successors would change the argument at precisely the
point where you follow the next arrow.
     A finite place to hold the answer. Suppose a move keeps every YES state at YES
and brings a NO state in. With K YES states, those states and the entrant give K + 1
sources landing in K places. Two arrows meet. The entering arrow need not be one
of them: a chain can run through the held states before meeting a fixed endpoint.
Section 3 gives the general count and its attaining constructions.
     Each part of that picture matters. An endless strip can keep moving to a different
YES state forever. A two-state toggle keeps the arrows one-to-one by turning YES
back to NO. A finite permanent holder has neither route available. For a single rule,
if its entered holding run were to repeat while remaining one-to-one, cancelling the
equal successors backwards would identify the unfinished entrant with a held state.
That is why the one-to-one alternative needs a fresh configuration at every later tick.
     Section 1 also follows finite noisy and unitary systems using their own preserva-
tion conditions. For a table of chances, both row and column sums enter the count.
For a unitary map, preservation of inner products supplies it. For the zoom argument,

                                                 333
334   20 The claims and their conditions


               keep track of the full states behind the coarse picture. The finite collection being
               counted must remain closed under the step; otherwise the next tick can move into a
               state the count left out.


               20.2 Putting a price beside the arrows
               A graph tells you which states meet. A price schedule tells you what a move costs.
               The finite holding count and a rule charging merging moves together force a charge
               on a permanent raise. Once the one-step toll is part of the machine, every run from
               NO to YES includes a charged crossing; adding nonnegative costs gives the universal
               floor (Section 2).
                  There are two useful schedules to keep separate. Charge by instruction name
               and repeating that instruction has the same price even after the flag is up. Charge
               by the source state and the schedule can ask whether this particular step raises the
               flag. The floor together with a ceiling of one unit per raise selects the latter charge,
               one for a raise and zero otherwise. When the same instruction performs the raise
               and the later idle, this state-sensitive policy lets the raise pay once and the idle stay
               free. The first is the cost signature in the basic definition; the second is the broader
               interface used in the source-charge and exact-pricing comparisons.
                  The three-card example makes the choice visible. Call the states blank, once and
               twice; once and twice read YES. A move sending once to twice and fixing blank and
               twice merges two states without raising the reading. A merge price charges it. A
               raise price leaves it free. The chosen reading and the chosen schedule specify which
               question the ledger answers.
                  With a halving allowance on each move, the list of possible starts can shrink only
               as far as the accumulated allowance permits. The entropy form additionally counts
               a supplied probability distribution. A physical heat reading uses Landauer’s premise
               for the device and process being described. These are the successive inputs to the
               arguments in Sections 3 and 5.
                  The four-state demon shows the distinction between learning and wiping. MEA-
               SURE copies onto a blank page reversibly; applied again it can return that page.
               WIPE sends different page contents to the same blank state. The first operation uses
               the prepared page; the second merges the alternatives. The price rule can therefore
               charge them differently.


               20.3 What reaches the reader

               Put a raising step and a quiet step behind a window that shows the same before-
               and-after pictures for both. Any price computed only from those pictures gives the
                                                           20.4 The concrete machine and its guests   335


same answer for both. It cannot both charge the raise and leave the quiet step free.
Let the window show the raise and that ambiguity disappears (Section 8).
    The same argument applies to a question about an earlier value. If a good and a
bad value leave the same complete retained observation, a reader of that observation
has one input for two required answers. Inspect the value while it is live and retain
an adequate answer, or retain the distinctions the later questions will need. Which
questions are allowed determines how much must survive.
    A permanent base-driven record has the latch form: it switches on at the first
occurrence of an event and stays on (Section 11). A toggle changes that task by
allowing the record to fall; a hidden clock changes what drives it. For a record
anywhere in an order, the readings “at least this place” give the row of cups in
Section 4, and the toll over the whole order is the toll on each cup. A chain with k
cups can have at most k + 1 different arrangements if cups only turn up.
    Entitlement adds a particular claim and the evidence permitting a later step to
use it. Its index count uses a covering tree whose depth the paid steps cover. The
uncovered narrowing example in Section 9 shows why that connection belongs
in the statement: narrowing a candidate list alone supplies no such bound on the
ledger.


20.4 The concrete machine and its guests

From a clean start, only CERTIFY raises the flag, only a successful COMMIT supplies
its channel, and only a successful CHECK supplies the matching fact. The counter’s
edition must still match at commitment. Following those entry points backwards
gives the earned chain and its minimum charge of three (Section 15). A claim such
as “this counter is at least zero” passes everywhere and still uses the same three acts.
The flag records their occurrence; the claim says what they established.
    The ledger starts at zero and each step adds its scheduled price. Induction on the
run then gives both its total and its uniqueness: two ledgers following that same
start and schedule agree before the first step and still agree after each addition
(Section 7).
    The universal program follows a guest through matching points, preserving
its halting, flag and ledger guarantees (Appendix C.1). The presented-machine
interpreter extends this to guests with computable transitions, prices and readings,
with the surcharge stated in Appendix C.2. Each interpreter earns its own flag
through the host’s instructions.
    Independent components compose by interleaving their moves. Each move
changes its own component, so the pair’s cost is the sum of the two component costs.
Keep each component’s own move order fixed and every interleaving has the same
336   20 The claims and their conditions


               final state. Nesting instead follows a guest through a host map; the record-order
               condition carries the guest’s crossings into the host’s accounting (Appendix D).
CHAPTER 21




The claim ledger

This section lists everything this book claims, one line each, with what kind of
claim it is and where it lives. “Proved” means proved under the premises printed
in that section, and nothing more. If a line here ever says more than its section
does, the section is right and the line is wrong. “Directly from the rules” means the
claim can be read off the stated operations by checking their cases. “Directly from
the interface” means its requirements already include the claimed behavior. These
claims are true, but carry almost nothing beyond what those definitions already say.
If you’re counting results, count those differently. I mark them so they don’t pad the
list, and where they’re stated in the book they carry the label observation, with two
exceptions: Theorem 15.6 and part (3) of Theorem C.8.
    Ledger is a good word for it, and it’s older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a
ledger was a book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from
the old verb leggen, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. Staying
put is the job here too. This is the one place where every claim lies still, so you can
come back and find it where you left it.


21.1 Claims about the model

The model comes first. Every line in this table is about any system that has the
pieces the line names: a state and a step, plus whatever the result asks for, a reading
and the toll, a counter and a price list, a window, programs. None of them is about
my machine, except the lines that run these results on it, which say so. The table
runs over several pages, in reading order, except that a line running a result on the
small machine sits beside the result it runs.
   There’s a way to use it that takes five minutes. Pick the sentence in this book you
trust least. Find its line. Read the Kind column before anything else. Then go to the
home section and check that the line says no more than the section does. If it says
more, you’ve found my mistake, and the end of this section says what I’d like done
about it.

21.2 Claims about the machine
Part III built one small machine, with the hosts that run it in an appendix, and
the ledger keeps them apart from the model. The machine is the small one of
Section 15, two counters and six instruction kinds, where commitments are earned
and universality is proved, with the universal program U on a host made of the same
instruction kinds, and the priced program UP that runs every computably presented
Thiele machine. Every line in the next tables is about those machines, or about the
physics section that closes Part III, or about the hosts and the machines built from
parts in the appendices, and nothing else, under the premises printed in its section.
