              21.3 What I propose
              What ties all of those results together is a proposal, and it’s mine: put the relations a
              computation carries, and what keeping them takes, into the state and the step. The
              items below spell that out, along with one narrower bet inside it, the pointer thesis
              about certification. Every one of them reaches past the theorems, and none of them
              adds to the physics, which stays in the premises the book names and the results it
              cites.
               • That the axis belongs in the step (Section 22, Section 23).
               • That the usual account of a computation is the flat case of the step, the shadow
                 a window on the flat part leaves, for machines whose control never reads their
                 record (Section 12). The proposal is that this is how to see computation in
                 general. The small machine’s control does read its own record: a commitment
                 that finds no fact traps. So for it the claim is about its flat part, not the whole
                 machine.
               • Within the record construction, that certification is the event selected by the
                 reliance criterion of the pointer thesis (Section 18).
               • That this is a structural account of computation, with a cost model as one part of
                 it (Section 22).
               • That the toll is the right thing to price. The alternatives are a wall or a penalty
                 for contradiction (Section 17, Section 23).
                  And there are three things this book doesn’t settle, each with what would settle
              it. Whether Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave every theorem standing
              and one premise unowned by the world: that takes measurements of real devices
              (Section 3). Whether certification really is the pointer event: that takes a way to tie
              the definitions to the systems the thesis is about, and Section 18 sets out the three
              comparisons needed. And whether there’s a smaller start than a partition: that takes
              a ruler someone can state and a smaller structure measured by it (Section 6).
                  That’s the whole ledger. If you find a claim in this book that isn’t on it, or a line
              that says more than its home does, that’s my mistake, and I’d want to hear about it.
CHAPTER 22




Scope

The definition asks for states, moves, readings and charges. To use a result elsewhere,
put that other system beside the drawing and match the pieces. Which states carry
the record? Which operation establishes it? What does the reader see, and what
does the price count?
    The following comparisons work through those questions for heat, computation
and the choice of record. They show which further connections an application needs.
    Physical interpretation of the counter. Choose a start and a price schedule and the
ledger is determined on reachable states. To read it as a physical quantity, specify
which states carry information and how the scheduled charge relates to dissipation,
under physical premises that hold together. The permanent-certificate theorems
supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a permanent reading. The two
premises are shown able to hold together whenever every counted step costs at
least one, and for a one-bit reset. The small machine’s unpriced steps merge states
and are charged nothing, so its ledger is not a heat meter for computing: whatever
those merges cost the hardware is off the ledger, and the two premises hold together
for the record steps only (Section 19). No joule value attaches to one unit of cost
without thermal and device premises (Section 3, Section 19). Once you pick the
start and the price list, the number is forced by arithmetic, and it isn’t energy. What
I’d need before it could be is the list at the top of this paragraph.
    Class separation. The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They
don’t stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No
separation of standard complexity classes follows from the collisions (Section 8,
Section 15). I’ll be blunt about why I’m careful here. Whether P equals NP is
one of the seven problems the Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on,
at a meeting in Paris in May 2000. One of the seven has been solved since, the
Poincaré conjecture, by the mathematician Grigori Perelman, who posted the proof
as preprints in 2002 and 2003. P versus NP hasn’t. If a two-state collision on my
machine settled it, I’d be owed a million dollars. Nobody owes me anything. A
window that loses a field is a fact about that window. A complexity class is a fact




                                                 361
362   22 Scope


             about what every possible program can do within a budget, and nothing in these
             collisions reaches that far.
                 Trace initiality, and what it doesn’t settle. The universal property of the trace
             fold is about evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there’s
             exactly one way to fold a list into it (Section 7). The counter’s uniqueness assumes a
             schedule. Rise-only pricing assumes an event, and a reference count that says what
             charging too much means (Section 8). Those results make the construction precise.
             None of them shows that the schedule I chose, or the event I chose, is physically
             necessary.
                 Other observables. Certification is one worked example. A family of other
             observations could turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own
             events, its own evidence, and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The
             window and oracle results are about what specific maps keep, and nothing more.
                 Program predicates versus state observations. The state-level collision (Section 8’s
             wall) and the program-level diagonal (Section 13’s wall) live in different domains.
             Linking them would take a theorem of its own. The diagonal (Section 13) keeps its
             explicit quantifiers and representability premises.
                 Entitlement bounds. The count is handed its tree and its covering, along with
             the payment condition. It doesn’t dig the tree out of an arbitrary run, and it isn’t
             a Shannon bound on every trace (Section 9). On the small machine the payment
             is the record moves, each costing exactly one; a branch that costs nothing can still
             narrow, the lists, tree and fibres are supplied, and the covering can’t be dropped.
                 The record axis. The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a
             base computation is a latch on an event; on a finite machine its write merges states;
             and the named windows don’t recover it. Certification is one instance. No theorem
             selects it as the unique event every system must record (Section 11, Section 18).
             A finite monotone multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches. One
             Boolean latch can’t hold it. Revocation, including revocation priced from the other
             side as in Casper, lies outside the permanent-record axis; a price on revocation
             doesn’t transfer to a price on the write (Section 17). Probabilistic records don’t
             inherit the uniqueness result either. Two honest random records can have the same
             branches and the same charges and still give those branches different weights, one
             choosing evenly and one two to one, so the schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities.
             And no single deterministic latch explains a record that can branch both ways from
             the same observation. Records that can come back down lie outside all of this:
             they’re limit computability’s, and Section 11 points at Ershov’s ladder.
                 Who it’s safe against. Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any
             list of instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says,
             one writer stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It
             doesn’t cover whoever sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts
                                                                                           363


nobody checked), a reset or a power cycle, the wire that carries the report, someone
who flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built the step, or a second writer that
changes a counter without bumping its edition. Those are the operator, the device
and the tool chain, and they’re outside this fence. A record read by someone who
didn’t watch it being made is only as good as their reason to believe the box that
shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote over measured state and a proof
that travels on its own, are in Section 8 and Section 17, and this book builds neither.
What the guarantee gives inside the fence is safety: no program forges the chain.
Availability is a different promise, and it isn’t given. A hostile program can put the
trap up or fill the table, and after that nothing useful gets done. The mathematical
machine uses whole numbers, which never overflow, so versions and the ledger
grow without bound. A build with fixed-width counters, versions or ledger has to
stop before any of them wraps, failing safe with the trap up, because a wrapped
version could make an old fact look live again and a wrapped ledger would fall.
Starting, restoring, resetting and that overflow stop belong to the implementation,
and none of them is proved here.
    The diagonal on the machine. What’s proved for the small machine’s programs is
that halting is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.5, for them and
for the universal program (Section 15; for the universal program, Appendix C.1).
The wall of Section 13 is stated over any substrate with a recursion theorem and a
representable flip, and uses neither the counter nor the toll.
    The five models. Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice;
the gas fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures;
the transparency verifier covers control flow and leaves collision resistance out; the
proof-carrying checker is a three-instruction memory-bounds language. None is a
claim about the real system beyond its fragment (Section 17).
    The machine. Part III has one small machine, with the hosts that run it in an
appendix, and this paragraph is its fence. The small machine of Section 15 (two
counters, six instruction kinds) is where commitments are earned: from a clean
start, a raised flag went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification
of the same claim, nothing is forged, and the cheapest such run adds exactly three
to the ledger, a price reached by a check that could have failed (the step doesn’t
police trivial checks: a check that can’t fail certifies for three too). It’s also where
universality is proved, by matching Minsky’s two-counter machines step for step
and using the halting reduction of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors. It’s
certified, in the sense Section 14.15 pins down, and it hides its record and ledger
from a window on its counters. The universal Thiele machine for the small machine’s
programs (Definition C.1) is a host with the small machine’s instruction kinds and
more counters, running one fixed program, U, with no guest step built in: it runs
364   22 Scope


             every program of the small machine from every clean start start( x, y), halts when
             the guest halts, raises its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if and
             only if the guest’s flag rises somewhere in the guest’s run, and keeps a ledger equal to
             the guest’s at every matching point. With one paid move added, one fixed program,
             UP , runs every computably presented Thiele machine: its step, prices and reading
             computed by programs, the reading decided on every state, the run fixed by a driver.
             The host halts when the guest stops, its flag is the latch of the guest’s reading, raised
             on its own earned chain whose claim is that reading, and its ledger is the guest’s plus
             a surcharge of at most two when the reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on
             that host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole
             ledger below three. A machine whose reading no program decides is outside. The
             small machine’s check price is flat, its fact table holds sixteen, and its certificate is
             historical (Section 15 lists the rest).
                 The comparison machines. The reversible result (Theorem 11.3) covers any base
             whose step is injective, and on a finite state space says only that no injective step
             raises a permanent reading. It is not a theorem about real memories or full reversible
             languages. The cost-semantics results are local correspondences, short of full cost-
             framework embeddings: the trace’s cost is a writer cost and a grade, and the toll is
             the potential method with one potential (Section 7). Nobody’s whole type system
             gets embedded either.
                 Outward consequences. I looked for results about real systems that would need the
             record axis. What’s proved are the five fragments of Section 17, each a transcription
             with its own named limit, and none is a theorem about the deployed system. Stronger
             candidates would need protocol or hardware semantics I haven’t formalised, and
             I’ve proved nothing about them. So none of this yields a new outside result that
             both needs the record axis and is ready to use.
                 Where each result lives is the premise column of the claims section (Section 21).
                 Models and processes. For a model of computation written down as states, a step
             and a reading that stays, what keeping takes is a theorem about the model, not a
             thesis. The thesis in the Conclusion is only the tie from a physical process to such
             a description. Here’s how far the theorems reach, and where they stop. A step
             that gives every state one next state, on any number of states: a run that raises a
             reading and keeps it up merges two of its own states or never visits a state twice
             (Proposition 3.5), and with finitely many states reading yes the move that raises it
             merges (Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.4). That takes in a Turing machine or a counter
             machine stepping by its program, and a cellular automaton stepping its whole grid
             at once. A model that halts has no next state at its halt, and slips past with no
             merge; give the halt a next state and the run is one rule again, so keeping the answer
             merges or takes fresh states, and with the halted state stepping to itself the step
             onto it is a merge (Theorem 1.2). Steps by chance on finitely many states: one
                                                                                             365


whose chances into each state add to one, which is what keeping the even spread
takes, never enters a finite set nothing leaves from a state outside it (Theorem 1.7).
A unitary step that keeps a finite-dimensional part of the space keeps the part at
right angles to it, so a state at right angles to the kept part stays at right angles
(Theorem 1.8).
    A model whose step may offer several next states, or none, comes in too: a
nondeterministic machine, a lambda term reduced at whichever redex you like,
a rewriting system, a proof system read as derivations made one rule at a time.
Nothing earlier in the book is stated for such steps, so here are the two arguments.
The first is the pigeonhole of Proposition 3.4 on one choice of next state, and the
second is the walk back of Proposition 3.5, stopped at the raise. First, suppose only
finitely many states read yes, none of them can step to a state reading no, each has
at least one next state, and some state reading no can step to one of them. Pick one
next state for each yes-state, and the outside state’s step into the yes-states: that’s
one more step than there are yes-states, each leaving a different state and landing
on a yes-state, so two land on the same one, and two different states share a next
state. That needs the yes-states finite; Hilbert’s hotel, everybody moving up one,
keeps a reading with no two states sharing a next state. Second, along any one run,
however its choices fall, take the step where a reading goes up, and suppose it stays
up for the rest of that run. If the run is in one state at two times after the raise, step
both times back together. They can’t stay equal past the raise, because the state at
the raise reads no and every later one reads yes, so at the first pair that differs, two
different states of that very run step onto one. So after the raise the run merges or
never repeats a state, on any number of states. Before the raise it can come back to
a state and then leave it for good with no merge, which one rule can’t do. A normal
form, with no next state, is the halt again: a reading kept by stopping is kept with
no merge, as Theorem 1.2 says. For such steps the first argument says little by itself:
in the lambda calculus every term N is one step from two different terms, (λx.x ) N
and (λz.N ) M with z not free in N, so two states sharing a next state is no news
there, and the second argument is the one that carries weight. And when a step
can branch, a shared next state doesn’t by itself bunch the crowd up, since a branch
spreads it out again; with chances on the steps and finitely many states, the count
that does is Theorem 1.7.
    Where they stop. Steps in continuous time have no next state to count, and
nothing here covers them. Steps by chance where endlessly many states read yes,
and unitary steps whose kept part has endlessly many dimensions, get none of the
finite results above, and the bilateral shift keeps a reading with no merge, a fresh
state every step. What still reaches them is the run: a unitary step is one rule, so
its runs are Proposition 3.5’s, and one run of steps by chance is a run the second
argument covers. And a truth isn’t a process at all: that a statement is provable is a
366   22 Scope


             fact with no step in it, and the theorems are about a run that derives it. What they
             give is the merge or the fresh states. The heat stays Landauer’s premise.
                 What I’m proposing beyond that. A way of describing computation in which the
             relations a computation carries live in the state, what each move does to them lives
             in the step, and a price list is one part of the description, not an afterthought. The
             permanent record is the one case I took apart all the way. The pointer thesis asks
             whether certifying is the thing that deserves that record in the systems it talks about,
             and it can be wrong without touching the latch or the window arguments, which
             never use it.
                 Underneath that is a question about which distinctions a description of a compu-
             tation ought to keep. The constructions show particular ways of keeping some, and
             what follows once you do, under premises I’ve printed. What that’s worth depends
             on what you need the description to answer. A program log with a proof about its
             updates may recover the required distinctions. A host can instead enforce those
             updates through every guest program. A system may prevent an act with a wall,
             penalise it afterwards, or charge it at the step. Comparing those choices means
             following what each one guarantees for the task.
CHAPTER 23




Conclusion

Put the blank cell, the triangle, the cups and the two computers back on the table.
The cell went from a specified blank state to a 0 and stayed under its write-once
rule. The rule merges blank and zero; a heat floor still needs the input preparation
and the thermal premises. Turning the triangle preserves relations you can check
with your fingers. Turning a cup records an act; a row of cups can distinguish stages
that one cup cannot. The two computers can leave the same answer while differing
in what they did to reach it. In each case I had to say what the things were, which
moves were allowed, which relations survived, and what my way of looking could
tell apart.
    Part I started at the bottom, with the cell. On any machine run by one rule, every
step lands on a fresh state, merges two into one, or goes round a loop, and a run that
raises a reading that stays either merges somewhere or never repeats a state, so it’s
paid in a merge or in fresh states, alongside the model-dependent thermal bounds,
more the faster it goes. The counting needs nothing but one rule and a reading
that stays. A single 0 written on a blank cell is already a merge, and every zoom
pays the same way. Then the model got an exact form: five parts, one rule, one
theorem you proved at the table, what keeping takes written into a step. Then the
rule stopped being only my preference. With finitely many yes-states and a flag that
stays up, the fresh states run out, every move that raises the flag merges, and under
the merge-pricing rule the toll follows. The collision belongs to the instruction, over
the states it’s allowed to act on; the state that just came in needn’t be one of the
two that collide. Turning that into heat takes a spread over inputs and Landauer’s
premise on top, its critics named; from a start somebody already knows, the premise
puts no floor under it, because that prepared distribution has no entropy to remove;
the step can dissipate under the stated thermal-model assumptions. The toll is a
derivation under three premises you can refuse one at a time, each with the machine
that walks past it built; what keeping takes, underneath it, isn’t. Learning borrows:
copying onto a blank page merges nothing, the copy can be handed back, and the
page is paid for when it’s wiped. Committing makes a record that can’t be handed




                                                 367
368   23 Conclusion


              back, so it pays. That’s as far as physics goes in this book, and I’ve tried to keep it
              exactly that far.
                  Part II gave the triangle and the cups their words: structure is relations among
              things, kept under the changes you choose, carried by whatever stuff happens to
              be there, relative to a frame. A partition turned out to be the smallest sorting by
              the ruler I picked, and a cell that goes from blank to 0 and stays is that smallest
              sorting, one yes-or-no question, kept. And making a grouping, keeping it, checking
              it and standing behind it came apart into four different acts. So the question became
              how an account of computation could carry what keeping the cell’s 0 takes, and the
              difference between those acts, in its step.
                  The rest of Part II was the logic, and what it earned comes next, in the order
              it was earned. The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window
              in which a raising step and a quiet one look the same can’t price the raise exactly,
              by a fact about functions far older than the machine. Entitlement is defined as
              an object, a checked relation, and a paid event; given lists, a tree and a covering
              somebody supplies, a run that paid a charged step for every level of the tree has
              paid for the index bits it commits to (that count doesn’t show a run has to pay
              them, the run doesn’t recover the tree, the lists count repeats, and the index bits
              aren’t the questions anybody asked); when the run makes the narrowing itself, every
              candidate dropped was dropped by a test the run paid for, and the index bits are
              at most k times the cost when each test keeps a 2−k share; on the small machine
              the same count, for a run from a clean start, is a theorem about its record moves,
              with the earned chain inside the run, and the count can’t do without the covering;
              and it is a license to lean on a claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true. Insight, in the
              sense the toll prices, is a distinction made to stay. A feeling doesn’t count. Its floor
              is flat: at least one, however deep. The claim behind the flag is something a check
              could have refused, and in the bare model nothing makes the commit wait for the
              check. Over any base, a base-driven record is a latch, with two unforced choices,
              the event and the price list; “only one substrate” is false and “one structure, many
              price lists” is true once the event is fixed. No procedure whose flip the substrate
              itself can represent decides the shortcut predicate, given a recursion theorem, by
              the same diagonal that broke Frege’s floor, and the machine’s answer is to record
              the commitment. It leaves the judgement unautomated.
                  Part III built an example that meets the definition. The small machine’s state
              ties a checked claim to an edition of a counter, and its step uses the tie: change the
              counter and the old check no longer lets you commit. So from a clean start a raised
              flag needs a passing check, a commitment about the same edition and a certificate,
              in that order. A cost of three is enough, and no such run pays less. Those are facts
              about the example, the check that can’t fail included, and its two-counter base is
              universal under Minsky’s packing.
                                                                                            369


    The universal programs ask whether those relations survive somebody else’s
machine doing the work. On the host with more counters, U runs the small
machine’s programs from clean starts, halts when they halt with their answers, earns
its own flag exactly when the guest raises one, and matches the ledger wherever the
two line up. With PAY added, UP runs every computably presented Thiele machine,
latches the guest’s reading through its own earned chain, and carries the guest’s
ledger to within the stated surcharge: at most two at the raise when the reading
starts at no. The theorems say which states match; this particular build takes a long
time to get there.
    Then I joined machines up, to see what carried over. Two machines side by side
need both records kept; one total loses which side did the work. Hand-offs and
nested runs each come with conditions of their own (Appendix D). Every one of
those constructions makes you say which relation survives the change and which is
lost, and that saying is the work.
    Of five record disciplines I modelled in fragments, one charges a fee at the write,
and which event to record is a thesis, with its refutations listed. And then came
what the counter has to do with physics. Two facts about the machine sit where
they belong. Its unpriced steps merge states, because that’s what forgetting scratch
work is; whatever those merges cost the hardware is off the ledger, so the toll on
this machine comes from the record’s merge premise, with no finiteness premise on
the whole machine; the only finiteness in it is the flag’s two readings. And a check
that cannot fail still certifies for three, because the step charges for the act, and the
entitlement count says what the claim bought.
    Part IV brings those pieces together (Section 20). A finite permanent holder has
to merge; the named price rule puts that merger on a ledger; a window determines
which part of it a reader can recover. The example machine then supplies the earned
path from a passing check to commitment and certification. Each argument has its
place in that chain, and the constructions show how to carry it out.
    Four contributions bring that chain into focus, each alongside the earlier work
it builds on. First, the toll isn’t only my preference: on a finite machine a reading
nothing turns off can only be turned on by a step that merges states, so if merges
are priced, raising it costs (Theorem 3.1, Observation 3.3); and on any machine
a raise that merges nothing needs endlessly many yes-states, so it pays in fresh
states instead (Proposition 3.4). The counting under it is the finite cousin of the
recurrence argument Zermelo threw at Boltzmann in 1896, and the abstract merge
price is motivated by Landauer’s reset example. Identifying that price with heat
needs the further premises stated in Part I. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) had
already put a physical price on that merge for finite automata, and Li and Vitányi
(1996) had already assumed a unit price on each irreversibly erased bit in a model
of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016) a price on instructions that
370   23 Conclusion


              destroy bits, so what’s here is the toll such a price forces on a reading that stays.
              Second, a window that shows a raising step and a quiet one the same can’t price
              the raise exactly (Observation 8.2); that a price computed from what a window
              shows can’t tell apart two steps the window shows the same is elementary, and
              what’s here is the pricing form. Third, a record driven by the computation that
              never switches off is a latch on one event, over any base (Observation 11.1); latches
              and history variables are old, and the theorem covers only records that never come
              down. Beside it sits the flat case: forget a machine’s record and its prices and what’s
              left is a computer, blind to what was kept and what it cost, and a window on the flat
              part can’t see either (Section 12). That forgetting a layer gives the runs back, where
              the step doesn’t read it, is the ghost-code erasure of Section 7; what’s here is that the
              forgotten layer still earns its record, and that what’s left can’t see it. Fourth, a record
              that’s priced, and on the small machine earned (Theorem 15.11), under the move of
              guaranteeing something about every program. That move isn’t mine at all. It’s the
              reference monitor’s (Anderson, 1972), made precise for monitors that watch a run
              (Schneider, 2000), and proved for monitors checked at every instruction (Azevedo
              de Amorim and coauthors, 2015). What I put together under it is built, and its idea
              isn’t new: the check bound to the edition it looked at, the toll charged on top, and
              universal programs that carry both to every program of the small machine and to
              every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag as they go.
                  And there is one thing I’d point at if you asked how far the proofs reach. It isn’t
              a fifth new thing. In the model, the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever
              its flip can be expressed inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed
              point, and it uses neither the counter nor the toll. On the small machine the wall
              stands by proof: halting for its programs is undecidable in the reduction sense of
              Theorem 15.5.
                  There are things this book doesn’t settle, by my count. It doesn’t settle whether
              the toll is the right thing to price; the five real systems mostly built a wall or a
              penalty for contradiction. It doesn’t settle whether certification is the pointer event.
              And it doesn’t settle whether Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave every
              theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world. And the question I’d
              most like someone to take from me: is there a smaller start than a partition, by a
              ruler they can state? I said in Section 6 it would change this book, and it would.
                  One more claim ties the counting to the world, the way Church and Turing’s
              ties computing to it, and I’ll state it as what it is, a thesis, the Thiele thesis: every
              physical process that computes with final answers has an exact description as a
              machine run by one rule, with a next state for every state, computably presented (its
              states written as whole numbers, and its step, its reading and its start for each input
              computed by programs that halt on every input), on which the answer is a reading
              that no run from any input ever turns off, on inputs accepted and rejected alike.
                                                                                           371


No proof settles it, because “a physical process that computes” isn’t a mathematical
object. A model of computation is one, and for a model written down as states, a
step and a reading that stays, what keeping takes needs no thesis: it’s a theorem, and
Section 22 says how far it reaches. The thesis is about what a physical computation
pays for what it keeps, which is Part I. A description run by one rule, with its program
loaded, is a Thiele machine in the flat case: either every move costs the same, a
clock, or its reading never rises, and either way the toll asks nothing of it. The
price shows only when the moves are offered before a program is chosen, and with
the program in the state a reading is a record, not a simulated bit, exactly when it
never comes down from any state. So the thesis is about physical processes and the
one-rule descriptions of them. The Thiele Machine is the model that prices what
such a description keeps. There is an established route to a conditional physical
description. Gandy’s work on mechanisms, restated by Arrighi and Dowek, starts
with homogeneity in space and time, finite local state sets, bounded propagation
and an initially finite departure from a preserved quiescent background. Their
classical theorem makes the resulting evolution computable. In the construction, a
cell consults finitely many neighbours through one finite table; a finite active region
can therefore be advanced by a program. These are substantive modeling premises.
They do not select a certification event or a price in joules, and they are not asserted
of every physical system here. The quantum extension uses different premises. See
Arrighi and Dowek, The physical Church–Turing thesis and the principles of quantum
theory, Section 2, https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.1612.
    What is proved sits on either side of the thesis. On one side, Part I applies to
every such description on the states its inputs reach, where the answer never comes
down: a run that raises it merges two of its own states or never visits a state twice
(Proposition 3.5). On the other, seen only through which inputs it accepts, the thesis
implies that every set a physical process accepts with final answers is one a Turing
machine can list. At that extensional level it has the physical Church-Turing thesis’s
conclusion. Run the description from every input, a step at a time across all of
them, and list an input the first time its reading says yes; no run turns its answer
off, so a yes seen once is the answer. The other way, a set a Turing machine lists
is accepted by the machine that searches the list for its input and then steps from
its halted configuration to itself, with the reading “halted,” which nothing turns off.
This converse constructs a machine with the same accepted set; it does not prove
an exact state-by-state description of the original physical process. Nothing about
how the keeping is paid survives that view: the same search held at its halt by a
step to itself, which merges, or by a counter that goes on ticking, which takes fresh
states, accepts the same inputs. And “final” has to cover the rejected inputs too. A
machine that starts at no, reads yes while program n is still running and falls to no
for good if it halts reads yes for good on exactly the programs that never halt, and
372   23 Conclusion


              no Turing machine lists those, since one that did, run beside the search for a halt,
              would decide halting.
                  And then there are the two computers of Section 14, the sorter and the copier,
              holding the same list. Walk the warehouse again. The list is in order on both. On
              the machine with the earned layer, a different part of the state tells you whether a
              check happened and a matching commitment followed it, and the rules keep that
              tied to the edition that was checked. Put your hand over that part of the machine
              and the difference between the two computers vanishes from where you’re standing.
              Change the counter and you can watch the old check go stale. Those are different
              operations with different consequences, and you can follow each one with your
              finger.
                  Carry a report out of the warehouse and you’ve got another question: what
              connects the report to the machine? The flag on its own doesn’t answer it. A
              window, a copy, a second machine and a reader each bring relations of their own,
              and the constructions in this book ask, one at a time, which of those relations hold.
              That’s how the example gets past the lamp: by what survives a change of view, a
              change of state, or a change of machine.
                  At the bottom of the Thiele Machine is one cell going from blank to 0, and the
              question of what that write keeps and what the chosen price rule charges. Built
              on that cell, the machine is structure held as state, acted on by a step, with an
              account of the changes and a view that may keep or lose their distinctions. What
              I’m arguing is that those relations are part of computation itself, and not something
              you bolt on afterwards. The record and its toll are the part of that I’ve worked all
              the way through, and there this much is proved: forget a Thiele machine’s record
              and its prices and what’s left is the flat case, a computer, blind to what was kept
              and what it cost; on the small machine a window on its counters can’t see either
              (Theorem 15.15). Run as one rule, a machine is a Thiele machine only as a clock or
              with a reading that never rises. The small machine and its interpreters are things
              you can take apart. Each theorem answers a stated question under stated premises.
              Put the computation, the record and its account on the same drawing, and you can
              follow what changes, what stays, and what the next reader has to work with.
CHAPTER 24




Afterword: how I got here

What I am is curious, past the point of good sense.
   I pick a thing up and cannot set it down until I have turned it over enough times
to see how it holds together, and this time it did not let go.
   I am not a programmer and I was never formally taught any of this.
   I was not trying to build a new model of computation.
   I would not have known what one was if it bit me.
   I was trying to build a 3D renderer.
   There was no plan behind it.
   Just a pull to make something real with my own hands, and the kind of stubborn-
ness that will not let a thing go until it stands up on its own.
   I have worked on it in off hours every day since.
   Once I started digging in, two things came clear fast. I knew nothing about
computers, and the field was already saturated, every obvious road paved and
crowded. So I needed an angle nobody else was standing on, and the angle I had
wasn’t a strategy. It was just the only way my head works. I did not know what
compositional meant. I had never heard of category theory. I called the thing I was
building digital DNA, because that is what it felt like in my hands, and I thought
about it in the only language I had: gravity pipes and directions and vectors, things
that were linear and somehow not linear at the same time, structure that flowed
and joined and came apart without my owning one proper word for any of it. I built
a custom rendering pipeline out of those intuitions, by feel, throwing out pieces that
did not sit right even when I could not have told you the rule they were breaking.
And then, the way I always do, I went looking for what I was actually doing, and
found out it already had a name. An old one. A deep one. What I had been reaching
for in the dark was composition. It was category theory, a whole field I had never
once heard of, sitting there describing the exact shapes I had been shoving around.
The moment that landed, the rendering pipeline stopped being a rendering pipeline
and started turning into a categorical engine, and I started swallowing the real
theory as fast as I could find the words for things I had already built.




                                                 373
374   24 Afterword: how I got here


                  I took it one concept at a time, and I would not move to the next until I could
              watch the current one actually run. Category. Object. Morphism. Functor. Monoidal
              product. It came together in pieces and never in chapters, the way a picture resolves
              out of static. The Yoneda lemma (a result buried deep in category theory) was the
              piece that made the rest snap into place.
                  Then within weeks I found out the engine I had built to draw pictures was
              general enough to run a physics simulation on the exact same primitives, without my
              rewriting any of it. I wrote Newton’s laws as a program in it, half expecting nothing,
              and it ran. I want to be careful about what that was and what it was not, because
              this is exactly the kind of thing that gets misread. It was not me deriving physics, and
              I am not claiming the machine explains gravity. It was the compositional structure
              being general enough to express a physics simulation the same way it had expressed
              a renderer, and that generality is what told me the structure was the point and the
              pixels never were. Somewhere in those weeks I crossed from debugging why one
              pixel would not show up to understanding that I had quietly built a categorical
              computing engine, and that the rendering had only ever been the first thing I aimed
              it at. The pixel did eventually show up, for what it is worth.
                  I kept going, because by then I could not not keep going. The night the engine
              first ran a program declaratively, meaning I told it what should happen and let it
              work out the how without my spelling out each step, I told my wife, Julie, I thought
              I was onto something. She said okay.
                  Then I hit a wall, and it is the wall this whole document is about. Every tool I
              had for settling questions about what I’d built could settle the small ones and fell
              over on the exact ones I needed answered, which left me staring down an infinite
              hallway of guess-and-test with no proof waiting at the end of it, ever. One night, not
              even working, I was watching a video about Flatland, the old story about a creature
              living in two dimensions who cannot so much as picture a third. And it landed on
              me sideways, all at once, the way the real ones always do. I said it out loud: I get it
              now. There is another axis. Classical computation only ever sees what it can read
              and write off its own surface, and there is a whole direction it is blind to. It isn’t
              broken. It was just never built with an eye that points that way. That’s how it landed
              that night, and it didn’t survive in that form: the direction turned out to be one
              an ordinary computer can reach, and what the usual rules leave out is the price
              (Section 2.3 says where the axis ended up). The two computers in Section 14 are my
              attempt to show you that blindness with something you can hold. That same night
              I gave the idea a name: the Thiele Machine. The name began as a working title
              and became the name of the model. It carries the larger claim plainly: the machine
              treats structural state as part of computation.
                  What survived the whole trip from there to here is not the renderer. Not one
              piece of it, and good riddance. What survived was a single commitment I made early
                                                                                          375


and never once let anyone talk me out of: structure is the state itself, the actual
thing the machine runs on. It is no metaphor laid over some realer state underneath.
Category theory was the first language I found for that structure. It is not what the
model is. The basic model asks for states, instructions, a step, prices and a reading.
The ledger and the window are further structure used in the constructions. None of
that needs category theory. The morphisms in that first engine, the night they first
composed correctly at two in the morning, were objects that remembered where
they came from; the records in the small machine I ended up with remember where
they came from too, and you can walk up to one and challenge it. The receipt grew
teeth. But the shape itself never moved. The shape was the substrate the entire time,
and everything else, every renderer and every proof, was me slowly learning to see
what I had already built. By the shape I mean structure held as state. Not category
theory. Category theory was just the first language I had for it.
    Every step pulled back to show another layer underneath that I had not known
was there, and I mean that plainly: I did not know what a Turing machine was when
I started, I did not know most of the words in this document existed. I learned each
one the same way, by walking face-first into a wall that needed it and not being let
past until I had it. The needing always came first. The learning came after, dragged
along behind the needing because it had no say in the matter.
    Large language models were my hands the whole way through, and I want
the division of labor exact, because it is the thing people most want to get wrong
about work like this. The hands had nothing like this to draw on: no reference
implementation, no prior project to point at. The ideas, the architecture, the
direction, the demand that the thing be true: those are mine, all of them, no asterisk.
The symbol-pushing, the code and the formal derivations, the models produced. So I
read every statement. A derivation can settle an empty question, and I had to refuse
that too. However the symbols got onto the page, the argument on it is checkable
by reading, and it would be exactly as right or as wrong if a million monkeys had
typed it. The monkeys could not have refused.
    A word on what I actually do, because it runs under everything after it. I do
not write code or math by hand. I do not pick constants. I do not grind through
derivations. I have never written a line of code on paper or in a notepad in my life.
What I do is see, and direct, and refuse. When I take hold of an idea it does not stay
a point. It opens up. It becomes a shape I can blow up and turn over and take apart,
lay across another shape to find where the two of them touch, run forward and then
back to where it started, zoom into until it is the only thing in the world and pull
back until it is one dot in a field of other dots, and the whole time it stays wired to
everything I have ever connected it to, the right connections and the wrong ones
both, all of them live at once. I am not reading that field neutrally, the way a search
would. The thing doing the looking is me, the whole of me, my gut and my mood
376   24 Afterword: how I got here


               and my stubbornness picking what lights up and which way I move through it, and
               that is the part you cannot lift out without turning me back into a search engine. So
               I see where a thing has to fit, the shape it is obligated to have, usually well before I
               could write it down in a single symbol. Then the model gives me the symbols, and I
               refuse anything whose argument does not hold or does not match the shape I am
               holding. That refusal is the one thing in this entire document that is mine and only
               mine: the demand that it be true, and the throwing-out of everything that wasn’t.
                   I am telling you all of this because it’s the engine. I did not come up through
               anywhere that hands you a foundation and says trust us, this part is settled. No
               professors, no colleagues, no field full of authority to lean back on when a claim got
               heavy. From the outside that is a deficit. From the inside it is the whole reason any
               of this is solid: when I meet a claim I either find the proof or I do not believe it, and
               that goes double for my own, because my own are the ones I most want to wave
               through. It is how I am built. It is the only way I know to hold a thing and actually
               trust that I am holding it.
                   So everything in here gets built from the ground up. It isn’t a courtesy to you. I
               build it because I do not believe I understand a thing until I have built it with my
               own hands, watched it stand up on its own, and tried to knock it over. I built this
               document the exact way I built the machine, brick by brick, refusing each brick until
               it held weight. That includes the parts you already knew cold before you opened
               this. I did not skip them for you, and I could not skip them for me.
                   The vocabulary I had to go look up to do any of this sits at the back of the book,
               so the argument comes first. If a word stops you, it is there. If you already know this
               material, you never have to open it. But if you catch something in the basics that is
               wrong, I want to know, and I mean that as a real ask. It isn’t politeness. Nothing in
               here is correct just because I wrote it. Especially the parts I wrote.
                   On the name. I wanted to call it the meta machine. Then, in October 2021,
               Facebook renamed its company Meta: a company taking a term for self-reference as
               its name and draining the word of meaning in the same motion. So I went one level
               up, where this machine already lives. The most meta move available, for a machine
               that runs on meta-level reasoning, was to put my own name on the cover and take
               the word back. That’s the whole of it, a meta move on a meta machine. It happens
               to be my dad’s name too, and my wife’s now. So I asked them before I did it. They
               said go ahead.
APPENDIX A




Words this book builds

These are mine, or mine in the sense that I pinned them down for this book. Each is
built properly in the chapter named; this is only a reminder.
    A few words first, because everything else hangs off them and each has exactly
one meaning. The model (or the abstract model) is the definition of a Thiele machine,
Definition 2.1, five parts and the toll, with the two-place record of Definition 2.2 as
its smallest case, plus exactly the extra pieces a given theorem asks for: a counter
in the state, or a window, or programs written as states and a recursion theorem.
A few theorems, the step law among them, use only the states and the step. The
name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. Parts I and II develop those general
arguments, and Part III applies them to the machine it builds.
    A substrate is the model’s shape with whatever extension a theorem names, and
nothing else; the word never means my machine, and never the side of a simulation
that does the stepping (Section 14.15).
    The example machine (also the machine I build, the build, the small machine, the
smallest honest machine, Section 15) is one small machine I defined to show the
definition can be met. It is an example of a Thiele machine, not the model. It fills in
those pieces at once: two counters with their versions, a table of checked facts, a
channel, a trap, a ledger and a flag, six instruction kinds and their prices, with its
hosts and universal programs.
    The scaffolding is the example machine and the constructions run on it, and the
model does not depend on any of it. It lives in Section 15 and in the appendices that
carry the machine on, the universal machines (Appendix C.1).
    A Thiele machine, lower case, is any system proved to fit that definition (Defini-
tion 2.1), five parts and the toll, on any order of records or on the two-place one of
Definition 2.2; the paper toys are, and so is the small machine. That bar is low on
purpose: a clock meets it, and so does every machine in the flat case, whose moves
never climb.
    Certified is what the small machine is held to beyond the definition (Sec-
tion 14.15): its flat moves cost nothing and can’t touch the record, a record that
stays up once it’s up and is raised from a clean state only after a passing check,


                                                 377
378   A Words this book builds


              which means its claim holds, a commitment to the same claim with the thing it’s
              about unchanged in between, and a certificate, at a cost of one for each of those
              three acts, and a claim whose check, commit and certificate raise the record from
              a loaded start exactly when the claim holds there, true at some loaded starts and
              false at others. The small machine meets it, and it hides its record and ledger from a
              window on its counters.
                  A universal Thiele machine is one fixed machine running one fixed program
              that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with every step of the guest’s
              computing done by the host’s counter moves and every rise of its record put where
              its program put it, and, in the certified case, each guest’s record earned again by
              the host’s own check, commit and certificate (Definition C.1). The ones in this book
              are U (Appendix C.1), a fixed program in the small machine’s instruction kinds,
              with no guest step built in, that runs every small-machine program with halting
              and flag exact and its ledger equal to the guest’s at every matching point, and UP
              (Appendix C.2), the same program with one paid move added, that runs every
              computably presented Thiele machine, one whose driver, step, prices and reading are
              computed by programs with the reading decided on every state, keeping its reading
              as a latch and, when the reading starts at no, its ledger to within two of the guest’s,
              a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the
              guest certifies with its whole ledger below three.
                  A computer running the small machine isn’t the small machine; it implements it,
              inside bounds, the way a laptop implements a Turing machine. When a word below
              belongs to only one of the two layers, the entry says which.
                  A partition is a sorting of a pile into groups, nothing in two groups and nothing
              left over (Section 6). A Thiele machine is a state type, moves, a step, a cost per
              move, and a record read into an order, plus one rule, the toll: a move that carries
              the record somewhere not at or below where it stood costs at least one; on the
              two-place record, a move that turns no into yes (Section 2). The rule is called A2 in
              the conditions table (Appendix B). A move merges when two different starting states
              land on the same end; one that never does is injective, it forgets nothing. A reading
              is permanent when no move turns it from yes back to no (Section 3).
                  A distinction that stays is something the world tells apart from something else
              and keeps telling apart: a cell that reads 0 and not 1 and not blank, a bead in the
              left well and not the right, a flag that’s up (Section 1). The step law says what any
              step of any machine with one next state for each state does to the states its run
              has used, with no finiteness anywhere (Theorem 1.1). It lands on a state the run
              hasn’t used yet, which uses up a fresh state. Or, the first time it comes back to a
              used state other than the start, it comes from a different state than the one that first
              got there, which is a merge, two states sharing a next state, and under Landauer’s
              premise a merge of states that were really possible carries a heat floor. Or it comes
                                                                                           379


back to the start, or retakes a step it already took, which is all a run does after its
first return: it’s going round a loop and makes nothing new. Merge, or a fresh state
every step is that law aimed at a reading that stays up: a run that raises one either
merges two of its states somewhere or never repeats a state (Proposition 3.5), and
that’s what keeping takes. Physical dissipation is additional only under physical
premises. In the specified thermal models a nonzero change of distribution has
a finite-time entropy-production bound, with fixed finite activity or mobility, and
slowness does nothing to the floor a merge adds. The book proves that for Bennett’s
walker (Theorem 1.9); the general finite-time bounds are physics (Schmiedl and
Seifert, 2007; Shiraishi, Funo and Saito, 2018). A reversible machine never merges,
so it owes no floor, but that doesn’t mean it pays nothing: each step can dissipate
under the stated thermal-model assumptions, and it pays in fresh states; on finitely
many states it comes back to its start and keeps nothing (Theorem 1.6). Finiteness is
what takes the column of fresh states away: when only finitely many states read yes,
a move that raises a reading that stays up has to merge (Proposition 3.4).
    The counter, which I also call the ledger: in the model, a number carried in
the state that starts at zero and that every step raises by exactly that step’s charge
(Section 7). My machine has exactly one, the ledger µ (Section 15). One other
thing gets called a counter, and each chapter says which: Minsky’s two bins on the
small machine. They aren’t the ledger. A price list says what each move costs; the
model takes it as given, and my machine’s table of what each instruction costs is in
Section 15. A receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum
of the charges on every path including the failures, and is the only such total, on
the states a run from the start reaches, for its price list (Section 7 proves it for any
system with a counter and a price list; on my machine the sum is a theorem too,
Section 15). In the model there is a reading into an order, two places at the smallest
(Section 2); on the small machine it’s the flag, set by a CERTIFY that passes and
never cleared.
    These words describe the example machine and its universal programs, and none
of them is part of the definition of a Thiele machine (Section 15). A two-counter
machine is Minsky’s: two counters holding whole numbers with no upper limit, and
two instructions: add one, and subtract one and jump if the counter is above zero,
or else go on to the next line; already enough that nobody can decide in general
whether one halts. The small machine is a two-counter machine plus HALT and
three instructions for the record, six in all: INC, DEC, HALT, CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY. A counter’s version is its edition number: it starts at 0 and goes up by
one every time the counter is written, so an edition never comes back. A fact is
a property, a counter and a version together, such as “A is even, as of edition 3”;
the properties come from a fixed language with three forms, is zero, is even and is
at least n. The same theorems also hold for any property language with an exact
380   A Words this book builds


              equality test whose checker is proved to say yes exactly when the claim holds, and
              one such language reads a counter as a list and asks whether it’s sorted. The fact
              table holds up to sixteen facts, and the only way in is a CHECK that passed; nothing
              ever leaves it. The small machine’s channel holds one committed fact or nothing,
              and COMMIT puts a fact there only if the table has it about the counter’s current
              edition. With the flag up from a clean start it names a commitment earned that way,
              and a later COMMIT replaces it, as a two-commit run shows. The trap is a bit that
              goes up when an instruction refuses, and then nothing in the core moves again. A
              commitment is earned when a passing check put its fact in the table first, about the
              same edition, with no write to that counter in between; on the small machine every
              flag raised from a clean start is earned, and that’s a theorem. CHECK, COMMIT
              and CERTIFY cost one each and everything else costs nothing, so from a clean start
              a run ending with the flag up adds at least three to the ledger, and a run whose
              check could have failed adds exactly three: CHECK is zero on A, COMMIT, CERTIFY,
              from a start where A is 0. The step doesn’t police trivial checks; is at least 0 passes
              every value and certifies for three too. The host machine is the small machine with a
              counter, called a register, for every whole number, and one property, Slot, true of a
              number that packs a property of the small machine together with a value it holds of.
              A slot is a register of the host used for nothing but holding one checked fact about
              the guest, and its mirror is a register beside it, safe to read, that says which claim the
              slot holds while its fact is live. U is the fixed program of host instructions that runs
              every small-machine program; it reads guest instructions out of one register, keeps
              the guest’s counters in two others, and puts every checked fact in a slot, because on
              this machine reading a counter above 0 into a program’s control flow writes it. The
              universal program’s guest is a program of the small machine, held as one number in
              a register of the host and run one instruction at a time by U’s fetch and decode. UP
              is U with one more handler, for PAY, an instruction that costs one and does nothing
              else; its guests are programs compiled from computably presented Thiele machines
              (Appendix C.2).
                 A window is any function that shows you part of a state (Section 8); a shadow,
              said loosely, is what a window leaves you with. A collision is two steps that look
              the same through a window, before and after, where one raises the flag and the
              other doesn’t (Section 8). Entitlement is what a run has when it carries an object,
              a checked relation between that object and a claim, and a paid event that put the
              object in place: a license to lean on the claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true
              (Section 9). A latch is a record that switches on the first time some event holds and
              never switches off (Section 11). The diagonal’s substrate (Section 13) is the model’s
              shape extended with programs, a run that may give nothing back, a counter that
              never falls, a way to write programs as states, the transformations the substrate
                                                                                        381


counts as its own, and its own recursion theorem for those; the proof of the diagonal
uses neither the counter nor the toll.
APPENDIX B




Every assumption in one place

This appendix gathers the conditions used throughout the book and shows what
each supplies. Use it to follow the connections between the results: which count
needs finiteness, which record needs permanence, and which charge follows from
which price rule. Each theorem also states its own hypotheses where the argument
is made.
    The labels A2 to A6 in this appendix are shorthand for the conditions listed below.
They are not additional claims: each label names the rule written beside it. There is
no A1: A2 is the toll’s name in the mathematical specification, and the others follow
it.


B.1 Systems and their conditions

Definition B.1 (Thiele machine with a two-place record). A Thiele machine (Defini-
tion 2.1) has a record in any order. The results of this appendix are stated on the
two-place record of Definition 2.2: a set of states S, a set of moves I, a step function
step : S × I → S, a cost cost : I → N, and a reading cert : S → {no, yes}, satisfying
the toll: every move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. This is
the condition of Section 2, called A2 in the table below. Every result stated “for any
Thiele machine” in this appendix assumes it.


Definition B.2 (Quantitative Thiele machine). A quantitative Thiele machine is
a Thiele machine with a witness, a function W from states to N, and a threshold
N ∈ N, satisfying: (A3) W (s) + cost(i ) ≥ W (step(s, i )), the witness grows by at
most what the move cost; and (A5) a state that reads yes has W (s) ≥ N. An optional
additional condition is (A4) W (s) ≤ W (step(s, i )).




                                 382
                                                                 B.2 The premises the derivations take   383




Theorem B.1 (The floor raised to a threshold). In a quantitative Thiele machine,
every run from a state with witness w to a state that reads yes has total cost at least
N −̇ w; from a state with witness 0 (this starting condition is called A6) that is at
least N.

Proof. Put the witness readings in a row: w0 = w, w1 , . . . , wn . Beside the move
from w j to w j+1 write its charge c j . A3 says that move can add no more than c j to
the witness: w j+1 − w j ≤ c j . Add these inequalities. Each intermediate reading
appears once with a plus and once with a minus, so only the last reading minus the
first survives:
                              w n − w ≤ c 0 + · · · + c n −1 .
At the end the reading says yes, so A5 puts wn at least at N. The bill is therefore at
least N − w. If the witness started above N, that subtraction is negative and supplies
no positive floor; the bill is still at least zero. That is what the truncated subtraction
N −̇ w says. At w = 0 the floor is N. For an empty run the same argument reads
wn = w and bill zero. Nothing here required the witness to rise on every move (A4),
or used the toll.
   A3 and A4 bound opposite directions, and neither implies the other: witness 1,
cost 0, witness 0 satisfies A3 and breaks A4, and witness 0, cost 0, witness 1 does
the reverse. These conditions describe a general setting. The small machine’s own
floor of three is proved directly (Observation 15.19) and never goes through it.
   The table below puts the labels side by side, so none of them is left without a
meaning.

 Label               Condition
 A2                  the toll
 A3                  the witness grows by at most the cost
 A4                  the witness never drops
 A5                  yes needs a witness at the threshold
 A6                  the run starts with witness zero

    Four remarks on the table. First, the recursion premise is what the diagonal
asks of a substrate (Section 13). Second, the substrate used for the diagonal also
carries a different rule from the toll: the counter never goes down on a step. Neither
implies the other, and the diagonal uses neither. Third, merge pricing is an abstract
lower bound on every merging instruction. It is the pairwise restriction of worst-case
entropy pricing, which is equivalent to the halving price. Landauer’s premise instead
bounds heat from the uncertainty actually removed under its thermal conditions. A
known starting state supplies no positive floor from that premise (Theorem 3.17).
Preparing or erasing an uncertain record of that start would be a separate physical
process with its own premises; knowing the start alone proves no payment. Under
the fixed-protocol entropy-balance assumptions in Section 3.7, a protocol merging K
inputs has a worst input with at least k B ln K of entropy production. This compares
inputs to one protocol rather than charging every known-state execution. Riechers,
Boyd, Wimsatt and Crutchfield (2020) derive additional work bounds under time-
symmetric control of metastable memories. Their low-error bound depends on the
initial distribution and the memory’s time-reversal behaviour; it is not a universal
heat charge on each logical move.
386   B Every assumption in one place


                 Fourth, finiteness, because it’s the premise people most often think the book leans
              on, and it leans on it less than it looks. The step law and the first half of merge
              or a fresh state need none: on any machine run by one rule, finite or endless, a
              run that raises a reading that stays up either merges two of its states somewhere or
              takes a fresh state at every step. Finiteness is what takes the second option away.
              With infinitely many states reading yes, a price list that charges only merges lets a
              machine certify at a cost of zero, the machine that keeps every history, the first way
              out (Section 3), by taking a fresh state at every step. That isn’t a way around what
              keeping takes; it’s a price list that charges nothing for the fresh states. And the finite
              set the count needs can be very small. When the record steers nothing and every
              move adds its own price to the ledger, the count runs over one state of the rest of
              the machine, on the record’s own readings, and for a flag that’s a set of two. That’s
              how the machine of Part III, which has no end, still pays for its raise in a merge
              (Theorem 3.19). Applying a finite-state count to a device requires a justified finite
              set of distinguishable states. The abstract theorem does not supply that physical
              premise.
APPENDIX C




The universal machines

This appendix carries the two universal programs of Section 16 in full: U, which
runs every program of the small machine, and UP , which runs every computably
presented Thiele machine, with the simpler host that has the guest step built in, the
diagonal on the small machine’s programs, and exactly what the universal machines
cover.


C.1 One machine that runs them all

The small machine raises its flag only by checking, committing and certifying, and it
pays for that. The next question is whether one machine can stand in for a whole
class of machines, the way Turing’s universal machine stands in for every Turing
machine. What I mean by that is a universal Thiele machine: one fixed machine
running one fixed program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with
every step of the guest’s computing done by the host’s own counter moves and every
rise of the host’s record put where the host’s program put it. No program running
on the host has to keep a convention for it. In full:

Definition C.1 (Universal Thiele machine). Fix a class C of Thiele machines, each
with its runs from given start states. A universal Thiele machine for C is a Thiele
machine H, the host, with one program P fixed for the whole class, a way to load
any guest M in C with any start s0 into a start state of H, and a way to read a
guest’s state off the host’s registers, such that: (1) H is a Thiele machine whose
counter moves cost nothing and can’t touch its record, and those are its computing
moves; (2) the run of P from the loaded state halts exactly when M’s run from s0
stops, and then shows the observable part of M’s last state, as the class names it,
its reading kept as a latch, and its ledger up to the surcharge; (3) the run passes,
in order, through host states that show the observable part of M’s states along its
run, at which the host’s record equals M’s reading kept as a latch and the host’s
ledger equals M’s ledger plus a surcharge, never negative and bounded by a number
fixed for the class; (4) the rise is the program’s: from every untrapped state, a record
move selected by P either traps, or leaves the flag up exactly when it was already

                                                  387
388   C The universal machines


              up or the current line is marked as raising by P. With the flag down and the move
              succeeding, that line decides whether it rises; (5) H is a register host: its counter
              moves are INC, DEC and HALT on registers, its record moves leave the registers
              alone and go to the next line or trap, and which move comes next depends only on
              the line and whether the trap is up; (6) each guest is loaded with the record down,
              no trap, a fixed line and the guest written into the registers, and the guest’s state is
              read off the registers in a coding fixed with the class, before any guest is named. A
              certified universal Thiele machine also has its host certified, with clean loads, and
              its record, whenever it’s up, standing on the host’s own check of the guest’s own
              justification, as the class supplies it.

                  For U the guest’s justification is its chain claim; for UP , the guest’s reading at a
              state of the run. For U the observable part I’ve proved it matches with all six clauses
              is the guest’s two counters, and in order it matches everything but the guest’s version
              numbers, which no run of the guest can show; for UP it’s the whole state.
                  The guest lives only in the loaded state; the machine and the program are fixed
              before any guest is named. For U the surcharge is zero; for UP it is at most two
              when the guest’s reading starts at no, and exactly three when it starts at yes, so
              three bounds it over the whole class. Both are certified universal Thiele machines,
              by the theorems of this appendix put together: each meets the six clauses, each
              host is certified, with clean loads, and each one’s flag stands on its own check of the
              guest’s justification.
                  The two that UP adds once a guest’s record is up is, at worst, the price of
              certification, not of universality. A certified host raises its record from a clean load
              only after three marks, so on a guest whose whole ledger is one when its reading
              first says yes it falls two behind at least. A host without certification can keep up
              exactly: on a host with registers, INC, DEC, HALT, a paid move TICK that always
              raises the record, a paid move PAY that never does, and a paid move MARK that
              raises it when register 0 is at least 1, which no program below runs and which a
              record that tells starts apart needs, since without it no run’s record depends on
              where it started, the program “count register 0 down to zero; TICK; HALT” runs the
              guests that count a pile down to zero and then raise their reading at a cost of one,
              each from its own pile, with surcharge zero. A guest whose reading is already yes at
              its start costs any host loaded with its record down at least one, and one is reached.
              And from a start at no one host keeps up exactly on the whole class: UP ’s compiler
              on that host, with the three-act chain at the first yes replaced by one TICK and the
              rest of that move’s price paid in PAYs. The toll on the guest makes that move cost
              at least one, so the TICK always fits inside it, and the host’s ledger is the guest’s at
              every matching point. On a host without certification the surcharge is zero from no
              and one from yes, and neither can be lowered. (And PAY is needed on such a host:
                                                                   C.1 One machine that runs them all   389


a guest that pays while its reading is down makes the host run a record move that
doesn’t raise, which is what PAY is.)
    Each clause stops something. For clauses (1), (4) and (5) there’s a host that
meets the others and fails it; (2) and (3) together stop a host that ignores its guest;
(6) I state in words below. Clause (1) stops a host that raises its record early and
lowers it again before anyone looks. Clause (4) stops a mark that reads the registers,
or a copy of the guest kept outside them, and raises when the guest would: the same
move on the same line would raise from one state and not from another. Clause
(5) stops a host with a move that takes one step of the guest. In the one I built
that move costs nothing on the guest’s unpriced instructions and traps on its paid
ones; costing nothing, it would have to be a counter move, and a counter move
never traps. Make such a move cost one instead and it’s a record move, which has to
leave the registers alone, so it can’t move the guest’s counters, which (6) puts there.
Clause (5) also stops a move costing nothing that fetches, decodes and carries out a
guest instruction on the registers, because that move adds one to one register from
