one state and to another register from another, which no single INC or DEC does.
Clause (6) makes the guest come in through the registers. It’s the one clause I’ve
stated in words without a theorem that it discriminates: a reading of the registers
that adds part of the guest back in isn’t excluded by anything I’ve proved. What
stops a host that ignores its guest is (2) and (3), on any class whose guests differ in
when they halt or what they record, which a universal class does. What the clauses
allow is exact too. By (1), (4) and (5), the line, the registers, the record and the
ledger of a run before any trap depend only on the line, registers, record and ledger
it was loaded with: each counter move acts on those alone, each record move leaves
the registers and moves the line, and its effect on the record is fixed by its line. So a
host may carry anything else along, even a copy of the guest that its counter moves
step, and what it carries along that way can’t touch anything the host shows. One
route I haven’t closed: a move that traps may read anything, and stopping the run is
all it can do. UP never traps on its class, so for it the route is shut. For U it’s shut too:
U is loaded with every version at 0 and an empty table and channel, so whatever
a trapping move of U reads was written by the run itself, from the registers it was
loaded with. For a host in general it stays open.
    None of this needs certification. UP ’s own program, read on a host with no
claims, no checker, no table and no channel but with that MARK, with CHECK,
COMMIT and PAY read as PAY and CERTIFY as TICK, meets (1) to (6) with the same
surcharge: UP never traps on its class, and while nothing traps the two hosts agree,
step for step, on the line, the registers, the record and the ledger. Certification adds
the tie to the guest’s own justification, and it needs (4) as much as anything: a host
that carries out a hidden copy’s own check, commit and certificate meets the tie and
fails only (4) and (5).
390   C The universal machines


                  And I want it the hard way. The easy way is to give the host a move that means
              “take one step of the guest,” and then “it runs any guest” is true because I wrote it
              that way. There’s a host like that two subsections on, after the two programs, and it’s
              useful as a picture. It isn’t Turing’s kind of universal. Turing’s universal machine has
              no instruction for “do what the machine on the tape would do.” It has the same kind
              of instructions every other Turing machine has, and one fixed table, and the table
              does the reading and the deciding and the carrying out. The bar here is the same,
              and clauses (4) and (5) make it exact: one fixed program, every computing step a
              counter move, and every rise performed by that program. The table, channel and
              trap still govern whether record operations succeed; the restricted computing-step
              claim is not independence from all auxiliary state.
                  Turing’s own explanation is worth having in your head, because the program
              below copies its shape. In the 1936 paper the universal machine’s tape starts with
              the machine to imitate, written out as a string of letters, its standard description, and
              after it the imitated machine’s complete configurations, one after another: where its
              head is, what state it’s in, what’s on its tape. To take one step, the universal machine
              finds the last configuration, looks through the description line by line, comparing,
              until it finds the line for that state and that symbol, and then writes out the next
              configuration the way that line says. Then it goes back and does it again. It leaves
              marks on squares so it doesn’t lose its place. Every bit of that is ordinary instructions
              on an ordinary tape, and nothing in its table knows any particular machine.
                  Turing’s universal program came first on paper, and one that people actually
              came to use arrived through the side door. John McCarthy, who had started the
              artificial intelligence project at MIT with Minsky, was writing up his new language
              Lisp around 1960 and wanted to show it was neater than Turing machines, so he
              wrote a universal function for it, eval, the language describing how to evaluate itself,
              and argued it was shorter and easier to follow than a universal Turing machine. In
              his own history of Lisp, that was for the paper, a thing to read; the notation for
              writing programs as data was made up for the paper with no thought of using it in
              practice. Then Steve Russell (S. R. Russell in McCarthy’s account), a programmer
              on that MIT project, noticed that eval could serve as an interpreter and coded it
              by hand, and there was a running language with an interpreter that nobody had
              planned. McCarthy adds that the surprise froze some decisions he’d made “rather
              lightheartedly” for the paper. So the trick has a habit: written to be read, it ends up
              being run. The program below goes the other way round, on purpose. It’s written to
              run, and the proofs show that what runs is what the page says.
                  The host. The program runs on a machine with the small machine’s instructions
              and the small machine’s prices: INC, DEC, HALT costing nothing, and CHECK,
              COMMIT, CERTIFY costing one each, with the same table of sixteen facts, the same
              channel, trap, ledger and flag. One change: it has a counter for every whole number,
                                                              C.1 One machine that runs them all   391


each with its own version, where the small machine had two. There’s no new
kind of instruction and no new price. Take away the table, the channel and the
flag and what’s left is old: a machine with as many registers as it needs, adding
one, taking one away and jumping on zero, is the unlimited register machine of
John Shepherdson and H. E. Sturgis, two logicians who proved in 1963 that such
machines compute every partial recursive function.

Definition C.2 (The host machine). The host machine is the machine of Defini-
tion 15.3 with one change: it has a counter, with its version, for every whole number
r (a register), and INC r, DEC r j, CHECK p r and COMMIT p r name one register
each. Its property language has one property, Slot. Write ⟨m, n⟩ for the number
(2n + 1) · 2m ; every positive number is ⟨m, n⟩ for exactly one pair, and 0 is no pair.
Number the small machine’s properties Zero 7→ 0, Even 7→ 1, Ge(n) 7→ n + 2.
The checker of Slot says yes at a value x exactly when x = ⟨m, v⟩ and the small
machine’s checker says yes to the property numbered m at v; its meaning is the
same with holds in place of the checker.

    There’s one place the guest’s machine shows up in the host. The host’s single
property knows how to read the small machine’s three-word property language:
“this number is the pair (property, value) and the property holds of the value.” It
doesn’t know the small machine’s step. Knowing the language and not the step is
the counter version of Turing’s universal machine knowing the alphabet its guests
write in.
    Two facts that force the design. Why more counters? The answer is two facts,
and the program looks the way it does because of them.
    The first is about reading. On this machine a program that wants a counter’s
value in its own control flow has to take pebbles out (DEC) and put them back (INC),
and every INC, and every DEC on a counter above 0, is a write, so the counter’s
version goes up. A fact is about one version, so a read done that way kills every
live fact about the counter. Not every look is a write: CHECK reads a value without
writing it, a DEC on 0 changes no version, and a fresh CHECK after such a read can
make a new live fact. But the guest’s counters are exactly the ones the host has to
read by taking pebbles out, again and again, to decide which way a DEC jumps and
to work out a property’s answer, and each of those reads kills whatever fact was
kept there. So the host can’t keep the guest’s facts on the copies it reads, and a copy
it only writes is what the second fact rules out.
    The second says that even if reading wrote nothing, a fixed program couldn’t keep
them by sending each guest property to one of a fixed, finite list of host properties
and checking it on the same register the guest’s fact is about. The theorem below
rules out that and nothing more, and the pigeonhole is what rules it out.
392   C The universal machines




              Theorem C.1 (No host fact on an exact copy of the guest’s counter). Take any host
              property language with an exact equality test and any checker, a finite list Q of host
              properties, and any translation of the small machine’s properties into members of
              Q whose host check passes whenever the guest’s check passes on the same number.
              Then there are n ̸= m, with Ge(n) and Ge(m) translated to the same host property,
              such that the guest program CHECK Ge(n) A; COMMIT Ge(m) A traps within two
              steps from every start, while on every host state with the trap down and room in
              its table, and some register holding a number at least n, the translated CHECK and
              COMMIT on that register both pass and put the committed claim in the channel.
                  So the host keeps the guest’s facts somewhere else: in slots, extra registers
              used for nothing but holding facts, one per checked fact, each holding the pair
              (property number, value) that the guest checked. The pigeonhole doesn’t bite a slot,
              because the property lives in the slot’s number. The instruction doesn’t have to carry
              it: CHECK Slot on a slot asks about whatever pair is sitting there, and there are
              infinitely many pairs. A slot’s number changes only when the program is moving a
              fact into it. And when the guest writes the counter a fact was about, the program
              gives every slot about that counter a nudge, one INC and one DEC, which leaves the
              number alone and pushes the version up, so the host’s facts go stale at exactly the
              moment the guest’s do.
                  The stored fact still names edition v. The two writes restore 18 but do not restore
              that edition. The intermediate row is inside the handler; the simulation promise is
              at the completed handler’s endpoint.
                  Count what costs anything. Fetching, unpacking, copying, nudging and branching
              are all INC and DEC, and all cost nothing, as computing does on the small machine.
              The only paid instructions are the CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY sites, and each
              guest CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY makes the program run exactly one of them.
              So the host’s ledger lands on the guest’s, unit for unit. And when the guest’s flag
              goes up, the host’s goes up by the host’s own CERTIFY, standing on the host’s own
              COMMIT and CHECK on a slot. The host isn’t copying a bit; it runs the same chain
              on its own registers.

              Definition C.3 (The program U, and loading a guest). U is the fixed list of 3728
              host instructions specified by its block expansions, starting at line 1 and mentioning
              registers 0 to 80; exactly 69 of them cost anything. For a guest program P and a
              start ( x, y), the loaded host hload( P, x, y) has register 0 at x, register 1 at y, register
              2 at the number of P, register 3 at 1 and every other register at 0, every version 0,
              line 1, an empty table and channel, the trap down, ledger 0 and flag down. Write
                                                              C.1 One machine that runs them all   393


grun(m) for m program steps of P from start( x, y), and hrun(n) for n program steps
of U from hload( P, x, y).



Theorem C.2 (U keeps pace with its guest). For every guest program P, start ( x, y)
and number of guest steps m, there’s a number of host steps n such that one of
two things holds. Either the host is back at line 1 with m ≤ n and related to the
guest: registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and B, register 3 holds the guest’s line,
the guest’s trap is down, the two ledgers are equal, the two flags are equal, and the
host’s table and channel hold, fact for fact, slot facts matching the guest’s facts and
channel. Or both have stopped, with the same counters, the same trap, the same
ledger, the same flag, and matching tables and channels. And from any related pair
where the guest hasn’t stopped, one guest step is matched by at least one host step
that lands related again, or with both stopped.



Theorem C.3 (Halting and answers match). For every P, x and y, the guest’s run
of P from start( x, y) halts if and only if U’s run from hload( P, x, y) halts. And
whenever the guest has halted at step m and U at step n, the host’s registers 0 and 1
hold the guest’s A and B, and the two traps, the two ledgers and the two flags are
equal.



Theorem C.4 (The host’s flag is the guest’s, and its ledger is exact). (1) The guest’s
flag is up at some step of its run if and only if the host’s flag is up at some step of
U’s run. (2) For every m there’s an n at which the two are related, with m ≤ n, or
both stopped, with µ(hrun(n)) = µ(grun(m)). And for every n there’s an m with
µ(grun(m)) ≤ µ(hrun(n)) ≤ µ(grun(m + 1)): in between matching points, the
host’s ledger never gets ahead of the guest’s next step.
    Equal ledgers at the matching points are a third sense of “exact,” and the plainest
of the three (Section 15 names all three): two ledgers holding one number.


Theorem C.5 (The host earns its own flag). If the host’s flag is up after n steps of U
from hload( P, x, y), then the instructions U executed contain, in order, a passing
CHECK Slot on a slot, then a passing COMMIT Slot on the same slot, with the slot
untouched and its version unchanged in between, then a passing CERTIFY; the slot
held ⟨number of p, v⟩ at the CHECK, with holds( p, v). And the guest’s own run from
394   C The universal machines


              start( x, y) contains a passing CHECK p c, then, with c untouched and its version
              unchanged, a passing COMMIT p c, then a passing CERTIFY, with c holding v at its
              CHECK.



              Theorem C.6 (The host is certified, and U’s halting is undecidable). (1) The host
              machine, with Slot as its property and one move per instruction, is certified in
              the sense of Section 14.15, over its own claim language, whose claims are “Slot
              holds of register r,” whose meanings are written without the host’s checker, and
              whose “unchanged” is “same value and same version of register r”; and U’s run from
              hload( P, x, y) is a run of it. (2) Read as a Thiele machine it obeys the universal
              floor; a run of U that raises the host’s flag costs at least 3 there. (3) U halts from
              hload( P, x, y) exactly when P halts from start( x, y), so the question “does U halt
              from this loaded host?” is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.5.
                  Put it together, plainly. One fixed program, 3728 instructions of the small
              machine’s six kinds, with no guest step built into anything, runs every program of
              the small machine from every clean start start( x, y). It halts exactly when its guest
              halts, with the guest’s answer in its first two registers. Its flag goes up at some step
              of its run exactly when the guest’s goes up at some step of the guest’s run, by its
              own check, its own commit and its own certificate. Its ledger is the guest’s, unit
              for unit, wherever the two line up. And the machine it runs on is certified. Since
              the small machine runs every two-counter program, through those guests U runs
              every computation, under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine. That’s
              a universal Thiele machine for the small machine’s programs, and the definition
              allows any other host that meets it; the next subsection carries it to every computably
              presented Thiele machine whose reading a program decides on every state.
                  There’s fine print, and it comes before you take that anywhere. The guests start
              clean, from start( x, y); the whole-run theorems are about loaded hosts, and only
              the one-step theorem is about any related pair. The host’s property reads the small
              machine’s three-word language, so a guest with a different property language needs
              a different host property; the host of the next subsection has one, a single property
              that reads a universal claim language. Sixteen slots per counter is the guest’s whole
              table size, reserved for each counter in case every fact is about that one. And it’s
              slow: for every guest step it unpacks the program number from the front again, and
              it copies a number one pebble at a time. That’s where its running time comes from.
              The theorems above say nothing about time; they match states and ledgers at the
              points where the two line up.
                  Enforcement in the step is the reference monitor’s move from Section 14, An-
              derson’s 1972 move: one mechanism everything has to pass through. What’s put
C.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  395

together here is a priced, earned record under that move, carried to every guest by
one fixed program. The move itself is Anderson’s. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett
and Fred Schneider (2006) worked out, in their model, which policies mechanisms
like that can enforce at all, and their paper is where I’d go to see why enforcing a
property of every run escapes the Rice-style walls that deciding one runs into.
    Why make such a fuss about proofs that walk every case? Because the first
universal machine had bugs. It’s the machine in Turing’s 1936 paper, and nobody
gets to call Turing careless. In 1947 Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a
problem of Thue, pointed out that the construction leaned on a convention it hadn’t
earned, and he patched a small defect in how the universal machine writes out
each complete configuration. Around the same time Donald Davies, who joined
the National Physical Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a computer,
worked through the universal machine’s tables and found more mistakes, much to
Turing’s annoyance, as the accounts of Davies’s life have it. (It’s the same Davies who
later named the packet in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed
in a collection edited by Jack Copeland, a philosopher and historian of computing
who runs an archive of Turing’s papers, The Essential Turing, in 2004. They may be
some of the first bugs ever written, in a program for a computer that didn’t exist
yet. That’s a lovely claim, and I haven’t been able to confirm it, so take it as a lead.
What it changes here: a universal machine is exactly the kind of construction where
a careful person leaves a hole, U has 3728 lines for a hole to hide in, and each case
of its simulation argument has to hold. The definitions are on the page so you can
examine what those cases establish.


C.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided,
    priced in whole units, carried as a latch

U runs the small machine’s programs, and through them every computation, under
Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine. But a Thiele machine from
somewhere else has its own states, its own moves, its own prices and its own
reading, and running it through the two-counter encoding keeps its computation
and nothing else. So the question Turing’s machine raises for this book is the bigger
one. Take any Thiele machine whose workings can be computed. Is there one fixed
program that runs every such machine as a guest, keeping its halting, raising its own
flag exactly when the guest’s reading would rise, on an earned chain of its own, and
keeping a ledger equal to the guest’s own prices, with the host’s flat ones nowhere
in it? There is, within limits I’ll list, and this subsection gives it.
    First the class, said plainly. A computably presented Thiele machine is a Thiele
machine in Section 2’s sense (states, moves, a step, a price for each move, a yes/no
reading, and the toll: a move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one)
396   C The universal machines


              together with a driver that picks the next move from the current state or says stop,
              and a way of writing states and moves as whole numbers. “Computably” means four
              little programs, written in the plainest language of computable functions there is,
              the one built from zero, plus one, picking an argument, composing, recursion and
              search: one computes the driver, one the step, one the price, and one the reading.
              The driver, step and price routines are required to halt and give the specified result
              on valid state and move codes; their behavior on other numbers is not constrained by
              the presentation. The reading routine is required to halt on every number, returning
              the reading on valid state codes and no on other numbers. State and move encodings
              have left-inverse decoders, so distinct states or moves cannot share a code. Run
              from a start s0 , the driver’s moves give one run. Its ledger after n moves is the sum
              of their prices, and its latch after n moves says whether the reading has been yes at
              any state so far.
                  The host gets one thing the small machine doesn’t have: a paid move that certifies
              nothing. On the small machine every charge comes from a CHECK, a COMMIT or a
              CERTIFY, and those can charge without raising the flag: one passing CHECK and six
              COMMITs of the same claim cost seven. But every passing CHECK takes one of the
              table’s sixteen entries for good, every COMMIT rewrites the channel, and a failing
              CHECK traps. So the host machine gets a seventh instruction kind, PAY: it costs one,
              goes to the next line, and changes nothing else; it never raises the flag, takes no
              table entry and leaves the channel alone. That’s why the compiler uses it.
                  How far the small machine gets without it is proved, and the count is short. Take
              a run that never traps and ends with the flag down. No CERTIFY ran in it, since
              a passing one raises the flag and a failing one traps. Every CHECK in it passed,
              since a failing one traps, and each passing CHECK filled one of the table’s sixteen
              entries, so there were at most sixteen. Every COMMIT in it committed a claim the
              table holds, and the table holds at most sixteen, so at most sixteen COMMITs can
              be of claims the run hadn’t committed before. Sixteen and sixteen make 32, and
              the only way past it is a COMMIT of a claim already committed earlier in the run.
              A claim names its counter’s version, and the version changes at every write, so a
              repeat needs its counter left alone since the earlier COMMIT. A guest that writes
              both counters between any two of its payments can’t do that, and it can’t commit
              at all, since a COMMIT needs its counter left alone since its CHECK, so it runs out
              of ways to pay after sixteen. Without that limit, 32 is reached: sixteen rounds of
              CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A; INC A pay 32 with no trap and the flag
              down. A guest that writes both counters at every move of the machine it simulates
              needs a fresh CHECK for each move it pays for, so it can pay for at most sixteen of
              them. A simulated machine that charges more often than that has to be paid for
              somewhere, and PAY is where. The 32 isn’t a ceiling on either machine: a program
              that checks one fact about a counter it never writes can commit that fact again and
                                               C.2 Every computably presented machine, on one host   397


again, at a cost of one each, with the flag down and no trap, because the counter’s
version never changes. On the small machine that leaves one counter to compute
with while it repeats, which is too few; the host has a counter for every whole
number, so on it the repeats cost the computing nothing. A program written for
the host’s registers doesn’t need PAY: it checks one true fact once, about a register
it never writes, and pays every later unit by committing that fact again. Those
commits overwrite the channel, so at the move where the reading first says yes it
runs the chain’s CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY back to back and pays the rest of
that move after the CERTIFY. UP can do without it on its class, and PAY is what it
needs beyond the class. UP names no register above 80 and its guest can’t name a
host register, so two sit untouched. Pay the first unit by raising one of them to 1,
which reads “zero holds at 0,” and checking it; pay every later unit by committing
that fact again, which passes because the register’s version never moves. A compiled
guest runs its chain back to back and pays after it, so the chain’s own commitment
is what its certificate finds, and its one check leaves the table at two facts. Every
payment costs one, the surcharge is unchanged, and the host is the register host
with no seventh instruction. Outside the class the trick fails: a guest that pays twice
and then certifies with nothing committed traps, and this host, with the pay-fact
sitting in its channel, would raise its flag instead. PAY leaves the channel alone, and
that is what those guests need. On a host without certification PAY is a necessity:
a guest that pays while its reading is down makes the host run a paid move that
doesn’t raise its record.
    Read as a Thiele machine, the host needs no filing at all: PAY is a paid move that
never raises the record. Certified, as Section 14.15 pins it down, sorts every paid
move into CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY, so PAY has to be filed under one of them,
and it’s filed as a CHECK of the empty claim, a claim that never holds. The filing
is for the interface. It isn’t what PAY does on the machine: a CHECK that fails on
this machine traps, and PAY goes on to the next line. With PAY filed that way the
host stays certified, over its own claim language, in which the empty claim holds of
no state. PAY costs exactly one, as the third of the four asks of a CHECK; its check
never passes, so it can’t stand in a chain; and it leaves the table, the channel and the
flag alone, so it can’t add to a chain or raise the flag either. For the same reason the
floor of three for a flag raised from a clean start still holds with PAY present: the
flag still needs a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY.
    The program is U with one more handler: a seventh branch on the guest’s opcode,
for PAY, that runs the host’s own PAY once. Call it UP ; it’s 3735 instructions, with
70 paid sites, the 69 of U plus the PAY. The guest it runs is a program of the small
machine with PAY added, and that guest is where the presented machine goes. Its
four programs are compiled into two counters, by the packing Minsky used, using
the standard translations from computable functions to counter programs; the guest
398   C The universal machines


              keeps the presented machine’s state coded in its counter B, takes one of its moves
              by running the compiled driver and step, runs the compiled reading on the new
              state, and pays the move’s price in PAYs; the first time the reading says yes, it
              checks, commits and certifies, and those three paid instructions count toward that
              move’s price. The host’s one property is fixed too: a claim is either one of the small
              machine’s three words about a number, or “run reading program r on the coded state
              v,” and the host’s checker evaluates that with one fixed routine for every presented
              machine there is. So nothing in UP knows any particular presented machine. The
              machine arrives as data, the way Turing’s guests arrived on the tape.
                  A fixed checker that runs whatever program it’s handed and always answers
              needs saying how, so here is the routine. A claim of the second kind carries a number
              r. The checker decodes r as a counter-machine routine: its instructions, where they
              sit, which register holds the answer, which register holds the fuel, and how many
              registers to load. If r doesn’t decode to a routine, the answer is no. Otherwise the
              checker loads the routine’s registers from v, reads a fuel number f out of v too (the
              fuel register’s entry in v’s prime factorisation), runs the routine for at most f steps,
              and says yes exactly when by then the routine has left its code with 1 in its answer
              register. Every input gets an answer within f steps, so the checker is total, and what
              it means is that bounded run: yes if and only if the routine halts within the fuel
              the value carries, with answer 1. That’s how it stays clear of the diagonal. A total
              evaluator E that agreed with every total yes-or-no program on that program’s code
              alone would let g(n) = ¬ E(n, n) contradict itself at its own code, as long as E is
              itself computable. This checker never evaluates a program on its code alone: the
              fuel comes with the claim’s value. The guest compiled from M runs M’s reading
              routine itself and puts at least the step count it took into the fuel register, and at
              such a value the checker says yes if and only if the reading says yes.
                  For the fuel rule, take a routine containing just one instruction: increment an
              answer register initially holding 0, then leave its one-line code. Give it fuel 0 and
              the check says no: it has not completed. Give it fuel 1 and the check says yes: it
              has left the code with answer 1. The first no did not mean the routine would never
              answer yes. It meant “not within this allowance.” You can run that distinction with
              a pebble and one instruction card. The real checker does the same job for any list of
              instructions, with the allowance handed in alongside the claim.


              Theorem C.7 (One host runs every computably presented Thiele machine). Let
              M be a computably presented Thiele machine, so that a driver picks its next move
              (one run per start), a program decides its reading on every state, and its prices are
              whole numbers; and let s0 be a start state. Load UP with the guest compiled from
              M’s presentation and s0 coded in. What the host carries of M’s reading is its latch.
                                               C.2 Every computably presented machine, on one host   399


Then: (1) UP halts exactly when M’s run stops. (2) For every n such that M hasn’t
stopped before move n, there’s a host time t at which the host’s register for the
guest’s counter B decodes to M’s state after n moves, the host’s ledger is M’s ledger
after n moves plus a surcharge, and the host’s flag is M’s latch after n moves; and
if M stops at n, such a t has UP halted as well. (3) The host’s flag is up at some
time exactly when M’s reading is yes at some state of its run. (4) If the host’s flag is
up at time t, the host’s own instructions up to t contain a passing CHECK on a slot,
then a passing COMMIT on the same slot with the slot untouched in between, then
a passing CERTIFY; and the slot held the claim “reading program r says yes of v” for
M’s own reading program r, that claim holds, and v decodes to a state of M’s run
where the reading is yes.
    There are two things the theorem doesn’t say. First, the host’s flag is M’s latch.
If M’s reading says yes at some state and no at a later one, the host’s flag stays
up, so it says the reading was yes somewhere in the run, and it doesn’t say the
reading is yes now. Second, what the host re-establishes is the reading: the claim
it checked is “M’s reading program says yes of this coded state,” and that’s all. A
bare Thiele machine needn’t tie its reading to anything true about sorting, proofs
or the world outside. If M’s reading is meant to say a list is sorted, that it does is
a separate correctness theorem about the reading, and the host doesn’t supply it.
The two universal programs also keep their own guests: U runs the small machine’s
programs over its three words about numbers, and UP runs computably presented
machines over the universal claim language.
    The surcharge comes next, because that’s where the ledger stops being exact,
and below three units it can’t be helped. The host raises its flag the only way the
host machine allows, by a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and those cost three.
If M’s first move that turns its reading to yes costs at least three, the host pays the
difference in PAYs and nothing more is owed. If it costs less, the host pays three
there anyway, which is the larger of three and the move’s price. The surcharge
starts at that move: while M’s latch is down it’s zero, so a run that never certifies is
matched exactly. Whether anything could do better depends on what M paid before.
When M’s whole ledger at the raise is below three, no program on the host machine
can match it, since a raised host flag costs three from a clean start. When M’s ledger
at the raise is three or more, this compiler isn’t always the cheapest. Take a guest
whose first move costs two and leaves its reading at no, and whose second costs one
and turns it to yes. This compiler carries it at 2 and then 5, against the guest’s 2
and 3. A program that looks ahead carries it exactly: inside the first move’s price of
two it works out the guest’s state two moves on, puts it on B, runs the CHECK and
the COMMIT of the reading’s claim about it, and puts the guest’s state back; inside
the second move’s price of one it runs the CERTIFY, which needs only a fact in the
400   C The universal machines


              channel, and nothing has committed since. Its totals are 2 and 3, and its flag stands
              on the guest’s reading at the first state where it said yes. Part (1) of the theorem
              below bounds this compiler, and part (3) is the only lower bound proved.


              Theorem C.8 (Exact, within two, and no better). Let M, s0 and the loaded host be
              as in Theorem C.7, and let M’s reading be no at s0 . (1) For every n before M stops
              there’s a host time at which the state is decoded and the flag matched as before,
              and the host’s ledger is M’s ledger after n moves while M’s latch is down, and that
              plus the larger of 3 − c and 0 once it’s up, where c is the price of the move that first
              turned M’s reading to yes; so the surcharge is at most two. (2) If moreover every
              move that first turns M’s reading to yes costs at least three, the surcharge is zero
              and the host’s ledger equals M’s exactly at those times. (3) If M’s latch is up after n
              moves while its ledger is below three, then no run of the host machine from a clean
              start, under any program at all, ends with its flag equal to that latch and its ledger
              raised by exactly M’s ledger. (4) If instead M’s reading is yes at s0 , then at the host
              time matching each move n before M stops, the host’s ledger is M’s ledger after n
              moves plus exactly three.
                  Part (3) is an observation in the sense of Section 2: it reads off Observation 15.19,
              which holds on the host machine with PAY for the reason given above. Part (4) is
              the same three paid at once: if the reading is already yes at the start, the host has
              to raise its flag before M has paid anything, and at that point no program can do
              better, since M’s ledger there is nothing. After it the three stay on only because this
              compiler doesn’t count them against M’s later prices.
                  And one machine is carried all the way, by proof, so the class isn’t empty. Its
              states are whole numbers, its one move adds one and costs three, its driver always
              picks that move, and its reading is “at least three.” The driver returns the fixed
              move; the step adds one; the price returns three; and the reading compares the state
              with three. Counter programs implement all four. Loaded into UP from 0, the host
              never halts, its flag goes up, at the host time matching move n its ledger is exactly
              3n and its flag is up exactly when n ≥ 3, and the raised flag stands on a host chain
              whose slot claims the machine’s own reading of a state at least three. That follows
              from the two theorems above: the reading is no at 0, and the one move that turns
              it to yes, from 2 to 3, costs three, so part (2) of the surcharge theorem makes the
              ledger exact.
                  Now the limits, each of which is in the statement, said plainly.
               • Readings that are decided. The reading’s program has to answer yes or no on
                 every state. A reading a program could only confirm, waiting forever on the no
                 cases, isn’t covered, and neither is a reading no program computes at all.
                                              C.2 Every computably presented machine, on one host   401


• One run per start. The driver picks the move, so the guest is deterministic. A
  machine whose next move is somebody’s unforced choice gets in only with that
  choice written into its driver.
• The record is the latch. The host’s flag is up once M’s reading has been yes at
  any state of the run, which is exactly the latch of Section 11. A reading that goes
  yes and then back to no is carried as “it was yes once.”
• The ledger is exact up to the surcharge. When the reading starts at no, at most
  two, and zero when the first raising move costs three or more; when it starts at
  yes, three. And no program on this host, run from a clean start, can do better
  when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three.
• Prices in whole units, paid one at a time. A move that costs a million is a
  million PAYs. The compiler also uses Minsky’s packing. Between them, those two
  choices set how long the host takes to pay for the guest’s moves.
• Proved; never run on a presented machine. The demonstration machine’s
  numbers come from the two theorems above. UP itself has run on guests small
  enough to finish; a presented machine’s compiled guest is far too large for that,
  and nobody has run UP on one.
APPENDIX D




Built from parts

Back in Section 2 I asked a question and only got halfway: bolt two Thiele machines
together, and do you get one? Everything real is built out of parts. A computer is
a processor and memory and a disk, a bank is branches, a proof is lemmas. If the
record and its toll only held for one machine at a time and fell apart the moment
you put two together, they’d be a property of toys.
   So put two Thiele machines on a bench, each box with its own panel, and wire
them up the three ways anybody wires machines. Side by side, with no wire between
them at all, so that every move is a lever pulled on one box or the other. End to
end, with the first box’s bins tipped into the second’s when the first is done. And one
inside the other, with the inner box running as a guest on the outer one. Some of it
holds and some of it provably doesn’t, and the places where it doesn’t were where I
learned the most.


D.1 Side by side

Two boxes on the bench, no wire between them. A move of the pair is a lever pulled
on one box or the other. The question is what the pair’s record should be, and my
first answer was the wrong one: a single count of how many certifications the bench
has made, one number, easy to read. I’ll come back to why it fails, because it’s in
the list of things that break. What works is to keep both panels showing. The pair’s
record is the pair of records, a place for the left machine and a place for the right
one, compared one side at a time.
    Since that record has more than two places, “certified” in this appendix means the
four things of Section 14.15 with the record allowed to be a place along a direction,
the way Section 4 set it up. Read on a direction, clean states all sit at one place, the
floor; a record never moves below where it was; and in the second of the four a
raised record is one that isn’t at or below where the run began, with the CERTIFY
the move that first takes it out. On two places this is exactly the two-place reading.




                                 402
                                                                                  D.1 Side by side   403




Theorem D.1 (Side by side). (1) The cost of any run of the pair is the left machine’s
cost of its moves plus the right machine’s cost of its moves, and the order in which
levers on the two boxes were interleaved doesn’t change where the pair ends up
or what it paid. (2) If both component state spaces are nonempty, the pair obeys
the toll exactly when both machines do. (3) Read through “either flag is up,” two
Thiele machines side by side are a Thiele machine with floor one; read through
“both flags are up,” a run that starts with both flags down and ends with both up
costs at least two, and two is reached when each part can certify for one. (4) Two
certified machines side by side are a certified machine. (5) In that pair, call a side’s
floor the place on its record axis where its clean states sit. A run from a clean start
that ends with each side at or above a point that isn’t at or below that side’s floor
makes at least six record moves and raises the ledger by at least six. Six is reached,
from suitable loaded starts, by a three-act certificate on each side; a particular pair
of target points can need more. (6) The pair of records is the product in the precise
sense: for any machine mapping into both, preserving records, there’s exactly one
map into the pair that does both jobs.

Proof. (1) A move of the pair is a lever of one box. It moves that box’s component by
that box’s step, leaves the other component alone, and costs what that box charges
for it. So the pair’s run is the pair of the two boxes’ runs along the projections of the
trace, each box’s moves in the order they came, and the cost is the left projection’s
cost plus the right’s. Two interleavings with the same two projections end in the
same state at the same cost. (2) The toll prices a step that takes the record out of
the down-set of where it stood. A pair is at or below another when both sides are, so
the down-set of a pair is the two down-sets side by side, and a move of the left box
leaves the pair’s down-set exactly when it leaves the left down-set, the right side not
having moved. So the pair’s exits are the left exits and the right exits, each priced by
its own box, and the pair obeys the toll exactly when both parts do; for the converse,
an exit at zero cost on one side is an exit at zero cost of the pair with any state at
all on the other. (3) Read through “either flag is up,” a step from neither to either
raises one side’s flag, and that side charges it at least one, so the pair is a Thiele
machine with floor one. Read through “both flags are up,” a run from both down to
both up raises each side’s flag on some step, no move touches both, and each such
step costs at least one; when each part can certify for one, the two certificates one
after the other cost two. (4) Give the pair the interface that reads a move as its own
box reads it, takes a claim to be a claim of one side, about that side’s component
and unchanged when that component is unchanged, with both sides clean as clean,
both sides loaded as loaded, the sum of the ledgers as ledger, and the left box’s
404   D Built from parts


              window as window. Clause (a) is the left box’s clause (a), since a left base move acts
              on the left window as its instruction does and a right move doesn’t touch the left
              component, and no base move of either side changes either record. Clause (c) is the
              two price lists added. Clause (d) is the left box’s witness claim with the right box
              idle. Clause (b) is the one with work in it. Take a run from both clean that ends with
              the pair’s record raised, and cut it just after the first move that takes the pair’s record
              out of where it began. That move is one side’s, and since pairs compare side by side
              it takes that side’s record out of where that side began. Project the cut run onto
              that side: a run from clean that ends with that side’s record raised, so by that side’s
              clause (b) it contains that side’s chain, a passing CHECK of a claim c, a COMMIT of
              c with c’s component unchanged in between, and a CERTIFY. Put the other side’s
              moves back where they were. None of them touches the component c is about, so
              the chain is a chain of the interleaved run. (5) If a side ends at or above a point
              that isn’t at or below its floor, its record ends not at or below its floor either, or the
              point would be at or below the floor by passing through it. The clean start puts that
              side at its floor, so the projection onto that side is a run from clean with its record
              raised, which by that side’s clause (b) has three record moves of its own, a CHECK,
              a COMMIT and a CERTIFY. The two sides’ moves are different moves, so six record
              moves at least, and by (c) a ledger rise of at least six; a three-act certificate on each
              side, from loaded starts where each side’s witness claim holds, makes exactly six.
              (6) A record-preserving map from a machine Z into a box is a map of states with a
              monotone map of records, the record of the image being the image of the record,
              and every move of Z simulated by some run of the box. Given one into each box,
              send a state of Z to the pair of its images. The record of the pair is the pair of the
              records, and a move of Z is simulated by the left box’s run followed by the right
              box’s, which is a run of the pair by (1). That map followed by either projection is
              the map you started with, and any map into the pair with those two projections
              agrees with it on every state, which is what equal maps means here.
                  Most of that is what you’d guess from the bench. Each box keeps its own ledger
               and nobody else pulls its levers, so the costs add, and it can’t matter which box you
               happened to work on first. The six in (5) is two certifications costing three each,
               one per box, with no discount for doing them on the same bench.
                  Machines, with maps that keep the record, form a category, and item (6) says
               these pairs are its products. Ask the maps to keep the cost too and the pair stops
               being a product: a machine mapped into both boxes would pay its cost once on
               each side, twice in all. What survives is a symmetric monoidal structure, which is all
               that side by side needs. Its pentagon, triangle and hexagon laws say that regrouping
               four boxes, inserting an idle box, or exchanging groups of boxes gives the same final
               wiring whichever permitted route you take. Label the boxes and follow each wire:
                                                                            D.2 One after the other   405


every rewiring only moves boxes around, so both routes put each wire at the same
labelled terminal, at the same cost.
   That paragraph is the most formal way I know of saying “side by side composes,
and nothing about the order of the parts matters.” It’s a lot of category theory to
confirm what the bench told me in a glance, and I’m glad to have it anyway. A
glance is where I’d have missed something.


D.2 One after the other
Now wire them end to end. Run the first box, and when it’s done, tip its two bins
into the second box’s start, at no charge on the ledger, and run the second. Programs
get chained that way everywhere, and my first thought was that the tipping couldn’t
matter, because it’s plumbing: pebbles go from one bin into another, nobody checks
anything, and plumbing has no business on a record. That turned out to be half
right, and the wrong half is item (4).


Theorem D.2 (One after the other). (1) Running one certified machine and then
handing its two counters to another through loads that cost nothing gives a certified
machine. (2) For any two programs of the two-counter machine, it computes the
composite: some schedule leaves the first machine’s window where the first program
takes the input, and the second’s where the second program takes that result. (3)
The hand-off keeps the toll when every state it can load into sits at one level of the
second machine’s record. (4) If some load lands the second machine at a record that
isn’t at or below another load’s, the hand-off loses the toll: it’s a certification nobody
paid anything for.

Proof. (1) Give the second machine a loadable form. A state is either pristine,
holding the second machine’s loaded state for some ( a, b), or running, a state of
the second machine. A move LOAD ( a, b) turns a pristine state into the pristine
state for ( a, b) and does nothing to a running one; the second machine’s own moves
move a running state as before and turn a pristine state into a running one. LOAD
is a base move and costs nothing. When the second machine is certified its loaded
states are clean and stand at the floor, so a LOAD leaves the record alone; the base,
the toll and the witness claim are the second machine’s; and the chain in front of
a raise lies after the last LOAD before the second machine’s first move, so it lifts
through the projection onto the second machine’s own moves. So the loadable form
is certified, and the composite, the first machine side by side with it, is certified by
Theorem D.1(4). (2) A wired schedule is the first machine’s moves, then a LOAD
of the two counters its window shows at that moment, then the second machine’s
406   D Built from parts


               moves. The first stretch runs the first program on the first window; the LOAD puts
               the second window at (1, a, b) for the counters ( a, b) the first stretch left; the last
               stretch runs the second program on it. If both programs halt, the two windows after
               the schedule are the two halting configurations, the second’s on the first’s output,
               and the wire cost nothing. (3) and (4) are one fact read two ways. A LOAD from the
               pristine state for one input to the pristine state for another costs nothing, and carries
               the record from where the first loaded state stands to where the second stands. If
               every loaded state stands at one level, no LOAD moves the record, the composite’s
               exits are the two machines’ own, and the toll is kept by Theorem D.1(2). If some
               loaded state stands at a record not at or below another’s, the LOAD from that other
               one to it, at zero cost, leaves a down-set, which is an exit nobody paid for, and the
               toll fails.
                  Item (4) is the one to remember. The tipping costs nothing, so it had better
               not tip in anything that counts as established. If pouring pebbles into the second
               box can land its panel somewhere that isn’t at or below where some other pouring
               would land it, the second machine gets a raised record without ever having checked
               anything, and that’s a forged certificate passed off as plumbing. My first thought
               was right about the pebbles and wrong about where they land.


               D.3 Connecting records and writers
               Joining two boxes also means deciding how to read their flags and who may write
               their workspace. The following examples trace those connections and the guarantees
               they affect.


              Theorem D.3 (What breaks). (1) Read the pair through “both flags are up” as a
              single flag, and any run that raises it from a clean start makes at least six record
              moves; certified asks for a claim that three moves can certify, so read that way the
              pair isn’t certified. (2) Two clocks side by side obey the toll with a two-counter
              machine inside. No move of the pair costs nothing, so composing that easy bar
              composes nothing. (3) Give the small machine a second writer that changes counter
              A without raising its version, and the run “check that A is 0, let the other writer
              change A, commit, certify” raises the flag, so the earned-record clause fails when
              the machine is read the small machine’s way, with the second writer as a base move.
              (4) Two windows that each price their own machine exactly can collide as a pair,
              so exact pricing isn’t preserved by putting machines together. (5) Count the pair’s
              certifications with one number, and the count can’t tell which side certified. The
              pair of records can.
                                                                D.3 Connecting records and writers   407


Proof. (1) Through the pair’s interface, a run from a clean start that raises “both
flags are up” ends with each side’s record raised, and by Theorem D.1(5) that takes
at least six record moves. Certified asks for a claim whose CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY, those three moves alone, raise the record from a loaded state. Three
moves aren’t six. (2) A clock is the two-counter machine with every move priced at
one and a reading over it. Two side by side have a two-counter machine running
inside, the left’s, and obey the toll by Theorem D.1(2); and every move of the pair
is a move of one clock, costing one. (3) Add to the small machine a writer that
changes counter A and leaves its version alone, read as a base move. The run
CHECK (A is 0), the writer’s move, COMMIT (A is 0), CERTIFY, from a start with A
at 0, passes its CHECK, finds its fact at the unchanged version at the COMMIT, and
raises the flag at the CERTIFY. The base and toll clauses still hold, and so does the
checker’s promise. What fails is clause (b). The small machine reads “unchanged” as
same value and same version, and the only chain in that run has the writer’s move
between its CHECK and its COMMIT, where counter A, the thing the claim is about,
changed its value. The COMMIT didn’t notice, because it looks only at the version,
and the version didn’t move. So a run from a clean start raises the record with no
earned chain in it. (4) Take a left box whose only step its window doesn’t see is a
certifying one, so the window still prices it exactly, charging that unseen transition
one; and a right box whose only step is a stutter, at zero cost, leaving its down-set
alone and its window unchanged, priced exactly at zero. In the pair, the left box’s
unseen certifying step and the right box’s stutter show the same pair of windows
before and after. One costs at least one and leaves the pair’s down-set; the other
costs nothing and doesn’t. So a price computed from the pair of windows is short
on the first or over on the second. (5) Replace the pair of records by the number
of sides that have certified. A run in which only the left side certifies and one in
which only the right side does both reach the count one, with the left record raised
in the first and at its floor in the second. The count can’t tell them apart; the pair of
records can.
    Item (1) puts one flag over two boxes. It costs what two certifications cost, six
record moves, and the definition wants a claim that three can settle, so a single flag
over both panels, read through the pair’s interface, is too expensive to meet the
definition. That holds for this interface; nothing here shows that no other interface
on the pair could meet it, and Theorem D.1(4) shows the pair meeting it through a
richer record. Item (4) says that a window exact for each box alone can be fooled
by the pair: two pair states with different costs can show the same pair of readings.
    Item (3) is the one with the most teeth, because it’s the bug from Section 14, the
file checked and then swapped. On the bench it’s a second hand reaching into a bin
while the box isn’t looking: two writers on one value, and a check that’s out of date
408   D Built from parts


              by the time anybody leans on it. The small machine’s version rule is exactly the fix,
              and this is what happens without it: the commitment goes through on a claim about
              a thing that changed underneath it. Database people and the people who build
              processors have been fighting this one since at least Kung and Robinson’s paper of
              1981 and the Livermore report of 1987, and that section gave it the security people’s
              name, time of check to time of use. Here it’s a theorem about the record, and the
              version number is what makes it go away. The second hand can still reach in, but
              with the version its reach shows on the tally, and the COMMIT traps.
                  Item (5) is my first guess from the side-by-side wiring, coming back to fail on
              schedule. It’s why the pair’s record compares one side at a time. Count only how
              many sides certified and the record forgets which side did it. That count answers
              "how many?" but cannot answer "did the left side certify?" An ordinary number
              could encode the full pair too: use 0 for neither, 1 for left only, 2 for right only and 3
              for both. It is the counting rule that loses the distinction, not the fact that its answer
              is one number.


               D.4 One inside another
              The last way to wire the bench: put one box inside the other, as a guest on a
              host. Part of this the book already has. The appendix on the universal machines
              (Appendix C.2) showed the fixed program UP runs any computably presented Thiele
              machine, and the small machine’s own programs, with the record earned again by
              the host. What’s new is putting those links in a row, a box in a box in a box, and
              asking what the outermost one pays.
                 My first guess was that it could pay less, even nothing for the guest’s climbs, since
              a host that’s clever about how it runs the guest could skip the guest’s costs. The first
              item below puts a floor under that: the host pays at least one for each step where
              the guest’s record went up. It’s a floor on rises, and it doesn’t keep the guest’s whole
              cost.


               Theorem D.4 (Nesting). (1) Let a host that obeys the toll simulate a guest faithfully:
               each guest state has an image among the host’s states and each guest record an
               image among the host’s records, the host’s record at the image of a state is the image
               of the guest’s record there, and each guest move is carried by some host run from
               the image of the state before it to the image of the state after it. Let the record map
               also reflect the order: when the image of one guest record is at or below the image
               of another, the first record is at or below the second. Say a run of the host follows a
               run of the guest when it splits into one stretch of host moves for each guest step,
               each stretch carrying the image of the state before that step to the image of the
                                                                          D.4 One inside another   409


state after it. Every run of the guest has a host run that follows it, every such host
run ends on the image of the guest’s end state, and every host run that follows a
guest run costs at least the number of the guest’s steps that turned a cup over. A
host run that only ends on the image of the guest’s end state can cost less. (2) In
each link the surcharge is 0 until the guest’s reading first says yes, and the bounds
below hold from then on. A small-machine guest on UP is carried with surcharge
exactly 0. A computably presented machine whose reading starts at no is carried,
through its compiled guest, with surcharge at most 2, and, when every move costs
at most one, exactly 2 once its reading has first said yes. One whose reading starts
at yes is carried with surcharge exactly 3. (3) Links compose, and their surcharges
add: a tower of k links has surcharge between the sums of their lower and upper
bounds. (4) A tower of presented machines, each level running the next on UP , adds
exactly 2 for every level above the first, on top of the first level’s own surcharge;
every level’s host run is presented by the next.

Proof. (1) The simulation gives, for each guest move, a list of host moves carrying
the image of the state before it to the image of the state after it. String those lists
together along the guest run: that host run follows it, and it ends on the image of
the guest’s end state, because each stretch ends where the next begins. Now take
any host run that follows the guest run, and a guest step that turned a cup over,
leaving the down-set of its record. Its stretch carries the image of the state before to
the image of the state after, and since the record map reflects the order, the image
after isn’t at or below the image before, or the guest’s record after would be at or
below the record before. If every host move in that stretch ended at or below where
it started, then chaining them, the end of the stretch would be at or below its start;
so some host move in it ends not at or below where it started, leaving the down-set
of where it stood, and the host, obeying the toll, charges that move at least one.
Different guest steps have different stretches, so the charges add up to at least the
number of such steps. The end alone isn’t enough: a guest on one cup that turns
it over and turns it back has one rise and ends where it started, and the host run
that does nothing reaches the image of the end state at no cost. (2) A link from a
guest to a host matches every point of the guest’s run with a point of the host’s, with
the record bits equal there and the host’s ledger the guest’s plus a surcharge, the
surcharge 0 while the record is down and between the link’s two bounds once it’s
up, and halting and the record’s first rising matching. A small-machine guest run by
UP is a link with surcharge exactly 0: that is the ledger equality of Appendix C.1,
carried to UP . A computably presented machine run as its compiled guest is a link
with surcharge at most 2 from a reading that starts at no and exactly 3 from one that
starts at yes, which is Theorem C.8; once the reading has first said yes the surcharge
is the larger of 3 − c and 0, with c what the raising move cost, since the host pays
410   D Built from parts


              the larger of c and 3 there, and when every move costs at most one, c is exactly
              one, the toll making it at least one, so the surcharge is exactly 2. (3) Match the
              points through the middle: a point of the bottom run has a matching point of the
              middle run, which has a matching point of the top run; the record bits agree along
              the way; the top ledger is the bottom ledger plus both surcharges, which is 0 while
              the record is down and between the sum of the lower bounds and the sum of the
              upper bounds once it’s up; halting and the first rising pass through. A tower of k
              links is that, k − 1 times. (4) Each level above the first is, by the presentation after
              this proof, a presented machine whose run is the level below’s host run, carried as
              its compiled guest on UP . Its moves are the host’s moves, which cost 0 or 1, so by
              (2) that link adds exactly 2 once the record is up, and by (3) the additions stack on
              the first level’s own surcharge.
                   Item (1) is the cleanest sentence in the appendix. However you build the outer
               box, as long as it obeys its own toll and doesn’t lie about the inner box’s record, it
               pays at least one for every step where the inner record climbed, on every run that
               keeps pace with the inner box step by step. The keeping pace is needed. A guest
               that turns a cup over and then turns it back ends where it started, and the host can
               reach that image by doing nothing at all, at no charge on its ledger. The step by
               step floor is the guest’s rises paid one by one, and the end alone can’t see them. It’s
               a floor on the climbs, and it isn’t the inner box’s whole cost. A guest can charge
               a hundred for one rise while a host charges one for the matching rise, and both
               obey their tolls. Keeping the whole cost takes a further demand on the simulation,
               that it carry the guest’s costs too, and for UP that’s the separate ledger theorem of
               Appendix C.2, with its surcharge.
                   Part (4) looks as if it needs a premise, and it doesn’t. Two links are plainly
               unconditional: from a presented machine to its compiled guest, and from that
               guest to UP running it. Going deeper needs the host’s own run, at each level, to be
               presented as a machine the next level up can run. All the host’s states together have
               no one-to-one code in one number, since there’s a register for every whole number.
               But a loaded state has only finitely many registers that aren’t at 0 with version 0,
               and no move changes more than one of them, so the states like that are a machine of
               their own, closed under every move, and each has a code: its line, its finitely many
               live registers with their versions, its table, channel, trap, ledger and flag. Programs
               that always answer compute its step, price and flag from that code, and the driver
               reads UP ’s instruction off the line and says stop when the host has stopped. Its run
               is the host’s run, and its toll is the host’s. So every level is presented by the next,
               and the tower adds 2 a level as deep as you like. The 2 comes from the compiler’s
               rule of stopping at zero; a compiler that carried the excess forward would add 2 at
               that level’s raise and give it back as the level below paid on.
                                                                          D.5 What this adds up to   411


D.5 What this adds up to
Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a Thiele machine on the
bench stays a Thiele machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What breaks,
breaks for reasons you could name before you saw the proof: a single flag for two
claims costs two claims’ worth, a clock is still a clock, a shared value without a
version can’t be trusted, and a hand-off that costs nothing can’t be allowed to carry
a certificate. None of those is a surprise in hindsight. All of them are now theorems,
and the composition question from Section 2 has an answer. Two Thiele machines
side by side are one under both readings I tried, “either flag” and “both flags.” The
“both flags” reading still fails certified through the pair’s interface, the second writer
breaks the earned-record clause through the small machine’s own reading, the clocks
and the two counterexamples fail outright, and simulation in general has a proved
floor.
   Three of my first guesses on this bench were wrong: the single count, the
harmless tipping, and the clever host that pays nothing for a climb. The last two
leaned toward a record that says more than anybody paid for, and the first toward
one that says less than it should. I didn’t see any of the three coming; the proofs did.

take the physical premise out of the heat bound; it stays a premise. And the papers
on records in the environment are where the pointer thesis got its shape; none of
them proves it.
